key_takeaways: FY26 has been a year of resilience and disciplined execution for Home First. We ended the year with healthy growth, record disbursements in Q4, over 41.4% profit growth for the full year, improving asset quality, and a balance sheet that remains very well capitalized.

Our assets under management stood at INR15,878 crores as of March '26, up 24.9% year-on-year and 6.4% sequentially. Disbursement in Q4 was the highest ever at INR1,572 crores, up 23.5% year-on-year and 19.3% q-o-q.
For FY26, PAT stood at INR540 crores, up 41.4% year-on-year. Reported return on equity for FY26 was 15.7%. And on a pre-money basis, adjusted ROE stood at 16.8%.

We are pleased with the pronounced improvement visible this quarter. Our 1+ DPD is at 4.7%, down 60bps sequentially. 30+ DPD improved to 3.2%, down by 50bps sequentially. Stage 2 reduced by 30bps to 1.4%. Gross Stage 3 improved to 1.8%, down by 20bps q-o-q.

Early indicators from April demonstrate good collection outcomes compared to the same month in previous years. Fresh slippage % is lower than what was seen in April 2025 as well as April 2024. We have not yet observed any significant impact from the ongoing war in the Middle East.
Based on where we are today, we are positioned to deliver around 25% year-on-year AUM growth.
Following the INR1,250 crores QIP completed earlier in Apr'25, our balance sheet remains very well capitalized.
In co-lending, disbursement for FY26 doubled, rising from INR153 crores in FY25 to INR307 crores in FY26. The co-lending book grew to INR593 crores and now represents 3.7% of AUM.
pressing_questions: How much is the funding cost differential between balance sheet borrowings and co-lending, and how does the co-lending/higher ticket size strategy compare to the target segment of larger housing finance companies? (Nischint Chawathe, Kotak Institutional Equities)

Given the loan book growth trajectory has come down from ~30% to ~25%, what gives conviction that this 25% trajectory will be sustained rather than tapering further? (Nischint Chawathe, Kotak Institutional Equities)
On risk-adjusted yields compared to peers — taking out credit cost from yield on a portfolio basis across different segments/states, how does this compare to peers? (Prashant Kothari, Pictet)
Can AUM CAGR of 30% (achieved between March'23 and March'26) be expected over the next 3 years, rather than the guided 25%? (Ravi Kumar Naredi, Naredi Investments)

MAANALU.about: Incorporated in 2003, Maan Aluminium Ltd is in the business of manufacturing & trading of aluminium profiles, anodizing and fabrication of profiles, aluminium ingots, aluminium billets etc.[1]

quarters.summary: Management indicated flattish volume growth for FY27 with a possible ramp-up towards year-end/early next year, as the sluggish export market (post-duties) is being realigned toward high-value domestic business. Focus for FY27 remains profitable growth, improving manufacturing mix, disciplined working capital, efficient capital allocation and strengthening return ratios; Dewas plant targeted online by mid of next year, and Pithampur Italian line expected to see significant contribution by mid of next year, with FY27 capex of ~INR166 crore planned over three years (INR90 crore for new plants under development, ~INR45 crore for Dewas), most of which will occur in H2FY27.

key_figures.label: Cost of goods sold and operating expenses
Cost pass-through to customers on gas/input cost increase

subsections.label: P&L detail
points: Revenue moderated sequentially from Q4 FY26 (INR255cr) to Q1 FY27 (INR232cr), attributed to normal quarterly fluctuations in volumes, product mix, and business activity.
Despite sequential revenue decline, profitability improved meaningfully — EBITDA up ~40% QoQ and EBITDA margin improved to ~3% from ~2%.
Key takeaway from Q1: although revenue moderated sequentially, profitability improved, reflecting better operating performance and cost discipline.
FY26 revenue was broadly in line with FY25, while EBITDA grew ~21% YoY, reflecting continued focus on quality and profitability of business rather than top-line growth.
FY26 PAT declined versus FY25 (INR13cr vs INR16cr), reinforcing the importance of ongoing initiatives around operating efficiency, product mix and higher value manufacturing.

subsections.label: Balance sheet and capital allocation
points: Balance sheet continues to strengthen; company has maintained a very low leverage position.
Working capital efficiency has improved significantly over the longer term.

Objective is to maintain a prudent balance between growth investments and financial discipline; will evaluate every capacity investment from the perspective of return on capital, cash generation and strategic relevance — not pursuing capacity merely for scale.
Company stated it has enough cash and does not anticipate taking on debt for capex; company is in fact deleveraging.

Working capital days increased from FY25 to FY26 due to raw material procurement to support capex investment readiness and extended credit periods given to some customers; expected to normalize once ramp-up stabilizes.

subsections.label: Cost management
points: Continued strong focus on cost control, working capital discipline, and efficient utilization of capital; objective is not merely to grow revenue but ensure incremental growth comes with better contributions and return on capital.

Other expenses have been gradually declining across the last 4 quarters (from INR18cr to INR13cr) despite elevated oil and gas costs from the Middle East crisis, due to increased conversion costs being transferred to customers.
Company transferred about 50% of the cost increase to clients over the last 2 quarters; balance 50% still being worked on via renewal of short-term and medium-term contracts.

Employee expenses are not expected to rise materially even as new capacities (e.g., Dewas) come online by mid-FY28, since the technical team and R&D personnel required for the new lines have already been hired and onboarded over the last 2 quarters.

subsections.label: Business model / margin structure
points: Trading is a vanilla pass-through business where commodity prices are passed on to customers directly.

Manufacturing business is mostly hedged; positions are taken based on orders — as soon as orders are received, the company hedges on LME or MCX; company strategy is to keep unhedged positions below 5%, so commodity price movement has minimal (<5%) impact.
Company operates as a pure converter with fixed margins; extrusion is a vanilla, low-margin business (6-8%/6-10%), while value addition (anodizing, machining, powder coating) lifts margins to 15%+.

Value-added products serve OEMs across applications such as windows, doors, processors, and car battery packs; the strategy is to maximize value addition on top of extrusion capacity, which naturally also attracts customers seeking a one-stop processing solution.

Business model is best assessed on an absolute EBITDA-per-ton / gross-profit-per-ton basis (over and above commodity price), rather than a percentage margin basis — management confirmed this understanding is correct.

subsections.label: Export vs domestic mix shift
points: Export duties have significantly impacted the export business, which used to be as high as 60-70% of the mix; now down to ~45% of manufacturing revenue.
Company is realigning that impacted export chunk toward high-value domestic business, which is taking time to convert but is where current focus lies.
Once the international market scenario improves, company expects to restart export growth and revert to high double-digit type growth numbers.

subsections.label: Capacity utilization ramp
points: Anodizing and machining facilities are not fully utilized (45-50% and ~55% respectively), leaving scope for margin accretion once ramped up within existing capacity.

Pithampur Italian press achieved 25% ramp-up versus an originally planned 3-year ramp-up curve of 35%/50%/75%; still developing tooling, aerospace-grade alloys, defense-grade alloys, and automotive-sector alloys.

Capacity was expanded from 1,200 MT to 12,000-24,000 MT near end of last year, implying ~1.5 years of planned catch-up; significant contribution from the new Italian line expected by mid of next year.

key_figures.label: Capex allocated to new plants under development
Dewas plant asset turn projection (peak utilization)

subsections.label: Integrated manufacturing platform
points: Maan is transforming from a conventional aluminium extrusion player into a high value-added aluminium converter, with an integrated platform comprising foundry, extrusion, anodizing, and machining.
Company is strengthening its manufacturing footprint with new facilities under development.

Strategy is to build a stronger, more balanced business by progressively increasing high value-added manufacturing contribution while continuing to leverage the legacy (opportunistic) trading business.

subsections.label: Capex roadmap
points: Capex roadmap for the next three years is clearly defined; cumulative planned capex of approximately INR166 crore includes investments in the existing Pithampur facility, new dyes and general capex, and other new plants under development.

Approximately INR90 crore is allocated toward new plants under development; investments intended to support the transition to higher value-added manufacturing and specialized applications, not capacity for scale alone.

Capex approach will remain disciplined, with close monitoring of implementation timelines, utilization ramp-up, customer development, and expected ROI; projected capex numbers are indicative and subject to management review.

In Q1 FY27, less than INR5 crore of capex was completed, as management is planning an overseas visit to finalize the extrusion press and other machinery for the Dewas plant input; the majority of capex will occur in H2 FY27.

subsections.label: Dewas facility (aluminium precision tubing)
points: Dewas project is described as strategic and a first-of-its-kind facility in India for aluminium precision tubing, targeting a niche segment requirement.

About INR15-20 crore of the total ~INR45 crore capex has been completed; the plant is currently being fed raw material by Pithampur as an interim arrangement, not the plant's intended long-term methodology.
The plant is expected to get its own capacity online within the next 6-8 months; expected to be low volume but high margin and high value-add (aerospace, defense, and automotive end-uses).

As a new plant and first mover in India for this process, it requires compliances, testing, customer onboarding, and technical development, which is taking time; management is targeting the plant online by mid of next year but declined to commit to firm dates.
Dewas plant asset turn is projected at two to three times at peak utilization.

subsections.label: Pithampur facility
points: Italian press is online at Pithampur; ramp-up curve was originally planned at 35%/50%/75% over 3 years, and the company has achieved a 25% ramp-up so far.
Tooling development, aerospace-grade alloys, defense-grade alloys, and special automotive-sector alloys are all currently in progress/mix.

Capacity was expanded from 1,200 MT to a 12,000-24,000 MT range near the end of last year, implying about 1.5 years of planned catch-up; significant contribution from the new Italian line is expected by mid of next year.

subsections.label: Export markets
points: Company serves customers across multiple international markets including the United States, UAE, Australia, U.K., Qatar, and Israel.
Exports give access to diversified markets and opportunities to develop relationships in specialized applications across geographies.

Company remains conscious of external risks in international markets, including currency movements, geopolitical developments, trade policies, and demand conditions; approach continues to be diversification and disciplined customer selection.
Export share of manufacturing revenue has fallen from a historic 60-70% to ~45% due to duties, prompting realignment toward high-value domestic business.

subsections.label: Logistics and shipment delays
points: Logistics and shipment delays seen over the past six months are still present; management stated there is little that can be done to mitigate them directly.
Business toward GCC and East Asia remains impacted because freight rates have risen sharply.
Strait of Hormuz disruption and general shipping issues are causing delays and backed-up shipping; freight prices have multiplied 5x to 10x.
Overall costs have risen significantly, impacting costing and margins; many customers are sitting back and waiting.

Management noted it is difficult to predict when the situation will improve; had expected improvement once the Middle East conflict cooled off, but the situation remains unresolved and freight rates remain high.
Business has not halted but continues under additional cost and delay pressure.

subsections.label: Working capital / raw material procurement
points: Working capital days increased from FY25 to FY26 due to raw material procurement to support upcoming capex investments and readiness for new capacity, plus extended credit periods offered to some customers.
Elongation expected to reduce once operations stabilize and ramp-up takes place.

subsections.label: Export duties impact
points: Export duties have impacted a major part of the export business, reducing export share of manufacturing revenue from a historic 60-70% to ~45% (Q1 export share ~40%).
Market has been pretty sluggish post the duties; company is trying to realign toward high-value domestic business, which is taking time to convert.

subsections.label: Logistics / freight cost inflation
points: Freight rates have risen 5x to 10x due to Strait of Hormuz disruption and general shipping issues linked to the Middle East conflict, impacting costing and margins.
GCC and East Asia business remains impacted; timing of resolution is uncertain as the Middle East situation remains unresolved.

subsections.label: Input cost inflation (oil and gas)
points: Gas prices have significantly increased due to the Middle East crisis, elevating other expenses.

Company has transferred about 50% of the cost increase to customers over the last 2 quarters; the remaining 50% is still being worked through via contract renewals (short-term and medium-term contracts).

subsections.label: Currency and geopolitical risk in exports
points: Company remains conscious of external risks associated with international markets, including currency movements, geopolitical developments, trade policies, and demand conditions.

subsections.label: FY27 focus areas
points: Focus for FY27 will remain on profitable growth, improving manufacturing mix, disciplined working capital, efficient capital allocation, and strengthening return ratios.

Four key investor-relevant areas going forward: (1) manufacturing mix becoming increasingly important in overall business mix; (2) value addition focus shifting to downstream processing and specialized products rather than basic extrusion economics; (3) capacity utilization ramp-up as new capacities become operational, alongside building the corresponding customer base; (4) return and cash generation discipline on working capital and capital allocation so growth translates into sustainable returns.

subsections.label: Volume/growth guidance
points: Guidance remains for flattish growth in volumes this year (quarter-on-quarter and for the full year), with a possible ramp-up towards the end of this year or beginning of next year.
When the international market scenario improves, company is confident of restarting export business and seeing high double-digit type growth numbers.

On manufacturing growth ballpark, management reiterated a flattish guideline and declined to give a specific forecast; if the company maintains what it did last year (~INR300cr manufacturing top line) purely due to market dynamics, management stated it would be 'okay' with that outcome even if not fully satisfied.

subsections.label: Facility timelines
points: Dewas plant targeted to be online with its own capacity within the next 6-8 months, and the overall project targeted (though not firmly committed) to be up and running by mid of next year.
Pithampur's new Italian line expected to see significant contribution by mid of next year.
Management is hopeful capex closure/renegotiation on Dewas machinery investment will be completed, aligning with prior guidance of closing this year (context from prior quarter).

subsections.label: Cost / margin outlook
points: Employee expenses are not expected to rise materially even as new capacities come online by mid-FY28, since the required technical team has already been hired and onboarded.
Management expects to recover the remaining ~50% of input cost (oil/gas) increase from customers within the next quarter or two as short-term and medium-term contracts get renewed.

guidance_ledger.statement: Similar flattish guidance this year, even quarter-on-quarter and for the full year; ramp-up may occur towards the end of this year or beginning of next year.
When the international market scenario improves, we are quite confident that we will restart that business and see the high double-digit type of numbers that we were expecting.

Sticking to the flattish guideline given previously; unable to give a specific forecast, though expects to be at least at the level of last year's ~INR300 crore manufacturing top line, ideally better.
Plant's own capacity (separate from Pithampur feed) expected online within next 6-8 months; overall project hoped to be up and running by mid of next year, though not committed to any firm date.
Total Dewas project capex is approximately INR45 crore, split into two phases.
We can only project means at least two to three times asset turn at peak utilization.
Margin profile at Dewas will definitely be much better than plain extrusion (6-10%), but management declined to give a specific number.
Hopeful by mid of next year we should see a significant contribution coming from the new Italian line.

Cumulative planned capex of approximately INR166 crores over next three years, including Pithampur, new dyes/general capex, and new plants under development (INR90 crore allocated to new plants); projected capex numbers are indicative and subject to management review.
Major capex will take place in H2 of this financial year, as management plans an overseas visit to finalize the extrusion press and other required machinery for the Dewas plant.
No debt anticipated for capex; company has enough cash and is in fact deleveraging.
Employee expenses should not increase as new capacities come online by mid-FY28, since technical team has already been hired and onboarded over the last 2 quarters.
Hopeful within the next quarter or two, we should be able to recover the remaining ~50% of cost increase as short-term and medium-term contracts get renewed.
Working capital cycle elongation due to raw material procurement for capex readiness will certainly come down once operations stabilize and ramp-up takes place.
Focus for FY27 will remain on profitable growth, improving manufacturing mix, disciplined working capital, efficient capital allocation, and strengthening return ratios.

guidance_ledger.statement: Ramp-up cost will add up to INR7 crores to INR10 crores in FY27 unless operating leverage is obtained.

Even if we are able to capture the market on 15%-20% year-on-year, we should achieve 80% of our capacities in the next three years... we should be in a very good position to achieve at least 75% of our capacities.

guidance_ledger.statement: Our improvement in profitability as utilization increase across extrusion, anodizing, fabrication, and tubing business will have a significant increase not this year, but next year, next to next year.
That is pending for us. But nevertheless, that's something that's going to be completed within the next six months.
We are hopeful that we are trying to close that this year and make the capex after we renegotiate our machinery investment contract.

guidance_ledger.statement: We are very positive that it will materialize this year... if it happens, we'll definitely see that those numbers this year.

themes.note: Company transforming from conventional extrusion player to high value-added converter via anodizing, machining and downstream processing, lifting margins from 6-10% to 15%+.

themes.label: Capacity expansion

themes.label: Margin pressure from input/energy costs
themes.note: Elevated gas prices raised other expenses, but ~50% of cost increase already passed to customers with remainder expected to be recovered within next quarter or two.

key_takeaways: So, the key takeaway from Q1 is that although revenue moderated sequentially, profitability improved, reflecting better operating performance and cost discipline.
Revenue from operations stood at INR232 crores, compared with INR211 crores in Q1 FY26, representing a 10% year-on-year growth.
EBITDA increased to INR7 crores in Q1 FY27, compared with INR5 crores in Q4 FY26, representing approximately a 40% quarter-on-quarter improvement in EBITDA.
Approximately 45% of manufacturing revenues are driven by exports.

The company has clearly defined the capex roadmap for the next three years with cumulative planned capex of approximately INR166 crores, of which approximately INR90 crores is allocated toward new plants under development.
The market has been pretty sluggish for exports post the duties that have impacted a major part of our export business; export share is down to 45% from an upward 60%-70%.
Freight prices have multiplied more than five times to ten times due to Strait of Hormuz and general shipping issues, impacting costing and margins.
Our focus for FY27 will therefore remain on profitable growth, improving the manufacturing mix, disciplined working capital, efficient capital allocation, and strengthening our return ratios.
pressing_questions: What would be the capacity volumes that we did this quarter? And what would be the EBITDA per metric ton?
Do the logistics and shipment delays that we were seeing in the past six months still exist? And if they do, what are we doing to mitigate these?

What is the status of the capex on the Dewas facility? When are we likely to see it online? And how much of the capex we have already done out of this INR45 crores that we are planning to do in FY '27?
Any broad projections in terms of growth on the manufacturing side?
Given our working capital days have increased a little bit from FY '25 to FY '26, do we anticipate taking any debt for this capex?

quarters.summary: Management flagged FY26 as a year of strategic transformation with flat revenue amid commodity volatility, export slowdown, and margin pressure; FY27 is expected to be a flattish/investment-and-commissioning year with ramp-up costs of ~INR7-10 crores, while margins are expected to normalize meaningfully only in ~2 years as newly created extrusion, value-added (anodizing, powder coating, fabrication, tubing) and Dewas precision-tube capacities ramp up utilization, aided by growing inquiry pipeline in defense, aerospace, solar and Make in India import substitution.

subsections.label: Revenue drivers
points: Revenue remained almost flat at INR809 crores vs INR810 crores in FY25, mainly supported by growth in domestic manufacturing business and better realizations.

subsections.label: EBITDA drivers
points: EBITDA increased 3% due to better operational controls, improved value-added product mix, and optimization of overhead costs.

subsections.label: PBT/PAT decline drivers
points: PBT decline of 18% mainly due to increase in raw material prices, lower export contribution, pressure on manufacturing profitability, and higher operating cost from the oil and energy crisis during the year.
Government restrictions on gas supply also impacted production efficiency and energy costs, affecting overall profitability.
PAT decline of 19% primarily in line with lower profitability at the PBT level and increased energy-related operational cost.

subsections.label: Net worth / balance sheet
points: Net worth increase primarily driven by the preferential capital raised (INR83 crores) along with retention of profits, strengthening balance sheet and long-term financial position.
Successful preferential capital infusion strengthened net worth, liquidity position, and balance sheet, enabling continued expansion and long-term growth initiatives.

subsections.label: Gross margin pressure
points: Gross margins fell to ~8% this quarter versus historical double digits; company is a converter and passes on higher aluminium prices but cannot immediately pass on higher operating costs (energy, finance cost, depreciation, ramp-up cost) though discussions with customers on this are underway.
As capacity utilization increases, fixed cost absorption is expected to come down leading to better margins.

subsections.label: FY27 cost outlook
points: FY27 will be an investment and commissioning year; ramp-up cost of INR7-10 crores expected via depreciation, finance cost, employee cost, and trial runs until operating leverage is achieved at 24,000 tons capacity.

subsections.label: Capex plans
points: Capex guided at INR40-50 crores for FY27 and INR35-40 crores for FY28.

subsections.label: Other non-current assets
points: Advances to customers of INR16.4 crores include an advance given for purchase of an office for the Delhi registered office plus some other normal operating business advances; not related to Dewas facility equipment.

subsections.label: Volume & realization clarification
points: Extrusion average realization of INR340/kg was clarified to actually be a blended EBITDA figure of about $300/ton (not INR340/kg), later further clarified as $340/ton.
Total sales realization for FY26 manufacturing business was approximately INR300 crores on 7,300 metric tons of combined extrusion and value-added volume.

subsections.label: Ramp-up strategy and aspiration
points: Management's ramp-up for the next three years is significant; a major capex/investment cycle occurred at end of last year and into this year, but conversion of that investment into revenue and profitability is taking longer than anticipated due to market dynamics.

In an ideal scenario, management would want to sell 100% of the 24,000 ton extrusion capacity as value-added product, but realistically expects to capture market share at 15-20% YoY, achieving 80% of capacity utilization in the next three years, with at least 75% considered achievable.
This year (FY27) is expected to be a flat year for volumes; faster ramp-up depends on commodity prices and overall economic environment correcting.

Focus is on customer qualification, value-added products, and operational stability at the higher end rather than aggressive volume growth at lower margins, positioning against volume-based competitors like Jindal or Hindalco Extrusions (no comment on their numbers/margins made).

subsections.label: Export vs domestic value addition
points: Value-added products on the export side took a hit this year because export markets offered better valuation plus margin benefit from value addition; company expects margins to increase once export demand returns and domestic value-addition play improves.

Working a two-way strategy: value-adding for existing standard-extrusion customers where possible, and separately serving customers who want fully value-added components; company does not turn away customers, qualifying them for either scenario to retain at least the basic business.

subsections.label: EBITDA per ton aspiration
points: Management declined to give specific numeric targets but said EBITDA per ton margins will increase substantially as value addition (mill finish getting machined/anodized, or drawn then anodized) creates a coupling effect on margin.
Significant profitability improvement expected as utilization increases across extrusion, anodizing, fabrication, and tubing business — expected not this year, but next year and the year after.

subsections.label: Italian extrusion press
points: New Italian extrusion press commissioned at Pithampur, increasing extrusion capacity from 10,000 to 24,000 tons per annum.

The press is a 9-inch, high-tonnage, close-diameter automatic press specifically suited for EV batteries, defense, and aerospace applications, capable of extruding special-grade alloys (2 series, 5 series, 7 series close to steel) that standard presses cannot handle without breaking.
Delivers stronger throughput for quality/technical/chemical parameters in the profile, and better quality, output, and performance versus standard presses.

subsections.label: Dewas facility
points: Acquisition and refurbishment of the Dewas facility completed, intended as the foundation for future tubing and downstream value-added business.
Dewas is a precision tube line, one of the first of its kind in India; requires additional machinery funded partly through the preferential issue.

Machinery costs increased, causing overall project cost to shoot up; company is in renegotiation of the machinery/overseas vendor contracts to optimize capital allocation, causing delay in the project.

Management is hopeful to close renegotiation this year and proceed with capex; exploring cooperation/joint-venture-type arrangement with technology providers to help run the facility, though nothing finalized.

This is a complete import-substitute business; management is confident of reaching 40-50% utilization in the medium term with better realizations and EBITDA per ton than most value-addition chains, though exact numbers were not disclosed.
Dewas plant itself is not yet qualified/audited for defense/automotive standards (unlike the main facility); qualification will take time as the plant comes online.

subsections.label: Capacity utilization ramp-up challenges
points: Commercial ramp-up of capacities has taken longer than anticipated due to customer qualification cycles, project approvals, slower industrial demand in certain sectors, and geopolitical uncertainty.

Management emphasized the challenge is one of timing and utilization rather than capability creation — capacities and infrastructure are largely established; focus now is on increasing throughput, expanding value-added offerings, and improving asset utilization.

subsections.label: Qualifications/certifications
points: Company performs about 8-10 compliance audits and regulatory approvals every year, and has completed all of them; facility is audited and fully geared up for most automotive and defense space (Dewas plant excluded).

Multiple defense customers have received submitted samples; company is a tier-two supplier to value-added defense-sector suppliers; a particular qualification/audit required to move up is pending but expected to complete within six months.
Company has developed alloys in-house at its foundry and sent samples out for defense/aerospace applications; inquiries have been more domestic than international.

subsections.label: US tariff and export impact
points: About 80-85% of exports go to the US, the largest, most profitable and fastest-growing export market, hence most impacted by tariffs.
Other export countries remain stable with a regular run rate of 2-3% YoY growth.

US aluminium duty of 50% has been in place and stagnant since 2024 under the American administration; aluminium commodity prices have risen over 50%, effectively raising net raw material cost by ~75%, causing customers to delay purchases or wait for better opportunities, driving the slowdown.
Expectation that if commodity prices cool off/stabilize, growth cycle will pick up again, similar to past 5-year inflation cycles requiring time to acclimatize.

subsections.label: Logistics/container disruption
points: Since last quarter, an insurance company invoked the terrorism clause, affecting container availability toward certain markets.

Dispatches into the Gulf/Middle East came to a standstill post-war and have not restarted as of the call date, significantly impacting Maan given its earlier significant international exposure delivering containers on CIF basis.

subsections.label: Export/domestic mix strategy
points: Export accounted for ~50% (about INR150 crores) of the INR300 crores total manufacturing sales realization in FY26.

Company is diversifying geographical concentration risk by focusing more on the domestic market, while renegotiating Incoterms with export customers to shift to FOB basis (from CIF) to pass on shipping/terrorism-clause risk and price risk.
Company is targeting new export markets, e.g., CIS market instead of US, and has appointed overseas consultants/brokers to source international orders.

Total exports of aluminium from India have dropped 50% (per an article); Maan's own exports fell 30-40% over the last three years, roughly 10-15% per year, attributed to US and international duty structures and subsidized material from other countries.

subsections.label: Raw material sourcing
points: No shortage of raw material (billets) currently or foreseen in India, barring temporary situations like a primary producer plant breakdown or renovation.
Promoter has 40-plus years of experience in the space; procurement and sourcing material at the right price domestically or internationally is considered a core strength.

Export customers, especially in the US and Europe, require declaration of raw material origin (Make in India / local smelting) to satisfy local government regulations; sourcing from China or Russia is generally not required/desired for these markets.

subsections.label: Customer engagement
points: Multiple qualifications in progress across aerospace, defense, and automotive sectors ('flavour of the year'); samples submitted to multiple defense customers, awaiting development and growth.

Company supplies as a tier-two supplier to firms providing more value-added products to the defense sector; tier-one companies have approached Maan, contingent on completing one pending qualification/audit.
Cannot disclose customer names but inquiries for defense-related work have been more domestic than international.

Regarding a previously mentioned agreement (referenced by an analyst as involving 'Tata', not confirmed by name): qualification process is lengthy; samplings completed and everything is ready; company is 'very positive that it will materialize this year'.

First qualification for this large customer has been submitted; second batch of samples will go out this month (June); pricing was originally quoted when raw material prices were 50-60% lower, requiring the customer to renegotiate; if it materializes, expected to be a significant chunk of revenue this year.

subsections.label: Competitive positioning
points: Company differentiates itself from large volume-based extruders (referenced generally as Jindal, Hindalco Extrusions, without commenting on their specific numbers/margins) by focusing on OEM relationships and value addition as its niche market.

subsections.label: Contract structure
points: No fixed-term or fixed-return supply contracts with clients; company generally uses non-disclosure agreements with design and confidentiality clauses.
No fixed commitment for supply/delivery; arrangements are open-ended and depend on requirement; forecasting may be provided by customers but is unpredictable.

subsections.label: Strategic transformation
points: FY26 marked the transition of the company from a traditional extrusion player towards a higher value-added aluminium converter.

Management's going-forward focus: increasing utilization of newly created capacities, expanding value-added segments (fabrication, anodizing, powder coating, tubing), improving EBITDA per kg through higher value-added products, strengthening domestic and strategic customer relationships, maintaining financial discipline, and prudent capital allocation.
Considering cooperation/joint-venture-type arrangement with technology providers for the Dewas precision tube line to help run the facility (nothing finalized as of the call).
Company purchased an office for its Delhi registered office (funded via the INR16.4 crore advance mentioned in balance sheet).

subsections.label: Risk factors
points: Volatility in commodity/aluminium prices.

Slowdown in exports, particularly to the US due to 50% tariff since 2024 combined with over 50% rise in aluminium commodity prices (effective ~75% increase in net raw material cost), causing customers to delay purchases.
Oil and energy crisis and government restrictions on gas supply impacted production efficiency, energy costs, and overall profitability.
Pressure on manufacturing margins; inability to immediately pass on increased operating costs (energy, finance, depreciation) to customers, though discussions are underway.
Geopolitical uncertainty and container availability issues after an insurance company invoked the terrorism clause, halting dispatches to the Gulf/Middle East (not yet restarted).
Customer qualification cycles, project approvals, and slower industrial demand in certain sectors have delayed commercial ramp-up of new capacities.
Dewas project delay due to cost increases in required machinery, now under renegotiation with overseas vendors.
Geographical concentration risk given high dependence (80-85%) on US export market.

subsections.label: Overall outlook
points: FY27 is expected to be a flat/investment-and-commissioning year for volumes given delayed ramp-up; faster ramp-up contingent on commodity price correction and broader economic environment improving.
Management targets achieving at least 75% (and ideally up to 80%) of the 24,000-ton capacity utilization within the next three years, assuming 15-20% YoY market capture growth.

Originally projected/forecasted (during roadshows) to achieve normalized margins next year, but management now expects this to take about two years due to commodity price disruption and machinery delays from cost increases.
Significant profitability improvement expected not this year, but next year and the year after, as utilization increases across extrusion, anodizing, fabrication, and tubing.
Management declined to give specific EBITDA per ton or realization numbers/percentages going forward but expects meaningful improvement with increased value addition.
Confident that investments made over the last two years will create meaningful shareholder value over the medium to long term.

risk_register.risk: Inability to pass on operating cost increases immediately
risk_register.note: Company passes on aluminium price increases but cannot immediately pass on higher energy, finance and depreciation costs to customers; discussions ongoing.

risk_register.risk: Container availability / geopolitical disruption
risk_register.note: Insurance company invoked terrorism clause last quarter, affecting container availability; Gulf/Middle East dispatches at standstill since war, not yet restarted.

risk_register.risk: Slower-than-expected capacity ramp-up
risk_register.note: Customer qualification cycles, project approvals, slower industrial demand, and geopolitical uncertainty have delayed commercial ramp-up of new capacities; described as a timing/utilization issue, not a capability issue.

risk_register.risk: Dewas project cost escalation and delay
risk_register.note: Required machinery costs increased, causing project cost to shoot up; company in renegotiation with overseas vendors, delaying the project.

risk_register.risk: Geographic concentration risk (US market)
risk_register.note: 80-85% of exports go to the US; company diversifying towards domestic market and new export markets like CIS to mitigate.

risk_register.risk: No fixed-term supply contracts
risk_register.note: Open-ended arrangements with customers with forecasting but no fixed commitment, creating revenue unpredictability.

themes.label: Value-added mix shift
themes.note: Strategic pivot from traditional extrusion to higher value-added converter (anodizing, powder coating, fabrication, tubing) commanding ~25% higher margins.

themes.label: Capacity expansion
themes.note: Extrusion capacity increased from 10,000 to 24,000 tons via new Italian press and Dewas facility acquired, but commercial ramp-up delayed by qualification cycles and demand.

themes.label: US tariff and export slowdown
themes.note: 50% US tariff since 2024 plus 50%+ aluminium price rise effectively raised net raw material cost ~75%, causing customer slowdown; exports fell 30-40% over 3 years.

themes.label: Margin pressure from input/energy costs
themes.note: Gross margins fell to ~8% due to inability to immediately pass on energy, finance and depreciation cost increases despite pass-through of aluminium price.

themes.label: Geopolitical/logistics disruption
themes.note: Insurance terrorism clause invocation halted container dispatches to Gulf/Middle East; not yet restarted.

themes.label: Defense/aerospace/Make in India opportunity
themes.note: Growing inquiry pipeline in defense, aerospace, solar sectors and import substitution opportunities under Make in India; tier-one customers approaching pending one audit.

themes.label: Balance sheet strengthening via preferential capital
themes.note: Preferential capital raise of INR83 crores lifted net worth 54% to INR274 crores, strengthening balance sheet for growth investments.

key_takeaways: FY26 has been a year of strategic transformation for the company... marked the transition of the company from a traditional extrusion player towards a higher value-added aluminium converter.
The revenue from operations remained almost flat at INR809 crores as compared to INR810 crores in FY25.
EBITDA increased by 3% to INR31 crores from INR30 crores last year.
Profit before tax decreased by 18% to INR18 crores as against INR22 crores in the previous year.
Profit after tax also reduced by 19% and stood at INR13 crores as compared to INR16 crores last year.
Net worth of the company increased significantly by 54% from INR178 crores to INR274 crores.
During the year, we successfully commissioned the new Italian extrusion press at Pithampur, increasing our extrusion capacity from 10,000 tons per annum to 24,000 tons per annum.
We also completed the acquisition and refurbishment of the Dewas facility, which will become the foundation for our future tubing and downstream value-added business.

We acknowledge that the commercial ramp-up of these capacities has taken longer than originally anticipated because customer qualification cycles, project approvals, slower industrial demand in certain sectors, and further geopolitical uncertainty have impacted the pace of utilization.
pressing_questions: What kind of ramp-up can we expect in extrusions given increased capacity, and what percentage of volumes will come from value-added products in FY27 and over the next one or two years?
Has the export/US tariff-related issue subsided or where does that stand for the export business going forward?
What is the expected cost increase in terms of employee or fixed costs associated with the increased capacity for FY27 given flat volumes?
Gross margins have taken a hit to close to 8% this quarter versus double digits earlier — what was the main issue, and is there a price pass-through clause in extrusion contracts?
Regarding the Dewas facility — what products are being manufactured, what are the orders, and how is it expected to scale up over the medium term (three years)?
Are audits taking place at the facilities for defense/aerospace, is there customer interest, and is there export opportunity/talks with export customers?
When do normalized margins come in and what might that number be?
What are the updates on the previously mentioned agreement (referenced as involving 'Tata')?
What would be the capex for FY27 and FY28?
What is the INR16.4 crore other non-current asset (advances to customers) in the balance sheet, and is it related to the Dewas facility equipment?

LENSKART.about: Incorporated in 2008,Lenskart Solutions is a technology-focused eyewear company involved in the design, manufacturing, branding, and retail of prescription eyeglasses, sunglasses, contact lenses, and accessories.[1]

quarters.summary: Management framed Q1 FY27 as evidence of an accelerating compounding story: revenue grew 34% YoY with PAT up 182% to ₹228 crores, India same-store sales growth of 18.3%, international revenue growth of 38% with EBITDA margin crossing 10% for the first time, and consolidated product margin crossing 70%. Forward focus remains on India store densification/white-space expansion, international margin scaling toward India-like economics, premiumization (Rodenstock/Tokai/Owndays, Under Armour) alongside mass affordability (₹500 Hustlr Club), and AI-led initiatives (self-eye test, B by Lenskart smart glasses) as long-term growth levers, with no new formal numeric guidance issued beyond reiterating strategic direction.

subsections.label: Headline commentary
points: A third more revenue has doubled post-rent EBITDA and nearly tripled PAT, indicating compounding is accelerating.
PAT for Q1 FY27 alone (₹228 crores, up 182% YoY) is nearly half of full-year FY26 PAT (₹530 crores).
Revenue grew 34% YoY in Q1 FY27.
Consolidated product margin was 70%+ in Q1 FY27, up from ~69% average over the prior 4 quarters.

subsections.label: Cash flow and capital allocation
points: ₹297 crores operating cash flow represented 82% EBITDA-to-cash conversion.

Cash generated was sufficient to fund store capex of ₹75 crores and plant capex of ₹132 crores (largely Hyderabad facility), leaving a positive net cash inflow of ₹116 crores before M&A and equity raise.
ROCE improved to 23% from 14.6% last year (corrected from an inadvertently stated 14%) as a result of improving profitability and disciplined capital allocation.

subsections.label: India segment drivers
points: Growth and profitability are positively correlated in the business model; EBITDA margin expansion accompanied revenue growth — India revenue of ₹1,531 crores grew 30.7% YoY, with EBITDA (pre-Ind AS 116) up 51.5% YoY to ₹236 crores, and margin expanding from 13.3% to 15.4%.
Product margin expansion to 64.2% absorbed currency headwind.
Marketing efficiency improved from 5.7% to 4.8% of revenue on the basis of brand pull.
Remote optometry scaled to 786 stores from 168 stores at FY25 end, powering volume-led growth in eyewear units (82 lakh units, up 22.8% YoY) and eye tests (63 lakh, up 42.7% YoY).

SSSG of 18.3% was broad-based across tiers; SPSG of 24% (corrected from an inadvertently stated 25%; also referenced as 24.3% in a footnote) ran ahead of it, proving densification continues to lock incremental demand.
Added 116 net new stores and opened 50 new cities in the quarter.
SSSG accelerated YoY (16% same quarter last year to 18.3% now) despite density rising from 1.5 to 1.6 stores per pin code, implying market share gains given SPSG running ahead.

subsections.label: International segment drivers
points: Growth broad-based across all markets and brands; volume-led, almost entirely same-store led — international revenue of ₹1,203 crores grew 38% YoY (29% constant currency).
EBITDA margin expansion (10.6% vs 4.5% prior year; EBITDA of ₹127 crores, roughly tripling YoY) driven by operating leverage and product margin improvement (product margin 77.1%).
Product margin expansion attributed to deeper supply chain integration of Owndays and Meller.

Core prescription business grew strongly with eye tests up 20.5%; sunglasses saw a pronounced seasonal peak (April-June) with units up 58.4%, contributing to Q1 seasonality where sunglasses (a higher net-margin business) makes Q1 stronger than other quarters.
Eyewear units grew 37.6% YoY and transacting customers grew 27.8% YoY internationally.
Just 16 net new stores added internationally, yet revenue grew 38% (29% constant currency), reflecting same-store-led growth rather than store count expansion.
International EBITDA margin has grown consistently YoY: 3.6% (FY25) to 7% (FY26 full year) to 10.6% (Q1 FY27); TTM international margin referenced at 8.6% in analyst discussion.

subsections.label: Premiumization vs mass adoption
points: Owndays premium lenses now doing over ₹1,500 crores of prescription eyeglass sales; Rodenstock and Tokai eyeglasses (progressives priced ₹30,000+) doing roughly ₹250 crores annually — company sees opportunity to build India's next iconic premium lens brands.
₹10,000+ price point mix grew from 18% (at DRHP filing) to 20% now.
Premium frames defined as above ₹5,000 ticket size (John Jacobs, Meller, Owndays, and newly launched exclusive brand Under Armour, the first third-party brand).
Lens category above ₹3,500 for single vision has historically been dominated by global brands — seen as a big opportunity for Lenskart to build next-generation iconic brands.

Onboarded largest ever number of customers in 'real Bharat' via Hustlr Club, offering ₹500 glasses with lenses and warranty included, ambition to democratize vision similar to telecom democratization in India.

It took time to profitably crack the ₹500 price point — required manufacturing scale-up, logistics optimization, and omnichannel customer acquisition cost management; management admits underestimating how fast customers would premiumize.

Cannibalization at the ₹500 price point managed via an omnichannel journey (face-scan verification, anti-duplication checks) and a house-of-brands strategy so different brands serve different customer segments/positioning.

Lower price points assessed as more margin-accretive from a unit economics perspective versus higher price points where absolute money is larger but margin is harder to achieve; unit economics were solved before launch, so no unit-level profitability challenge expected even if ₹500 SKU expands significantly.
Meller brand grew from USD35 million at acquisition to tracking over USD70 million currently.
Singapore Lenskart holds 25%+ volume market share.

subsections.label: Dual brand strategy (Owndays vs Lenskart) internationally
points: Strategy differs by market — in Singapore, dual-brand strategy (Lenskart + Owndays) worked well, with Lenskart holding over 25% volume market share even before Owndays was strong there; both brands coexist serving different consumer segments and price points (Lenskart as platform brand, Owndays as D2C brand).
Same dual-brand approach being followed in Thailand, where Owndays operates at a different price point from Lenskart.
In Japan, dual-brand strategy is not currently planned; approach evolves market by market.

subsections.label: Meller / celebrity brand positioning
points: Meller priced around EUR50 for sunglasses but carries strong authenticity-driven visibility (Virat Kohli, Tanmay Bhat, Blackpink wearing Meller), reflecting a view that next-generation brand building is about authenticity rather than superficial premium positioning.

subsections.label: Self eye test / AI
points: Self-eye test entered pilot stores this quarter, built on one of India's largest recorded eye test data sets.

Positioned as an engineering solution to the shortage of optometrists globally (India trains only a few thousand per year) — cannot scale eye testing to a billion tested eyes by training optometrists alone, so must engineer the solution.
AI eye test aims to deliver consistent outcomes every time, unlike traditional subjective eye tests where results vary by optometrist and by patient response.

Remote optometry via Tango Eye (an acquired computer vision company) is used to monitor whether all steps in the eye test process are followed correctly via CCTV, producing a consistency/process score; accuracy is tracked indirectly via customer power-change exchange rates, though not all exchanges indicate an incorrect test.

subsections.label: B by Lenskart (smart glasses)
points: B by Lenskart is live, with sign-ups reaching 80,000+.
Manufacturing is scaling, with a few hundred glasses shipping daily.
Product is improving weekly based on consumer feedback.
Management views eyewear's 12-hours-a-day facial presence as giving Lenskart a unique position at the intersection of eye care, AI, personal health and data.

subsections.label: Progressive lens R&D
points: Progressive lens opportunity requires precise post-eye-checkup markings/fittings, traditionally done manually with limited scalability/precision; Lenskart is building tech-enabled solutions to automate marking.
Owndays progressive lens series has been engineered in-house by a dedicated R&D team, leveraging AI to run customer fitting data into lens design models, significantly lowering R&D cost.
The Owndays adaptive customized progressive lens reportedly has higher customer satisfaction than even the most expensive lenses currently sold.
Quality (not price) has become the primary reason customers buy from Lenskart (~60% cite quality), even in single vision, informing the progressive lens strategy.

subsections.label: In-house manufacturing / branded lens arrangements
points: For branded lenses such as Rodenstock, Lenskart acts as both manufacturer and brand licensing partner — manufacturing in its own factory using certain raw materials and design information from the brand partner; in some cases products may still be imported directly.
This manufacturing/licensing arrangement started in India only but is expanding into international markets one by one, based on India response.

subsections.label: Hyderabad facility
points: Plant capex of ₹132 crores in the quarter was largely pertaining to the Hyderabad facility.
Hyderabad plant coming online expected to further aid insourcing and cost structure improvement, supporting margin resilience against currency headwinds.

subsections.label: Backward integration
points: Structural initiatives to offset currency impact on product margin include increasing in-house manufacturing of frames, negotiating vendor volume-based discounts, and optimizing overall product mix.
Backward integration is described as an ongoing journey that will continue as insourcing improves.

subsections.label: Three directions of growth
points: Grew deeper: densification within existing 1,517 pin codes raised store density from 1.5 to 1.6 (about 150 net new stores) while SSSG held at ~18% and same pin code sales growth ran at 24%, indicating demand is being added not divided.

Grew wider: entered 152 of 2,821 previously unserved pin codes within existing cities (as flagged in Q2 FY26), leaving over 2,650 pin codes of white space where brand, supply chain and delivery network are already operational; average revenue per store in these towns tracking at ₹18 lakhs per month.

Grew further: entered 140 entirely new towns this year (e.g., Hassan in Karnataka, Balasore in Odisha, Tura in Meghalaya, Gandhidham in Gujarat), with strong unit economics reported in these new stores.

In nine months, 455 net new stores added — the fastest expansion in company history — consuming about 5% of the 6,400 pin code white space mapped in the Q2 FY26 letter; over 6,100 pin codes still await a first store, and densification allows for at least another 3,000 stores, pointing India's store potential past 10,000.
Bangalore reached 189 stores (13 net additions in last 9 months) with SSSG of 20%.
Visakhapatnam added 11 net new stores and Kolkata added 10 net new stores (8 of which were in new pin codes) in the last 9 months.

subsections.label: India market opportunity framing
points: 78 crore Indians need vision correction today, heading towards 94 crore by FY30 — framed as a market to build, not capture.
India eyewear penetration is only about 35%, expected to grow, especially given rising myopia rates among kids.
Progressives is a category where Lenskart historically was not the strongest player but is now gaining market share.
Price spectrum expansion (sub-₹1,000 and above-₹10,000 with lenses) has made the brand relevant to previously unserved cohorts.

subsections.label: International store strategy and geography
points: International markets are at different growth stages: Thailand is adding many stores; Middle East is being doubled down on; more mature geographies like Singapore and Japan have better unit economics, reflecting maturity rather than fundamental market structure differences.
Japan is one of the fastest-growing international markets currently, driven by a market phenomenon of consumers moving from expensive traditional opticians to D2C brands despite high penetration.
The unit economics/playbook used internationally mirrors India's approach exactly.

GeoIQ acquisition enables geo-analytics data mapping for international markets similar to India, guiding store site selection; eyewear is viewed as a neighbourhood model similar in structure across markets (e.g., UK's Specsavers, Australia).

subsections.label: Market creation vs competition
points: Management frames its role as creating the market, not competing in it — roughly 35,000 Indians per day discover for the first time in Lenskart stores that they cannot see clearly.
63 lakh eye tests conducted in India this quarter, growing every year; over 1 crore first-time eye tests conducted in FY26.
Eye test volume is described as a discovery problem more than a competitive share-shift problem, given the belief that 70% of adults have vision issues.
As long as eye test growth continues (top of funnel), volume growth follows via conversion; this drove much of the quarter's ~23% eyewear unit growth.
Comparison to China's eyewear market growing at ~13% CAGR, with India seen as following a similar path.

subsections.label: NPS / customer experience
points: SSG, SPSG and NPS moderated this quarter versus prior trend but management does not see it as concerning; some confusion/miscommunication about certain policies on social media affected NPS temporarily, since clarified, with NPS bouncing back to near original levels.
Company remains highly committed to NPS and continuous enhancement of customer experience as store network scales, citing plans for continued newness in the customer experience.

subsections.label: Eye test funnel and conversion dynamics
points: A significant majority of people who take an eye test eventually buy glasses, if not immediately then within a few months; first-time test-takers take longer to convert than repeat test-takers.
As top-of-funnel eye tests increase, conversion rates naturally get diluted, requiring better CRM engineering to bring these customers into the fold over time.
Managing queues and wait times from increased eye test volume is a key reason for investment in remote and self eye test technology.

subsections.label: Brand campaigns
points: Run for Frame campaign in Thailand (over 40,000 runners) extended to India (more than 5 lakh people); a new initiative 'Drishti ki Daud' (a run for vision) launching this Independence Day in collaboration with the Lenskart Foundation, where running 20,000 steps donates a pair of glasses to someone in need, with an additional pair for every additional 10,000 steps.

subsections.label: M&A / acquisitions referenced
points: Proforma financials reflect acquisitions of Dealskart, Meller, and GeoIQ as if always part of the company for like-to-like comparison; for Q1 FY27 there is no difference between proforma and reported financials.
GeoIQ acquisition specifically enables the team to build geo-analytics/mapping data capability for international markets, mirroring India's data-driven store site-selection approach.
Tango Eye (computer vision company) acquisition underpins remote optometry monitoring for eye test process consistency.

subsections.label: Long-term company vision
points: Management describes the broader ambition as building 'the infrastructure of vision for the billion people no one has ever served,' beyond simply selling glasses.

Achieving this requires manufacturing at unprecedented category scale, a fast design-to-shelf engine, distribution into hard-to-reach towns, omnichannel access, AI-scaled eye testing, multiple brands for different cohorts/price points, data capability, global talent, and capital.

subsections.label: Currency / FX headwind
points: A significant part of revenue comes in non-INR currencies, providing a natural hedge at the full P&L level.

Product margin has been protected from currency impact via structural initiatives (in-house frame manufacturing, vendor volume discount negotiations, product mix optimization), but short-term headwinds could persist if currency worsens further.
Continued backward integration and cost structure improvement are the company's ongoing response to currency risk.

subsections.label: Talent and execution risk
points: When asked which of product, real estate or talent is the biggest medium/long-term worry, management cited talent and culture — specifically maintaining organizational agility and speed at scale, and having sufficient engineering talent capable of leveraging data/AI to solve scaling bottlenecks.

subsections.label: Supply-side execution risk in Tier 2/3 expansion
points: Serving Tier 2 markets is described as 'a muscle that needs to be built' — requiring logistics solutions, manpower hiring and training, and willingness of people to work in these locations.
Remote optometry was described as the biggest unlock enabling store expansion pace in Tier 2 to date; without it, current pace of Tier 2 store openings would not have been possible.
Logistics network had to be re-engineered for Tier 2 (air+train+bus ecosystem) since the network built for Tier 1 delivery (air-based) doesn't work for Tier 2.

subsections.label: NPS-related communication risk
points: Some confusion/miscommunication about company policies on social media temporarily affected NPS this quarter; has since been clarified and NPS is recovering.

subsections.label: Down-trading / cannibalization risk from ₹500 price point
points: Risk that existing higher-ASP customers could down-trade to the ₹500 price point is managed via an omnichannel journey (face scan verification against duplication) and a house-of-brands approach so different brands target different customer segments.

subsections.label: International margin trajectory
points: Full year FY26 international EBITDA margin was about 7%, up from 3.6% two years prior (FY25); management expects continued YoY improvement in international margin but declined to give a specific full-year FY27 number, noting Q1 seasonality (sunglasses peak) makes Q1 stronger than the eventual full-year average in some periods.

Time is coming closer for international store expansion acceleration, but this varies market by market and depends on completing technology integration to protect customer experience; acceleration not expected 'this year' broadly, though plans are being made in select markets such as Thailand.

subsections.label: Store expansion pace
points: India store additions accelerated from about 100 stores/year historically to 300, now to 450+ per year, with an intent to continue accelerating internationally similarly.

Densification and unserved pin code white space suggest India's total addressable store count could go past 10,000 (from around 2,700 stores currently), though this is not stated as a firm formal target.

guidance_ledger.statement: Net new store additions for FY27 are expected to be around FY26 levels (prior guidance); this quarter management reiterated an intent to accelerate store additions in India and internationally similar to the trajectory of moving from 100 to 300 to 450+ stores/year.

guidance_ledger.metric: Long-term steady-state EBITDA pre-Ind AS margin
guidance_ledger.statement: Long-term steady-state EBITDA pre-Ind AS margin expectation (previously ~25%) not explicitly restated this quarter but implied to remain the direction of travel as margins continue to expand (India at 15.4%, international at 10.6%).
Prior target was working towards 100 million eyewear units milestone (from 29 million in FY26); not explicitly restated this quarter, though unit growth of 22.8% YoY continues.

Prior ambition was 100 million eye tests at least, eventually a billion; this quarter reinforced with 63 lakh eye tests in the quarter and over 1 crore first-time eye tests in FY26, and repeated emphasis on scaling eye tests via remote and self/AI eye test as the path to that ambition.

Prior long-term runway was 4,500 stores, expected to expand given Tier 2 demand surprise; this quarter management indicated India store potential now points past 10,000 stores given remaining white space (6,100+ pin codes) and densification potential (3,000+ more stores), an implicit upward revision though no single formal number given.
No update provided this quarter on same-day delivery target; not discussed.
No update provided this quarter on KSA-specific breakeven timing; not discussed.

Margin in international reached 10.6% in Q1 FY27, up from 4.5% last year and up from 7% full-year FY26 and 3.6% FY25; management reiterated margin will continue to grow but declined to commit to a specific full-year number, citing Q1 sunglasses seasonality.
Management reiterated that compounding effect of revenue and margin will continue, evidenced this quarter by revenue growth of 34% translating into doubled post-rent EBITDA and near-tripled PAT.

Management indicated time is coming closer to accelerate international store expansion, contingent on completing technology integration market by market; explicitly stated acceleration is not expected 'this year' broadly but plans are being made for select markets like Thailand.
Constant endeavor to keep doing backward integration and improving cost structure to serve consumers better, especially as Hyderabad plant comes online and insourcing improves.

guidance_ledger.metric: Branded lens manufacturing expansion to international markets
guidance_ledger.statement: In-house branded lens manufacturing arrangement (e.g., Rodenstock) started in India only but is expanding into international markets one by one, based on India response.

risk_register.risk: Currency / FX headwind on product margin
risk_register.note: Natural hedge exists from non-INR revenue mix; structural initiatives (in-house manufacturing, vendor negotiations, product mix) have offset impact so far, but short-term headwinds could re-emerge if currency worsens further.

risk_register.risk: Talent and organizational agility at scale
risk_register.note: Cited as the biggest medium/long-term worry among product, real estate, and talent — need for engineering talent that can leverage data/AI to solve scaling bottlenecks.

risk_register.risk: Tier 2/3 execution risk (logistics, manpower, training)
risk_register.note: Remote optometry described as the biggest unlock enabling Tier 2 store expansion pace; logistics re-engineered with air+train+bus ecosystem for Tier 2 delivery.

risk_register.risk: NPS / customer experience volatility
risk_register.note: SSG, SPSG and NPS moderated this quarter due to social-media miscommunication about company policies; since clarified and NPS has bounced back to near original levels.

risk_register.risk: Down-trading / cannibalization from ₹500 price point
risk_register.note: Managed via omnichannel journey (face-scan anti-duplication) and house-of-brands strategy to segment customers by brand/positioning.

risk_register.risk: Eye test funnel conversion dilution
risk_register.note: As top-of-funnel eye tests increase, conversion rates naturally get diluted, requiring better CRM engineering; first-time testers take longer to convert than repeat testers.

risk_register.risk: Same-store growth sustainability at scale (10,000-store ambition)
risk_register.note: Pushback concern on whether SSG will come under stress as store count scales from ~2,700 to ~10,000; management sees eye test growth and premiumization/lower-price cohorts as offsetting factors, with supply-side engineering (queue/wait time reduction, RFID rollout) as the key lever.

risk_register.risk: Currency / rupee depreciation on imports
risk_register.note: Biggest cost variable; offset so far by 42% international mix and vertical integration; RMB move from 11 to 14 plus dollar-rupee depreciation offset structural margin gains this year, keeping India product margin flat at 64%.

risk_register.risk: Geopolitical uncertainty and demand cycles
risk_register.note: Flagged as a source of potential short-term bumps for FY27; no material impact seen so far on Indian or international demand.

risk_register.risk: Middle East regional disturbance / store traffic dip
risk_register.note: Temporary, smaller dip in traffic that bounced back quickly; eyewear category proved resilient though some discretionary/fashion element exists.

risk_register.risk: Discretionary consumption pressure
risk_register.note: If consumers move toward cheaper alternatives amid consumption pressure, management believes Lenskart's value-conscious offerings could be a strong alternative.

risk_register.risk: Competitive intensity in smart glasses
risk_register.note: Space getting more competitive with entrants like Google (using Gemini Live); no player yet has a clear winning form factor, requiring Lenskart to stay agile.

risk_register.risk: Freight and raw material cost impact
risk_register.note: No meaningful impact seen so far as these costs are a fraction of total cost base.

themes.label: Operating leverage / margin compounding
themes.note: 34% revenue growth drove PAT up 182% to ₹228 crores, with post-rent EBITDA doubling — compounding accelerating across India and international.

themes.label: Tier 2+ demand opportunity
themes.note: 455 net new stores added in nine months across densification, white-space entry, and new towns, with India store potential now seen pointing past 10,000 stores.

themes.label: International expansion maturity
themes.note: International EBITDA margin crossed 10% for the first time, up from 4.5% last year, with product margin at 77.1% on deeper Owndays/Meller supply chain integration.

themes.label: Currency headwind
themes.note: Natural non-INR revenue hedge plus backward integration offset FX impact on product margin, though short-term headwinds could persist if currency worsens further.

themes.label: AI-led transformation
themes.note: Self-eye test entered pilot stores this quarter as an AI-engineered solution to optometrist scarcity, alongside remote optometry scaling to 786 stores.

themes.label: Smart glasses / B by Lenskart
themes.note: B by Lenskart live with 80,000+ sign-ups, a few hundred glasses shipping daily, product improving weekly with consumer feedback.

themes.label: Premiumization alongside mass adoption
themes.note: Owndays/Rodenstock/Tokai premium lens sales scaling (₹1,500cr+ and ₹250cr annually) even as ₹500 Hustlr Club pair launched profitably for mass-market Bharat customers.

key_takeaways: Revenue grew 34% year-on-year and PAT grew 182% to ₹228 crores.
India same-store sales grew 18.3%, international revenue grew 38%, and consolidated product margin crossed 70% for the first time after four quarters at around 69%.
Every single day now, roughly 35,000 Indians walk into Lenskart stores and discover for the first time in their lives that they cannot see clearly. 63 lakh eye tests in India in this quarter.
78 crore Indians need vision correction today, heading towards 94 crores by FY30.

In nine months, we added 455 net new stores, the fastest expansion in our history, and it consumed about 5% of the 6,400 pin code white space we mapped in our Q2 FY26 letter. Over 6,100 pin codes still await their first Lenskart store, and densification allows for at least another 3,000 stores. India alone points past 10,000 stores now.
This quarter, international grew 38%, with EBITDA pre-Ind AS margin crossing 10% for the first time.
Owndays is now one of Asia's most respected eyewear brands, and Meller, which was a USD35 million brand when we acquired it, is tracking to be a $70 million plus brand already.
This quarter, our self-eye test entered pilot stores, built on one of India's largest recorded eye test data sets.
pressing_questions: Could you give us a sense on how store growth kind of behaves based on age? Because one of the pushbacks, the concerns that emerges as you go on this journey from 2,700 stores to around 10,000 stores, will your sales on the same store basis kind of come under stress?
Given you have like, RetailIQ, GeoIQ, the store addition pace can pick up from where you are currently? And what will it take to do so?

SSG, SPSG, NPS all moderated this quarter, though individually they don't look particularly concerning, but given the base and the noise around NPS, do you see any common thread here? Has NPS improved in the following months also after the quarter ended?
Out of the three inputs, product, real estate and talent, over the medium to long term, which of the three worries you most in getting to the vision you have laid out?

Would it be possible to rank even directionally where Japan, Southeast Asia, Middle East and others rank in terms of margins versus let's say our 8.6% TTM, which are the geographies which are above and which are below?

In the international business, the Y-o-Y store count was up 10% while revenue growth was much higher, close to 30% in constant currency. How much more can you sweat these stores? Or do you think to maintain the current growth rate you would need to look at accelerated store additions internationally as well?

What percentage of people who do eye tests at your store do not buy eyewear at your store at least immediately in the next few weeks? And what percentage of people who do buy prescription eyewear in your store come with a prescription from outside?
Last year your full year margin was higher than the margin that you did in Q1. So, do you think that's a fair estimate to take for FY27 as well?

If I look at your international margins, they are now very similar to what your India margins were in FY25. So do you think you are now at that stage where the store expansion can significantly be accelerated?
If this ₹500 eyewear were to expand very significantly, would that have any sort of drag effect on profitability?
For brands like Rodenstock where you indicated that you're manufacturing the lenses here, how is that arrangement? Is this just a brand licensing arrangement or something deeper?

quarters.summary: Lenskart delivered its strongest quarter as a public company in Q4 FY26 with 41% YoY revenue growth and EBITDA margin expansion, and management guided for FY27 net store additions around FY26 levels, unchanged long-term steady-state EBITDA pre-Ind AS margin target of ~25%, with continued compounding of revenue and margin, while flagging currency, geopolitics and demand-cycle risks as sources of short-term volatility.

subsections.label: Margin drivers
points: EBITDA margin expansion in India was broad-based across the P&L: employee cost improved 2.7 pp, marketing improved 80 bps despite higher absolute spend, other expenses (excl. marketing) improved (stated as 1.3 pp, noted as inadvertently misstated vs correct 2.3%), and rent reduced 70 bps driven by same-store growth.
India product margin held steady at 64% because rupee depreciation absorbed all the benefit from vertical integration and premiumization.
International EBITDA margin improvement was led by both product margin improvement and operating leverage.

subsections.label: Capital allocation
points: Operating cash flow of ₹887 crores in FY26 fully funded store capex for 603 net new stores while also funding investment in manufacturing, including the new Hyderabad facility.
Closing net cash balance excludes IPO-related payables which were largely settled in April.
ROCE of 23% (excluding undeployed IPO proceeds) expanded 9 pp versus prior year.

subsections.label: Three-year compounding trend
points: 25% revenue growth is translating into near doubling of EBITDA every year; PAT has scaled from negligible to ₹530 crores over three years.
India is at ~14% pre-Ind AS EBITDA margin today with roughly another 10 pp of runway to the steady-state margin expectation of ~25%.

International margin (7%) at 718 stores compares to India's 0.3% margin at nearly twice the store count at the same stage in FY23, indicating international is earlier in its journey but progressing faster.

subsections.label: Demand drivers
points: India volume growth was primarily volume-driven, powered by 50% increase in eye tests to 6 million in the quarter.
Same Store Sales Growth of 24% in Q4 was broad-based across Metro, Tier 1 and Tier 2 markets; Same Pincode Sales Growth of 31% confirms store densification continues to unlock incremental demand.
Management noted eye tests growing ~50% YoY versus volume growth of ~25%, indicating a large opportunity to improve conversion post eye test — this will be a key area of focus.

Management stated ASP/volume split for SSG is not disclosed by value and volume, but clarified analyst's calculated volume-only SSG estimate (implying ~10% volume growth) is not correct and the actual number is meaningfully higher; quarterly ASP/volume mix fluctuates as the company opens both low-cost (OPP) and premium offerings simultaneously, so a 12-month view is recommended.

Management noted growth in Metros and Tier 1 is not slowing — a large part of SSG is coming from Metro/Tier 1 stores, and eye test wait-time reduction solutions are being worked on more aggressively in Metros.

subsections.label: Pincode/store clustering strategy
points: Store expansion decisions are based on bottoms-up mobility-pattern data science (via GeoIQ) rather than top-down pin-code mapping; the company optimizes for market share within a 10-minute travel radius.

Management stated cannibalization concerns from adding stores in the same pincode should not materialize under this model; cited data shared in Q2 letter showing store count tripling in some cities while revenue doubled.
A large part of this year's SSG came from stores in pincodes/cities with multiple Lenskart stores.
