Opening order book of INR1,110 crores (as of 1 Apr 26) plus INR2,000 crores new bookings less ~INR1,900-1,950 crores revenue implies closing order book of at least INR1,250-1,300 crores at start of next fiscal
Utilization guided to reach 70%+ (even 75%) this financial year without booking further orders, from 44% in Q1

Post Ghiloth second sandwich panel line, Mambattu additional line, and Vithalapur 50,000-ton structural steel line, total peak revenue potential close to INR2,700-2,900 crores (blended PEB + sandwich panel)

risk_register.risk: Commodity/steel price increase due to Middle East war
risk_register.note: Abrupt steel price increase of 12-15% post war start caused ~100 bps EBITDA margin contraction in Q1 (vs estimated 200 bps); impact managed via fixed-price contracts repriced weekly and smart sourcing; management expects margins to normalize from Q2 onwards as older low-price orders get executed/repriced.

risk_register.risk: Monsoon-related execution delays
risk_register.note: Monsoon causes delays in civil works done by customers (e.g., the INR165 crore renewable order customer committed 1-month civil works completion but faced monsoon delays); management does not see major challenge to EPACK's own execution role.

risk_register.risk: Fixed-price contract risk from raw material timing mismatch
risk_register.note: Orders are booked at fixed price; raw material procurement, production, logistics and installation happen at different points in time, creating risk if commodity prices move abruptly between order booking and execution; company mitigates by booking orders based on current prices almost every week.

risk_register.risk: Low win/pipeline conversion ratio (~20%)
risk_register.note: Pipeline conversion/win rate sits at 15%-20%; company deliberately does not chase 100% of quotations due to customized/technical nature of buildings, capacity constraints, regional availability mismatches, and selective focus on serious customers; management considers 20% a good hit rate versus industry range of 10-12%.

risk_register.risk: Data center design/pricing inexperience
risk_register.note: Company lost 2 data center structure bids due to design optimization issues (new to designing) and pricing inexperience (still learning to price this segment perfectly).

risk_register.risk: Capacity constraints limiting order acceptance
risk_register.note: Regional capacity mismatches (e.g., north capacity available but project in south where facility is full) lead to lost projects to avoid creating a bad image for EPACK in the market.

risk_register.risk: Heavy structure capability limitation
risk_register.note: Company is not capable of doing ROBs (railway over bridges) or structures requiring much wider span/web width; no current business in railways.

risk_register.risk: Steel price increase due to minimum import barrier duty/anti-dumping duty
risk_register.note: Caused 70-80 bps margin decline in Q4 FY26 due to fixed-price contracts; company obtained price increases from over 80% of contracts to offset.

risk_register.risk: Fixed-price contract exposure to raw material cost swings
risk_register.note: Inventory of 32,000 tons held at pre-increase pricing will not fully match new contract pricing, causing some but not major EBITDA impact this quarter.

risk_register.risk: Geopolitical/war-related disruption
risk_register.note: Caused brief uncertainty in demand but companies have continued capex plans over the last month, viewing disruption as short-term; no major disruption seen in capex cycle or order inflow.

risk_register.risk: Sandwich panel line underutilization (Mambattu)
risk_register.note: Utilization was low at ~25% in FY26; management is addressing via sales engine rebuild, restructured sales team, new leadership and go-to-market changes.

risk_register.risk: Order book execution delays
risk_register.note: About 5-10% of order book can be delayed due to environmental clearance not being cleared or customer funding issues.

risk_register.risk: Partial price pass-through
risk_register.note: Not 100% of price increase is passed through to customers; some accepted full pass-through, others lesser, but overall a good amount of increase was achieved.

risk_register.risk: Competitive intensity limiting margin expansion
risk_register.note: Industry has 3-4 large players with good capacity; competition limits ability to command higher margins, so company is prioritizing capacity utilization and growth over margin expansion.

themes.label: Growth guidance
themes.note: Q1 FY27 revenue grew ~25% YoY; company reiterates FY27 revenue target of INR1,900-1,950 crores (~30% growth) backed by order book of INR1,380 crores.

themes.label: Steel input cost inflation
themes.note: Middle East war-driven steel price increase of 12-15% caused ~100 bps EBITDA margin contraction to 9.4% in Q1, better than the 200 bps initially estimated; margins expected to normalize to 10.5%+ from Q2.

themes.label: Capacity expansion
themes.note: Ghiloth second sandwich panel line, Andhra Pradesh second line, and Vithalapur (Gujarat) 50,000-ton plant are progressing, with commissioning staggered through FY27 into Q4 FY27/April FY28.

themes.label: Sandwich panel ramp-up
themes.note: Mambattu continuous sandwich panel line utilization rose to 44-45% in Q1 FY27 from 25% in FY26, with guidance of 70%+ utilization for the full year even without further order booking.

themes.label: New-age sector demand
themes.note: Order book increasingly driven by energy sector (renewables, transformers, wires & cables) and emerging data center opportunity, including formation of EPACK Data Center Solutions subsidiary with INR75 crore proposed investment.

themes.label: Order book & win-rate dynamics
themes.note: Record order booking of INR580 crores in Q1 (150% YoY growth) alongside a modest 15-20% pipeline win rate, which management attributes to selective bidding and capacity constraints.

themes.label: Geographic mix shift (West market)
themes.note: Early-stage exports of insulated sandwich panels to Africa (~INR2.5 crores in Q1); PEB exports remain limited mostly to SAARC nations (Bhutan, Nepal, Sri Lanka); no meaningful international contribution yet.

key_takeaways: Revenue growth of about 25% YoY in Q1 FY27
Order book grew 150% YoY - INR580 crores booked in Q1 FY27 vs INR240 crores in Q1 FY26
Biggest ever single order of INR165 crores received from a renewable energy company for solar cell and solar module plant
First order received from an automobile company for a manufacturing plant
Total revenue in Q1 FY27 was ~INR366 crores vs INR295 crores in Q1 FY26
EBITDA grew from INR30.9 crores to almost INR35 crores YoY, but EBITDA margin contracted from 10.5% to 9.4% due to steel price increase from Middle East war
PAT margin was 5% in Q1 FY27 vs 5.4% in Q1 FY26
Total order book as on 30 June 2026 was almost INR1,380 crores, giving visibility for 6-8 months and for FY27
FY27 revenue target of INR1,900-1,950 crores, a growth of ~30% over FY26
All four manufacturing plants running at almost full capacity; prefab division average capacity utilization was 75%+
Sandwich panel line at Mambattu, AP utilization ramped up to ~45% from 25% in FY26
EPACK Data Center Solutions subsidiary formed with proposed INR75 crores investment to tap data center opportunity
pressing_questions: Sir, your Q2 FY26 order book to revenue ratio was 1.5x with an 8-month completion cycle, but your own FY27 guidance of INR2000 crores order book against a INR1920 crores to INR1950 crores revenue compresses that ratio to 1x. So, by your own numbers, your order book coverage has nearly halved. So, what explains that compression and how are you thinking about rebuilding that ratio going forward?

As you have consistently described trust and execution speed as your core competitive moat and your ability to deliver 2 to 3 months ahead of competitors is genuinely impressive, but your own pipeline conversion ratio sits at 15% to 20%. So, 80% of the customers who evaluate EPACK choose someone else. So, I would generally like to understand what is driving that 80% loss rate, and how do you reconcile that number with the confidence placed in the moat narrative?

On the data center opportunity - can you at least give some sense on revenue potential? What kind of working capital this business would involve? How it will compare with your base business? And basically is it ROCE accretive versus the 18% to 20% you do currently in the PEB business?
How would this INR75 crores be utilized, any approximate timelines that you have in mind and whether we would be taking on any new debt for this to fund this venture?

quarters.summary: FY26 was EPACK's first full year as a listed company with revenue up 35% to INR1,525 crores, expanded EBITDA margins, PAT up 56%, and INR107 crores of debt repaid. For FY27, management guided to 30% growth in the Prefab division (revenue of ~INR1,920-1,950 crores), an order booking target of INR2,000 crores plus, and margins maintained at 10%+ (range-bound 10.5%-11.5%), with three new capacity additions (Mambattu line 2, Ghiloth greenfield, Gujarat greenfield) coming online through FY27.

subsections.label: Revenue & profitability
points: FY26 was the first full year as a listed company; revenue up 35% at INR1,525 crores, EBITDA margins expanded, PAT up 56%.
Every commitment made at the time of the IPO has been met, per management.
Credit rating has improved as the company heads towards becoming debt-free.

subsections.label: Cash generation quality
points: Generated around INR135 crores of free operating cash flow last year, approximately 85% of EBITDA converting into cash.
Management characterizes this as exceptional cash discipline for a fast-growing company deploying significant capital — growing while generating real cash.

subsections.label: Margin drivers
points: Margin reduction of 70-80 bps in Q4 was mainly due to steel price increment caused by minimum import barrier duty being imposed, since a lot of contracts are fixed price contracts.
Company was able to get price increments from most customers who understood the increase was due to tax/anti-dumping duty changes, not a normal increase.
In over 80% of contracts, the company was able to get a price increase, limiting the impact.
Some Q1 impact expected from steel price increase, but Q2 not expected to see major challenge since most contracts have received price increases.

Company holds inventory of close to 32,000 tons which will cover the entire quarter, but that inventory is not priced at the level fixed in contracts, so some EBITDA impact is expected though not major.
Gross margin decline was majorly because of a sudden burp in steel prices, more so in March; management expects margins to fall back to original levels given price increments obtained this quarter.

Packaging business margin profile is about 100 bps better on EBITDA than Prefab business (10-10.5% range), but sandwich panel margin is not guided separately since raw material (steel) is common with Prefab structural steel.

subsections.label: Debt & interest cost
points: Debt repayment of ~INR107 crores (term loan ~INR70 crores plus some working capital loan), taking total debt repayment to about INR108 crores.
Interest cost in P&L still ~INR8 crores quarterly despite debt reduction because interest cost includes LCs used for vendors, BG commissions, apart from interest on term loans and WCDL.
Finance cost currently about 2.1%; expected to go down by about 20-25 bps in FY27 as full impact of repayment comes through.

subsections.label: Working capital
points: Average debtor days around 62-63 days, described as commendable, achieved on back of good collections.
Payment policy: 20% advance, 10% on GA drawing approval, balance ~60% prior to dispatch; most customers are B2B and understand payment terms since raw material must be paid for in advance.
Payables reflect use of LCs of 120 days, helping manage working capital and pull cash from operations.
Target is to bring receivable days down to 60 in FY27.

subsections.label: Capital allocation
points: IPO proceeds earmarked for Ghiloth and Mambattu expansion should take care of those; company has money in bank account which should take care mostly of the Gujarat capacity.
Total capex plan of close to INR150 crores in FY27 to ramp up capacities for fabricated steel and sandwich panel line.

subsections.label: Order book visibility & execution
points: Overall order book stands at INR1,117 crores (also referenced as INR1,127 crores in a later exchange), giving clear visibility of the next six to eight months.
Company is booking orders from some of the biggest companies in the country; Q1 expected to be a good quarter for order booking, which will give further clarity on total revenue guidance.

Entire order book of INR1,100+ crores is expected to be executed within FY27, as the business typically requires execution within six to nine months; only about 5-10% of order book faces delay risk due to EC not cleared or customer funding issues.
This quarter's order booking run rate is much better than last quarter; pending order book at end of quarter expected to look very strong.

subsections.label: Order booking run-rate & guidance confidence
points: Order booking is a project business, making a monthly average run rate difficult to guide — certain bigger projects take time to finalize but make up for the entire quarter when they close.
Order booking target for FY27 is INR2,000 crores, in line with 30% growth guidance in the Prefab division.
Management is 'doubly sure' of achieving the order booking and turnover targets given market, pipeline, experience and capacities being added.

30% growth guidance viewed as easily achievable and possibly exceedable, given current pipeline of inquiries, order book, and inflow of further capacities; historically company had grown at higher rates (35-40%) but 30% is the guided number to the market.

subsections.label: Pipeline dynamics
points: Total pipeline (short gestation + long gestation) is around INR5,000 crores, expected to close over next two to three quarters.
Pipeline is dynamic: some inquiries close, some get pushed to next quarter, some get lost, and new inquiries get added every quarter, so pipeline is continually replenished.

subsections.label: New-age sector demand drivers
points: Renewables, data centers, logistics and semiconductors are growth drivers; as of April 1, ~35-38% of order book was from these sectors.

Renewable companies have committed investments under PLI; last two years saw module/solar cell manufacturing facility builds, now inquiries are coming for wafer and ingot plants, which are typically bigger and heavier in tonnage — a good business opportunity.

Data centers have mainly used insulated sandwich panels (Rockwool panels) in the last two years, now widely accepted in market; company in discussion with at least three data center companies to also support the structural steel part of construction to expedite build.
Last year the company had no data center orders; this year it executed four data center orders, alongside focus on EV sector, driving growth from new customers.

subsections.label: Demand resilience amid war/disruption
points: When the war-related disruption started there was a little uncertainty, but over the last month companies have continued with capex plans as they view it as a short-term phenomenon and do not want to derail expansion commitments made to government (schemes) and customers.
No major disruption seen in the capex cycle; order inflow and pipeline remain strong.

subsections.label: Revenue split confirmation
points: Of INR1,525 crores total revenue, INR1,382 crores was from PEB business and rest INR131 crores from EPS panel and packaging business, confirmed by management.

subsections.label: Sandwich panel utilization & economics
points: Sandwich panel line at Mambattu underperformed potential in FY26, with capacity utilization low at around 25%; management candid about this miss.
Sales engine has been rebuilt, go-to-market strategy re-looked, new leadership in place, and sales team restructured with sharper market focus to drive utilization this year.

Order book of 4 lakh square meters (50% of line capacity) already booked, giving confidence of substantial utilization this year; management hopeful Mambattu plant utilization will be at least 75-80% this year.

This sandwich panel line is fully automated in terms of operating cost and 'very light'; overall revenue impact on the company won't be much — will add another INR70-90 crores; margin-wise slightly better than structural steel business but won't meaningfully move overall company margin.
Currently 75% of the 4 lakh sq meter sandwich panel order book is captive consumption (packaged with structures) and 25% is product sales to external customers.

Sandwich panels do not command a price premium per se, but give priority/preferred-vendor status for buildings requiring both insulated panels and structure, since customers otherwise face design coordination challenges across two vendors.

subsections.label: Margin bifurcation across segments
points: Bifurcating margin profile precisely across Prefab/sandwich panel/packaging is difficult; packaging business margin is about 100 bps better on EBITDA than the Prefab business (10-10.5% range).

Sandwich panel margin not guided separately since a lot of raw material used is common with Prefab structural steel; most projects are integrated with both structural steel and insulated panels, and company evaluates margin at the project level, not by component.

subsections.label: Regional revenue mix shift (West vs South)
points: Revenue/order book mix from the West has continuously declined even though the company has capacity planned there, because the company added capacity in the South a couple of years back and has been focusing there, while the West has been served from the North plant.
Order book share from West was ~30% in FY24-25 but declined to 17-18% in FY26.
Company has been subsidizing freight cost to serve West projects without a local plant; since demand in South is high, company does not want to subsidize freight there to the same extent.
Management denies losing market share in the West; presence remains strong (worked in every state over last 3 years); large orders booked from South make the South percentage look large.
West pipeline currently looks very strong; company will build order book from West until the West plant comes online, after which West's revenue share is expected to substantially grow.

subsections.label: Volume growth
points: PEB volume grew from 75,000-76,000 metric tons in FY25 to about 1,07,000-1,08,000 metric tons in FY26.
Targeting ~30% growth in volume/output in line with overall sales growth guidance for FY27.

subsections.label: Differentiation strategy
points: Management states there is typically no differentiation possible in the base product (steel is bought from the same vendors as competitors); main differentiation is in service, divided into design service and installation service.
Design service: three design centers with around 150 people working to optimize buildings — lighter structures that meet requirements and are aesthetically strong.

Installation service: company positions itself as an industry leader in fast execution, with a track record of delivering projects faster than the industry; holds a world record of constructing 1,51,000 square feet in just 6 days.
Overall differentiation stems from project communication, on-time delivery, quality and installation service across the project lifecycle.

subsections.label: Multi-story building opportunity
points: Multi-story/commercial buildings using pre-engineered building (PEB) solutions seen as a large market opportunity going forward given time-to-revenue benefits versus RCC construction and space constraints in dense cities.
Acceptability of PEB for multi-story buildings is currently penetrating the market, with consultants increasingly working on PEB solutions for multi-story buildings.
Company already executing a few multi-story building projects and plans to further penetrate this sector.

subsections.label: Capacity utilization trend
points: Prefab capacity utilization (structural steel fabrication) rose through the year: 58% in Q1, 77% in Q2, dipped to 67% in Q3, and hit 83% in Q4 — running close to full capacity by year end, justifying capital investment in new capacity.
14,000 tons of new capacity added in the last quarter has become operational from this month.
Based on demand trajectory, incremental capacity added/about to be added is expected to be absorbed significantly this year.

subsections.label: Three simultaneous capacity expansions
points: Mambattu brownfield line two has already been commissioned; second line is in execution phase and will be operational next quarter.

Ghiloth greenfield project in Noida/North India progressing well; commercial production from the new continuous sandwich panel line expected in Q3 (October-November), and will add ancillary/steel component capacity that was earlier outsourced (not another continuous line).

Gujarat greenfield project (Vithlapur) civil construction in full swing; Phase 1 will add close to 50,000 tons of PEB capacity to serve fast-growing industrial markets of Maharashtra and Gujarat; capacity planned by end of Q4 FY27, with utilization starting from next FY.
All three plants (three geographies) coming online in FY27, with total capex of close to INR150 crores planned this financial year to ramp up fabricated steel and sandwich panel line capacities.

Precedent: when a large-capacity facility was set up in the South previously, it was immediately taken up and capacity had to be increased within 18 months; management expects similar dynamics in Gujarat given it is one of the fastest-growing markets after South India.

subsections.label: Capacity economics
points: Peak capacity revenue potential: PEB (1,47,000 tons) plus sandwich panel capacity is about INR2,200-2,300 crores, plus EPS business of about INR200 crores, taking total peak-capacity revenue potential to about INR2,300-2,400 crores.
Industry benchmark: 70-75% capacity utilization is considered a great utilization level given quarter-to-quarter variability; Q4's 83-84% was described as peak.

Asset turn is in the range of 5x overall; excluding the EPS business (which has relatively high fixed assets), Prefab business asset turn is about 6x — noted as high not just for the company but for competitors as well.

Incremental 50,000-ton Gujarat capacity expected to generate INR500-600 crores of revenue at peak capacity, though ramp-up takes time as seen with earlier plants; generally, PEB capex of about INR100 crores can be expected to generate five to six times asset turn in revenue.

subsections.label: Export markets
points: Company has been tracking export opportunities for the last couple of years, monitoring how much export activity happens from India to other countries.

Currently doing projects in Bhutan and exporting to Nepal and neighboring countries; has executed two projects for Africa and is currently executing two more export projects for Africa; in discussion for four-five projects in Africa and a couple of projects in America.

Market size for America and Africa has not been considered great enough as of now for major focus; current plan is to expand more in India given the Indian market's promise (data centers, renewables, EV sector).
Focus on exports is not a priority right now but will be monitored and pursued as opportunities arise; export foothold will increase once management feels the market is big enough.

subsections.label: West India regional strategy
points: Order book share from West has declined from ~30% in FY24-25 to 17-18% in FY26 because capacity has been in the South, and West has been served from the North plant with subsidized freight.

Company plans to set up a plant in the West (Gujarat) to reduce reliance on freight subsidization and capture more of the fast-growing Maharashtra/Gujarat market; expects West's revenue share to substantially grow once the Gujarat plant comes online this year.
Company maintains it has not lost market share in the West and has strong presence across the country, having worked in every state over the last 3 years.

subsections.label: Raw material sourcing & input costs
points: Majority of purchases are domestic; steel is the primary raw material, so there is no extra input cost tied to imports/exports from the geopolitical conflict.
Domestic steel prices have increased due to minimum import barrier duty; company discussed with customers and most understood the situation and granted price increases.
Company holds inventory of 32,000 tons which will cover the entire current quarter, though that inventory is not priced at contract-fixed levels, implying some near-term margin impact.

subsections.label: Working capital management
points: Receivable/debtor days managed at 62-63 days, attributed to good collections; policy of 20% advance, 10% on GA drawing approval, 60% balance prior to dispatch helps manage cash.
Payables reflect use of LCs with 120-day terms, helping the company manage daily working capital and driving strong operating cash flow (INR135 crores, ~85% of EBITDA).

subsections.label: Competitive positioning
points: Industry has three to four large players with good capacity, limiting ability to command a huge margin due to competition; more important for the company to utilize capacity and target growth than to chase margin at this moment.
Company's differentiation vs competition is service-based (design + installation), not product-based, since steel input is sourced from the same vendors as competitors.
Company is a preferred vendor for buildings needing both structure and insulated sandwich panels, solving the design-coordination problem customers otherwise face across two separate vendors.

subsections.label: Customer mix and repeat business
points: Repeat orders from existing customers are 35-40% of order book, driven by focus on new-age sectors; balance comes from new customers being added, e.g., four data center orders executed this year (versus zero last year) and growing EV sector customers.

subsections.label: Reasons customers choose EPACK
points: Speed of execution is the primary reason new-age players (renewables, data centers, semiconductors) choose EPACK — Prefab construction is at least 60% faster than conventional RCC, and EPACK's overall execution ability is faster than peers.

subsections.label: Steel price / anti-dumping duty impact
points: Steel prices increased tremendously in Q4 due to minimum import barrier duty being imposed, impacting margins by 70-80 bps since many contracts are fixed price.
Company managed to get price increment from most customers (80%+ of contracts) as they understood this was due to tax/duty changes, not a normal cost increase.
Some Q1 impact expected to carry over from the steel price spike, but Q2 not expected to see major challenge; inventory of 32,000 tons will cushion the quarter but at different cost basis.
Price pass-through to customers has not been 100% — some customers accepted full pass-through, others accepted lesser pass-through; overall a good amount of price increase has been achieved.

subsections.label: Geopolitical / war-related disruption
points: War-related disruption caused a little uncertainty in demand initially, but companies have continued with capex plans over the last month as they view the disruption as short-term and do not want to derail commitments made to government schemes and customers.
No major disruption seen in the capex cycle or in order inflow/pipeline as of the call date.
No additional input cost from imports due to the conflict since the majority of raw material (steel) purchase is domestic.

subsections.label: Sandwich panel line underperformance
points: Sandwich panel line at Mambattu underperformed potential in FY26 with utilization at only around 25%; management candidly acknowledged the miss and has rebuilt the sales engine, go-to-market strategy, leadership and sales team structure to address it.

subsections.label: Order book execution risk
points: About 5-10% of the order book can face delays due to environmental clearance (EC) not being cleared or customer funding issues.

subsections.label: FY27 outlook
points: Prefab division guided towards 30% growth, translating to revenue of around INR1,920-1,950 crores (also stated as INR1,925-1,950 crores) for FY27.
Order book target of INR2,000 crores plus for FY27, in line with 30% growth in order booking.

Margins guided to remain 10%+ throughout the year, in the range-bound 10.5%-11.5% band that has been the long-standing guidance; some quarter-to-quarter variation possible (e.g., Q1 impact) but pan-India annualized basis margin maintained.
Company believes the 30% guidance is conservative and easily achievable/exceedable given current pipeline, inquiries, order book and capacity inflows, despite historical growth rates of 35-40%.
PAT margin expected to rise to around 6.5% (from 6.1% in FY26) aided by ~20-25 bps reduction in finance cost as debt repayment impact fully plays out.

Multi-year outlook (3-4 years): management expects continued growth at a rate that beats industry average, supported by ongoing capacity additions (Gujarat, sandwich panel line in Mambattu), promising new-age sectors, multi-story building and data center markets.

subsections.label: Capacity-linked guidance
points: PEB capacity to increase from 1,47,000 tons currently to about 1,70,000 tons after Mambattu second line and Ghiloth additions, reaching ~2,20,000 metric tons by end FY27 with Gujarat capacity included.
Sandwich panel capacity to increase from 13,10,000 sq meters currently to about 21,10,000 sq meters by end FY27 (Ghiloth addition of 8 lakh sq meters by end Q3 FY27).
Mambattu capacity to reach ~96,000 tons by end FY27 (from current 82,000 tons).

themes.label: Capacity expansion

themes.label: Steel input cost inflation

themes.label: Cash generation & deleveraging

themes.label: Growth guidance
themes.note: Prefab division guided to 30% revenue growth and INR2,000+ crores order booking target for FY27, with management confident of achieving/exceeding this.

themes.label: Geographic mix shift (West market)
themes.note: West India order book share declined from ~30% to 17-18% due to lack of local capacity; Gujarat plant expected to reverse this trend.

key_takeaways: So we said we will deliver, and we have delivered. FY26 was our first year, or rather first full year as a listed company, and revenue is up by 35% at INR1,525 crores. EBITDA margins have expanded. PAT is up by 56%. We have paid down around INR107 crores of debt.
We have generated around INR135 crores of free operating cash flow last year, which is approximately 85% of our EBITDA converting into cash.
Our prefab capacity utilization: 58% in Q1, 77% in Q2, 67% in Q3, and 83% in Q4 — running close to full capacity by the end of the year.
We have already added 14,000 tons of capacity in the last quarter, which has become operational from this month onwards.
Our sandwich panel line that we put up last year in Mambattu did not perform to its potential. The capacity utilization was low at around 25%.
Our Prefab division is guiding us towards a 30% growth. Our overall order book stands at INR1,117 crores today, giving us a clear visibility of the next six to eight months.
We are compounded at 36% for the last consecutive five years.
Margins have always been guided to be range bound between 10.5% to 11.5% and we could achieve 10.5% last year. FY27 also our guidance is the same, it will be at least 10% plus throughout the year.

Is the 30% guidance given based on some conservative guidance or because we were all these years growing North of 40% or maybe more than 30% at least 35% to 40%?

HINDOILEXP.about: Hindustan Oil Exploration Company Limited was incorporated in 1983, It is engaged in the exploration, development and production of crude oil and natural gas in India, both onshore and offshore. The company is India's first private E&P company and its assets are geographically spread across Tamil Nadu, Maharashtra, Gujarat, Assam and Arunachal Pradesh (both offshore and onshore). [1][2][3]

quarters.summary: Management flagged continued operational challenges at B-80 (higher water cut, subsea well interventions planned) and PY-1 (production loss, rig-less intervention underway), alongside progress on Assam (Dirok) pipeline evacuation constraint (common carrier status, hot-tapping expected by December 2026) and Kharsang (doubled production, second workover phase and gas pipeline route survey underway). The company is raising debt to fund the B-80 workover/drilling campaign while relying on internal accruals for Kharsang and PY-1, with cash flow expected to improve materially once Dirok gas flows post-December 2026 and B-80 wells are worked over/drilled through FY27.

subsections.label: Revenue drivers
points: Improvement in current quarter revenue was driven by higher production from the Kharsang field (mainly crude) and favorable Brent prices, augmented by commencement of liquidation of B-80 crude, although at a slower than expected pace.
Previous quarter's negative standalone revenue was due to reversal of the HPCL sale of INR259 crores.

subsections.label: Profitability drivers
points: Standalone PBT decline vs previous quarter mainly due to offset to cost from higher inventory of crude in the previous quarter; previous quarter's HPCL sale reversal resulted in a lower cost offset to overall operating cost.
Movement of profitability needs to be viewed in context of the quarter's cost structure, mainly the impact of changes in inventory of crude stored in tankers and not sold till the appropriate time.

subsections.label: Other income composition
points: Standalone other income includes release of a long-due escrow balance pertaining to cost recovery (~INR8 crores), income from an admitted insurance claim (INR2 crores), and top-up of the Adbhoot acquisition as at March (~INR2.3 crores).

subsections.label: Inventory mark-to-market / HPCL crude loss
points: Company has sold roughly 15% of the HPCL-stored crude so far, incurring losses in the range of INR4-6 crores depending on Brent price movements.
Management estimates a further 7-10% loss on the remainder but cautioned this should not be taken as guidance.
CFO declined to quantify EBITDA excluding inventory/profit-petroleum/sale adjustments, citing technical complexity, and said he would revert.

subsections.label: Capital allocation and funding
points: Focus ahead is cost reduction and cash management to maximize the potential of existing reserves.

Company is raising debt in the market to fund the B-80 workover and three-well drilling program, as capex budget has increased (contingency-driven, not full spend commitment) given short supply of rigs and rising oil prices.

Own cash flows will improve after workovers, funding part of the program internally; company is talking to investors and banks to raise funds to execute workover and three wells unhindered from a cash position.
Kharsang program and PY-1 rig-less intervention are being funded from internal accruals (self-funding), while B-80 program depends on external debt raise.
By November/December 2027, cash flows expected to be sufficient to fund growth for B-15; further blocks would require separate funding decisions.

subsections.label: B-80 (offshore, flagship asset)
points: Production during the quarter was impacted by higher water cut from one producing well, resulting in lower output; water cut continued to increase despite prior work-over plans, but production continues.
Compressor train configuration on the MOPU platform changed to operate with lower suction pressure, allowing wells to flow more even as flowing pressure decreases; currently in test mode.

Workover of two existing wells (D1 and D2) on track; in discussion with rig for final award this month, mobilization by October, at which point water zones will be shut off and new oil/gas zones opened to increase production.
Meaningful progress made on resolving the HPCL issue, though offtake by road has faced delays; crude continues to be resold to third parties.

Production never fully shut during monsoon, though asset integrity work was needed in the splash zone on one well due to severe corrosion; compression reconfigured from parallel to series to suck at lower suction pressure allowing partial production; expected to reach full production by end of month.

Drilling campaign: two workovers (10-20 days each) followed by three new wells (30-40 days each), targeting completion towards end of March/early April 2027, followed by installation of a jacket and production deck before starting production.
Plan: two worked-over wells on production by November/December 2026; three new wells on production by June 2027, subject to offshore risks like stuck tubing causing delays.

Confidence in production improvement stems from rig-based intervention allowing complete water zone shut-off (vs. prior chemical treatments with mixed results) and re-perforation of new producing strata, feasible only via rig on subsea completion wells.
Workover expected to yield 500-800 barrels per well and 3-5 million standard cubic feet per day per well.

New wells expected to deliver 1,000-1,500 barrels per well based on reservoir simulation, though actual could range 700-1,400; drilling sequence is first well, test, then second, then third, informed by logging for oil/gas saturation.

HPCL crude inventory (~1,18,000+ barrels on FSO) expected to be sold starting October, in tranches of ~120,000-150,000 barrels using smaller tankers to avoid demurrage charges on larger tankers; expectation that entire inventory will clear from HPCL's Chembur refinery by end of October/early November.

Tamil Nadu protests reported regarding drilling of two wells near allocation area; fields are approved by MOPNG (central government is final arbiter); state government kept informed and shown approvals; management hopeful issue will not escalate.

HPCL dispute: agreement already signed to reverse the sale; HPCL has been cooperative, created additional gantries for offtake; matter to go through conciliation process with a High Court Chief Justice appointed; management wants an amicable resolution given long-term partnership, will not renege on agreed terms despite potential Brent-driven losses.

subsections.label: B-15 (new block)
points: FDP under preparation; evaluating three to four concepts, including connecting to existing ONGC platform to reduce capital costs.
Drilling planned for FY28; reserve levels (16 MMBOE) to be reappraised after further processing and the first well, with hopeful upside.

subsections.label: PY-1 (East Coast)
points: Three wells on the platform suffered serious production loss; contract awarded for rig-less intervention to increase production from existing wells before drilling two new wells.

Drilling of two new wells (previously planned for Q4 next year) is now contingent upon gas buyers (IOCL/GAIL) committing to lift gas, to avoid repeating the historical scenario where wells were shut for lack of buyers and became watered out.

Management intends to secure a take-or-pay agreement with GAIL or IOCL before spudding new wells; in the interim, rig-less completion is being used to increase production, funded from internal accruals.

Historical context: PY-1 wells came on 15 years ago with 50 million standard cubic feet/day from three wells, among the best in Bombay offshore, but were shut due to lack of buyers, and water overwhelmed the gas zones in the basement reservoir; PetroVietnam re-analysis suggests two new wells could still deliver 15-20 million standard cubic feet/day.
Drilling of new PY-1 wells depends on firm gas sales agreement; rig-less intervention on existing wells continues as short-term measure funded from own books.

subsections.label: Dirok (Assam, onshore)
points: HOEC is operator with ~27% stake; reservoir extremely prosperous, with 3,000 PSI header pressure from six wells, but only 50-70% of well capability is produced due to lack of evacuation route.

PNGRB has made the DNPL pipeline (operated by AGCL) a common carrier (previously captive to NRL/Oil India); some pipeline sections had degraded, reducing overall capacity; new pipeline sections have been laid alongside degraded sections requiring hot-tap tie-back.

Hot tapping intended to restore full capacity from current degraded 1-1.5 MMSCMD to 2.5 million standard cubic meters/day; work being done by Assam Gas Company Limited (AGCL), with HOEC providing technical support in discussions.

Expected completion of hot taps and pipeline capacity restoration by December 2026; a 100-200 meter pipeline section within NRL premises also needs to be laid to connect DNPL to the gas grid, though this is considered a minor task compared to the hot-tap critical path.

Confidence in December timeline driven by stakeholder alignment amid national energy security push; hot tapping avoids need for a 7-15 day NRL refinery shutdown (previously required to depressurize and flush the pipeline), which had been a bottleneck; floods in Assam caused some disruption/delay to tender timelines, but conditions are normalizing.

DNPL pipeline maximum pressure containment capacity is 90 bars, yielding 2.5 MMSCMD; currently operating at 40-50 bars due to degradation, yielding 1-1.3 MMSCMD; full capacity restoration expected once degraded sections are isolated and new sections tied in.

NRL has also been made a re-seller, and with DNPL as a common carrier, NRL can sell HOEC's gas on the exchange (similar to B-80 in Bombay offshore) without requiring a firm buyer; management expects ramp-up could occur within days of pipeline capacity coming online, given the exchange-based route.

Company's locked-in gross Dirok gas volumes are 0.5-0.7 MMSCMD; pipeline capacity increase from ~1.1 MMSCMD to 2.5 MMSCMD could allow additional 50-60 million standard cubic feet/day to flow; management expects to be able to sell all well-stock gas once pipeline capacity is online.

subsections.label: Kharsang (onshore)
points: Nine-well program successfully completed, doubling production versus last year.
Continued workover of previously non-producing wells (23 additional wells identified); five to six workovers completed so far, incrementally increasing production.
Preparing for second phase of nine wells; rig identified, award imminent, tubulars being ordered (expected in one to two months) ahead of second drilling phase.

Virgin gas found in two wells, but monetization delayed due to lack of pipeline; pipeline route survey tender out, closing the next day, to commission a 24km pipeline tying into Oil India's existing pipeline at Bordumsa (which connects onward to NRL and the national gas grid).

Regulatory clearance challenge as pipeline route passes through forest area; management confident of navigating this given assurances to environmental/forest officials; expects pipeline laying to start in six to eight months.

Right-of-way approval process: six to eight months expected for approval, followed by another six to eight months to lay the 24km pipeline; ideal-case target is pipeline completion by December 2027 (14-18 months given difficult terrain, forest areas, highway/river crossings).
Oil currently sold to Digboi Refinery and various buyers, mostly IOCL.

subsections.label: Cambay Basin (Gujarat) — Asjol, Balol, Palej
points: New belt technology implemented at Balol (in trial phase) — a belt mechanism that goes down, soaks up oil, and is squeezed to extract oil.
Palej facility debottlenecked using thermionic heaters and similar measures to increase production.
Palej has significant potential requiring additional new wells; sucker rod pumps have been ordered.
New exploration block near Palej field in final stages of approval; new exploratory wells planned once approved.

subsections.label: Crude storage and offtake logistics
points: HPCL-stored B-80 crude offtake has been slower than expected by road; entire crude inventory expected to clear from HPCL's Chembur refinery by end of October/early November.
Smaller tankers being used in October to sell crude to avoid demurrage charges associated with larger tankers when volumes are insufficient to fill them fully.

subsections.label: Adbhoot acquisition
points: Adbhoot acquisition top-up of approximately INR2.3 crores recorded as at March 2026, included within standalone other income.

subsections.label: Samudra Manthan scheme evaluation
points: Samudra Manthan scheme (government support scheme) is essentially targeted at deepwater assets; HOEC operates in shallow water, so eligibility for support is still under evaluation.

subsections.label: Operational and reservoir risks
points: B-80: higher water cut at one producing well causing lower output; offshore subsea well interventions carry inherent risk of delays (e.g., stuck tubing).
PY-1: serious production loss across three wells; drilling of new wells contingent on securing gas buyer commitments (take-or-pay) to avoid repeat of historical well-shutdown/water-out scenario.
Reservoir uncertainty remains inherent given wells are ~4 kilometers below the mud line; production ranges given (e.g., 8,900-13,000 barrels/day) reflect this uncertainty.
Rig availability in short supply as oil prices rise and everyone seeks to drill, contributing to capex contingency increases.

subsections.label: Financing and funding risk
points: B-80 program funding depends on successful debt raise from the market; failure to secure funds could pose a challenge, though some funding will come from internal accruals.
Capex budget increase from Q4 presentation reflects contingency planning (facility to draw down as needed), not a firm commitment to spend the full amount.

subsections.label: HPCL dispute risk
points: HPCL crude inventory sale is subject to Brent price fluctuation risk; company already booked INR4-6 crores in losses on ~15% sold and expects a further 7-10% loss on the remainder (not guidance).

Matter is in a conciliation process with a High Court Chief Justice appointed; management seeks amicable resolution to preserve long-term relationship with HPCL rather than pursue full liability recovery.

subsections.label: Regulatory / social risk
points: Protests reported in Tamil Nadu regarding drilling of two wells related to area allocation; company has engaged with state government and shown approvals, though final drilling authority rests with central government (MOPNG).

subsections.label: Evacuation infrastructure risk
points: Dirok gas monetization has been delayed for approximately two years due to pipeline evacuation constraints; hot-tap completion timeline (December 2026) depends on external parties (AGCL, NRL) and has already faced delays from floods in Assam.
Kharsang gas monetization delayed due to lack of pipeline; pipeline route survey faces regulatory clearance challenges as the route passes through forest area.

subsections.label: Historical execution risk
points: An analyst noted that production has drastically reduced from 2024 levels despite repeated statements about future increases; management acknowledged the HPCL invoice stuck-up (~INR260 crores plus interest, ~INR300 crores total) as a key reason for delay, which otherwise would have allowed workovers in November of last year.
Globally, $400 billion is spent every year just to keep production at a plateau (not decline, not growth) — underscoring the scale of continuous investment required in the sector.

subsections.label: Overall Outlook
points: Management reiterated confidence in long-term fundamentals of the sector supported by country's 7-8% growth driving energy demand, despite short-term operational challenges across the portfolio.
Focus remains on operational execution, production optimization, and development projects while maintaining strict capital allocation discipline.

Priority order for capital: Kharsang (self-funding) and PY-1 rig-less intervention (funded from own books) are not major funding concerns; B-80 is dependent on external debt raise, making it the key funding risk factor.
Company reiterated it is 'not resting at B-80' and will move to B-15 once B-80 program is delivered; overall cash flow situation expected to improve significantly once Dirok is fully on stream.

themes.label: Production ramp-up / growth trajectory
themes.note: Kharsang production doubled YoY and Cambay Basin targeting 20-30% increase, but B-80 and PY-1 continue to face short-term operational setbacks (water cut, production loss) delaying the path to targeted volumes.

themes.label: Pipeline evacuation constraint
themes.note: DNPL made a common carrier with hot-tapping expected to restore Dirok pipeline capacity to 2.5 MMSCMD by December 2026; Kharsang gas monetization also pipeline-constrained with a new 24km line under route survey.

themes.label: HPCL crude sale dispute
themes.note: Offtake continues with third parties amid a cordial but unresolved conciliation process; ~15% of crude sold with INR4-6 crores loss booked and further 7-10% loss estimated on the remainder.

themes.label: Reserve base and asset quality
themes.note: B-80 2P reserves of 26 million barrels (only 1.5-2 million produced so far) and B-15 reserves of 16 MMBOE support continued development; Dirok reservoir prospectivity highlighted by high header pressure.

themes.label: Rig availability and cost inflation
themes.note: Rigs in short supply as oil prices rise, contributing to an increased capex contingency budget for B-80.

themes.label: Capital discipline and funding
themes.note: Company relying on internal accruals for Kharsang and PY-1 while raising debt from market/banks for the B-80 program; gearing remains low at 0.04 with only INR20 crores of bank debt currently.

themes.label: Regulatory and stakeholder alignment
themes.note: National energy security push has driven stakeholder alignment on PNGRB common-carrier status and hot-tapping for DNPL, though Tamil Nadu drilling protests present a new localized regulatory friction point.

key_takeaways: The quarter unfolded against a backdrop of continued focus on energy security, with domestic hydrocarbon production and infrastructure development across the oil and gas sector being a heavy lift for the country.

At B-80, production during the quarter was impacted by a higher water cut from one of the producing wells resulting in lower output; compressor train configuration on the MOPU has been changed to sustain production and is in test mode.
Workover of two existing wells (D1 and D2) at B-80 remains on track, with rig award discussions this month and mobilization by October.

Meaningful progress made on resolving the HPCL issue, though offtake by road faced delays; crude continues to be resold to third parties, with entire inventory expected to clear by end of October/early November.
At Dirok, PNGRB has made the DNPL line a common carrier, and hot-tapping work by Assam Gas Company Limited is expected to restore pipeline capacity from ~1-1.5 MMSCMD to 2.5 MMSCMD by December 2026.

Kharsang successfully completed a nine-well program, doubling production from last year, with a second phase of nine wells being prepared; virgin gas found in two wells but monetization delayed pending a new 24km pipeline.
In Cambay Basin, new belt technology trial at Balol and debottlenecking at Palej are expected to drive a 20-30% production increase going forward, following a 5-6% increase last quarter.

Consolidated revenue from operations for the quarter was INR124 crores, with net consolidated revenue at INR114.17 crores after profit petroleum and revenue sharing; consolidated PBT before exceptional items was INR6.5 crores.
pressing_questions: What is the current status and expected timeline for the Northeast grid connectivity that Dirok depends on? Is the pipeline interconnection actually complete now, and once ready, by when is Dirok production expected to ramp to decent levels?
What is the view on B-80 currently — how is production and monetization progressing given the HPCL dispute, and when is the issue expected to be resolved?
How much was the impact on the P&L because of mark-to-market losses on the inventory being held, and what would EBITDA have been excluding these adjustments?
What is giving confidence now on the Assam grid connectivity after a long history of delays over the last two years, and what are the actual risks involved with the connectivity?
What gives confidence that B-80 is structurally fixable this time, given past re-working attempts (chemicals, equipment) have not worked historically?
Why has the capex budget increased from the Q4 presentation — is it due to escalating costs or incremental opportunities?

Given production has drastically reduced from 2024 levels despite repeated statements about future increases over the last three years, how can investors trust the stated target of 11,000 barrels per day by June 2027?
If HPCL's agreement is on an as-is basis and Brent price has fallen causing a loss, why isn't this liability being passed on to HPCL rather than the company absorbing it?
Realistically, given the funding crunch, how firm is the plan for drilling wells in Kharsang and PY-1, and which field will take priority if B-80 workovers don't deliver expected output by Q3?
Post-Dirok ramp-up, would it be fair to assume all cash flow constraints will be over by the end of the financial year?

quarters.summary: HOEC frames FY26 as a challenging but transformational base year, with an active pipeline of ~20 wells in various stages of preparation across offshore and onshore assets. Management targets production growth from current ~1.5 thousand BOE/day (with 0.4–0.7 thousand BOE locked in due to infrastructure constraints) to 10,000–11,000 barrels by June 2027, 22,000 barrels by 2028, and 32,000 BOE by 2029, funded via internal accruals and bank facilities under strict capital discipline; detailed FY27/FY28 debt and EBITDA guidance deferred to next quarter, and HPCL crude realization/conciliation and Dirok pipeline connectivity are expected to resolve within 1-3 months to 2-3 years depending on the item.

subsections.label: P&L drivers
points: Consolidated P&L reflects income and operations of the entire group; performance impacted by decrease in production and the acquisition of producing properties (40% share) from Adbhoot.
Net income is lower mainly because of the impact of the HPCL sale reversal.
Balance sheet growth is steady, reflecting the increase in producing properties from the Adbhoot acquisition and the increase in B-80 participating interest.
Everything else defined mostly by lower production this year.
Standalone results show cost base continues to be strong, evidenced by lifting cost broadly stable YoY.

Exceptional item of INR32 crores booked as a fair value/valuation gain (non-cash) resulting from Ind AS requirement to fair value the entire stake upon business combination (Adbhoot 40% acquisition); netting off of estimated field value and JV outstanding in the books.

subsections.label: HPCL crude sale/inventory issue
points: HPCL sale was reversed (invoice canceled, credit note issued); crude mutually agreed between parties and resold to third-party buyers while still physically stored at HPCL.
Sale proceeds will come in over 2-3 months, not in one go; weekly truck pickups of 300-700 tons, with advance payment received per pickup.

Pricing initially firm for a few weeks, then linked to Brent minus a discount (Brent minus X%); realization is near what was originally sold to HPCL, with buyers bearing additional costs such as higher diesel costs.
Buyers took crude samples and analyzed via third parties; crude picked up on an as-is-where-is basis without further processing by HOEC or HPCL.
Inventory valuation methodology used a discount to Brent factoring in a downside risk; management believes this protects against loss.
No further commercial interaction/compensation issue with HPCL currently; matter to go through a conciliation process per COSA, outcome awaited over next few months.
Q4 consol PAT of INR9 crores included INR14 crores from derecognition of HPCL revenue linked to inventory valuation; without that, Q4 would have shown a loss despite higher prices.

subsections.label: Capital allocation / funding
points: Funding for growth pipeline planned via internal accruals and bank facilities/debt raise from institutions and banks, underpinned by strong capital discipline to avoid unnecessarily diluting gearing ratios.
Operations largely funded by internal cash generation to date; limited capex funded internally; plans to access bank loans/facilities going forward to advance drilling program.
Equity fund raise not confirmed; management stated it will do whatever makes commercial sense for management, Board and shareholders, but declined to elaborate further at this stage.

FSO/tanker crude storage: technical (not commercial) constraint on selling smaller parcels — smaller cargo pickups may incur demurrage on daughter tankers; ~100,000-150,000 barrels considered a good parcel size to sell; currently at ~150,000+ barrels and looking at options to sell even now, subject to finding right buyers and vessels.

subsections.label: National gas demand context
points: Huge national requirement/necessity to capture every molecule of gas that can be produced to meet shortfall, driving collaborative efforts among HOEC, Oil India, NRL, Assam Gas Company, PNGRB to unlock stranded production.

key_figures.label: Locked-in production due to infrastructure constraints

subsections.label: B-80
points: Flagship offshore oil development block with substantial remaining reserves (26 million BOE 2P, only ~1 million produced so far).

Plans: workovers on 2 existing subsea wells, production optimization via facility configuration changes to reduce suction/backpressure and enable more gas/oil flow, additional development drilling, reservoir management improvements, and facility debottlenecking.
Workover delayed from last quarter due to financial constraints (INR260 crores tied up in invoices for crude sales); to be taken up post-monsoon.
3 more wells planned to drill; facilities (MOPU) and tanker already have sufficient capacity to handle additional gas and oil.
Target: liquidate entire B-80 work program (3 wells + 2 workovers) by June of next year, dependent on weather (drilling window from November), funding, and rig availability.
Zero contamination established from the wells based on biweekly/weekly sampling over recent months; second part of contamination question (during transit) not addressed.
Offers significant operational leverage as core infrastructure is already in place; may support B-15 development by evaluating bringing B-15 crude to B-80.

subsections.label: B-15
points: Newly awarded block; company has begun FDP maturation quickly, evaluating 2-3 development concepts before finalizing one via stage-gate process (identify, assess, select, define, execute).
After concept selection, FEED will take a few months, followed by FID and execution; long-lead procurement and reservoir modeling underway in parallel.
3 to 5 wells may be needed to develop in-place reserves of 15 million BOE (concept stage); target production of 4,000-5,000 barrels and ~10 million SCF of gas.
Located 50-60 km from existing B-80 facility; options being evaluated include tying back to B-80 facility or building separate export line.

subsections.label: PY-1
points: Long-standing (nearly 2 decades) development project; originally produced 45-50 million SCF/day before offtake issues arose.
Has offshore platform facility, 55-km subsea line to onshore facility, onshore gas processing infrastructure, and significant redevelopment potential.
Plan: drill new wells, reservoir activation, production optimization to restore meaningful gas production.
Benchmarked against PetroVietnam's White Tiger field (similar basement reservoir, once producing 100,000 barrels) for remaining potential assessment; results were positive.
Campaign: 2 firm wells, 1 exploration well, and 1 additional well depending on first 2 results (total 4 wells, one straddling exploration/appraisal).

subsections.label: Dirok (Assam)
points: High-focus area amid national gas shortfall; strong reservoir quality with 3 zones (Girujan, Tipam, Barail) and untapped potential.
Wells have been choked back since COVID-era shutdowns; short-notice opportunity exists to ramp production back up.

Plan to drill 3 more wells to raise potential from 45 to higher; further upside from North Dirok exploration well (potential 10-15 million SCF, to be confirmed post-drilling) and Greater Dirok (100% HOEC-owned, additional wells planned).

Overall Dirok potential could triple from the existing 45 million SCF/day gross if all wells drilled at right time, contingent on pipeline evacuation network completion (DFL-Duliajan line, 2-3 years out).
Gas production carries associated condensate liquids; volumes to scale with gas production increase.

subsections.label: Kharsang
points: One of the largest medium-term growth opportunities in the portfolio; production has doubled after drilling 9 wells; found oil.
Unexpected large gas volumes discovered (commercial surprise), requiring evacuation planning.
Plan to drill 9 more wells to double production again.

subsections.label: Greater Dirok and Umatara
points: Important exploration and appraisal upside areas.
Objective: disciplined exploration focused on commerciality, infrastructure-led monetization, and capital-efficient development pathways given remote location.

subsections.label: Cambay (Gujarat)
points: Legacy assets (company started operations in Gujarat ~40 years ago).
Focus areas: revisiting development philosophies, workovers, production enhancement, secondary recovery, and low-cost incremental production growth.

subsections.label: Reserves
points: 1P (P90) ~40 million BOE, 2P (P50) 60 million BOE, 3P (P10) ~109 million BOE (over 100 MMBOE cited earlier).
Reserves certified by independent global agencies.

Value creation levers: better reservoir management, history matching, infill drilling in areas of accumulated reserves, 'produce the limits' workshops to optimize existing wells, and infrastructure enhancement.

subsections.label: Drilling & rig plans
points: Two rigs planned to drill on B-80 and PY-1 simultaneously (with possible overlap) to avoid costly mobilization/demobilization delays.
PY-1: 2 wells + 1 coiled tubing intervention planned by one rig.
B-80: 2 workovers + 3 interventions/wells planned by another rig.
Timeline could slip from March to May due to rig tow insurance expiry constraints; management targets completion of B-80 program (3 wells, 2 workovers) by May of next year.
No plans currently to purchase a rig (e.g., ONGC tender) as owning a rig only makes commercial sense with continuous, high well-count usage; company will continue to hire rigs as needed.
Workover risk: uncertainty over reusability of existing subsea Christmas trees; contingency plans (Plan A/B/C) being prepared including backup subsea trees.

subsections.label: Pipeline infrastructure (Assam/Dirok)
points: DNPL line (16-inch x 192 km) currently flows ~1 million (gas units); has capacity to go up to 2.5 million; working with Assam Gas Company, NRL, and Oil India to utilize additional capacity.
A 55-km patch of the DNPL line needed replacement due to asset integrity issues (pipe thinning); new pipeline segment has been laid but needs to be connected back to the main line.
Connection requires either a full NRL shutdown to purge and cut/connect the line, or alternative methods being explored to avoid shutdown; expected resolution in 1-2 months.

NRL may not be ready to use its full expanded capacity immediately; a short 300-400m connector line to link IGGL to NEGG (National Gas Grid) is being worked on by NRL, which could allow NRL to become a reseller of surplus gas.
DFL-to-Duliajan line (24-inch, 175 km) needed to unlock full pipeline capacity for incremental 35 million SCF from Dirok wells; expected in 2-3 years.

Alignment among all stakeholders (PNGRB, NRL, Oil India, Assam Gas Company, other operators) to fast-track evacuation solutions given national gas shortage; ownership of pipeline is being treated as secondary to getting molecules to market.

Oil India has publicly indicated DNPL may not become a common carrier and only Oil India gas would flow through; HOEC is pushing for shared use of any ullage/spare capacity in the pipeline regardless of ownership.

subsections.label: Asset geography
points: Portfolio spans India's key hydrocarbon basins: offshore assets (B-80, B-15), onshore Assam assets (Dirok, Greater Dirok, Umatara, Kharsang), PY-1 (offshore with onshore processing tie-in), and Cambay (Gujarat) legacy assets.

subsections.label: Operational cost pressures
points: Rising global energy market costs, especially diesel and other offshore-operations commodities, increasing cost of running operations.
Rig availability constrained as high oil prices lead everyone to want to drill as much as possible, creating short supply of rigs.
Diesel shortage affecting crude buyers' ability to transport/collect crude quickly from HPCL storage (long queues, e.g., 6-7 km long queues for diesel), slowing realization pace of crude sales.
Crude storage/logistics: buyers arranging vessels/tankers to pick up crude from HPCL storage; smaller parcel sizes incur demurrage risk for daughter tankers.

subsections.label: Leadership strengthening
points: New CFO Allen Joseph Andrade: 40 years experience across British Gas and Shell India, deep expertise in oil & gas joint ventures.
New Head of Offshore Operations Sanjay Kundu: 30 years experience spanning Shell and BG across UK and India, including offshore operations.
New Principal Reservoir Consultant Parthasarathy Bandopadhyay: 30 years experience across India, British Gas, PTTEP in Thailand, Total, and World Bank.
Continuing CTO Krishnan Raghavan with extensive global and HOEC-specific (Eastern and Western blocks) experience.

Corporate structure: HOEC (consolidated and standalone entity holding PSC participating interests) has two 100% subsidiaries — Hindage (owns vessel storing oil) and Geopetrol International Inc. (owns Geopetrol Mauritius Limited, which owns GeoEnpro Petroleum Limited, holding a participating interest in Kharsang).

subsections.label: Adbhoot acquisition
points: Acquired 40% share of producing properties from Adbhoot during the year, impacting balance sheet (increase in producing properties) and P&L (exceptional non-cash fair value gain of INR32 crores under Ind AS business combination accounting).

subsections.label: Strategic priorities
points: Maximize value from existing producing assets (low-hanging fruit) and accelerate monetization of discovered resources.
Improve operational efficiency through technology and disciplined execution; capital efficiency is key.
Embed a high-performance execution culture underpinned by strong governance, uncompromising safety standards, and disciplined capital allocation.
Preserve value (higher facility uptimes) and increase value across the portfolio.

subsections.label: Operational & commercial challenges (FY26)
points: Delays in certain monetization initiatives (drilling, workovers) driven partly by inability to complete commercial settlement on crude sales (HPCL issue).
Infrastructure constraints, especially in the East (Assam pipeline evacuation bottleneck).
Global energy market cost inflation, particularly diesel and other offshore operating commodities, raising cost of operations and rig costs.
Rig availability shortage due to high oil prices driving industry-wide drilling demand.
B-80 workover delayed due to financial constraint (INR260 crores tied up in invoices for crude sales).

subsections.label: HPCL dispute
points: HPCL crude sale invoice reversed; conciliation process required per COSA terms to formally close the dispute; outcome and potential compensation implications not yet determined.
Realization pace of resold crude slowed by diesel shortage affecting buyer logistics/trucking capacity.
Uncertainty on whether final realization results in a loss or breakeven versus March 31 inventory valuation, to be clarified after 2-3 months of sales.

subsections.label: Pipeline/evacuation dependency risk
points: Dirok and Greater Dirok production growth entirely dependent on third-party-owned pipeline infrastructure (Assam Gas Company/DNPL/NRL/Oil India), with no guarantee on allocation of capacity or timeline certainty.
Oil India public comments suggest DNPL may not become a common carrier, creating uncertainty over whether HOEC's gas will be allowed to flow through jointly-owned infrastructure.
B-15 development timeline dependent on drilling execution and tie-back/export concept decisions, still at concept stage.

subsections.label: Well intervention / drilling risk
points: Workover of subsea wells carries inherent uncertainty (e.g., whether existing Christmas trees will function or need replacement).
Drilling timelines subject to weather (drilling window from November), funding availability, and rig availability/tow insurance expiry (by May).

subsections.label: Guidance qualifications
points: Targets described as backed by drilling opportunities and reservoir study potential, contingent on investor/stakeholder support to help realize them.
Management explicitly frames targets around a June 2027 (not March 31, 2027) timeline, since drilling programs run through May-June of the following year.
Detailed FY27/FY28 debt and EBITDA guidance deferred; management to provide details next quarter to avoid premature/incorrect figures.
Funding of capex plan via internal accruals and bank facilities/debt, with capital discipline to protect gearing ratios; equity fund raise not ruled out but not confirmed.
Next quarter, management to provide more clarity on offshore-onshore capex mix and oil vs gas production mix once capex program is better defined.

AMAGI.about: Founded in 2008, Amagi Media Labs Ltd. is engaged in cloud-based broadcast and connected TV technology. [1]

quarters.summary: Amagi delivered its highest-ever quarterly revenue (INR437 crores, up 32% YoY) with expanding profitability (adjusted EBITDA margin 11.5%, PAT margin 7.5%), driven by broad-based, volume-led growth across segments and continued operating leverage. Management expects gross margins to stay in the 67-69% range for the year, sees Q2 FY27 facing a ~600bps YoY headwind from prior-year rev-rec base effects, and continues to view AI (via Newspulse and a broader upcoming product suite to be unveiled at industry conferences in Q2) as an early-stage but structurally positive growth driver, alongside a large and AI-expanding $17 billion TAM.

subsections.label: Revenue Drivers
points: Revenue was broad-based and largely volume driven across segments; segment mix broadly unchanged, supporting the broad-based growth narrative.
FIFA World Cup workloads were priced within normal commercial models and did not materially change Q1 revenue.
Prior year base had a one-time rev rec benefit related to a large deal that impacted the first half compare, mostly affecting cloud modernization comparison.
One-off base effect impact on overall revenue growth was ~450 basis points in Q1 FY27; excluding this base effect, overall growth would have been 35% reported and ~23% in constant currency.

subsections.label: Margin Drivers
points: Q1 is historically a seasonally softer quarter due to annual salary raises/increments kicking in, yet margins still expanded YoY and sequentially (adjusted EBITDA margin rose to 11.5% from 5% a year ago, and improved 1.2 percentage points sequentially vs Q4 FY26; FY26 full-year adjusted EBITDA margin was 10.3%).

Operating leverage stems from much of growth coming from existing customers already on the platform, so sales, marketing and customer success scale lower than revenue (23% of revenue vs 27% a year ago); R&D also scales sub-linearly due to shared platform layer investments (21% of revenue vs 27% a year ago), even as the adjusted EBITDA cost base grew 24% YoY.

Gross margin YoY movement (67.3%, down 2.2 points YoY but up 0.5 point QoQ) reflects segment mix, live event delivery intensity, select commercial engagements (pricing adjustments), and the prior year accounting base effect; direct costs rose to 33% of revenue from 31%.

Pricing approach is disciplined — adjustments made only when volume run-rate clearly outweighs price trade-off; one customer example tracking at >30% run-rate growth even after a pricing adjustment, a net revenue tailwind.
$282,000 in monthly run-rate gross margin cloud cost savings from FinOps were reinvested into AI-related initiatives to fund durable long-term growth.

Incremental adjusted EBITDA flow-through of ~31% of incremental revenue is about 3x the reported EBITDA margin, reflecting the land-and-expand model's core operating leverage; revenue grew INR107 crores YoY and adjusted EBITDA grew INR33 crores YoY (from INR17 crores in Q1 FY26 to INR50 crores).

PAT margin expansion (to 7.5% from 1.1%, a 6.3-point improvement, with PAT rising to INR34 crores from INR4 crores) driven by adjusted EBITDA expansion and lower ESOP costs as % of revenue; a one-time non-cash FX charge of INR6 crores from aligning a legacy customer advance to its contractual rate did not affect EBITDA or cash flow and is not expected to recur — PAT excluding this charge was INR40 crores.

subsections.label: Cash Flow
points: Q1 is structurally the weakest cash quarter due to annual incentive payouts, increments and software renewal lapping.
Operating cash outflow narrowed to INR65 crores from INR141 crores a year ago; free cash outflow narrowed to INR68 crores from INR143 crores.

Both periods included one-time items: last year buyback payments (INR57 crores), this year residual IPO expenses (INR25 crores); excluding one-time items, operating cash outflow was INR41 crores vs INR84 crores a year ago, a reduction of INR43 crores.
Cash burn narrowing was primarily driven by higher adjusted EBITDA; receivables (DSO) improved sequentially by 8 days vs Q4 FY26.
Cash and investments stood at INR1,616 crores.
Numbers are better assessed on a full-year basis rather than Q1 given seasonal cash outflow patterns.

subsections.label: Capital Allocation / M&A
points: Organic investment remains first priority; most growth has been organic so far.
Inorganic focus is capability-led, targeting areas that extend the media industry cloud vision.

Since January 2026, the company has evaluated 33 M&A opportunities, passed on 23, and has 10 under active evaluation as of Q1 FY27; disclosure is for visibility only — not a signal of an imminent deal or binding commitments; appropriate disclosures will be made at the right time.
Company remains sensitive to cash balance but is actively looking at deploying cash when price is right.

subsections.label: Historical Phasing Context
points: Q2 FY26 had the same rev rec timing benefit, creating a ~600bps YoY headwind for the Q2 FY27 compare.

H1 phasing: in FY26, H1 was ~47% of full-year revenue and ~37% of full-year adjusted EBITDA — EBITDA is historically more back-half weighted because annual merit increases occur early while revenue scale builds through the year, so operating leverage flows through better in later quarters.
This is historical context, not prescriptive guidance, provided because this is Amagi's first full year as a public company covering all quarters.
