subsections.label: Segment Growth Drivers
points: Streaming Unification revenue grew 39% YoY to INR249 crores, driven by both existing customers expanding with Amagi and channel deliveries reaching almost 10,000 (9,900+) with distributor count reaching 451 (up 21% YoY).
Monetization and Marketplace segment revenue grew 30% YoY to INR110 crores, volume-driven, with monetized impressions reaching a record high of 13.6 billion (up 59% YoY, 21% QoQ).
Cloud Modernization segment's reported growth of 17% YoY was affected by the prior-year rev rec base effect; excluding that, growth would have been ~32%.
Content processed reached 959,000 hours, up 43% YoY.

subsections.label: Convergence & Global Wins
points: Broadcast and FAST are converging into a unified cloud-native platform: an Australian broadcaster launched 4 FAST channels, while a U.S. news network moved its whole broadcast operations to Amagi, unifying FAST and traditional playout.
Adoption is global — wins span the U.S., Australia, Middle East, India and broader APAC region.
Momentum spans monetization to channel operation as an end-to-end capability, not concentrated in one part of the business.
An Indian news network selected Amagi to expand CTV distribution and drive monetization across channels.
A larger U.S. FAST platform selected Amagi's ADS PLUS and THUNDERSTORM to monetize in-content ad format.

subsections.label: Customer Retention / Stickiness
points: Gross revenue retention (GRR) is not a disclosed metric per DRHP routine disclosures, but logo churn is in low single digits and average vintage of top 10 customers is about 5 years, indicating stickiness.

Trailing 12-month NRR is 125%, reported on a trailing-12-month, reported-currency basis (not constant currency); it can only be disclosed at Q4 per DRHP intellectual honesty, but a TTM figure is shared directionally each quarter.

Approximately 26 of the 31% total growth rate is estimated to come from existing customers (NRR as % of total growth), offered as the closest proxy for dissecting new vs. existing-channel delivery growth, which is not tracked internally as a discrete metric.

subsections.label: Live Event / Mission-Critical Delivery Proof Points
points: Amagi's infrastructure aired all 104 FIFA World Cup matches for key customers, delivering 100% availability for a major U.S. broadcaster.
Supported more than 300 hours of FIFA and, for one U.S. broadcaster, 325 different events and 450 hours of events including shoulder programming, with 100% on-air availability.
These live events do not create one-time uplift or drag in quarterly financials; growth is secular and not dependent on any particular marquee event.

subsections.label: Distribution Platform Dynamics
points: Motivation to add distribution platforms stems from content-owner customers moving into more geographies (globalization trend); examples include Kogan TV (Australia), Vodafone (Germany), Virgin (UK).
Distribution platforms sometimes also become Amagi customers, but that is not a prerequisite for partnership — partnerships are in service of content owners reaching new geographies.

Ad impression growth this quarter was organic, driven by expanding connected TV (CTV) penetration in the U.S. and other geographies and more content being fed into platforms — no correlation with FIFA World Cup.
Platforms are generally looking to outsource ad insertion rather than in-source, given rising scale and complexity of ad management; management is not aware of any in-sourcing risk trend.

On platforms where Amagi is the ad insertion partner, all channel content flows through Amagi; on platforms where Amagi is only a delivery partner, there's no direct correlation to ad insertion revenue.
Channel deliveries vs. THUNDERSTORM ad-insertion penetration delta is not tracked as a discrete metric; directionally, growth is assumed to come mostly from existing channels adding more deliveries.
With personalized viewing and content fragmentation (shorts, vertical formats), the concept of a channel as a limiting factor is diminishing; runway should be viewed medium-to-long term.
Amagi serves 400+ content providers, 400 distributors, and 80+ advertisers.

subsections.label: Newspulse / AI Progress
points: Newspulse, Amagi's first AI agentic newsroom platform, was shipped last quarter with its first paying customer signed.

This quarter, more than 10 active pilots are underway across different customers, and a major U.S. news network selected Newspulse to transform itself into an AI-first newsroom — a vote of confidence in the product.
Company is investing beyond news across multiple content genres and plans to introduce a broader AI product suite at flagship industry conferences in Q2 FY27 (plans are indicative).
Commercial logic of AI products: reduce operational costs for customers, help expand distribution, and monetize assets better.
Company is building telemetry with the Newspulse customer to measure cost leverage and revenue expansion trends, working toward outcome-driven pricing over time — but this is very early stage.

Introduced an 'AI credit' pricing option for agentic media operations, measured on credits akin to token-based enterprise pricing; credits can be used flexibly (e.g., language translation, metadata enrichment), resembling a cost-plus model.
Company is mapping AI pricing models to underlying cost structures to avoid cost run-up disconnected from revenue base.

AI is not yet having a material or deflationary structural impact on revenue base or pipeline; ask from customers is a holistic view of the operating layer, not just software, aimed at revenue increase and cost reduction — currently viewed as a net tailwind.

AI gross margin impact is starting but from a relatively small base — not yet substantial; management expects an S-curve over a 2-3 year view, similar to historical gross margin trajectory (from ~64% several years ago to current ~67-69% target band), with AI expected to follow a similar multi-year curve.
No single AI business model has been presupposed; directional clarity expected in a few more quarters given the breadth of planned product offerings and agentic workflow infrastructure already built.

subsections.label: Video Fabric / Platform Architecture
points: Amagi operates end-to-end across the media value chain ('glass-to-glass') — from content creation to production, preparation, distribution and monetization — serving content providers, distributors and advertisers on a single cloud-native platform.

Underlying 'video fabric' — the mesh of compute, networking, storage and orchestration — is described as the harder engineering problem and the foundation enabling AI and all other capabilities, differentiating from an application-layer view of the industry.

subsections.label: TAM & AI Opportunity
points: TAM is roughly $17 billion across modernization, unification, and monetization/marketplaces; only about 10% of playout has moved to the cloud, indicating early-stage market.
AI could nearly double this opportunity over time (directional view, not a forecast); more proof points expected in coming quarters.

For customers, opportunity comes via two dimensions: operating leverage (cost) — customers spend roughly $2-$4 on human toil for every $1 on technology, an opportunity for AI-enabled replacement — and revenue growth via more content, new audiences and increased engagement.
Streaming is nearing half of U.S. television viewing, and as pay-TV declines this share is expected to rise, benefiting the business and industry.
Advertising is becoming central to streaming economics, citing the Fox-Roku deal and Netflix's new ad formats as industry evidence.
AI adoption among broadcasters remains early (27% usage today) with a significant runway ahead.

subsections.label: Customer Advisory Board Themes
points: Customers consistently emphasized three needs: (1) consolidate vendors given high tool proliferation and workflow complexity (one large customer cited using 800 tools); (2) trust in Amagi's mission-critical, end-to-end 'system of action' platform across technology, operations and business workflows, with embedded intelligence for efficiency and future autonomy; (3) this trust is supported by scale — 400+ content providers, 400 distributors, 80+ advertisers.
Vendor consolidation is viewed by customers as a cost lever and forcing function to simplify workflows via AI, positioning Amagi favorably given its end-to-end capability.

Existing customers are Amagi's first adopters of new AI product offerings, seeing them as natural extensions of existing infrastructure Amagi already owns and operates for them (e.g., the first Newspulse U.S. news network customer is an existing Amagi customer).

subsections.label: Consolidation & Fragmentation Dynamics
points: Both consolidation (mergers of media companies) and fragmentation (spin-offs) are occurring; fragmentation creates a tailwind since spun-off units need new infrastructure/facilities.

Amagi, connecting supply side, demand side and advertisers, is positioned as an end-to-end, neutral ecosystem player ('Switzerland of the ecosystem'), which structurally benefits it whether consolidation or fragmentation occurs.
No material net headwind observed so far from either consolidation or fragmentation trends.

subsections.label: Pricing Methodology
points: Current pricing largely tied to hours of content processed and channel deliveries; management is exploring changes but no material structural or deflationary AI pricing impact seen yet on revenue base or pipeline.

Disciplined pricing approach: price adjustments made only when volume run-rate clearly outweighs the trade-off; cited customer example tracking >30% run-rate growth even after a pricing adjustment, framed as a net revenue tailwind.

subsections.label: Flagged Headwinds
points: One-time non-cash FX charge from aligning a legacy customer advance to its contractual rate impacted PAT but not EBITDA or cash flow; not expected to recur.
Q1 is seasonally the weakest cash quarter due to annual incentive payouts, increments, and software renewal lapping.
Prior-year base effect from a rev rec timing benefit created comparison headwinds in Q1 (cloud modernization segment) and is expected to create a ~600bps headwind for Q2 FY27 as well.

Gross margin faces puts and takes from segment mix, live event delivery intensity, and select commercial (pricing) engagements; management does not view this as structural deterioration but flags ongoing monitoring.
AI is very early stage with a thin read on structural or deflationary pricing impact; no material flow-through yet observed in revenue or pipeline.
Elongated sales cycles associated with industry vendor consolidation could be a factor, though management frames consolidation/fragmentation as a net tailwind rather than headwind currently.

quarters.summary: This was an educational webinar ("AI in Media") explicitly excluding company-specific financial, operational, or business outlook disclosures; management (Baskar Subramanian) discussed industry-wide AI transformation across content production, preparation, distribution, and consumer discovery, framing agentic AI, GenAI, VLMs, and world models as reshaping the media value chain, with directional views that automation drives business expansion (Jevons' paradox) rather than pure cost deflation, and that outcome-based commercial models may emerge over time as agentic AI deployment matures.

subsections.label: Video value chain stages
points: Content flow starts at the camera (e.g., a cricket match at the stadium) with multiple cameras connected to an OB van with a satellite antenna, beamed to a studio; commentary boxes and a production room handle camera switching.
Preparation stage occurs typically in a studio: adding scorecards, team logos, multiple audio tracks, advertising and ad breaks.
Distribution occurs via cable or streaming platforms; monetization can be advertising or subscription; viewership can be global.
Analogy drawn to retail value chain: production (factory) → preparation (warehouse/packaging) → logistics/distribution (trucks) → retailers/consumers (quick commerce/e-commerce).

subsections.label: Agentic infrastructure — definition and evolution
points: Coffee machine analogy used to explain agent evolution: (1) Non-agent = pre-programmed automation (press button, get espresso); (2) Agent = AI-enabled system that proactively predicts needs (e.g., anticipates you want an espresso based on facial expressions/time of day) without being explicitly programmed for that scenario; (3) True AI agency (AGI-like) = system learns, decides, and evolves by itself, inventing new outcomes (e.g., 'inventing a new drink').
Media industry is currently in the 'Agentic Era' (step 2), progressing toward true AI agency (step 3).

Digital agents in media are described as 'glorified coffee machines' — AI-enabled software that understands video, audio, and storylines to automatically extract/create metadata (artwork, program guide ratings, story summaries) without human intervention.

subsections.label: Content production disruption via GenAI
points: Content business getting disrupted by GenAI tools (Google Omni, Google Nano Banana, Runway, etc.); high-quality AI production systems are starting to evolve, still early stage.
Cost of content production is expected to deflate as AI capability improves, requiring the economics of the value chain to be rethought.
New AI-first studios are evolving that fuse AI tools with human creative/storytelling capability; seen in India and globally.

View that live sports may be the only content category to remain largely non-AI-generated, given human/emotional appeal of live competition; all other content may become indistinguishable as AI- vs human-generated.

subsections.label: Metadata / content preparation problem
points: Metadata includes artwork/image, storyline description, program guide ratings, actor/episodic info, content advisories, audio tracks/subtitles, creator/copyright info, PG ratings.
Metadata explosion arises from needing to produce this across many countries, languages, and differing regulations, driving a 'headcount crisis' in media companies.
AT-time report (referenced, released about a week prior to the webinar) flagged 'messy media'/metadata problems as one of the largest industry bottlenecks slowing scaling.

Agentic scheduling example: system builds full TV channel schedules autonomously overnight (2-5 a.m.) using taste/genre understanding, new content awareness, business needs, prior-day viewership analytics, and social signals (e.g., recognizing a celebrity birthday); human operator reviews and confirms in minutes instead of spending a full workday.

subsections.label: Inter-agent transactions and Agentic Discovery
points: Distribution/negotiation between content creators and OTT platforms today is a highly manual, human-to-human process (email/phone) repeated across hundreds of content owners and tens/hundreds of platforms across 40+ countries.

Future concept: 'inter-company agent transactions' where AI agents representing platforms and studios negotiate commercials, legal terms, and content planning (e.g., Diwali content planning) directly with each other, functioning like a marketplace.

'Agentic Discovery' concept: personal conversational bots (ChatGPT/Claude/Gemini-like) could become the primary interface for content discovery and consumption, replacing website/app-based discovery; bots would understand a user's mood, emotions, and cross-platform viewing behavior rather than being tied to one OTT surface (Netflix/Prime/YouTube).

subsections.label: Content transformation / new storytelling formats
points: AI removes human/hardware bottlenecks that today homogenize content consumption (same camera switches, commentary, graphics for all viewers).

Future vision: a single sports match (e.g., football/cricket) could be rendered as multiple personalized storylines — tactical fan view, home-fan view, Gen Z multi-camera/chat experience — with tailored commentary, statistics, and graphics per persona.

Microdrama trend: existing long-form content libraries (built over the last 50 years) could be repurposed into new short-form/microdrama formats (e.g., a 3.5-hour Sholay movie reformatted into 3-minute micro-episodes totaling ~30 minutes), previously impossible pre-AI due to human scaling limits.

subsections.label: Technology stack complexity: LLMs, VLMs, world models
points: Content/video business technology is more complex than typical text-only enterprise AI because it must jointly handle audio, video, and text.
Large Language Models (LLMs) serve as the base for text; Small Language Models are used for less resource-intensive reasoning.

Vision Language Models (VLMs) are needed to extract information from video/audio ('eyes and ears' understanding of scenes, actions, e.g., basketball dunk, goal, foul, yellow card) — currently very few VLMs exist and they are described as expensive and slow.

'World models' are the next step — predicting the next state of a real-world environment from a current scene (originating in autonomous-vehicle use cases); applicable to sports for physics-based prediction (e.g., ball trajectory, air drag) and to create more immersive experiences (e.g., viewing from a goalie's gloves or a player's shoes) beyond what fixed camera positions allow; expected to be a major industry research area over the next couple of years.

Because of low-latency and cost/performance requirements in live content (e.g., real-time camera-switching decisions in a football game), the industry needs hundreds of custom, narrow audio-video models (e.g., sport-specific models for basketball, soccer, ocean scenes) rather than general-purpose LLMs like ChatGPT/Claude/Gemini.

subsections.label: Cost vs. revenue-expansion dynamics (Jevons' paradox)
points: Management view: customers are largely using AI/automation to expand capabilities and revenue opportunities rather than purely to cut costs — described via Jevons' paradox (more automation historically leads to doing more, not less).
On a per-job basis there may eventually be a deflationary cost trend, but the multiplier of total jobs/tasks customers want to do is seen as expansionary overall.

Token cost is described as only a small part of AI cost in video businesses; GPU cost (for custom video/audio models) is the more relevant cost driver, and GPU cost is said to be far lower than the human cost it replaces.
Early evidence cited: speech-to-text has largely solved subtitling needs; dubbing is becoming viable; artwork/promo creation (previously human jobs) are changing due to AI.

OTT/cable AI content adoption is described as still 'in bits and pieces' — not yet a full 'factory approach'; VFX cost reduction and use of AI for background creation/specific storytelling elements cited as early real-world examples; broader OTT/content-creation platform adoption is currently small but expected to grow substantially ('big tsunami') over time, with more visible activity currently in microdrama.

subsections.label: Network effects and moat
points: Question raised on network effects from agent-to-agent communication and first-mover advantage.

Management view: agentic infrastructure connecting distinct parts of an ecosystem (vs. within a single company) has a much higher network-effect multiplier; inter-agent communication, protocols and standardization are still very early across every industry.
Time compression is expected in areas like legal/commercial negotiations between ecosystem partners as agents take over routine coordination, while key decisions remain human-driven.

On vertical vs. horizontal SaaS/hyperscaler threat: management (from a vertical media-software vantage point) argues that mission-critical software/services in media provide a moat because business/technology/operating context (not just reasoning, which may commoditize) is the key differentiator; whoever owns that context is best positioned to drive future workflows.

subsections.label: Commercial model evolution
points: Question raised on how industry commercials between vendors and clients may change as the industry moves toward Agentic AI deployment.

Management view: very early stage; there are directional conversations across industries (e.g., call centers) around outcome-driven pricing models (per-transaction, per-result, per-success-criteria basis).

Media is described as somewhat different; core existing value-based pricing is expected to continue, with new revenue-share or outcome-linked models potentially applying to incremental/expansionary capabilities; how pricing would be linked to outcomes is still to be determined and not yet playing out materially in media.

subsections.label: Reliability/hallucination risk in agentic AI
points: Analyst question flagged that clients operate under SLAs up to 99.9999% and that Agentic AI can be prone to hallucination and unpredictability.

Management response: focus is on bringing determinism to an indeterministic problem via guardrails and systems engineering; predictability is critical when processing hundreds of thousands of hours of content; getting AI solutions from demo/POC stage to reliable production use at scale is described as the hardest engineering challenge.

subsections.label: Technology complexity as a barrier
points: Video/audio AI is inherently more complex than text-only AI because it must jointly process audio (speech, music, background sound), video (action, emotion, scene context) and text (summaries, scene descriptions) together.
Current VLMs are described as expensive and slow, limiting real-time application (e.g., not fast enough for live camera-switching decisions).

risk_register.risk: Agentic AI hallucination/unpredictability risk versus stringent client SLAs (up to 99.9999%)
risk_register.note: Management stated focus is on bringing determinism to an indeterministic problem via guardrails; production-scale reliability (vs. demos/POCs) is described as the hardest ongoing engineering challenge.

risk_register.risk: High complexity of building AI models jointly across audio, video and text (vs. simpler text-only enterprise AI)
risk_register.note: Current VLMs described as expensive and slow; need for hundreds of custom narrow audio-video models due to low-latency requirements in live content scenarios.

risk_register.risk: Early-stage/immature technology for world models and VLMs limiting real-time, immersive use cases
risk_register.note: World models and VLMs are described as very early-phase; VLMs are expensive/slow and not yet fast enough for real-time decisions like live camera switching.

themes.label: Agentic AI adoption
themes.note: Media industry progressing from non-agent automation to Agentic Era systems that predict and act, moving toward true AI agency (AGI-like self-learning agents).

themes.label: Content production cost deflation via GenAI
themes.note: GenAI tools are expected to deflate content production costs over time, prompting rethinking of value-chain economics, while AI-first studios fusing AI with human creativity are emerging.

themes.label: Metadata/preparation automation
themes.note: Agentic infrastructure is automating metadata creation and scheduling work that today causes a 'headcount crisis', citing an 8-hour manual scheduling task reduced to a 10-minute confirmation.

themes.label: Inter-agent transactions & Agentic Discovery
themes.note: Future vision of agents negotiating directly between content creators and platforms, and personal conversational bots replacing traditional content discovery surfaces.

themes.label: Revenue expansion over cost deflation (Jevons' paradox)
themes.note: Management believes customers are primarily using AI to expand capabilities/revenue rather than purely to cut costs, per Jevons' paradox reasoning.

themes.label: Vertical AI moat vs horizontal SaaS/hyperscalers
themes.note: Management argues mission-critical, context-owning vertical media software provides a durable moat even as generic AI reasoning commoditizes.

themes.label: Outcome-based commercial models
themes.note: Early, unresolved industry-wide shift toward outcome-driven pricing models as Agentic AI deployment matures; not yet playing out meaningfully in media.

pressing_questions: Given that we have strict SLAs up to 99.9999% with clients, Agentic AI can be prone to hallucination and be at times unpredictable. What are the safeguards we have in place to mitigate such risks?
Regarding the prep work, are we seeing any improvements in the speed in work due to AI? Does it in turn reduce pricing because of AI-led deflation?
Can AI become a lever for getting production and pre-production workflows to be hosted in cloud?
Have we seen increase in OTT cable based content because of AI? Any real life examples on cost that has been reduced?
Is there any evidence on cost savings, for production prep, etc, especially given the higher token costs?
Are there any network effects that can come from agent-to-agent communication opportunities you discussed? Is there any benefit to being the first mover here?
Does AI help strengthen the business with deeper engagement with clients? Does this create a threat to horizontal SaaS or cloud companies like hyperscalers, etc?
With the rapid adoption of Agentic AI across media, do you expect it to materially reduce operating costs for your customers? If so, could this create pricing pressure as we go about things?
How do you see industry commercials between vendors and clients change from its current form as industry moves more towards Agentic AI deployment?

MAXHEALTH.about: Max Healthcare Institute Limited is primarily engaged in the providing healthcare services through primary care clinics, multi-speciality hospitals / medical centres and super-speciality hospitals providing operation and management, medical services, clinical, radiology, pathology services and related healthcare services. [1]

quarters.summary: Max Healthcare started FY27 with 16% YoY revenue growth and 15% YoY operating EBITDA growth, continuing capacity expansion (Max Smart, Nanavati Phase 2, Vaishali new tower, Bhubaneswar integration, Pune SPV acquisition) and entering the medical education business pending regulatory change, while oncology in-patient mix continues to normalize downward and is expected to stabilize by Q3/Q4 FY27; management expects EBITDA flow-through to improve as new brownfield beds ramp occupancy-first then revenue/EBITDA over the next 2-3 quarters, and guided that opex will not see material further increase until Gurugram (Sector 56) comes online.

subsections.label: Cash flow bridge (EBITDA growth vs FCF growth divergence)
points: EBITDA grew 15% YoY but free cash flow/EPS growth was much lower (3%) due to movement in accounts receivable, particularly lumpiness in CGHS and other PSU collections.
DSO increased from 87 days to 95 days, with an AR build-up of around INR 250 crore in the quarter compared to Q4 last year, absorbing working capital and hurting FCF conversion.
Effective tax rate (ETR) has also gone up, increasing tax outflows compared to last quarter.
Normal FCF conversion range is 62-65%, but this quarter it was around 56%, mainly due to the AR build-up.
Management expects this to normalize going forward as CGHS's new portal, which was earlier not processing bills, has started showing collections.

subsections.label: Net debt trajectory
points: Net debt increase during the quarter includes INR 153 crore towards Kalinga and the put option liability for the balance stake in Yerawada (Pune project).
Net debt-to-EBITDA remains below 1x; management would be comfortable going up to 2.5x net debt-to-EBITDA via acquisitions.

Barring acquisitions, ongoing capex (including the newly approved INR 425 crore Vaishali tower and Shaheed Path) means cash generated will be consumed and some debt may be taken to finance projects, so net debt could marginally rise by year-end.
Over a 3-4 year horizon, capex is expected to be funded and debt paid down depending on cash flow generation.
Free cash flow generated of INR 397 crore in Q1 FY27, with INR 386 crore deployed towards Kalinga & Yerawada acquisitions and INR 337 crore invested as capex in ongoing expansion projects.

subsections.label: Cost structure
points: Direct costs grew 16% versus revenue growth of 15%; the incremental 1% gap is attributed to clinician costs.
No significant impact from crude/consumable price increases on direct costs; some impact seen in indirect costs but not material on direct cost side.
Increase in clinician costs tends to normalize over time as revenues ramp up.

Large sequential increase in indirect/operating expenses (even adjusting for Bhubaneswar) is due to new capacities operationalized at Mohali, Nanavati and Smart, combined with Bhubaneswar; no significant further increase expected until Gurugram (Sector 56) comes online, after which revenue and EBITDA flow-through should increase.

subsections.label: CSR and community initiatives
points: Free treatment provided to over 56,000 patients from economically weaker sections worth INR 78 crore at hospital tariff.

Around INR 6 crore spent on CSR initiatives including medical scholarships to underprivileged students, promoting maternal and newborn health, vocational skill training, and environmental projects such as pond rejuvenation and tree plantation.

subsections.label: Max Bhubaneswar contribution
points: Max Bhubaneswar contributed INR 19 crore revenue and INR 2 crore EBITDA post-acquisition in Q1 FY27, versus FY26 (pre-acquisition) full-year revenue of INR 154 crore.

key_figures.label: Increase in operational bed capacity YoY

subsections.label: Occupancy and utilization trends
points: Average occupancy for the Network continued to be more than 75% despite a 13% increase in operational bed capacity YoY, with most units operating at near-optimal capacity.
ALOS reduced by 4% over the trailing quarter, reflecting concerted efforts on this front.

New brownfield beds follow a standard ramp trajectory: occupancy ramps first (using whatever ARPOB comes), then revenue ramp-up, then EBITDA ramp-up which eventually overtakes revenue ramp-up; management expects revenue and EBITDA ramp-up to play out by the second or third quarter of operations for beds like Max Smart.
Max Smart and Nanavati Phase 1 commissioned beds both running at 80% occupancy in Q1 FY27.

subsections.label: Long-term sector demand outlook
points: Management does not believe top hospital chains can reach 100,000 beds each in 20 years given India's total current bed base is ~100,000; largest chain today is 10-11,000 beds, requiring 10x growth, which management views as a major execution and capital challenge.

Management foresees continuing capacity doubling roughly every 4-5 years (e.g., from 5,000 to 10,000 to 20,000 to 40,000 beds) but stresses no specific plan exists beyond investing available cash flows into capacity.

ARPOB growth (historically 7-8%, a couple of points above inflation) is expected to remain structurally superior to inflation because of novel treatments and technology adoption, a trend management expects to continue for the next 10-15 years as long as sector innovation continues.
Demand-supply gap for private hospital beds versus consumer preference for private care is expected to persist given the scale of investment required to meaningfully close it.
Less than 2% of institutional business patients qualifying for NEET find medical college seats, underscoring the scale of unmet demand for medical education capacity.

subsections.label: Oncology revenue mix decline
points: Discontinuation of select high-value chemotherapy drugs for institutional patients caused the share of oncology in in-patient revenues to drop to 22% from 26% in Q1 FY26.
Excluding oncology, gross revenue grew 20% and ARPOB grew 9% YoY, showing strong underlying growth in non-onco specialties.

Oncology is expected to start normalizing from Q3 FY27 onwards, since the action of discontinuing ORC drugs for institutional patients was taken mid-Q3 FY26 following a new MOU signed in October 2025; by Q4 it should be fully normalized.

Max's oncology franchise was the largest among peers with 25%+ of revenues from oncology historically, so the impact was proportionately higher versus peers; Max also had the highest institutional business and largest CGHS share due to Delhi presence, explaining why the impact is more visible at Max than peers.

Institutional patient bed share has come down this quarter versus previous quarter even as capacity was added; management expects this reduction trend to continue absent significant acquisitions of institutional-heavy capacity.

subsections.label: Payor mix
points: Institutional revenue share is deliberately being brought down as a result of concerted effort, not expected to revert to the earlier ~22% level.

subsections.label: International patient business
points: International patient revenue reached INR 247 crore, up 18% YoY, representing 9% of hospital revenue.

subsections.label: Digital and strategic business units (Max@Home, Max Lab)
points: Digital revenue reached INR 941 crore, 32% of overall revenue, supported by website traffic of 97 lakh sessions, up 41% YoY.
Max@Home revenue grew 32% YoY to INR 78 crore, across 16 service lines in 15 cities, with 56% repeat transactions.
Max Lab revenue grew 20% YoY to INR 58 crore, covering 60+ cities and serving 6 lakh+ patients.
Both strategic business units continue to deliver steady growth in revenue and profitability.

subsections.label: Kalinga (Bhubaneswar) turnaround plan
points: Occupancy of 50% and ARPOB of INR 35,000 provide significant levers for growth versus corporate average; management expects a 50% to 80% enhancement in both occupancy and ARPOB.
Turnaround plan involves integrating operations, renovating infrastructure, upgrading technology, and enhancing clinical programs over the next 12 months.
Hospital currently makes a marginal profit; management has prior experience executing similar turnarounds at Lucknow and Noida acquisitions.
Alongside turnaround, an additional 200-250 beds will be built at the site.
Revenue post-acquisition of INR 19 crore and EBITDA of INR 2 crore in Q1 FY27, versus FY26 (pre-acquisition) full-year revenue of INR 154 crore.

subsections.label: Institutional/CGHS business economics
points: Institutional business has never been profitable historically and contributes to fixed costs rather than bottom-line profit; relying solely on this business would create a continuing issue.
There is inherent lumpiness in institutional payments (up-down), which management does not view as a major concern given it is a small part of the overall business mix trend.

subsections.label: Max Smart brownfield tower
points: Currently operationalized 50% capacity of the 400-bed brownfield tower; remaining 50% beds are expected to be handed over to operations during the course of the current quarter.

Oncology is the focused specialty at this facility; beds already opened are running at 80% occupancy despite being opened in a phased manner through the quarter, with occupancy filling in as beds come on stream.

subsections.label: Nanavati Max
points: Remaining 50 beds will be operationalized this quarter; Phase 2 expansion work has commenced.
Phase 1 beds already opened are running at ~80% occupancy; occupancy has significantly picked up ahead of revenue and EBITDA is now catching up and expected to surpass revenue ramp-up soon.
Phase 2 (271 beds) requires shutting ~100-odd existing beds first; will take about 2.5 years to complete.
Margin improvement at Nanavati is expected to come through even in Phase 1 given the high ARPOB business, not solely dependent on Phase 2.

subsections.label: Max Vaishali
points: Board approved capex of INR 425 crore for a new brownfield tower adding 202 beds to existing 387-bed capacity.
Building plans have been approved and construction activities have already commenced; project expected to be commissioned before FY30.
Confirmed to be the same 200-bed tower previously flagged in earlier presentations for FY29, not a fresh additional tower.

subsections.label: Pipeline of expansion projects (next 2-3 years)
points: Max Lucknow: additional 100 beds in the existing 468-bed facility to be commissioned over next two quarters.
Sector 56 Gurgaon (500 beds): phased commissioning expected to start by end of this year.
Bhubaneswar (250 beds): renovation of existing facility to be completed within 12 months.
Nagpur (100 beds): project on track, commissioning expected by FY28.
Zirakpur, Mohali (400 beds): project on schedule, commissioning expected in FY28.
Max Dwarka onco day care block (Phase 2): project work complete, awaiting occupancy certificate.
Dwarka (260 beds, next phase): Dwarka hospital already running full; to be commissioned by FY30.
Pitampura (200 beds): project on track, commissioning expected in FY29.
Patparganj (400 beds): D-wall work started, commissioning expected by end of FY29.
Nanavati Phase 2 (271 beds): work started, commissioning in FY30.
Pune (450 beds): IOD received, project expected to be commissioned by FY30.

subsections.label: Thane and Shaheed Path greenfield status
points: Thane: regulatory approvals are progressing; stage-one approval received for the overall master plan for the site; specific building plan drawings to be submitted next.
Shaheed Path: drawings prepared, discussions ongoing with authorities; will be submitted after broad clearance on the concept.
For both projects, approval is expected in another six months, after which delivery will take about 30-36 months.

subsections.label: Medical education infrastructure plan
points: For-profit companies previously curtailed from opening medical colleges (only not-for-profit entities allowed); a draft notification now permits for-profit companies to open medical colleges, which management assumes will become law.

Estimated ~INR 300 crore spend needed for a 150-seat medical college; colleges will generally be set up within existing hospital campuses (e.g., 27-acre Lucknow campus is the planned first site), followed by other locations with available land such as Delhi and Bhubaneswar.

Previous guidelines had restrictions on hospital charges attached to medical colleges and infrastructure/ward requirements, all of which have now been removed; a hospital is now a prerequisite for medical college seats since students must train there.
Company already trains DNB and MBBS students, has existing faculty and curriculum, making entry into medical education a natural, near backward-integration move.
Management sees >25-30% ROCE currently and intends to pursue this at scale; entire medical education business will sit within the consolidated listco with 100% economic interest, no leakages.

Plans to also start postgraduate (PG) courses; would consider meaningful acquisitions to kick-start the process sooner; intends to fund entirely through internal accruals; commercial operations expected to start over the next few years.

subsections.label: Regional disclosure discontinuation
points: Company has discontinued providing regional (state-level) revenue disclosures because in some states/regions (e.g., East, represented solely by Bhubaneswar) there is only one hospital, making the data effectively hospital-specific and competitively sensitive.
Management is considering reinstating some regional disclosure using an 'Others' bucket to avoid disclosing solo-hospital-level data, in response to an analyst request.

subsections.label: Bhubaneswar (Kalinga) acquisition and integration
points: Integration of Max Bhubaneswar into the Network is proceeding as planned.

Minority shareholders holding 39% equity (based outside India, in the UAE market) are undergoing liquidation proceedings against themselves and their parent setup; their shares are considered non-transactable per company legal counsel.

Minority shareholders requested their shares also be bought as part of the transaction, and have gone to court seeking this; company's position is that their shares are currently untouchable absent a court order.
No issue on the promoter side — company has bought shares from promoters and has full control of the company.

subsections.label: Pune project (Yerawada)
points: Company has acquired the SPV for the Pune greenfield project, which is now a subsidiary of the company.
Balance stake in Yerawada carries a put option liability, part of which contributed to the net debt increase during the quarter.

subsections.label: Research and academic ecosystem
points: Recently established a standalone Max Research Centre, marking a landmark milestone in the company's research journey.
Built an integrated clinical research ecosystem with patents generated and capabilities translating scientific discovery into better patient care.

Secured several research grants and awards from prestigious institutes including ICMR Centre for Advanced Research in Precision Diabetes, ANRF MAHA MedTech Mission, DBT European Union Dengue Program, and India AI Mission initiatives with the National Cancer Grid, among others.
Research capabilities complemented by the Max Institute of Medical Education (MIME), a dedicated education arm.

Cumulative track record includes 750+ clinical trials conducted, 2,200+ investigator-initiated studies completed, ~3,500 papers published in indexed journals, and 30+ competitively funded research projects secured.
MIME trains 12,000+ healthcare professionals annually across 180 training programs; postgraduate ecosystem includes 600+ DNB students.

subsections.label: Medical education board approval
points: Emboldened by the above research/education ecosystem and the change in recent National Medical Commission guidelines, the company has decided to embark upon the medical education business and received in-principle board approval.
Management believes this will be a significant line of business in years to come.

subsections.label: Track record of past acquisitions (Lucknow, Noida, Nagpur)
points: These acquisitions, now about two to two-and-a-half years old, were operating at low occupancy levels at acquisition; all three have seen very high ramp-up in occupancy, revenue, and profitability.

Company is now moving towards capacity expansion at all three, with brownfield capacity expansion leading straight to the bottom line; qualitatively all three deemed successful, consistent with the company's playbook.

subsections.label: Prior Shaheed Path approval context
points: (Referenced from prior guidance) Board approved investment of INR 1,400 crore for a 700-bed greenfield hospital at Shaheed Path, Lucknow, expected to take about 3 years to build; current update indicates drawings prepared and discussions ongoing with authorities, approval expected in ~6 months with 30-36 months delivery thereafter.

subsections.label: Parliamentary Standing Committee recommendation
points: The recent committee report speaks about affordability but management believes viability and the need for new hospital beds must be considered alongside it.

Management has not been reached out to by the committee; report speaks about certain FDI caps among other things; this is the 176th report by the committee and needs to be viewed in balance, which management expects ministries will also do.

Management does not believe the report changes or requires reassessment of the company's expansion plans; believes eventually any policy will be rational, and the company as an efficient healthcare provider would have superior returns even under a risk-free-return viability scenario; any adverse policy situation could become a consolidation opportunity for the company.
Management does not see the report affecting the viability of expansion plans in light of ongoing execution.

subsections.label: CGHS and institutional payor dynamics
points: Institutional business (including CGHS) has never been profitable; it is loss-making but contributes to fixed costs — reliance solely on this business would create ongoing issues.
There is inherent lumpiness in institutional payments; management does not view this as a major concern, treating it as a normal to-and-fro part of the business.
CGHS reimbursement flow was previously delayed for super-specialty rates but has started flowing from June onwards; company is on track versus its earlier flagged number.

CGHS's new payment portal was previously not processing bills, causing collection delays, but collections from the new portal have now started, and DSO/AR build-up is expected to normalize going forward.

subsections.label: Insurance company negotiation dynamics
points: Ongoing negotiations with GIPSA and other insurance companies; insurance companies that had prior discussions are up for renewal in September-October, and the company hopes for a price increase.
Previously, during a stalemate with insurance companies, a 6% automatic price revision was agreed, which is set to occur upon renewal.
There is also engagement with IRDAI and insurers (via CII) for an automatic price increase linked to inflation levels going forward.

Media articles have highlighted insurance companies trying to dictate admission/care terms; management clarifies that admission decisions rest solely with doctors, not hospitals, and any standardization would require agreement between insurance companies, IMA and the medical council; no occupancy impact has been observed so far from this dynamic.

subsections.label: Oncology drug discontinuation impact
points: Discontinuation of select high-value chemotherapy drugs for institutional patients reduced oncology's share of in-patient revenue and impacted overall reported margins, with impact expected to fully normalize by Q4 FY27.

Impact has been proportionately larger for Max versus peers because Max previously had the largest oncology franchise (25%+ of revenue), largest institutional business, and largest CGHS share due to Delhi presence.
Analyst estimate (not confirmed by management) pegs the combined EBITDA impact from new hospital overheads and onco drug discontinuation at INR 100-150 crore versus Q1 FY26.

subsections.label: Cost inflation and construction delays
points: No material impact from crude oil / consumable price increases on direct costs; slight impact seen in indirect costs only.
Direct cost growth outpacing revenue growth by ~1% attributed to clinician cost increases, which tend to normalize as revenue ramps up.
Historically, import delays (e.g., importing furniture for hospitals from overseas) contributed to project delays, though management states much of that is now behind them.

subsections.label: New capacity cost absorption during ramp-up
points: Opening new beds requires staffing ahead of full occupancy (e.g., staffing a 400-bed hospital ahead of ramp-up), so costs rise ahead of matching revenue in early periods; management does not view this as incremental new cost but as a timing effect that will yield revenue as occupancy catches up.
Break-even for a brownfield expansion is much lower than for a greenfield project.

subsections.label: Near-term EBITDA/revenue trajectory for new beds
points: For Max Smart, revenue and EBITDA ramp-up is expected to play out over the next couple of quarters, with meaningful improvement expected by the second or third quarter of operations, following the standard occupancy-then-revenue-then-EBITDA trajectory.

For Nanavati, occupancy has already picked up ahead of revenue, and EBITDA is expected to catch up and surpass revenue ramp-up soon; margin improvement is expected even from Phase 1 given the high ARPOB nature of the business.

subsections.label: Opex and net debt outlook
points: No material further increase in opex expected until Sector 56 Gurgaon comes online; incremental beds at Nanavati and Smart should not cause a similarly large increase in indirect costs going forward, and revenue/EBITDA flow-through should improve.
Net debt-to-EBITDA remains below 1x currently; management would be comfortable going up to 2.5x via acquisitions.

Barring acquisitions, ongoing capex (Vaishali INR 425 crore, Shaheed Path, etc.) means net debt may marginally rise by year-end as cash generated is consumed and some debt may be taken for project financing.
Over a 3-4 year horizon, capex is expected to be funded and debt paid down, depending on cash flow generation.

subsections.label: CGHS reimbursement run-rate
points: Company is on track for the INR 140 crore CGHS reimbursement number for the year, having realized INR 35 crore in Q1 FY27; super-specialty rate flow started from June onwards, implying a run-rate of INR 140/4 crore per quarter going forward from June.

key_takeaways: Average occupancy for the Network continued to be more than 75% despite a 13% increase in operational bed capacity year-on-year, with most units continuing to operate at near optimal capacity.
Occupied Bed Days (OBDs) were up by 10% year-on-year and 5% quarter-on-quarter.
Average Length of Stay (ALOS) reduced by 4% over trailing quarter, reflecting concerted efforts on this front.
Average Revenue Per Occupied Bed (ARPOB) for the quarter stood at INR 81,900, growing by 5% both year-on-year and quarter-on-quarter.

Network gross revenue stood at INR 2,982 crore compared to INR 2,574 crore in Q1 last year and INR 2,664 crore in previous quarter. This reflects an increase of 16% year-on-year and 12% quarter-on-quarter.

Due to the discontinuation of select high-value chemotherapy drugs for institutional patients, share of oncology for in-patient revenues dropped to 22% from 26% in Q1 FY26. Excluding oncology, gross revenue grew by 20% and ARPOB grew by 9% year-on-year.
International patient revenue was INR 247 crore, registering a growth of 18% year-on-year and accounting for 9% of the revenues from hospitals.

Digital revenue from online marketing activities, web-based appointments and digital lead management was INR 941 crore, accounting for approximately 32% of overall revenue. Website traffic crossed 97 lakh sessions during the quarter, growing by 41% year-on-year.
Network operating EBITDA stood at INR 704 crore, reflecting a growth of 15% year-on-year and 3% quarter-on-quarter.

Network operating EBITDA margin was 24.8% for the quarter, compared to 24.9% in Q1 FY26 and 26.8% in trailing quarter. The margin was relatively muted due to the recent commissioning of new brownfield capacities and the acquisition of Kalinga Hospital.
Net debt for the Network stood at INR 2,384 crore compared to INR 1,908 crore at the end of March 2026, while the net debt-to-EBITDA ratio continued to remain below 1.

The board has approved a capital expenditure of INR 425 crore for a new brownfield tower at Max Vaishali, adding 202 beds to the hospital's existing capacity of 387 beds, expected to be commissioned before FY30.
pressing_questions: Karan Vora requested reinstating regional (state-level) revenue disclosure that used to be provided in the past, as it was helpful to understand regional performance; management indicated concerns over disclosing competitively sensitive solo-hospital-level data and suggested an 'Others' bucket as a compromise, without committing to full reinstatement.

Abdulkader Puranwala asked whether new hospital overheads plus onco drug discontinuation had a INR 100-150 crore impact on EBITDA YoY; management declined to frame it that way, saying it is a timing/staffing cost effect rather than incremental new cost.

quarters.summary: Max Healthcare closed Q4/FY26 with continued double-digit revenue and EBITDA growth (22nd consecutive quarter of YoY growth), while FY27 priorities center on scaling recently commissioned brownfield/greenfield capacity, integrating the newly acquired Kalinga Hospital (Bhubaneswar), and progressing expansion projects including Sector-56 Gurgaon (expected commissioning by end of FY27) and the newly Board-approved INR 1,400 crore, 700-bed Shaheed Path, Lucknow greenfield hospital.

subsections.label: Oncology drug discontinuation impact
points: Share of oncology in in-patient revenues dropped due to discontinuation of select high-value chemotherapy drugs for institutional patients (CGHS/ECHS), where margins had turned negative after CGHS mandated a 30% discount to MRP.
Discontinuation impacts both top line and OBDs, as some day-care chemo patients were also admitted overnight; oncology OBDs fell 5-6% YoY as a result.

Management does not expect oncology's share to return to 25-26% levels; expects it to hover around 21-22%, with other specialties filling the vacuum — overall Network OBDs still grew despite the oncology decline.
Impact is industry-wide, but Max is disproportionately affected as it does the largest proportion of oncology business and the largest proportion of institutional (CGHS/ECHS) business among peers.

Annual chemotherapy drug billing (top line) impact from discontinuation: INR 200 crore in gross terms (drug billing); previously quantified onco drug impact around INR 80-crore range referenced by an analyst.
Margins on these discontinued drugs were previously ~15-16% (MRP-based); after CGHS mandated a 30% discount to MRP, margins turned negative, prompting discontinuation.

Net benefit calculation: CGHS rate revision gave a gross net benefit of INR 200 crore, which nets to INR 140 crore after GST impact; of the INR 140 crore, about INR 100-110 crore has already flowed in on an annualized basis, and INR 30-40 crore (linked to pending super-specialty rate implementation) is yet to flow in.

CGHS rate revision benefit has started flowing through in Q4 for all rates except super specialty rates; two hospitals have received super-specialty rates so far, balance pending and expected to phase in over the year.

This CGHS price change (first in 14 years) applies to all chemotherapies, not just specific drugs; CGHS patients can still access the drugs at a discount via CGHS dispensaries, but ECHS and other PSU patients lack dispensary access, causing patient complaints and potential reversal risk that management could not commit a timeline to.

Q4 FY26 already reflects the full impact of the drug discontinuation, which began in October 2025; Q1 FY27 onward will also reflect full impact, while CGHS price gain will only start showing fully from this quarter as more hospitals get super-specialty rates.

Occupancy ramp curve: units generally break even at 50-55% occupancy; perform well at 60-65%; the largest incremental margin/EBITDA benefit ('hockey stick') comes from moving occupancy from 60-65% up to ~80%.

subsections.label: Phased brownfield/greenfield rollout approach
points: Brownfield and greenfield capacity has always historically been opened in a phased manner (Nanavati, Mohali, Smart, and previously Shalimar Bagh, Vaishali) — as soon as floors are ready, there is immediate demand ('tearing need') for those floors, so they are put to use as quickly as possible.
Costs related to brownfield capacity are not linear; full operating leverage benefit is realized only as balance beds progressively get occupied over subsequent quarters.
New bed openings temporarily push up ALOS as hospitals are less efficient with new capacity than pre-expansion; this shows up as slightly lower ARPOB even as occupancy stays high.
For a facility like Max Smart (400 beds), rollout started with about 100 beds before phased addition of the balance.

subsections.label: Gurgaon greenfield rollout plan
points: Gurgaon greenfield (500 beds) commissioning pushed to end of FY27 (previously guided second half, now end of second half) due to labour attrition around Bengal elections/festive season and an LPG shortage disrupting labourer meal access; company has since started providing meals on-site for ~1,100-1,200 contractor workers to mitigate this.
Similar to the Dwarka playbook (300 beds, started with 140), Gurgaon will start with roughly 200 beds operational, break even on that base, then progressively roll out balance beds.
Management guides FY28 breakeven for the Gurgaon greenfield within the year of operation, based on the Dwarka precedent (guided 1-year breakeven, actually achieved in 6 months).

subsections.label: Lucknow multi-location cluster strategy
points: Two land parcels in Lucknow — 27 acres at Gomti Nagar and 5+ acres at Shaheed Path — will be developed as a multi-location cluster rather than a single mega-facility, enabling two separate senior clinician teams (avoiding a choke point on senior specialists such as a single Chairman of Cardiology/Oncology).

Shaheed Path (14 km from Gomti Nagar) is viewed as complementary/multi-location rather than cannibalizing; land capacity there could ultimately support up to ~900 beds versus the initially planned 700.

Gomti Nagar capacity plans to expand further (200-300 more beds) even as Shaheed Path is built out; over the next decade Gomti Nagar alone could reach close to 2,000 beds, reflecting the strength of clinical programs in the region.
Cluster approach mirrors the benefits already seen in Delhi and other markets — combining the benefits of brownfield expansion with the benefits of multiple locations.

subsections.label: Expansion pipeline delays context
points: No regulatory clearances are currently pending beyond what has been anticipated for the pipeline projects.

Past delays were caused by external/incident-driven factors rather than regulatory approval issues: GRAP 3 pollution-related construction shutdowns, LPG shortage-driven manpower shortages (linked to the Iran war), and a Delhi tree-transplantation Supreme Court contempt matter (Lieutenant Governor vs Supreme Court) that stalled forest approval.

subsections.label: CGHS chemotherapy drug discontinuation risk
points: CGHS rate revision (first price change in 14 years) required all chemotherapy drugs to be provided at a 30% discount to MRP; since prior margins were only ~15-16%, this made continued dispensing loss-making, prompting discontinuation for institutional (CGHS/ECHS/PSU) patients — this is an industry-wide phenomenon but disproportionately affects Max given its outsized oncology and institutional-business mix.

ECHS and other PSU patients cannot access CGHS dispensaries (unlike CGHS pensioners), creating access issues, patient complaints, and uncertainty; management believes it 'stands to reason' this could be reconsidered/reversed but could not provide a timeline.

There is uncertainty on whether/when displaced patients return to hospital pharmacies versus continuing with alternate (potentially less clinically preferred) medicines or moving to disorganized-sector/smaller nursing homes.

The Network generated free cash flows of INR 581 crore during the quarter. INR 328 crore was deployed towards ongoing capacity expansion projects and facility upgrades at newer facilities.

FIRSTCRY.about: Founded in 2010, Brainbees Solutions Limited offers products for mothers, babies, and kids through its online platform 'FirstCry'.[1]

quarters.summary: Consolidated revenue grew 13% YoY in Q1 FY27, the strongest in five years, with a 34% YoY improvement in loss reduction after tax. India multi-channel delivered its strongest growth in seven quarters (17.7%-18%) and remains PAT positive; international business grew 12% YoY with adjusted EBITDA losses down 22.3% YoY; GlobalBees was flattish in revenue but adjusted EBITDA grew 308% YoY (temporary flatness due to a planned brand transition expected to normalize by Q3); the pre-school segment grew 47% in revenue and 65% in adjusted EBITDA. Management expects India multi-channel growth to remain elevated on the back of RocketBees, FC Qwik and offline width-to-depth initiatives, gross margin recovery (280 bps Q4 YoY loss, 20 bps recovered in Q1) to accelerate from Q2 onward as diapering competitive intensity eases and manufacturing input costs are fully passed on to customers by end of Q2, with full margin normalization expected by Q3/Q4.

subsections.label: Gross margin bridge (India multi-channel)
points: Q4 FY26 saw a 280 bps YoY gross margin decline driven by two factors: (1) competitive intensity in diapering category (~15% of business) pressuring margins, and (2) manufacturing business margin impact from rupee depreciation and increase in crude-linked raw material prices.

Only 20 bps of the 280 bps lost margin was recovered in Q1 FY27, but management expects faster recovery in subsequent quarters as diapering competitive intensity eases and manufacturing input costs are fully passed to customers by end of Q2 FY27.

EBITDA margin YoY decline of 290 bps in Q1 FY27 is bridged as: 260 bps from gross margin reduction (Q4 onwards) + 30 bps net impact of increased logistics costs (RocketBees/FC Qwik initiatives) offset partly by operating leverage recovery in marketing spend and fixed costs.

subsections.label: Capital allocation / cash
points: Management stated the company has not discussed buybacks or acquisition-related matters internally or at the board level despite having sufficient cash (context from prior guidance ledger carried forward as unaddressed in this call).

subsections.label: India Multi-Channel
points: Core business segment reflecting highest ever revenue growth, driven by initiatives shared over the last several quarters.
Offline GMV grew in the mid-teens, aided by product portfolio realignment from width to depth strategy, driving footfalls and conversions.
Business remains PAT positive for Q1 FY27.
Diapering category witnessed heightened competitive intensity during the quarter but has started to soften in the ongoing quarter.
Non-diapering portfolio (85% of GMV) remains robust and continues to perform well.
Revenue growth of 18% YoY accompanied by moderation in gross margin YoY, resulting in lower EBITDA margin YoY.

India revenue growth (18%) exceeded GMV growth (12%) due to the mix of online, offline and manufacturing revenue, plus a minor MRP reduction impact from GST 2.0 implementation in Q2, which affects GMV (MRP-based) more than net revenue.

subsections.label: International Business (Middle East)
points: Continued focus on sustainable growth while reducing adjusted EBITDA losses.
Geopolitical disruptions ongoing in the Middle East; however business sustained healthy growth with higher potential once environment stabilizes.
Objective is to achieve EBITDA-neutral business as soon as possible.

Breakeven timeline not disclosed specifically, but trajectory of gross margin expansion, reducing losses, and improving unit economics viewed as key inputs; comfort should come from input metrics (home brand mix, high-margin brand curation, high-quality customer acquisition, service levels) rather than a specific quarter target.

subsections.label: GlobalBees
points: Revenue was almost flattish for the quarter — described as a temporary state, not a long-term structural change.

Key factor affecting growth was a planned transition in one of the core brands involving shifting of business warehouse and inventory; transition expected to complete in Q2, with growth expected to bounce back starting Q3.

If a nominal growth assumption plus the ~2% Flipkart settlement impact is added back, YoY growth for the quarter would have been in the high teens, supporting management's view that this is not a structural issue.
Growth is entirely organic; last acquisition was in September 2022.
Margin profile for core brands remains strong; continued focus on expanding margins despite slight gross margin drop, with overall adjusted EBITDA improving meaningfully.

subsections.label: Pre-school segment (fourth business segment)
points: Both revenue and EBITDA growth were very strong in Q1, described as best-in-class growth for the segment.
Currently around 500+ pre-schools under the FirstCry Intellitots umbrella; management aims to grow rapidly, targeting not less than 1,000 preschools over the next couple of years.
Business model is royalty-based, meaning segment revenue will always be a small proportion of overall consolidated revenue relative to the much larger revenue accrued at the franchisee level.
No near-term M&A plans in this vertical; management stated it is too early to comment on M&A and the current focus is on organic growth via partnering with more franchisees/business partners.
Strategic fit: many parents/kids in the preschool ecosystem are also power users of FirstCry retail.

subsections.label: RocketBees (internal faster delivery framework)
points: Started around calendar year start of last year (Jan-March 2026 period); expanded from 62 to 72 cities since last update.
Reached target of covering ~50% of total online shipment volume under RocketBees umbrella by end of June quarter, as promised.
Delivering approximately 20% improvement in turnaround time (TAT) versus third-party delivery framework, with lesser RTOs and improved customer experience.
Management plans to continue growing network and area under coverage.

subsections.label: FC Qwik (quick delivery layer)
points: Started as an experiment/pilot around December last year; expanded from a pilot in 5 cities to a full-fledged strategy in 12 cities.
Leverages COCO stores, dark store infrastructure and warehouses built out in specific cities/pincodes.

TAT reduced from three hours to two hours in many cities/pincodes; management aims to reduce further, though not to 10-15 minute quick-commerce timelines given the far larger product assortment (fashion and non-fashion).
Overall ambition is 10% of total shipment volume onto FC Qwik platform, with 20% target within specific operating pin-codes.

subsections.label: Offline product assortment realignment (width to depth)
points: Product portfolio realigned from width to depth strategy, fully scaled out; impact visible from last quarter and continuing this quarter.
Strategy drove both footfalls and conversions, contributing to 15% GMV growth in offline channel.
New store expansion had been paused to align product portfolio and restore capital efficiency; company now resuming store expansion given two quarters of positive impact observed.

subsections.label: Diapering competitive intensity
points: Diapering category (15% of business) witnessed heightened competitive intensity during the quarter, driven by aggressive quick-commerce and horizontal e-commerce/pharmacy players entering with capital and offering disproportionate/aggressive limited-period pricing, echoing a similar dynamic seen in 2015-2016.

Competitive intensity has started to soften/ease in the ongoing quarter (Q2), with market signals showing reduced intensity; management expects normalization over the next couple of quarters, aided by capital market dynamics (e.g., IPO postponements) pushing competitors to focus more on gross margin and bottom line.

New entrants such as Apollo Pharmacy and MedPlus launching their own diaper private labels cited by an analyst as a competitive risk; management noted diapering is a complex, retention-sensitive category where private labels struggle to achieve high retention given it is used on a baby.

subsections.label: Input cost / currency-driven margin pressure
points: Manufacturing business gross margin impacted by rupee depreciation and increase in crude-linked raw material prices.
Company has started passing on these increased input costs to customers and expects to fully recover the impact by end of Q2 FY27.
Combined with diapering competitive intensity, these two factors accounted for the 280 bps YoY gross margin decline seen from Q4 FY26 onward.

subsections.label: Geopolitical disruptions (Middle East)
points: Ongoing geopolitical disruptions in the Middle East affecting the operating environment for the international business, though the market has sustained healthy growth and has higher potential once the environment stabilizes.

subsections.label: Logistics cost front-loading
points: Increase in logistics cost attributable to RocketBees and FC Qwik initiatives contributed to part of the EBITDA margin decline (part of the 30 bps residual in the 290 bps YoY EBITDA margin bridge for India multi-channel).

subsections.label: India multi-channel growth outlook
points: Management believes structural growth rate will remain elevated in subsequent quarters, driven by online and offline initiatives, not a one-off phenomenon.
Growth rate for India multi-channel expected to remain elevated for FY27 based on RocketBees, FC Qwik, and offline assortment initiatives.

subsections.label: Gross margin recovery outlook
points: Margin recovery in subsequent quarters expected to be much faster than the 20 bps recovered in Q1, as diapering competitive intensity eases and manufacturing input cost pass-through completes by end of Q2 FY27.

Expect diapering-related margin loss to reduce dramatically in H2, though full normalization of the diapering component may take until Q4; rupee depreciation/crude-linked cost component expected to be fully recovered by Q2/Q3.
Non-diapering portfolio (85% of business) expected to continue accruing higher margins via increasing fashion and home brand contribution.

subsections.label: International business outlook
points: Continue focus on reducing adjusted EBITDA losses sustainably while growing revenue; objective to become EBITDA neutral as soon as possible.

No specific breakeven quarter provided; management prefers to track input metrics (home brand mix, high-margin brand curation, quality customer acquisition, service levels) as leading indicators of the path to profitability.

subsections.label: GlobalBees outlook
points: Growth expected to bounce back starting Q3 FY27 once the planned brand transition (warehouse/inventory shift) completes in Q2.

subsections.label: Pre-school segment outlook
points: Management remains bullish, expecting continued organic growth; targeting not less than 1,000 preschools over the next couple of years.
No near-term plans for M&A in this vertical; too early to comment.

subsections.label: Store expansion outlook
points: Plans to add close to 100 stores (net of attritions) in the current fiscal year (FY27).
FY28 expected to be even better given no lost quarter of preparation, as the transition period impacting new store openings is now behind the company.

quarters.summary: Management guided to a much superior FY27 growth for India multi-channel (both offline and online), continued international loss reduction toward breakeven, GlobalBees sustainable growth post brand-rationalization (completing by Q1 FY27), and continued expansion of RocketBees/Qwik initiatives, while flagging transitory gross margin pressure from rupee depreciation/crude-linked inputs (expected to recover by Q2 FY27) and prolonged (4-6 quarter) diapering category competitive intensity.

subsections.label: India Multi-channel
points: Despite competitive intensity continuing in the quarter, offline channel initiative (mentioned in last 2 quarters) went live in Q4 SH26 and yielded mid-teens GMV growth in offline channel.
Management believes trajectory of sequential quarterly better growth will continue in FY27, expecting overall better growth for FY27 vs entire FY26.
India multi-channel business remained PAT and cash flow positive for the entire FY26.
Diapering category continued to witness heightened competitive intensity during the quarter, pressuring both growth and margins.
Non-diapering portfolio (>85% of GMV) remains robust and continues to perform well.

80 bps of EBITDA loss recovered in Q4 owing to operating leverage benefits.
Offline growth driven by product-mix fix (width to depth strategy) launched around March SH26, which significantly improved COCO business performance.
Online GMV growth roughly steady at 10.5%-12% across FY26 quarters; management attributes lower relative growth partly to front-loaded logistics costs with lagged benefit.

subsections.label: International (Middle East)
points: Continues to face elevated promotional pressures from horizontal commerce players that entered the market in late Q3 FY25.
Management remains focused on sustainable growth, targeting reduction of adjusted EBITDA losses to zero via gross margin improvement, home brand expansion, and sales mix expansion.

Significant gross margin expansion (250 bps) attributed to home brand share growth (incl. fashion share within home brands), improved margins in both home brand and third-party brands, and operational efficiencies as business scales.
International business ~5 years old has already achieved gross margins comparable to India multi-channel at 8 years old — considered on-track.
AOV in international ~4x higher than India business.
Live in UAE since October 2019 and in KSA since August 2022; app available in both English and Arabic; operates largely as an online platform in both markets.

Favorable demographics: birth rates slightly higher in KSA vs India; higher per-capita spend in KSA/UAE vs India; childcare market size forecast significantly high in international markets (though lower than India).

subsections.label: GlobalBees
points: Structured into four broad categories: home utilities, home appliances, fashion & lifestyle, and beauty personal care/health & personal care.

Over the last year, portfolio rationalization has focused on brands driving growth and profitability; brands with lower revenue growth and losses are being rationalized, nearly at trail end, with completion targeted by Q1 FY27.
20% consolidated revenue growth is lower than 27%/28% core category growth purely due to brand rationalization.
All growth mentioned is organic — last acquisition made at GlobalBees was in September 2022.
Continuous improvement trend in bottom line: FY23 negative, FY24 EBITDA neutral, FY26 at 3% adjusted EBITDA post-corporate expenses (including rationalization impact, adjusted for ESOP cost).

subsections.label: Others (Preschool)
points: Preschool business continuously growing — count more than doubled from 208 (end FY24) to over 400+ equivalent by end FY26; student enrollment nearly 3x in 2 years.
Healthy revenue growth of 11% with 220 bps EBITDA margin improvement.

subsections.label: 6-12 Years Age Category Expansion
points: Positive traction continuing in the 6-12 years age category, which remains the fastest growing part of the business by children's age group.
Assortment being built to be more conducive to this segment.
Long-term cohort data (in supplementary slides) shows strong retention — consumers acquired 10 years back continue to transact, indicating good future potential for this segment.

subsections.label: Competitive Landscape / Diapering Pressure
points: Diapering margin pressure is a platform phenomenon, not specific to any low-cost or particular brand — seen across both listed and unlisted Quick-commerce and horizontal commerce platforms.

Price competition from both Q-commerce and horizontal players considered irrational; typically such cycles subside after a few quarters (4-6 quarters expected, based on precedent from 2016-2017 when a similar situation normalized).

subsections.label: Delivery Model vs Competition
points: Management declines to directly compare RocketBees to competitors' (e.g., Amazon, Nykaa, Flipkart) delivery models, citing category complexity (SKU size range from 10-gram diaper pin to 30kg toy car) requiring specialized supply chain handling.
Different companies use different last-mile models — some third-party aggregated, some dedicated; no single industry-standard model.
Company aims to continue improving RocketBees coverage but considers reaching 100% RocketBees coverage very difficult.

points: Expanded from 13 cities (Q2) to 22 cities (Q3) to 62 cities (Q4 FY26).
