subsections.label: Competitive dynamics on price points
points: Some competitors continue selling at INR 4.50/INR 9 price points (below Britannia's INR 5/INR 10) rather than moving to full price points, though management expects other biscuit players to gradually move to full price points.

A competitor (implied Parle) reportedly stated double-digit volume growth in media interviews; management attributes this possibly to that competitor's higher wholesale/rural channel mix (as high as ~40% of business vs Britannia's 25%) giving a volume advantage in the currently-stressed dual-pricing channels.

On value-share basis, management does not see meaningful share shift from the INR4.5/9 vs INR5/10 price point dynamic, though acknowledges some wholesalers/rural retailers may prefer competitor packs opportunistically for higher margin.

subsections.label: Growth vs margin strategy
points: When asked to choose between growth/market share and margin, management stated intent to keep growing market share while remaining adept at managing margins — described as a 'careful orchestra' — with smarter fund allocation and marketing spend directed where it has the most impact.

subsections.label: Snacking category comparison
points: Management does not believe there is a dramatic consumption shift toward other snacking categories (chocolates, noodles) reporting ~30% growth; attributes their faster growth to more visible/noticeable price drops from GST reduction on higher-priced packs (independent of the INR5 conundrum), not to a shift away from biscuits.

subsections.label: Strategic priorities
points: Continue driving efficiencies in sales, distribution and supply chain channels via existing efficient networks.
Stronger investment in brand experiences, with more experiential brand-building strategies.
Intense work on innovation, adjacencies and future platforms to build a portfolio for the future.
Realigning teams to create a 'Many Indias' structure — agile, start-up-culture teams enabling faster, regionally customized decision-making; output expected over coming quarters.
Commitment to sustainability across all initiatives.

subsections.label: Future growth vectors and platform expansion
points: Management confirmed intent to add more platforms/adjacencies going forward, describing signature brands (Treat, Little Hearts, Jim Jam) as currently underleveraged and needing amplification alongside new platforms.

Company aims to move toward being a 'more complete foods company', balancing continued relentless cost/efficiency focus (now ingrained in company DNA) with new growth pillars including brand investment, premiumization, and new verticals.

subsections.label: M&A stance
points: Company has not done inorganic acquisitions to date but is actively scanning opportunities with serious intent.
Acquisition criteria: must help address something new, address an unaddressed consumer need, or provide a skill/technology/capability the company lacks.
Company has created a new platform in the health space, which will be an active consideration for expansion in coming months.

subsections.label: West Asia conflict / geopolitical risk
points: Strait of Hormuz lockup disrupted vessel dispatch for international business manufactured out of Oman/Dubai, impacting international revenue and profitability.
Sharp rise in fuel costs and ocean freight rates due to the conflict.
Domestic concerns initially arose around LPG shortage but were managed without material disruption to Indian manufacturing operations.
Laminate price inflation attributed to the war impact in the Middle East raising granule prices; laminate prices rose again from March and remained elevated into April.

subsections.label: Dual pricing / GST transition risk
points: Dual pricing in the market (competitors at INR 4.5/9 vs Britannia at INR 5/10) caused transaction slowdown in rural and wholesale/B2B channels (25% of business), impacting growth through January-March, worsened by West Asia in March.
Management could not quantify precise bps impact but confirmed the effect on transactions; expects normalization during the current quarter.

subsections.label: Commodity/input cost inflation risk
points: Fuel (LPG/CNG) inflation affecting all players; laminate inflation ongoing; milk prices seasonally rising with added uncertainty from potential El Nino/warming; palm oil prices up (though covered via forward buying); wheat/flour prices recently rising due to unseasonal rains, heat and arrival quality issues after an earlier favorable trend.

subsections.label: Competitive/channel risk
points: Competitor with higher wholesale/rural exposure may have gained relative volume advantage during the dual-pricing disruption period.

subsections.label: Near-term normalization outlook
points: Management expects wholesale/rural channel pricing to normalize and volumes to recover during the current quarter (Q1 FY27) as dual pricing fades and competitors move to full price points.

West Asia supply chain has been de-risked via shifting sourcing/manufacturing (e.g., Mundra) so as not to depend on the Hormuz Strait route going forward; optimization of India/international sourcing for key geographies expected to be fully operational by mid-May.
Biscuit industry expected to see sequential growth pickup from June onward due to monsoon and school reopening season.

subsections.label: FY27 outlook
points: Management expressed confidence in generating demand and having a good year in FY27 via strategic levers (premiumization, future platforms, Many Indias, higher ad spend/marketing investment), while flagging external uncontrollable factors like monsoon.

On pricing/elasticity, management does not expect major elasticity impact from calibrated price increases given category dynamics and because the increases essentially normalize conditions to levels of ~6-7 months ago when demand was good.

On margins for FY27, management stated confidence in managing cost pressures (fuel, laminate inflation) within a certain band via strong CEP discipline and selective, ROI-driven brand investment, without providing a specific margin number.

subsections.label: Pricing actions
points: Calibrated price increases starting this quarter (Q1 FY27) to mitigate cost pressures, including both grammage adjustments and price increases on packs priced above INR 10.

guidance_ledger.statement: With pricing getting normalized, we can see that during this quarter, they will get normalized, and hence, volumes in those channels will come back.

guidance_ledger.metric: West Asia supply chain de-risking / sourcing optimization
guidance_ledger.statement: We are also optimizing our sourcing between India and international manufacturing facilities for key geographies to mitigate supply-related challenges, expected to be fully operational by mid-May.
We are quite confident that by the end of the quarter, the market would quite likely stabilize on the domestic front... we are quite confident that we will do better this quarter.
We are quite confident that our portfolio, the strategy... we are quite confident that we will be able to generate demand and have a good year.
I don't think that pricing either a bit upwards or either a bit downwards is going to have any major impact from an elasticity point of view... the demand situation will remain fairly strong.
There will be calibrated price increases starting from this quarter... this includes both grammage adjustment and some of the packs which are above INR 10, some kind of a price increase.
The team is confident that within a certain band, we'll be able to manage it [margins amid cost pressure and investment].
We also know that the biscuit industry starts to have a sequential growth from June onwards when monsoon starts to hit and when children start going back to school.

guidance_ledger.metric: Value/realization growth from GST pack economics
guidance_ledger.statement: We are also positive that we will have a good realization... if it happens like that, we are happy that you brought it to the fore.
We will be adding more platforms, and you will hear about that... you would hear about them in the future.

There is active scanning and there is a very serious intent... we also have created a new platform on health. So that also would be an active consideration as we will expand this in the coming months.
We have to keep going stronger on market share, but... we are also adept at managing margins. So it is a careful orchestra which we will play very nicely.

risk_register.risk: West Asia conflict (Strait of Hormuz lockup) disrupting vessel dispatch and manufacturing logistics for international business (Oman/Dubai)
risk_register.note: Impacted international revenue and profitability last quarter; also drove up fuel costs and ocean freight rates.

risk_register.risk: LPG/fuel supply constraints in India due to West Asia conflict
risk_register.note: No material disruption to Indian manufacturing operations; managed well despite initial concerns.

risk_register.risk: Laminate price inflation
risk_register.note: Prices fell toward end of Q4 but rose again from March and remained elevated in April due to war impact in Middle East raising granule prices.

risk_register.risk: Dual pricing / GST transition impact on wholesale and rural channels
risk_register.note: Caused transaction slowdown in B2B/wholesale (25% of business) through Jan-Mar; expected to normalize this quarter.

risk_register.risk: Milk price inflation with El Nino uncertainty
risk_register.note: Prices on an upswing; usually decline in winter, but El Nino/higher warming expected and could impact this dynamic.

risk_register.risk: Wheat/flour price uptick
risk_register.note: After a receding/positive trend, last 1 month saw prices rise due to unseasonal rains, high heat and quality issues in arrivals.

risk_register.risk: Palm oil price rise correlated with fuel costs
risk_register.note: Company forward-buys and is covered for next 5 months at a favorable rate.

risk_register.risk: General fuel (LPG/CNG) inflation
risk_register.note: Inflationary for all players; company pays market rate inflation.

risk_register.risk: Competitive volume advantage from wholesale/rural mix during dual-pricing disruption
risk_register.note: A competitor with higher wholesale/rural exposure (~40% vs Britannia's 25%) may have gained relative volume advantage.

themes.label: West Asia geopolitical disruption
themes.note: Strait of Hormuz lockup disrupted vessel dispatch from Oman/Dubai manufacturing, hitting international revenue/profitability and raising fuel and freight costs; company shifted North America-bound manufacturing back to Mundra to mitigate.

themes.label: GST dual-pricing transition
themes.note: Dual pricing between INR 4.5/9 (competitors) and INR 5/10 (Britannia) packs caused transaction slowdown in wholesale/rural channels through Jan-Mar, expected to normalize this quarter.

themes.label: Input cost inflation
themes.note: Wheat/flour recently turned inflationary after a favorable trend; palm oil, laminate, fuel and milk all inflationary, though palm oil and wheat are well covered via forward buying/inventory.

themes.label: E-commerce / quick-commerce acceleration
themes.note: E-commerce salience rose to 6% (adjusted ~12%+) of domestic sales with quick commerce at ~70% of e-commerce (rising toward 85%), enabling premiumization of assortment and adjacency growth at 2.7-3x.

themes.label: Premiumization and brand investment
themes.note: Company stepping up advertising/brand investment (driving 18% growth in other expenses) and new launches (Cheeze Dipped, Doodh Marie Gold, Good Day Butter, Fudge It) to build premium and adjacency portfolio.

themes.label: Cost efficiency program (CEP)
themes.note: CEP discipline has grown 10x versus 2013-14 and doubled versus 2021, seen as key lever to manage margins amid fuel/laminate inflation and rising brand investment.

themes.label: Growth vs margin balance / market share strategy
themes.note: Management stated intent to keep gaining market share while also managing margins carefully via smarter, ROI-focused fund allocation amid competitive and cost pressures.

pressing_questions: What is the rough order of magnitude (in bps) by which the dual-pricing issue in wholesale/rural channels dampened sales growth — 200, 500, 700 bps?

Given the mathematics of INR 5/INR 10 packs under lower GST leading to higher per-pack realization for the company (as seen in noodles/chocolates), should biscuits not see a significant/faster acceleration in value growth once the pricing transition stabilizes?
Is there any implication for EBITDA margins in FY27 given cost pressures alongside innovation/strategy investments, or are cost-saving efforts sufficient to mitigate these investments?

Given calibrated price hikes across the industry and transitory fuel pricing pressure, will FY27 see stronger sales growth than FY26, and how does management view the domestic demand environment and price elasticity?

HNDFDS.about: Hindustan Foods Limited is an India-based company, which is engaged in contract manufacturing of various FMCG products including food, home care, personal care, beverages etc. They also do manufacturing of leather shoes and accessories

quarters.summary: Hindustan Foods delivered its highest-ever quarterly PAT (up 33% YoY) in Q1 FY27 despite temporary footwear cost headwinds, and reaffirmed FY27 PAT guidance of INR200-220 crores (34-48% growth over FY26). Management expects to commercialize manufacturing capacities exceeding INR500 crores in FY27 (signed projects of ~INR340 crores plus INR150 crores carried forward from FY26), is optimistic about sustaining growth into FY28 and beyond, and expects the footwear division to return to profitability in the coming months as H2 order books are full.

subsections.label: P&L drivers
points: Total income growth of 18% YoY reflects strong start to FY27.
EBITDA growth of 26% YoY reflects improving operating leverage and better asset utilization across the manufacturing platform.
PBT and PAT both grew 33% YoY, marking the highest ever quarterly PAT, attributed to resilience of diversified manufacturing platform, disciplined execution and improving operating leverage.
Quarter's performance was impacted by cost pressure in footwear business from higher raw material costs and revised wage rates, totaling ~INR6 crores impact for Q1 FY27.

Company is proactively addressing footwear cost headwinds by securing alternate raw material sources, working with customers on cost pass-through mechanisms, and driving operational efficiency; expects these to progressively mitigate impact and support margin recovery over coming quarters.

subsections.label: Capital allocation
points: Company follows a disciplined, customer-led approach to investing with clear focus on returns, capital efficiency and timely commercialization.
FY27 capex (~INR500 crores) is expected to be larger than the record capex executed in FY26.

Company aims to continue investing internal accruals on a 1:1 basis (no reliance on outside funds) to sustain growth for the next few years, while maintaining 1:1 debt-equity ratio even for new projects, leading to some interest cost outflow.
Endeavour is that shared manufacturing facilities should deliver a much higher ROCE than the 18% threshold, but current numbers are not there yet mainly due to the shoe business drag.
No revaluation of assets has been done despite many factories being old and depreciated; business model is not contingent on revaluation, but that value sits unlocked on the balance sheet.

subsections.label: GST / accounting matters
points: Duty inversion in GST continues to affect cash flows of some business units.
Steps taken to address GST inversion issues will continue to result in higher growth in profitability numbers compared to revenue numbers.

Because of GST inversion, company is encouraging some customers to move to a model where customers supply raw material and packing material, so revenue will recognize only conversion cost — this will cause disproportionate rise in gross block, EBITDA and PAT versus sales growth.

key_figures.label: Footwear order book/capacity status Q2 FY27 onwards
Company scale-up (PAT)
key_figures.value: from INR12 crores to INR200 crores

subsections.label: Home & Personal Care (HPC)
points: HPC remains at maximum capacity, supported by consistent demand and efficient manufacturing operations; traction seen in demand across all categories and all sites.
Division delivered a record performance this quarter.
Integration of the Aurangabad Personal Care facility successfully completed, production stabilized, plant operating seamlessly within the network.
Liquid category of home care is growing double-digit in volumes across the country, becoming a tailwind for HFL.
Management is 'materially' more bullish on HPC now vs. 3-6 months ago given increased traction/demand, though remains cautious given macro variability.

subsections.label: Food & Beverages
points: Continued healthy momentum across multiple categories; Coimbatore, Nashik and Mysore units operating at record production levels supported by efficient operations and sustained demand.
Beverage division had an excellent season, validating belief that beverages will be a major growth avenue for this division.
Expanding manufacturing platform with addition of a Greek yogurt facility in Goa, marking entry into another high-growth category.

subsections.label: Ice Cream
points: Delivered another strong quarter supported by robust summer season and record production volumes across facilities.

Successfully commissioned state-of-the-art Panipat facility (20,000 tons capacity) during the quarter; continuing to expand ice cream manufacturing capacities to cater to growing customer demand and support long-term category growth.
Continuing to improve asset utilization at Nashik operations by adding new customers across both ice cream and cone manufacturing facilities.

subsections.label: Healthcare / OTC Pharma
points: Strengthening capabilities by adding new customers across syrup, tablets and lozenges while progressing ayurvedic wellness expansion at Baddi.
Initiated certification process for Class III medical devices at Chennai facility, supporting expansion into regulated international markets.
Actively pursuing new export opportunities for personal care portfolio manufactured at Baddi; engaging with international customers/partners.

OTC Pharma site approved; started commercial production for 2 more multinational companies in addition to existing customer; Baddi facility expected to reach 100% capacity utilization in the next 6 months to a year; no new capex announced for this segment currently due to customer gestation timelines.

subsections.label: Footwear
points: Made steady progress by expanding manufacturing footprint and strengthening customer relationships; added new customers; expanded capacities across North and South India.
Order book and capacities from Q2 FY27 onwards are full for rest of the financial year; strong demand from reputed industry brands.

Operations hit by Middle East geopolitical crisis causing short-term logistics/supply chain disruptions; had to procure material at higher prices and increased freight; also hit by large minimum wage increase in Haryana (~30% increase).

Shoe industry works on fixed pricing for the season — prices for finished goods and raw materials fixed 6-12 months in advance; cost increases could not be passed through to brands mid-season, unlike other business categories with pass-through mechanisms.
Company is in discussions with brands for the coming season to convince them to absorb some of the cost, which they have agreed to; may be able to pass on costs going forward.
Price inertia could work in HFL's favor when Middle East crisis resolves and commodity prices fall, since brands won't reduce prices either.
Confident division will return to profitability in coming months; customers expected to support in mitigating losses.

Full order book driven by both existing customer wins (higher order books) and new customer wins domestically and among multinational companies; some customers who had stopped business during the transition have returned.
South units (previously on the learning curve) now also have a full order book.
Consolidation of operations over ~2 years is starting to pay off, expected in H2 FY27.

Headcount of ~5,000 people; capacity utilization in Q1 was poor due to material availability issues and freight disruptions; from August onwards utilization improved to 80-90%; company ramping up via more hiring given labor-intensive nature.
Prior FY27 footwear turnover target of INR700-800 crores was referenced in prior quarter guidance; no explicit reiteration/update given this quarter beyond order book commentary.

subsections.label: Customer relationship / scale
points: Company has scaled from ~INR500 crores revenue to ~INR4,500-5,000 crores and from ~INR12 crores PAT to ~INR200 crores PAT over the years.
Company believes it defined the FMCG contract manufacturing industry in India and is the largest and most diversified contract manufacturer.
Established 5 different BUs with experienced CEOs bringing domain expertise, strengthening customer confidence.
Company likened its dependency by customers to a national airline — if it were to shut down for a few days, FMCG industry would face trouble.

Across all 5 BUs (HPC, Food & Beverages, Beverages, Ice Cream, Shoes, OTC Pharma) company is a significant partner for most customers; in some product categories may be the only manufacturer in the country, in others one of the largest.

key_figures.label: FY27 investment breakup - Home & Personal Care (Lucknow)
Total FY27 capex incl. carryforward from FY26
Silvassa facility expected full operational restoration

subsections.label: Expansion projects & commissioning timelines
points: Brownfield expansion at Silvassa expected to commence production during Q2 FY27.
Greenfield Lucknow facility continues to progress as planned for commissioning later this year.
Panipat ice cream facility successfully commissioned during the quarter (state-of-the-art), representing continued expansion of ice cream manufacturing capacity.
Food & Beverages investment of INR210 crores spread across 5 units: Coimbatore, Mysuru/Mysore, Goa, Aurangabad and Hyderabad (for the beverage part).
Ice Cream investment of INR80 crores at Panipat.
Home & Personal Care investment of INR50 crores at Lucknow, for a bar and a liquid line.
Beverage units (INR210 crores) expected to come online by December/January to catch the beverage season starting in January.
Most of these projects are on an anchor-tenant basis, i.e., capacities underwritten by the principal customers, reducing capacity utilization risk unless execution timing/production is missed.

subsections.label: Silvassa flood disruption
points: Silvassa manufacturing facility disrupted by record rainfall in the region during July.
Production already partially restored; facility expected to be fully operational by end of August.
Facility is adequately insured; no material impact expected on long-term operations or growth plans.
Anecdote: a machine being imported from China for the Silvassa factory has been stuck at an Iranian liner ship for ~2.5 months due to the Middle East crisis, illustrating disruption severity.
Teams worked overnight to partially resume production within a week despite ~10 feet of water in the factory; expected fully back on board within August.

subsections.label: Capex trajectory and disclosure policy
points: FY27 will likely see capex larger than the record capex executed in FY26.
Company's policy is to announce capex only after projects are signed; hence prior quarter's disclosed figure of ~INR150 crores did not reflect the full pipeline under discussion.
Current project pipeline under discussion with customers (not yet signed) is approximately INR1,000 crores.
Hit/conversion ratio for pipeline-to-signed-project varies by customer and BU; company declines to quantify it, focusing instead on disclosing capex once signed.
Company expects to have a carryforward at end of FY27 similar in magnitude to the carryforward from FY26.

subsections.label: Capacity utilization disclosure policy
points: Company gives out footwear capacity utilization because it is a shared manufacturing site and does not reveal customer-specific performance.
Company avoids disclosing capacity utilization for dedicated factories because it could act as a proxy for a specific customer's business performance.

subsections.label: Export markets
points: Entire Dr. Scholl portfolio currently being exported to U.K., EU, Australia, New Zealand and Japan.

International business team (IBD) working strongly to open up the Middle East; had extended discussions with companies in UAE and Saudi Arabia, but this has been put on hold again due to the ongoing Middle East crisis.
Exports have taken a back seat in the last couple of months due to the Middle East crisis.
Discussions ongoing with large box retailers in the U.S.; ambiguity on tariffs continues, delaying conversion of potential orders.

Received potential orders for personal care products to be shipped to the U.S. from a U.S. personal care brand; all product development, trials, and mold investments completed, but orders on hold pending tariff/freight situation resolution.
Discussions have begun to leverage the India-U.K. FTA and India-EU FTA for footwear exports.
Class III medical device certification at Chennai facility will support export expansion into regulated international markets (EU, U.K.) over time.

subsections.label: Footwear raw material sourcing
points: ~50% of footwear raw materials are imported — fabrics, laces, eyelets, soles, and labels.

Middle East geopolitical crisis caused short-term logistics and supply chain disruptions, requiring procurement of material at higher prices and increased freight to maintain uninterrupted production.
Company securing alternate sources of raw materials to mitigate footwear cost pressure.

subsections.label: Regulatory / competitive landscape
points: FSSAI clampdown on label claims (e.g., '100% pure, natural') is expected to cause some disruption for brands in the near term, but management believes it will help move production toward the organized market in the long run, which should benefit contract manufacturers like HFL.
Label claims and marketing are under the purview of the brand, not the contract manufacturer, so HFL assumes no risk from such regulatory notices.

Management sees competition weakening as a positive dynamic as HFL scales, diversifies its customer base, and expands its product range, expecting improvement in profitability margins and capital-based ratios (ROE, ROCE) over time.

subsections.label: Category diversification outlook (3-year view)
points: Continued traction expected across at least 4 of 5 BUs.
Beverages continue to grow rapidly.
Ice cream had a fantastic season aided by weather; expected to continue delivering growth in coming years.
HPC liquid category witnessing double-digit volume growth nationally, becoming a tailwind.
Footwear expected to deliver from H2 FY27 given full order book and capacity expansion underway.

OTC Pharma: no new capex announced currently due to customer gestation timing, but Baddi site approved with commercial production starting for 2 more MNC customers; expected to reach 100% utilization in 6 months to a year.

subsections.label: New category entry
points: Management currently has no plans to enter other contract manufacturing categories like EMS, textiles/garments given full order book, ~INR500 crores of capex this year, and ~INR1,000 crores inquiry pipeline occupying management bandwidth.

subsections.label: Backward integration
points: Company has started a backward integration journey with the acquisition of a cone manufacturing facility for ice cream and setting up of a stick manufacturing facility in Lucknow.
Good experience in the last 1 year: managed to get existing customers to source from these 2 units, and also seeded new customers not currently part of the contract manufacturing business.

Backward integration seen as an interesting avenue to increase wallet share of existing customers and cross-sell to other customers; company actively exploring further backward integration and will share specific plans in the future.

subsections.label: Governance / risk management suggestion
points: An analyst suggested creating a risk management committee to address diverse risks (natural calamities, people/attrition risk, sourcing risk, geopolitical risk, team/personnel risk) given the company's diverse products, geographies, and categories; management called this an excellent suggestion.

subsections.label: Footwear-specific risks
points: Middle East crisis caused polymer prices to increase by ~50-60% and freight rates to nearly double (later cited as 4x increase), which could not be baked into fixed seasonal pricing.
Haryana minimum wage rates increased by ~30%, impacting footwear labor costs; this was a local/state-specific issue, not related to the new national labor code.

Footwear industry's fixed pricing structure (prices fixed 6-12 months in advance) makes it uniquely difficult to pass through mid-season raw material or wage cost increases, unlike other HFL businesses which have pass-through mechanisms.
Management believes such raw material/wage cost pass-through difficulty is unique to the footwear business and not expected in other divisions.

subsections.label: Natural disaster / logistics disruption
points: Record rainfall in July disrupted the Silvassa manufacturing facility; production partially restored, expected fully operational by end of August; facility is insured, no material long-term impact expected.
A machine being imported from China for the Silvassa factory has been stuck at an Iranian liner ship for ~2.5 months due to the Middle East crisis.

subsections.label: Geopolitical / macro risk
points: Middle East geopolitical crisis caused short-term logistics and supply chain disruptions across the footwear business.
U.S. tariff ambiguity is delaying conversion of potential U.S. personal care export orders.
Middle East expansion discussions with UAE/Saudi Arabia companies put on hold due to ongoing crisis.
Management remains circumspect about macroeconomic variability, citing volatile oil prices and flare-ups in the Middle East.

subsections.label: GST inverted duty structure
points: Duty inversion in GST continues to affect cash flows of some business units; steps being taken to address these issues.

key_figures.label: FY27 PAT guidance growth over FY26

subsections.label: Outlook commentary
points: Management reaffirms FY27 PAT guidance of INR200-220 crores (34-48% growth over FY26) despite footwear headwinds; too early to say PAT will land at the lower end of the guidance range due to footwear stress; will revisit with more granular details in coming quarters if needed.
Optimistic about sustaining growth momentum into FY28 and beyond, supported by continued customer engagement on new projects.

Priorities for FY27: commercialize new capacities on schedule (expected FY27 commercialized capacity >INR500 crores, with INR340 crores of new projects already signed), improve asset utilization, allocate capital prudently, and consistently enhance returns.

Long-term opportunity for FMCG contract manufacturing in India remains compelling, driven by increased outsourcing by consumer brands, rising consumption, premiumization, and growing preference for asset-light manufacturing.
Company will continue to invest internal accruals into productive assets targeting threshold ROCEs of 18%, aiming to grow without accessing outside funds.
Project pipeline under discussion with customers (not yet signed) stands at approximately INR1,000 crores.

guidance_ledger.statement: We reaffirm our FY27 PAT guidance of INR200 crores to INR220 crores, representing healthy growth of 34% to 48% over FY26.
Including investments already signed and projects under implementation, we expect to commercialize manufacturing capacities exceeding INR500 crores during FY27.
We have already signed on various projects totaling around INR340 crores in this financial year, in addition to INR150 crores worth of projects carried forward from FY26.
We continue to engage with customers for various new projects, which makes us optimistic about sustaining this growth in FY28 and beyond.
We are confident that our customers will support us in mitigating the losses incurred due to these causes and that the division will return to profitability in the coming months.
Starting from something like August onwards, we have nearly 80% to 90% capacity utilization; we are ramping up capacities by employing more people.

Our endeavor is that shared manufacturing facilities should deliver a much higher ROCE number than the threshold number of 18%; unfortunately, current published numbers are not there yet mainly because of the shoe business.
Project pipeline under discussion with customers is about INR1,000-odd crores; whether all will convert into orders is uncertain, but capex will continue to be announced as and when signed.

We will continue to invest monies generated from business into productive assets giving threshold ROCEs of 18%, growing without accessing outside funds, giving enough headroom to grow for the next few years.
I think the Baddi facility itself should be working at 100% capacity utilization in the next 6 months to a year.
After having executed record capex in FY26, it appears that FY27 will be larger than the previous year.
We will have an opening carryforward at the end of FY27 of a similar amount as last year.
Prior guidance was INR700-800 crores turnover for footwear in FY27; not explicitly reiterated or revised in this call.

Because of GST inversion and customer-supplied raw material arrangements, you will continue to see a disproportionate rise in our EBITDA and PAT as compared to revenues; likewise gross block, EBITDA, PAT rising disproportionately vs sales growth.

guidance_ledger.metric: Shared vs dedicated gross block split
guidance_ledger.statement: We believe it will be on the same range [61%-39%, roughly 60-40] in INR2,150 crores also.
We were hoping to be able to make this transition starting from Q1 and finish it by Q2. Now it looks like it will start in Q2 and finish by Q3.
EBITDA 10% is definitely achievable.

If all customers agree to change to conversion cost model, PAT margin could reach 10%, but purely as an accounting entry since sales would fall; on like-to-like basis it would be surprising for a contract manufacturer to achieve 10% PAT margin.
Mandate given to management is to grow EBITDA at 20% in each BU and deliver 20% ROE numbers, and company as a whole should grow at 20%.
At an individual project level, the minimum threshold remains the same, which is about 18%-odd.
We strive to be between 16% to 22% ROEs pretax, where we negotiate depending on customer, product category and location.

guidance_ledger.metric: New capex pipeline signed for FY27
guidance_ledger.statement: New projects worth approximately INR150 crores have already been signed up for FY27, including ~INR50 crores each in beverages, HPC and ice cream capacities; expected to grow with further announcements during the year.
Panipat facility alone (20,000 ton capacity) represents a 50% jump purely in ice cream facility production versus FY26's 35,000-40,000 tons; total production quantum will see a jump of more than 50%.
Currently avoiding giving guidance on sales numbers because of discussions on revenue recognition changes and inflation-driven pass-through effects, both of which do not affect company performance.
It is definitely achievable to get to 20% growth across BUs; by 2030, if consumption recovers and inflation eases, it should be easier given tailwinds.

guidance_ledger.metric: Silvassa liquid detergent & Lucknow detergent bar facility commissioning
guidance_ledger.statement: Silvassa liquid detergent project and Lucknow detergent bar facility are progressing well and expected to become operational during FY27.
Company is expanding its beverage platform through a new bottle capacity in Aurangabad and South India, both of which are expected to be commissioned during FY27.
We will probably, at the end of FY27, become the single largest independent bottler of beverages in the country.

risk_register.risk: Footwear raw material cost inflation (Middle East crisis-driven polymer/fabric price increases of 50-60%, freight up to 4x)
risk_register.note: Fixed seasonal pricing model in footwear prevents mid-season cost pass-through, unlike other HFL businesses.

risk_register.risk: Minimum wage rate increase in Haryana (~30%)
risk_register.note: Local/state-specific wage hike impacted footwear division; ~INR3 crores impact for the quarter; not related to the new national labor code.

risk_register.risk: Silvassa facility flood disruption (record July rainfall)
risk_register.note: Production partially restored; facility expected fully operational by end of August; adequately insured, no material long-term impact expected.

risk_register.risk: Middle East geopolitical crisis
risk_register.note: Caused logistics/supply chain disruptions in footwear, delayed a machine shipment stuck on an Iranian liner for ~2.5 months, and put Middle East export expansion discussions (UAE, Saudi Arabia) on hold.

risk_register.risk: U.S. tariff ambiguity

risk_register.note: Analyst suggested forming a dedicated risk management committee given company's diverse products/geographies; management agreed it was an excellent suggestion.

themes.label: Record profitability / operating leverage
themes.note: Highest-ever quarterly PAT (INR42.8 crores, +33% YoY) driven by EBITDA growth of 26% YoY and improving operating leverage across the diversified manufacturing platform.

themes.label: Footwear cost inflation headwind
themes.note: Footwear division hit by ~INR6 crores cost impact from Middle East crisis-driven raw material inflation (50-60% polymer/fabric price rise, 4x freight) and a ~30% Haryana minimum wage hike, with fixed seasonal pricing preventing pass-through; expected to return to profitability in coming months as H2 order book is full.

themes.label: Capex-led capacity expansion
themes.note: FY27 capex expected to exceed FY26's record levels, with INR340 crores of new projects signed and total commercialized capacity expected to exceed INR500 crores, spanning Food & Beverages, Ice Cream (Panipat) and HPC (Lucknow); project pipeline under discussion is ~INR1,000 crores.

themes.label: GST inverted duty structure / revenue recognition shift
themes.note: GST inversion continues to affect cash flows; customer-supplied raw material model shift will cause profitability metrics (EBITDA, PAT, gross block) to grow disproportionately faster than revenue.

themes.label: FY27 PAT guidance reiteration
themes.note: Company reaffirmed FY27 PAT guidance of INR200-220 crores (34-48% growth over FY26) despite footwear headwinds, stating it is too early to guide toward the lower end.

themes.label: Segment diversification & capital allocation transparency
themes.note: Management disclosed a ~INR1,000 crores project pipeline (beyond signed capex) for the first time, and reiterated policy of announcing capex only once signed, while declining to disclose category-level EBITDA or dedicated-facility utilization to protect customer confidentiality.

themes.label: Natural disaster / geopolitical disruption
themes.note: Silvassa facility disrupted by record July rainfall (insured, expected fully operational by end of August) and Middle East crisis caused logistics delays, including a machine stuck on an Iranian liner for ~2.5 months, and put Middle East export/expansion talks on hold.

key_takeaways: We delivered our highest ever quarterly PAT with a growth of nearly 1/3, 33% over last year.
We have already signed on various projects totaling to around INR340 crores in this financial year.
Including these investments and the projects already under implementation, we expect to commercialize manufacturing capacities exceeding INR500 crores during FY '27.
This gives us the confidence not only to reaffirm our FY '27 PAT guidance of INR200 crores to INR220 crores, but also makes us optimistic about sustaining this growth in FY '28 and beyond.
Total income for the quarter stood at INR1,207 crores, registering a growth of 18% over the corresponding quarter last year. EBITDA increased by 26% year-on-year to INR106.3 crores.
Profit before tax grew 33% year-on-year to INR56.6 crores, while profit after tax also increased 33% to INR42.8 crores, marking our highest ever quarterly PAT.

The quarter numbers were impacted due to cost pressure faced in our footwear business arising from higher raw material costs and revised wage rates, totaling to around INR6 crores impact for Q1 FY '27.
We remain confident of delivering our FY '27 profit after tax guidance of INR200 crores to INR220 crores, representing the healthy growth of 34% to 48% over FY '26.

Just extending that, if you want to maintain the internal in terms of your threshold ROCE, et cetera, among the pipeline, what is your hit ratio?

quarters.summary: FY26 was a record year for HFL with total income up 17% YoY to INR4,264 crores, EBITDA up 20% YoY to INR377 crores, and PAT at a record INR149 crores (+29% YoY), on the back of an ~INR700+ crore capex cycle. Management reiterated FY27 PAT guidance of INR200-220 crores, backed by a new INR150 crores project pipeline signed since April, ramp-up of newly commissioned capacities (Panipat, Aurangabad, cone/stick facilities), while flagging footwear division cost pressure from petrochemical/freight inflation and GST inverted-duty-structure related revenue recognition changes (gross-to-net) as ongoing headwinds being managed without impact on absolute profitability.

subsections.label: Balance sheet & capital allocation
points: FY26 marked commercialization of one of the largest investment cycles undertaken by the company.
Gross block increase reflects scale-up underway across multiple growth categories.
Company maintained prudent mix of internal accruals and debt while maintaining balance sheet discipline even during peak investment phase.
Net debt to equity of 0.84x is well within the company's internal comfort level of 1x.
Adjusted ROCE of 18.9% is after normalizing the newly commissioned and underutilized assets.

Cash flow during the year impacted by higher working capital deployment, primarily due to GST rate changes under the inverted duty structure effective September '25 and proactive inventory buildup to safeguard supply chain continuity amid geopolitical environment.
Working capital investment is currently not limiting or constraining capex investment; company has secured working capital credit across product lines.

Cash generation from operations as a percentage of EBITDA has declined given working capital constraints (inventory buildup and GST inversion), flagged by an analyst and acknowledged by management as an important shareholder monitoring parameter.

subsections.label: Capital employed reconciliation (Ind AS / Baddi)
points: Difference between reported net capital employed (per annual report) and disclosed net capital employed (per slide) is mainly due to Ind AS accounting treatment for the Baddi acquisition from Reckitt.

Baddi was an older plant with high gross block and high accumulated depreciation in the seller's books; company records the net difference (~INR220 crores) as its actual capex/cash paid, versus the higher accounting gross block and depreciation.
Management measures capital employed based on actual cash paid, not accounting gross block, to assess returns on money actually deployed.
Net capital employed figures are based on average equity (average of two years) and net debt reduced by cash on balance sheet.

Underutilized/to-be-commissioned asset base of INR508 crores is large because a large sum was invested in FY26, with many projects (e.g., Panipat, Aurangabad, cone facility) not contributing for the full year - Panipat started commercial production only in April, Aurangabad integrated from April 1, cone facility contributed only a couple of months.
Guidance assumes these assets will contribute for a full year once ramped to entire capacity.

subsections.label: ROCE/ROE framework
points: Company evaluates each project/acquisition on an 18% IRR threshold over a longish period.
Shared manufacturing assets are expected to deliver much higher ROCE than dedicated manufacturing assets, since shared manufacturing carries higher risk.
Dedicated manufacturing business targets ROEs (pretax) between 16% and 22%, depending on customer, product category, and location; returns are more humble but well predicted with low variability.

Blended shared:dedicated split of ~60:40 for the company as a whole may not hold true for individual segments — e.g., shoe business is 100% shared manufacturing, so its ROCE expectation is much higher than the company blended ROCE.
Blended ROCE is not being given as guidance for FY27 given the mix of assets at various stages of commercialization; instead an absolute PAT guidance number is given.

key_figures.label: Expected jump in ice cream production volume (Panipat ramp-up)

subsections.label: Footwear division
points: Footwear division finally gained a grip on the business and started performing well on deliveries and profitability, but faced the maximum impact from war/geopolitical conditions affecting petrochemical prices this quarter.
Large part of footwear raw materials imported from Far East; freight rates have risen substantially and polymer prices (used in soles) have increased by nearly 50-60%.

Unlike other businesses where price increases are immediately passed on to customers, footwear price pass-through is not instantaneous; management is in discussions with customers who understand the changes and are engaging on pricing.
Division continues to be affected in Q1 as well as far as the P&L is concerned.
Company has order book visibility for the shoe season through the end of the year and believes it will be well above previously targeted growth rates.
Footwear profitability target not disclosed due to raw material price variability and ongoing customer discussions.
Footwear business broke even at EBITDA level in Q2 FY26 (not Q3) and is now PAT positive; it was never cash-loss making.

100% of the footwear business is shared manufacturing, so its ROCE expectation is much higher than the company blended ROCE; this quarter it did not meet the higher ROCE expectation for reasons beyond company control.
Engagement and discussions with customers on cost pass-through have started; management expects to work with customers within about a month on passing on some costs.

subsections.label: Home & Personal Care (HPC)
points: Maintained steady momentum during FY26, supported by investments across home care, personal care and allied categories.

Aurangabad Personal Care facility successfully integrated into the network, strengthening HFL's ability to cater to emerging D2C and premium product categories requiring even small production batches.
Silvassa liquid detergent project and Lucknow detergent bar facility progressing well, expected to become operational during FY27.
HPC segment continues to see more emphasis on dedicated manufacturing, or a hybrid 'anchor tenant' model where part of capacity is dedicated and part is shared.

subsections.label: Ice Cream division
points: Delivered strong Q4 performance aided by favorable seasonal demand and ramp-up of newer capacities.

Backward integration achieved through acquisition of cone manufacturing facility and commissioning of stick manufacturing facility, enabling better service to existing customers and development of new relationships.
Panipat plant commissioned in April 2026 in a record time of less than 10 months.
INR50 crores investment announced for ice cream capacity is a brownfield expansion across both Lucknow and Panipat (not a separate location from Panipat).

subsections.label: Food & Beverages
points: Continues to scale operations across beverages, dairies, snacks and other fast-growing consumption categories.
Several facilities recorded peak production levels during the summer season, reflecting strong customer demand and improved operational efficiencies.
Entering the Greek yogurt segment as part of strategy to expand into higher value and wellness-oriented dairy categories.
Expanding beverage platform through new bottle capacity in Aurangabad and South India, both expected to be commissioned during FY27.

Strategy for beverages is to set up multiple units across the country; company aims to become the single largest independent bottler of beverages in the country by end of FY27 (independent meaning no affiliation to any single brand, manufacturing for multiple brands).
Beverages business, given its growth trajectory, will be a shared manufacturing model.

subsections.label: Healthcare (Pharma/OTC)
points: Continued to strengthen manufacturing quality and product development capabilities during FY26.

Added new customers during the year (3-4 new customers signed for the Baddi facility) and completed several domestic and international regulatory audits, reinforcing credibility in regulated and export-oriented markets.

Continued to increase presence in wellness and Ayurveda-focused categories; currently establishing a dedicated ayurvedic wellness manufacturing facility at Baddi alongside modernization initiatives at the existing facility.
Inherited Baddi facility has all regulatory approvals including US FDA and Russian FDA.

A new Head of Exports has been nominated to focus on export growth; company has taken a contrarian approach and started talking to customers including large modern trade players in the US, despite global supply chain uncertainty.
OTC pharma segment sees traction in both shared and dedicated manufacturing, evenly split.
Segment expected to start contributing well going forward given new customer wins.

subsections.label: Segment strategy / capital allocation
points: Company does not disclose segment-wise EBITDA/profitability because in some product categories its numbers would be indicative of customer performance, and it doesn't want to be used as a proxy for customers.
Organization broken into 5 divisions, each with new leadership, with mandate to grow EBITDA at 20% and deliver 20% ROE.
Company is agnostic across the 5 categories and will invest wherever it sees growth.
Currently seeing more engagement in home care, beverages and ice creams in terms of client inquiries/pipeline activity.

Management declined to disclose customer/brand names due to confidentiality but stated it works with largest brands as well as emerging D2C brands across all segments; considering disclosing number of new customers acquired over the years in future.
By FY2030, if consumption numbers for the country recover and inflation eases, achieving 20% growth across BUs should be easier, providing tailwinds versus current headwinds.

key_figures.label: Ice cream capacity capex within new pipeline

subsections.label: Capacity commissioning & integration
points: FY26 was a milestone year with an ambitious capex goal of investing more than INR700 crores, delivering capacities across geographies and product categories despite macroeconomic and geopolitical headwinds.

Company achieved successful pivoting of the business to a more broad-based manufacturing platform by deepening existing customer relationships, bringing in new customers and scaling up new product categories.
Smooth commissioning of newer factories and integration of acquisitions further added to performance.
Two factories were temporarily affected by LPG shortage during the quarter.

Focus for FY27 is accelerating utilization ramp-up across recently commissioned assets, continuing to judiciously invest in new capex, and ensuring sustained improvements in earnings and returns across all platforms.

The new INR150 crores pipeline represents new contracts signed since April (last 45 days), not full-year guidance; company expects the pipeline number to grow through the year with further announcements.
FY26 gross block came in about INR190 crores short of the ~INR2,000 crore target, with the shortfall expected to be completed over the coming year.

subsections.label: Portfolio strategy
points: Company undertook an ambitious capex program exceeding INR700 crores in FY26, laying the foundation for continued compounding growth across revenues, profitability and manufacturing capabilities.
Onboarding of new management leadership across the 5 verticals to support sustained profitable growth.

Baddi facility was acquired from Reckitt; an older plant with high gross book value and accumulated depreciation, with the actual cash paid recorded differently from the accounting gross block due to Ind AS treatment.
Cone manufacturing facility acquisition and integration supports backward integration in the ice cream value chain.
Company evaluates every expansion/acquisition against an 18% IRR threshold over a longish period.

Strategy differs by BU: beverages aiming to become largest independent bottler via shared manufacturing; footwear fully shared manufacturing; HPC moving toward dedicated/hybrid anchor-tenant model; OTC pharma evenly split between shared and dedicated.

subsections.label: Geopolitical & input cost risk
points: Company successfully maneuvered disruptions caused by geopolitical conditions through strategic buildup in inventories and working capital investment, continuing to serve customers with agility.
Two factories temporarily affected by LPG shortage.
Footwear division faced brunt of rising petrochemical prices this quarter; freight rates from Far East imports have risen substantially and sole polymer prices increased ~50-60%.
Unlike other businesses with immediate cost pass-through, footwear pricing changes with customers are not instantaneous, though customers are engaging on the topic.
Footwear division impact continues into Q1 FY27 as well.
Management does not have visibility beyond anyone else on how long this uncertainty (geopolitical/inflation) will persist; will update if the situation changes materially next quarter.
Despite the footwear headwind, management does not expect it to be significant enough to change FY27 PAT guidance, as other categories are expected to compensate.
Uncertainty around global supply chains cited as a headwind, though also being used contrarian by healthcare/export business to engage new customers.

subsections.label: GST / inverted duty structure risk
points: Cash flow during FY26 impacted by higher working capital deployment, primarily due to GST rate changes under the inverted duty structure effective September '25.

Discussion with customers to transition certain businesses from gross to net revenue recognition (from Q3 FY27 onwards, delayed from earlier expectation of starting Q1/finishing Q2) — this is an accounting reclassification with no impact on absolute profitability or cash generation, but reported revenue for those businesses will show a reduction.

Most food categories have been shifted to 5% GST duty, while packaging material and some raw materials continue to attract a much higher GST rate, causing duty inversion mainly affecting the foods segment.

Discussions on this transition were pushed to the back burner as customers and company focused on managing inventory stocking amid geopolitical disruptions; transition timeline shifted to start in Q2 and finish by Q3 (from earlier Q1-Q2 timeline).
Management to update on how many customers have agreed to the new business model in the next investor call.
This transition, once executed, will make EBITDA/PAT margins look better since the denominator (sales) reduces, without affecting absolute profitability.

subsections.label: FY27 outlook
points: Company reiterated its FY27 PAT guidance of INR200-220 crores, backed by improving utilization across newly commissioned capacity, rising operating leverage, and healthy execution momentum across business verticals.
Company achieved the FY26 guidance communicated despite a dynamic external environment.

Management avoids giving sales/revenue guidance given planned gross-to-net revenue recognition changes and inflation-driven pass-through effects on sales, neither of which affects underlying company performance.

Volume growth is expected to be significant even if value/turnover growth is not like-for-like, due to full-year ramp-up of newly commissioned assets (e.g., ~50% jump in ice cream production alone from Panipat ramp-up).
Company remains confident that PAT guidance will be met despite footwear cost headwinds, as other categories are expected to more than compensate.
EBITDA margin of 10% (as % of sales) is considered achievable, though management cautioned about conflating this with PAT margin.
Mandate for each of the 5 business verticals is to grow EBITDA at 20% and deliver 20% ROE, extrapolated to potentially support growth through 2030 if macro consumption tailwinds emerge.

guidance_ledger.statement: We remain confident in sustaining profitable growth and delivering FY27 PAT guidance in range of INR200 crores to INR220 crores.
We should be about INR700 crores to INR800 crores of turnover as far as shoes is concerned in this FY27.

Profitability target is something that I would much rather not talk about, especially for this division right now because there's just too much variability in terms of the raw material prices and our discussions with the customers are still ongoing.
Upon completion of the announced capex by FY27, gross block of approximately INR2,150 crores.

We were hoping to be able to make this transition starting from Q1 and finish it by Q2. Now it looks like it will start in Q2 and finish by Q3.
EBITDA 10% is definitely achievable.

If all customers agree to change to conversion cost model, PAT margin could reach 10%, but purely as an accounting entry since sales would fall; on like-to-like basis it would be surprising for a contract manufacturer to achieve 10% PAT margin.
Mandate given to management is to grow EBITDA at 20% in each BU and deliver 20% ROE numbers, and company as a whole should grow at 20%.
At an individual project level, the minimum threshold remains the same, which is about 18%-odd.
We strive to be between 16% to 22% ROEs pretax, where we negotiate depending on customer, product category and location.

guidance_ledger.metric: New capex pipeline signed for FY27
guidance_ledger.statement: New projects worth approximately INR150 crores have already been signed up for FY27, including ~INR50 crores each in beverages, HPC and ice cream capacities; expected to grow with further announcements during the year.
Panipat facility alone (20,000 ton capacity) represents a 50% jump purely in ice cream facility production versus FY26's 35,000-40,000 tons; total production quantum will see a jump of more than 50%.
Currently avoiding giving guidance on sales numbers because of discussions on revenue recognition changes and inflation-driven pass-through effects, both of which do not affect company performance.
It is definitely achievable to get to 20% growth across BUs; by 2030, if consumption recovers and inflation eases, it should be easier given tailwinds.

guidance_ledger.statement: Silvassa liquid detergent project and Lucknow detergent bar facility are progressing well and expected to become operational during FY27.
Company is expanding its beverage platform through a new bottle capacity in Aurangabad and South India, both of which are expected to be commissioned during FY27.
We will probably, at the end of FY27, become the single largest independent bottler of beverages in the country.

key_takeaways: FY26 was a milestone year for HFL, a culmination of various initiatives taken over the last few years, with an ambitious capex goal of investing more than INR700 crores despite macroeconomic and geopolitical headwinds.

Total income increased by 17% Y-o-Y to INR4,264 crores, while EBITDA grew by 20% Y-o-Y to INR377 crores, and Profit after tax for FY26 stood at a record high of INR149 crores, registering growth of 29% year-on-year.
The company achieved the guidance communicated despite operating through a dynamic external environment.
Net debt to equity as on March '26 stood at 0.84x, well within the company's internal comfort level of 1x, with adjusted ROCE of 18.9% after normalizing newly commissioned and underutilized assets.

Footwear division faced the maximum impact from war and geopolitical conditions affecting petrochemical prices, with raw material (polymer) prices up nearly 50-60% and rising freight rates; impact continues into Q1 FY27.

Company is in discussion with customers to transition certain businesses from gross to net revenue recognition from Q3 FY27 onwards (pushed out from earlier Q1-Q2 timeline) due to the inverted GST duty structure; this is an accounting reclassification not impacting absolute profitability or cash generation.
Company remains confident in sustaining profitable growth and delivering FY27 PAT guidance in the range of INR200 crores to INR220 crores.

pressing_questions: I would request some of the clarifications on the numbers... when I look at the presentation numbers in terms of ROCE, capital employed, everywhere, 2 things becomes very common. We are unable to go back to the reported balance sheets and able to reconcile any of the numbers, firstly. And secondly, all of the numbers have got some kind of asterisks, hyphens adjustments which makes it very difficult for us to understand... last time also I had requested capital employed is not getting reconciled, the fixed assets, the gross fixed assets commissions, which is there for the year is not getting reconciled with the cash flows. Can you help us reconcile all of that?

So the net capital employed, what is the net capital employed as per balance sheet when we look at very simple definition of equity plus borrowings, which is there, that number needs to be -- why should that be different?
I appreciate, Sameer, but the problem is this underutilized capacity of underutilized assets of INR508 crores.

Considering FY27 was anticipated to be year that your bottom line is going to be driven by the operating leverage that will come in. Just wanted to understand how this cost pressure in 2 businesses is not going to impact the PAT guidance because we have reiterated that PAT will remain same, while we are saying that we are seeing significant impact wherein some of the prices of the raw material have gone up by 50%, 60% and still we are very confident to achieve the guided PAT.

TRAVELFOOD.about: Incorporated in 2007, Travel Food Services Ltd provides Travel QSR and Lounge services in India and abroad.[1]

quarters.summary: Management expects a temporary disruption from the Middle East conflict to ease, with H2 FY27 anticipated to see a strong bounce-back in passenger traffic as suspended international long-haul routes are restored from September/October; over 50 outlets under development and ~90 units mobilized in the last 12 months are expected to normalize and drive meaningful revenue/earnings uplift over the next 12-18 months, supported by a debt-free balance sheet and continued expansion into new airports, international markets (Asia focus via Dubai/Indonesia entities), and highway wayside amenities.

subsections.label: Gross margin accounting treatment
points: Gross profit margin reflects accounting treatment of the lounge aggregation business, where revenues are recorded in sales while related service costs are classified under other expenses.

Adjusting for reclassification of INR223 million of lounge aggregation cost from other expenses to cost of sales gives adjusted gross profit margin of around 81%, which remains well within the guided range.

subsections.label: Cost drivers
points: Employee cost increased primarily due to annual compensation revisions and onboarding of additional manpower to support recently opened outlets at Noida and Cochin airports, both currently in ramp-up phase.
Increase in employee cost also reflects staffing for the newly launched passenger services business at Noida Airport.
Other expenses witnessed a similar increasing trend, driven by investments in these growth initiatives.

EBITDA margin moderation to 35.8% reflects the impact of higher employee cost and operating cost associated with recently commissioned airports and new business initiatives; these investments are described as strategic, aimed at supporting future growth and scaling of the business.

Excluding the lounge aggregation reclassification, other expenses increased 22% YoY, in line with business growth, driven by higher pre-operating costs from ramp-up/mobilization of units at Cochin, Delhi and Noida; expected to normalize within ~12 months as units perform.
Labour code impact on the ~5,000+ employee base (majority on company roll) is minimal, below INR8-10 crores.

subsections.label: Profitability drivers
points: Overall improvement in profitability driven by continued sales growth despite flat passenger traffic, along with higher other income including the GST provision write-back following a favorable rectification order.

subsections.label: Balance sheet and capital allocation
points: Debt-free balance sheet as of June 30, with consolidated cash balance of approximately INR9.7 billion, providing substantial headroom to fund airport expansions, lounge and highway growth opportunities, passenger services, and other strategic initiatives.
Capital allocation strategy is prudent, driven primarily by units currently in ramp-up phase, while constantly exploring new opportunities in target airports.
Approach is to target returns at maturity that mimic the rest of the portfolio; the company will not chase growth unless it delivers sustainable long-term profits for stakeholders.

subsections.label: Cost structure (fixed vs variable)
points: Roughly 8-10% of costs tend to be fixed, mainly occupancy cost / CAM charges levied by airport operators, which are fixed in nature with full visibility on growth/ramp-up over the contract.

Labour is semi-variable since India is a fixed-wage market; economies of scale come from back-of-house efficiencies (stores, procurement) and ability to shift staff from international to domestic terminal sides when needed.
The proportion of cost that is variable versus fixed varies year-on-year depending on ramp-up cycles; ramp-up years see higher variable pre-operating cost expense base.

subsections.label: LFL growth drivers
points: Consolidated LFL sales growth was driven by menu innovations, promotional initiatives, and calibrated pricing.

A few markets saw softer LFL performance during the quarter, notably Mumbai and Guwahati owing to traffic migration to new airport infrastructure, and certain South India markets given higher exposure to Middle East traffic.
Excluding these specific markets, like-for-like sales grew around 7% YoY across the wider network.

Management indicated it tends to be in the range of more than passenger traffic, somewhere 5% to 7% above that, in terms of LFL performance — a trend expected to continue as passenger traffic returns.
LFL growth is a blend of price (limited price escalation this year given cost challenges), premiumization initiatives, bundling, and in limited cases brand edits/changes.

Normalized-year expectation: passenger traffic historically around 8-9%, plus 5-7% LFL delta, reaching normalized LFL of around 14-15%; this year, given flat passenger traffic, LFL is expected in a similar range to what would normally be seen relative to traffic.

subsections.label: Net contract gains commentary
points: Net contract gains reflect contribution from recently commissioned units across Delhi, Cochin, Noida, and other key locations.

Net contract gains are described as lumpy year-on-year (sometimes 30, sometimes 50, sometimes 20 outlets won), not a straight line, but the company has been consistent in the ballpark historically at ~16% system-wide this quarter.

subsections.label: Contract renewal rate change
points: Moderation in contract renewal rate from ~94% to ~92% attributed to some highway outlets (smaller pilot sites) which the company chose not to renew, as strategy has shifted toward larger wayside amenity (WSA) investments rather than smaller highway pilots.

key_figures.label: Adani F&B and lounge revenue growth

subsections.label: JV vs non-JV/consol business dynamics
points: JV/associate business growth (~15%) was relatively muted compared to consol growth, versus Adani F&B and lounge revenue growth of 55% YoY and GHL/GMR reported growth of ~22% YoY.

Reason 1: In JV markets, some units have to move to the company or JV structure over a scheduled period of time as contracts move over, creating a mismatch between JV growth trajectory and overall growth at airport operator partners.
Reason 2: A lot of airports on the western side, which had Middle East as a strong market, have been impacted in passenger traffic and overall sales; these form a bulk of the JV portfolio.
JV portfolio is not limited to India-based JVs (Adani, GMR) — it also includes a significant portion from the Malaysia business and other international JVs.

Two clear drivers of growth: joint ventures with partners (used typically when an operator runs multiple airports, making a JV structure efficient) and direct concessions (used for single-airport operations, which is the global norm by a wide margin), with similar underlying growth drivers (passenger traffic) for both, and growth broadly balanced/robust across JV, non-JV, large and small airports during normalized periods.

Delhi T3 was previously a JV in the form of an SPV where TFS had a majority share and hence consolidated it; going forward the plan is to bid through a different, long-term joint venture (not an SPV) with GMR where TFS's shareholding is 30%, and hence it would not be consolidated going forward but would contribute via profit pick-up.

Margin profile is described as similar irrespective of JV or direct concession structure; the more relevant factor for profitability is the timing/maturity of a contract (new build vs mature) rather than entity type.
New tenders for JV structures like Delhi T3 tend to be for a larger set of outlets than what was operated directly previously, reflecting a strategy to scale via JVs when tenders are sizeable.

subsections.label: Average selling price (ASP) across airports
points: ASPs remain similar between JV and non-JV structures given the same way of operating.

Across airports, larger metro airports (Delhi, Mumbai) have higher spends due to nature of travel, international travel propensity, and per capita income in those cities, supporting premium brand offerings (e.g., Gordon Ramsay at Delhi T1, Wagamama at Mumbai).

subsections.label: Contract economics — MG and revenue share structure
points: Contracts are largely structured as minimum guarantee (MG) and/or revenue share, whichever is higher; the company tends to consistently exceed the minimum guarantee via revenue share.

MGs normally have a built-in escalation; revenue share percentages in some contracts may have marginal escalation (0.1-0.2%) but generally no meaningful jump, and remain fixed/contractually backed for the life of the contract; they can only be revised upon contract renewal, not arbitrarily each year.

subsections.label: Passenger services / EATS platform
points: Successful launch of passenger services at Noida International Airport under the Elite Assist brand, including meet-and-greet and porter services.

These offerings complement the existing lounge network and will integrate into the EATS technology platform, allowing passengers to use them alongside other experiences, strengthening the ability to offer a comprehensive suite of airport hospitality and services through a single connected ecosystem.
Company intends to progressively expand the passenger services platform to additional airports, building on the encouraging early response at Noida.

subsections.label: Technology and customer engagement
points: Increasingly leveraging technology to deepen engagement with passengers and partners while creating additional avenues for monetization on the lounge side.

key_figures.label: System-wide footprint (travel QSR outlets and lounges)
Units mobilized/activated (trailing 12 months, incl. QSR and lounges)

subsections.label: Recent openings and unit ramp-up
points: Commenced operations at Noida International Airport during the quarter, taking system-wide presence to 21 airports.
Significant additions over the last 12 months at Mumbai, Delhi, Hyderabad, Cochin, Navi Mumbai, and Noida airports.

Many of these assets are still in the early stages of ramp-up, meaning a significant part of their earning potential is yet to be realized; as passenger traffic normalizes, these units are positioned to contribute progressively and increasingly to performance.

Existing/running airport units typically take 12-18 months to hit normalized profit levels; greenfield airports (built from scratch) take 18-24 months, given time needed for passenger traffic to build, understanding gate usage/brand fit, and occasional brand changes.

subsections.label: Upcoming growth catalysts
points: Bhogapuram Airport opening on 17th August marks another significant milestone, where multiple outlets will operate under the JV, GHL.
Over 50 outlets currently under development across the network; as these open and mature over the coming 12-18 months, they are expected to provide meaningful uplift to revenue and earnings.

The 50 outlets are outlets already secured/won on contracts 3-8 months ago that are in build-out, spread across multiple airports already announced (e.g., Delhi, Navi Mumbai, Bhogapuram), not new bids.
Some of the ~90 units mobilized/activated over the last 12 months are hitting normalization; a large part activated in the last 2 quarters will hit normalization over the next ~12 months.

subsections.label: Renewal-related mobilization
points: When contracts are renewed, changes may be more limited than fresh construction, but there is still some level of asset refresh/brand change and associated cost, normalizing probably on the lower end of the 12-month scenario.

subsections.label: Domestic vs international traffic
points: Domestic traffic registered modest growth during the quarter, while a significant decline in international traffic resulted in overall passenger traffic being broadly flat YoY.

May saw domestic traffic return to growth with a temporary easing of geopolitical tensions, resulting in the highest ever single month of domestic air traffic in India, notable against a softer base in the same month last year.
International traffic continued to face headwinds despite improving conditions in May, and traffic softened again in June following renewed conflict-related disruptions.

Q2 FY27 (to date, through mid-August): domestic traffic reportedly down ~6%, international traffic down ~4% per public data, with a trend broadly similar to Q1; international traffic remains where the delta sits, given suspension of long-haul international routes by two of the largest airlines toward end of May, with restoration expected from September/October.

subsections.label: International expansion focus
points: Success in Malaysia (expanded post-COVID) and Hong Kong (won a second lounge in January); those units are maturing/ramping up and performing well.
Focus areas historically called out as Middle East and Asia; given current Middle East situation, Asia is the more immediate focus until Middle East normalizes.
Set up an entity in Dubai to focus on the Middle East region, and another entity recently in Indonesia to pursue opportunities there, since local entities are required to bid in those markets.
Company sees opportunities coming up to bid/pitch for in these markets and plans to be focused on participating this year.

subsections.label: Domestic airport pipeline
points: Won a prominent KFC outlet at Bangalore T1, one of the busiest outlets there, as T1 undergoes a massive upgradation plan; expects more opportunities to bid for over the next 12 months, coming in phases.
Tier 2 airports and other AAI airports represent opportunity; example cited is Pune coming up in the next 2 years (one of the top 15 airports where the company is not yet present).
Highways identified as a medium-to-long-term opportunity given the government's wayside amenities (WSA) plan and expressway rollout.

subsections.label: Highway / wayside amenities strategy
points: Highways are compared to where airports were in 2008-2009 when the company entered that business, now nearly 17-18 years later.

Government investment is coming into wide multi-lane, access-controlled expressways with limited retail F&B development through wayside amenities (WSAs); about 1,000 WSA plan already announced by government.

Company is doing back-end work — analysis, engagement, talking with potential partner brands, landlords, oil marketing companies — and will target WSAs as they come online in a calibrated manner, prioritizing financial return benchmarks over immediate scale.
Approach on highways is medium-to-long term rather than an immediate jump; a few smaller highway pilots entered earlier were not renewed as strategy shifts toward larger WSA investments.

subsections.label: Operational flexibility
points: Economies of scale at existing airports allow efficiencies in back-of-house operations, including stores and procurement strategies.
Ability to move staff/manpower from international to domestic side of the terminal when international traffic is impacted, providing operating leverage.
