subsections.label: In-city Platform Growth Story
points: In-city platform spans 17 assets across 7 major cities (6-7 million sq ft), providing access to more than 20 million consumers within 30-minute driving distance.
Combination of proximity, scale and Grade-A infrastructure creates a differentiated, hard-to-replicate platform.
Grew from 3-4 assets to 17 assets; no institutional-grade in-city logistics stock exists today, so significant expansion runway remains and this is a key management focus area.
When fully completed, in-city portfolio (~7 of 61 million sq ft, ~10% of area) is expected to contribute nearly 25% of top line given a 2.5-3x rental premium versus big-box parks.

Entered in-city strategy largely through partnership with Central Warehousing Corporation (CWC) on a revenue-share basis; even after revenue share, tracking 13-14% yield on cost versus 11-12% on big-format parks.

First in-city delivery expected in Pune (Pimpri) by Q4 FY27; described as top-notch global construction standard with ramps and aprons, expected to redefine in-city logistics/industrial real estate in India.
In-city asset parcel sizes will be a mix, likely 10,000 to 100,000+ sq ft (smaller than typical 300,000-500,000 sq ft big-format leases); company may act as consolidator for occupiers.
In-city construction cost guided at INR4,500 per sq ft, roughly INR500 per sq ft more than standard industrial galas.

subsections.label: Customer Base & Sector Mix
points: Serves large blue-chip corporates across e-commerce (Amazon, Colgate, Unilever, Zara) and industrial/manufacturing (Schneider, SIG, Lumax, Tata, Vestas) among others.
Supports renewables, EVs, automotive, plus sunrise sectors like data centers, semiconductors, aerospace, defense — collectively nearly half (~50%) of portfolio.
Total customer base has exceeded 120 partners.
Infrastructure is largely agnostic — no dedicated industrial or warehousing parks; coexistence of industrial and warehousing customers within same parks using common infrastructure.

subsections.label: Lease Tenure & Rent Differentiation by Customer Type
points: Deep industrial companies sign longer leases (9-15 years) given substantial investment inside buildings, providing similar lock-ins to Horizon.
Industrial segment commands ~20% premium rent over standard bare-bone warehousing (INR29+ vs INR24 per sq ft), an average 15-20% better rental.

subsections.label: In-city Asset Construction Technology
points: Construction technology for in-city multi-story assets (e.g., Pimpri) is described as top-notch, global standard, featuring ramps and aprons — a product quality/scale that India has not previously seen.
This is expected to redefine how in-city infrastructure and real estate for logistics and industrial use is viewed in the country.

key_figures.label: Total fully-paid land bank for further development
Time to double large-park operational footprint

subsections.label: Platform Scale & History
points: Horizon achieved a sixfold expansion, growing to 61 million sq ft, making it India's largest industrial and logistics real estate platform, from establishment in 2020.
Business spreads across 9 states, 10 markets, and 46 assets, owning 2,300 acres of land.
Grew from 10 million sq ft to 60 million sq ft over 6 years through both consolidating sub-scale platforms and acquiring greenfield land parcels.

subsections.label: Development Pipeline
points: Delivered 1 million sq ft this quarter; on track to achieve 6 million sq ft completion target for FY27, enhancing operational area to nearly 35 million sq ft (from 29.5 million sq ft as of 30 June 2026).

25 more million sq ft of large-park land already fully paid for, with approvals and financing largely in place in most locations; annual throughput of 5-6 million sq ft over last 12-18 months implies doubling of large-park development footprint over next 4-5 years.
In-city development on track for first delivery in Pune by Q4 FY27; in-city network to deliver 6 million sq ft over next 3 years (~2 million sq ft annually).
Fully-paid land bank will deliver 30 million sq ft of further development in total; financing and approvals materially in place.
240-member high-caliber team drives the operating platform.

subsections.label: Value-Added Infrastructure (Solar, Worker Housing, Hospitality)
points: Rooftop solar presence has reached nearly 38 MW, of which ~20 MW is operational and another 17-18 MW is being operationalized, largely serving industrial customers with larger power requirements.
Rooftop solar generates healthy yield on cost since no additional land purchase or grid infrastructure investment is required — power is captively consumed on-site.
Currently pouring concrete on 6,000-7,000 worker accommodation beds, to be delivered over next 12-18 months.
Building India's first on-site residential hotel, to be delivered in next 18-24 months.

Worker accommodations, hospitality, and skill centers largely driven by demand from deep industrial customers, effectively creating a broader business ecosystem within existing parks without requiring additional land or FSI expenditure, generating accretive yield on cost.

subsections.label: Market Presence & Expansion Strategy
points: Company operates across 9 states and 10 markets; these are described as the deepest industrial and consumption micro-markets in the country, driving 60-70% (or more) of overall throughput and goods movement.
Company has entered newer markets like Nagpur, Goa, and Nashik and will continue to opportunistically explore lucrative Tier 1-minus/Tier 2 markets.
Significant scope remains to increase market share within existing Tier 1 markets, given more than 90% of stock in the sector today sits in fragmented, non-compliant, poor-quality assets.
Institutionalization/formalization of the economy and the logistics/industrial real estate sector is viewed as a major megatrend supporting continued market share gains in existing markets.

subsections.label: Competitive Landscape Benchmarking
points: Grade-A industrial/logistics stock in India today is not even 500 million sq ft, compared to a single market like Chicago having over a billion sq ft of Grade-A stock.
Grade-B/Grade-C stock in India could be in the range of five to tens of billions of sq ft, indicating the market can absorb much more institutional competition ('tens of Horizons').

subsections.label: Competitive Intensity
points: Management views increased institutional competition as welcome given the vast under-penetration of Grade-A stock in India versus global benchmarks (e.g., Chicago).
Comparison drawn to early 2010s commercial and residential real estate sector evolution, which went from negligible Grade-A stock to about a billion sq ft in commercial.

subsections.label: Demand Evolution Narrative
points: Business built initially (2020) to enable rapid growth of organized e-commerce via large-format fulfillment centers for e-com, retail, FMCG, and 3PL companies.

As India's manufacturing ecosystem gathered momentum (PLI, Make in India, global supply chain diversification), customer requirements evolved beyond warehousing toward plug-and-play infrastructure for assembly, manufacturing, processing and value-add operations, prompting expansion into the industrial segment.

More recently, exponential growth of quick commerce and hyperlocal fulfillment created demand for infrastructure closer to end consumers, addressed via the in-city platform given absence of institutional-grade in-city logistics infrastructure.

subsections.label: Growth Strategy — 4-Pronged Approach
points: 1) Contractual 5% annual rent escalations plus embedded mark-to-market opportunities in existing leases.
2) Continued development expansion of big-format parks, expected to double operational capacities over next 4-5 years.
3) Rapid expansion of in-city strategy, delivering 6 million sq ft over next 3 years at 2-3x rentals versus big-format parks.
4) Expansion of value-added services (rooftop solar, worker accommodations, hospitality, and other new ventures), expected to deliver nearly 5-10% of revenues in next 5 years.

subsections.label: IPO & Blackstone Sponsorship
points: IPO completed in August, raising INR4,250 crores of fresh primary capital, marking a defining milestone in Horizon's journey.

Logistics has been a high-conviction investment theme for Blackstone globally, which owns and manages over a billion sq ft of logistics assets worldwide; Horizon was established in 2020 with this backing to build industrial and logistics infrastructure in India at scale.

Blackstone did not sell a single share as part of the INR4,250 crores capital raised between December and August; overall hold period for Blackstone in the company to date is significantly less than 5 years, and the fund has historically held some investments in India for over a decade (per management's own observation, not a formal commitment).
CEO clarified he represents the company, not the shareholders, and cannot give a definitive answer on Blackstone's exit timeline or further dilution plans.

subsections.label: Acquisition Strategy
points: Historically grown via both consolidating sub-scale platforms and acquiring greenfield land parcels — this is expected to remain central to acquisition strategy going forward.

Company already has sufficient land/raw material to execute growth over next 4-5 years without further acquisitions, but continues to develop an acquisition pipeline opportunistically given growth headroom from the IPO.
No specific quantified annual target for new acquisition additions was provided ('tough to say that today').

subsections.label: Litigation Risk
points: A Delhi High Court case is challenging the tender for the company's 13 in-city warehouses; matter is sub judice and management declined to comment further, but stated confidence in the company's position and in continuing to execute its strategy and plan on those assets, expecting to deliver a large part of those assets over the next 12-24 months.

subsections.label: Non-cash P&L Drag
points: Reported net loss of INR12 crores in Q1 FY27 continues to be impacted by non-cash depreciation and interest expense, which management flags as distorting the true cash profitability picture.

subsections.label: Forward Outlook Summary
points: Management expects FY27 to deliver 6.5 million sq ft of leasing (~30% growth vs last fiscal) and 6 million sq ft of completions, taking operational area to ~34-35 million sq ft with high-90% occupancy targeted.
In-city first delivery (Pune/Pimpri) targeted for Q4 FY27.
Reported P&L expected to turn profitable (black) from Q2/Q3 FY27 onward as non-cash depreciation and interest burdens ease post-deleveraging.
Post-deleveraging, cost of debt (currently 8.2%) expected to fall by 40-50 basis points on improved credit ratings.
Value-added services (solar, worker housing, hospitality, skill centers) expected to contribute 5-10% of revenue over the next 5 years.
In-city portfolio expected to contribute nearly 25% of top line when fully completed.
Large-format park operational capacity expected to double over the next 4-5 years; in-city network to add 6 million sq ft over next 3 years.
Incremental capex on ~25 million sq ft of forward pipeline expected to generate 13-14% yield on cost, with further improvement expected as product mix shifts toward industrial and in-city.
Guided in-city rents of INR70-75 per sq ft against guided in-city construction cost of INR4,500 per sq ft.

This will double our operational capacities over the next 4 to 5 years.
This will deliver 6 million square feet over the next 3 years.
This will deliver nearly 5% to 10% of our revenues in the next 5 years.
When fully completed, this should be nearly 25% of our top line.
You'll see another, call it 4 million square feet to 4.5 million square feet of incremental leases that we will sign over the next, call it 9 months.
Our capex requirements over the next 3 years are more or less in the INR1,500 crores to INR2,000 crores zip code, which we look to roughly manage 1/3 internally and 2/3 with incremental debt.
INR70, INR75 is a good guidance today, and we will continue to update the market as we gun ahead with the construction and the leasing of these.
This will be at roughly about INR4,500 a foot on construction cost.

risk_register.note: An analyst noted FY26 net loss came in about 3.5x worse than forecast; management attributed this to non-cash book depreciation and interest impact rather than operational underperformance.

themes.label: IPO & Deleveraging
themes.note: IPO raised INR4,250 crores, bringing proforma net debt down to INR2,500 crores (12.5% of enterprise value) and strengthening balance sheet flexibility.

themes.label: In-city Expansion
themes.note: In-city platform (17 assets, 6-7 million sq ft) commands 2.5-3x rentals versus big-format parks and is expected to reach 25% of top line at full completion.

themes.label: Re-leasing Spread Strength
themes.note: Re-leasing spreads of 12% in Q1 (12-15% historically) outpaced the 5% contractual escalation, supported by high single-digit market rent growth.

themes.label: Development Pipeline Execution
themes.note: Fully-paid 30 million sq ft land bank with approvals/financing largely in place supports doubling of large-format park footprint over next 4-5 years plus 6 million sq ft in-city over 3 years.

themes.label: Cash PAT vs Reported PAT
themes.note: Reported net loss of INR12 crores contrasts with pro forma cash PAT of INR116 crores after adjusting for non-cash depreciation and pro forma interest savings; P&L expected to turn profitable Q2/Q3 FY27.

themes.label: Value-Added Services Ecosystem
themes.note: Rooftop solar (38 MW), worker accommodation (6,000-7,000 beds) and hospitality ventures expected to contribute 5-10% of revenue in next 5 years, driven largely by industrial customer demand.

themes.label: Litigation Overhang
themes.note: Delhi High Court case challenging tender for 13 in-city warehouses remains sub judice, though management expressed confidence in delivering these assets over 12-24 months.

key_takeaways: In August, we successfully completed our IPO and raised INR4,250 crores of fresh primary capital. The proceeds have been deployed for deleveraging, which brings our net debt down to INR2,500 crores, proforma as of end-June or 12.5% of enterprise value.

Horizon has achieved a remarkable sixfold expansion, growing to 61 million square feet, making us India's largest industrial and logistics real estate platform. Today, our business spreads across 9 states, 10 markets, and 46 assets. We own 2,300 acres of land. We serve over 120 customers and are rapidly building India's largest last-mile network.

Q1 has been our strongest ever quarter. We delivered revenue of INR200 crores, representing 23% year-on-year growth, EBITDA of INR161 crores while maintaining a very healthy EBITDA margin at 80%. Our contracted revenue run rate today continues to grow strongly and has reached nearly INR970 crores as of end June.

On the operating side, we leased 1.9 million square feet across 13 transactions. We onboarded nine new customers and added INR65 crores to our contracted revenue kitty. Notably, three-fourths of our leasing during this quarter came from the industrial customers.
We are on track to deliver 6.5 million square feet leasing for FY27, which will translate nearly to about a 30% growth compared to the last fiscal.

While we reported a net loss for the quarter of INR12 crores, this continues to be impacted by non-cash depreciation and interest expense... Adjusting for these, our pro forma cash PAT stands at a healthy INR116 crores.

The way we are thinking about our growth strategy, it's a 4-pronged growth strategy, which includes: the contractual 5% rent escalations and embedded mark-to-market opportunities; continued development expansion of big format parks (doubling operational capacities over next 4-5 years); rapid expansion of in-city strategy (6 million square feet over next 3 years at 2-3x rentals); and expansion of value-added services (5-10% of revenues in next 5 years).

There is a Delhi High Court case going, which is challenging the tender for your 13 in-city warehouses... That's sub judice, so I will not be able to comment much more on that. But we remain very confident on our position.

GOKEX.about: Gokaldas Exports Limited is engaged in the business of design, manufacture, and sale of a wide range of garments for men, women, and children and caters to the needs of several leading international fashion brands and retailers [1]

quarters.summary: Q1 FY'27 was a broad-based strong quarter with consolidated income up 21% YoY and consolidated EBITDA up 17% YoY, led by 16% YoY growth in India (vs a 12% YoY decline in Indian apparel exports overall) and 45% YoY growth in Africa (aided by AGOA renewal and a weak year-ago base). Management guided to overall revenue growth better than the earlier 15% mid-teens target, Africa revenue visibility of $112-115 million (against a $120 million aspiration), BTPL merger on track for Q3 FY'27 with EBITDA turning positive by Q3 and PBT positive by Q4, and reiterated confidence in margin expansion aided by rupee depreciation, capacity additions in low-cost regions, and operating leverage, even as wage inflation, RM/logistics costs, and AGOA/RoSCTL policy uncertainty remain watch items.

subsections.label: Margin drivers and pressures
points: Margin performance was hard earned: wages rose across both India and Kenya reflecting local inflation.
Higher oil prices increased cost of shipping fabric and trims and simultaneously drove up fuel and logistics costs.
Container availability constraints and shipping delays disrupted material flow with consequent effects on production planning and throughput.
Company optimized overhead and grew operating leverage to limit the financial impact of cost pressures.
Continued investment in automation is delivering measurable productivity gains and greater consistency in product quality.

Rupee weakened but company has not yet fully realized the value of the weaker rupee in P&L since it hedges via forward dollar sales (70% hedged at ~INR89 forward cover rate in Q1); remaining 30% naturally hedged via imports — expected to provide a cushion going forward.
Capacity increases are happening in lower-cost regions of the country, which will also help offset margin pressure from external macro factors.

Minimum wage hikes are inevitable and factored into planning; company pays above minimum wage so % impact on total wage bill is lower than the headline minimum-wage hike (e.g., Haryana 35% minimum wage hike and Noida 25% hike translated to only 14-15% overall wage increase for the company; Karnataka CPI-linked hike is a more modest 5%).
India salary/wage costs rose ~INR20 crore in Q1 FY27.
One quarter is typically inadequate to fully absorb wage hikes; automation efficiencies are a continuous process to help improve margins.

Raw material (RM) costs such as fabric are largely passed through to customers via costing; but ancillary costs like poly bag cartons and fuel caught the company by surprise in Q1 as they were not factored into pricing set back in January; these are now being factored into pricing going forward.
Cotton and polyester prices are a reality but may cool off from peaks; polyester will move in tandem with oil prices.

Other expenses rise attributed to two factors: (1) utilities cost — gas, fuel and chemicals cost increases (~INR5-6 crore hit) and (2) inbound/outbound logistics cost increases; this may partially neutralize in H2 if situation improves, otherwise will be factored into new order costing.
ETR expected to come down substantially by year-end with contribution from international operations, estimated between 20-22% for the year.

Global wage comparison: China minimum wage is 500+ USD, Vietnam is 300+ USD and growing, while India wage level is 210-240 USD — underscoring India's continued cost competitiveness even as wages rise.

subsections.label: Policy/incentive risk to margins
points: Company engaging with government at industry level to preserve incentives (refund of state/central levies embedded in cost structure, e.g., diesel/electricity outside GST remit); reduction could alter industry financials.
Worst case scenario for RoSCTL is it halves from current 3.5% to 1.75%; company believes it can offset this impact through its own performance.

In totality, if Indian incentives halve, offsetting factors — BTPL contribution and rupee — should help balance out; overall EBITDA margin should be higher than current base, per management, regardless of AGOA outcome.

subsections.label: Reported growth metrics
points: Consolidated income grew 21% YoY and consolidated EBITDA grew 17% YoY in Q1 FY27.

India operations EBITDA grew 14% YoY on India business revenue growth of 16% YoY, against an industry backdrop of Indian apparel exports declining 12% YoY over the same period — indicating market share gains.
Africa business revenue grew 45% YoY in Q1 FY27, with Africa EBITDA margin at 8%.

subsections.label: Order book visibility
points: Growth came from across geographies and customer base rather than any single customer or market; recorded growth across all major accounts.
1 new customer onboarded during the quarter, with operations expected to commence in Q2.
Strong order book visibility across customer base; company continues to diversify customer portfolio.

Q1 and Q2 are already booked (booked long back); Q2 revenue profile expected to be similar to Q1 despite Q2 typically being a seasonally weak quarter (winter-season/synthetic products favor China/Vietnam/Cambodia), because Gokaldas has strong outerwear presence.
Q3/Q4 orders being booked currently; projections looking good notwithstanding US 2027 inflation/consumer behavior concerns.
Spring '27 orders (executed in Q3 FY27) show fairly good revenue traction similar to Q1.

For H2 in Africa, order booking beyond December (post-AGOA expiry) appears robust; customers seem confident about Africa's cost economics and possible AGOA extension, and are proceeding with orders regardless of duty uncertainty.

subsections.label: Volume vs value dynamics
points: India volume growth of 3.4% YoY described as somewhat of a misnomer because Q1/Q2 production skews toward high-value outerwear (garments with 150-250 minutes of stitching content) versus simpler garments like shirts (22-25 minutes) made in spring/summer; so volume can be a misleading metric.
No YoY drop in overall business; on the contrary, strong growth.

subsections.label: Customer engagement / new product additions
points: New product additions being seen across all major customers (including large retailers like Carhartt, Gap) for next year summer onward.
Product mix for new additions is a blend of ASPs — ranging up to $40-50 per garment for high-ASP products, with overall average in a broad ballpark including sub- and above-INR700 ASP items.
New UK customer engaging for onboarding; not yet signed, dependent on profitability assessment.
Existing UK customer volumes growing due to UK FTA; UK contributes 4-4.5% of total revenue currently.

subsections.label: BTPL performance and outlook
points: BTPL merger process on track, expected to conclude in Q3 FY27 (likely latter half of Q3); BTPL will merge into Gokaldas for roughly the last 4 months of the year.
Business seeing consistent improvement in operating metrics; secured nominations from multiple brands for fabric sourcing and has started exporting fabrics.
BTPL fabric sales turnover was INR170 crore in Q1 FY27, currently operating at ~50-53 lakh meters/month capacity, expected to grow by another 30% in near future.
Increasing capacity utilization, investment in product mix, and rising average realization expected to drive margin growth.
Moving toward higher-value products like linen, linen blends, and certain bottom-weight fabrics where price realization is better.
Q1 FY27 EBITDA loss (-7.5% to -8%) was relatively higher due to chemical and fuel cost increases; these cost increases are being factored into pricing going forward.
Target trajectory: EBITDA positive by Q3 FY27, PBT positive targeted for Q4 FY27 (prior call had targeted breakeven by H1, which slipped).
By time of merger (end of calendar year), anticipated to generate mid- to high single-digit EBITDA margin and contribute positively to Gokaldas post-merger.
Consistent good quality delivery from the unit; several new customers nominating it for fabric procurement, augurs well for utilization.

subsections.label: India operations breakup (bookkeeping)
points: All new capacity added in central India is now part of Gokaldas; company has amalgamated Matrix operations and no longer distinguishes them separately in reporting, though the data was pulled out on request (Matrix volume 1.5 million pieces at ASP INR613).
Referring only to old Gurgaon units, volume is 1.53 million pieces with average ASP of INR613.

subsections.label: Fabric type mix
points: Cotton is almost 65% or a little higher of garment fabric mix on an annual basis; polyester/nylon/spandex fibers contribute up to 30%.
Mix varies quarterly — Q1 and Q2 have more man-made fiber garments due to higher share of outerwear production in those quarters.

subsections.label: India capacity ramp-up
points: Karnataka facility completely on track and progressing.
Madhya Pradesh on track and progressing well; second unit ramping up as we speak, expected to reach near full capacity utilization by Q4 in terms of manpower ramp-up.
All existing and newer India capacities shaping up very well; central India factories currently running at 85% capacity utilization.
In Karnataka, one factory being taken to full capacity utilization (incremental facility); in Ranchi, 2 units in operation — one at full capacity, other being taken to full capacity.
New brand-new units (one each in Karnataka and Ranchi) mentioned separately will be effective in 2029, distinct from the existing units being ramped up now.

Planned addition of 2,000-3,000 extra machines by end of this year, likely coming into operation in later half of next financial year, contributing to FY29 and beyond revenue; steady-state revenue per 1,000 machines added is ~INR175-200 crore (more like 200).
Early capex may happen in FY27 but larger capex will happen in FY28; internal go-ahead decision expected within next 3 months.

New capacity in Jharkhand and Karnataka: total investment ~INR100 crore for both facilities (INR50 crore each), INR70-75 crore to be spent this financial year; facilities to come on stream H2 FY28, full potential realized in FY29 (created over 1.5-2 years); each unit expected to reach ~3.5 million pieces and ~INR175 crore revenue run rate at steady state, combined incremental revenue of ~INR350 crore.

Older Bhopal facility fully running and working to plan; second Bhopal facility to reach full capacity by Q4 of this year (manpower ramp-up); new Bhopal capacity (~3.5 million pieces at ~INR500 ASP assumption) should yield revenue from H2 and beyond and add ~INR175 crore incremental revenue at steady state, with next year being its first full financial year.

Incremental capacity planning targets ~15-20% YoY revenue growth, of which 4-5% comes from productivity gains in existing factories, and the rest from incremental capacity (planned well in advance, yielding revenue in FY29 and beyond).

Already-commissioned expansions (Bhopal Phase 2, Karnataka, Ranchi) expected to add a shade under ~INR275 crore incremental revenue; further new expansions expected next year to add another ~INR250 crore; earlier plan for Karnataka/Ranchi contemplated adding 500-700 machines this year.

subsections.label: Africa capacity
points: African capacities being managed well, currently running at 80-85% utilization; second shift operations not increased beyond previous level as Q2 is seasonally weak.
Q3/Q4 order book expected to force stepping up capacity via second shift operations again, based on seasonal flows.
Company has ability and access to swing capacity, particularly in Africa where running a second shift is easier.
Also experimenting with second shift in Bhopal and Ranchi, both locations running second shift operations with reasonable success.
Existing Africa capacity already created; current capacity should support annual revenue delivery of about $120 million; quarterly run-rate of $30 million approaching full capacity utilization.
No plans for significant capex in Africa until existing capacity/second-shift potential exhausted.

subsections.label: Leasing / Bangladesh option
points: Leasing facilities remains an option if a good facility becomes available, though such facilities often have some defect or inadequacy that requires care in selection.
Currently doing subcon work out of Bangladesh; may consider more direct expansion there in future if conditions are favorable.

subsections.label: US/UK demand environment
points: End consumer demand in both US and UK recorded strong growth through first 6 months of CY'26, though US growth pace softened in June.

Apparel imports into EU and UK declined steadily for first 5 months of FY'26 — seen as reflecting a mix shift toward lower value apparel and continued inventory destocking by retailers rather than genuine contraction in underlying retail demand.
May marked first month of positive US import growth since beginning of CY'26 — an early but encouraging indicator.

subsections.label: Trade policy developments
points: US tariff under Section 301 places India on equal footing with competing sourcing destinations while preserving advantage over China and Vietnam (both subject to 12.5% tariff).
India-UK FTA implementation will bring India to parity with Bangladesh and Vietnam in UK market while providing duty advantage over China.

These developments do not create demand themselves but remove a structural disadvantage from customer sourcing decisions, expected to strengthen customer confidence and support higher order placement across key markets.

A 2.5% tariff advantage is not seen as remarkable — competitors may discount to offset; however directionally, when India's tariff is at par or better than rest of world, global placements gravitate to India.

Seeing broad interest from Europeans and Americans rebalancing sourcing portfolios toward India; India traditionally strong in fashion/high-value items (outerwear) but now also seeing interest for shirts and bottoms (typically Bangladesh-category products) in low-cost India regions.
Denim inquiries and business currently dominating trend flows into India, though such fashion trends change over time.

subsections.label: UK market strategy
points: UK FTA has resulted in some UK clients stepping up business; other geographies also growing.
Company working with select UK customers for long-term relationships; new UK customer in onboarding discussions.
UK contributes 4-4.5% of total revenue currently.

Given UK market is more fragmented than US, company's strategy is to target larger customer profiles (e.g., Marks & Spencer-type) since company is geared to handle larger customers; remaining margin-conscious in selecting business portfolio.

subsections.label: European FTA outlook
points: Eagerly awaiting European FTA, hoped to happen by H2 of calendar 2027; would open a large duty-free market and provide tremendous growth advantage.
Already ramping up relationships with European customers and growing with them ahead of FTA; real benefit expected once FTA is in execution.
Business being planned according to anticipated FTA timeline.

subsections.label: Africa AGOA/tariff dynamics
points: Under Section 301, Africa (Kenya) faces no tariff, unlike India/rest of Asia which face a 10% tariff — a Kenya-specific benefit.
AGOA gives Kenya duty-free access to US but expires in December; a bill to extend AGOA by 2 years has passed the Senate with bipartisan support, now needs House and President's consent.
AGOA extension would give more time to negotiate individual free trade agreements with countries like Ghana and Kenya, which are high on the agenda for such FTAs in Africa.

Business booking for Africa beyond December appears robust regardless of AGOA uncertainty, as customers see strong cost economics of Africa and are also taking a calculated risk on continued business.

Compared to Bangladesh (10% reciprocal tariff + 20-30% underlying tariff depending on cotton vs synthetic), Kenya has no duties at all — a very different value proposition drawing business (and Chinese companies setting up factories) to Africa; Egypt is another region seeing capacity build-up.
Africa FY27 revenue guidance range is $112-115 million, with company pushing for $120 million.

subsections.label: Shipping and logistics disruption
points: Strait of Hormuz and Houthi issues occasionally shutting down Red Sea routes; typhoons in China also impacting sailings from China to rest of world — both impacting container availability and shipping schedules.

Outbound shipping sometimes delayed by 2 weeks even though selling FOB — finished goods delivered to Indian port but take about 2 weeks to catch a ship, leaving company sitting on inventory and unable to realize receivables until goods are boarded.

Management believes current period represents the worst of the disruption; expects easing over next 2 quarters as war tensions may not hold, typhoon situation may improve, and global logistics improvement efforts continue; logistics costs may also get rationalized.
Working capital optimization continues to be pursued despite challenges like long shipping lead times.

subsections.label: Raw material cost pass-through
points: Fabric costs are largely passed through to customers via costing/pricing mechanism.
Ancillary costs (poly bag cartons, fuel) caught company by surprise in Q1 as not factored into pricing set months earlier (January); these are now being priced into new orders.

subsections.label: Customer/product strategy
points: Company positions itself as a versatile business partner able to handle any type of product, allowing it to benefit whatever the current fashion trend (e.g., current denim demand surge).
New product additions being seen across all major customers for next year summer season onward, including large retailers like Carhartt and Gap; high-ASP product examples range $40-50.
Focus in UK remains on larger customer profiles given company's operational scale, remaining margin-conscious in business selection.

subsections.label: M&A stance
points: Currently focused on existing business; not working on any inorganic (acquisition) moves outside India at this time.

key_figures.label: Revenue growth target Y-o-Y for capacity planning
Productivity gains contribution to revenue growth

subsections.label: BTPL merger
points: BTPL merger process on track, expected to conclude in Q3 FY27, subject to process; BTPL will effectively merge into Gokaldas for roughly the last 4 months of the year.
Focus on BTPL performance, ensuring the business performs strongly by end of calendar year; early signs encouraging.

subsections.label: Capacity planning approach
points: Company has already evaluated and identified opportunities for capacity expansions in low-cost parts of the country; awaiting internal go-ahead, decision expected within next 3 months.

Approach captured in philosophy 'plans are worthless, but planning is everything' — not positioning business around a single macro outcome but ensuring capacity, cost structure and customer relations to respond decisively to whichever direction the situation takes.
Revenue growth target for capacity planning is 15-20% Y-o-Y, of which 4-5% is expected to come from productivity gains.

subsections.label: Management-flagged headwinds (closing remarks)
points: Possible changes to RoSCTL incentive scheme.
Disruption to logistics.
US retail demand trajectory.
Tariff volatility — though on tariff side, situation currently looks good; company gearing for business volatility and feels confident it can handle it as long as within reasonable levels.

subsections.label: Cost inflation risks
points: Wages rose across India and Kenya reflecting local inflation.
Higher oil prices increased shipping, fuel, and logistics costs for fabric and trims.
Container availability constraints and shipping delays disrupted material flow affecting production planning and throughput.

Steep minimum wage revisions in select states this year (e.g., Haryana +35%, Noida +25%) versus Karnataka's more modest CPI-linked +5% increase; Karnataka non-textile minimum wage proposal considered 'outrageous' and high, but management does not foresee this applying to textiles/apparel — matter still being settled.
Cotton and MMF (polyester) raw material cost increases; ancillary costs like poly bags, cartons and fuel not factored into earlier pricing caught company by surprise in Q1.

subsections.label: Geopolitical/trade risk
points: Renewed US-Iran engagement has resulted in shipping reroutes and elevated freight costs, introducing uncertainty to global supply chain.
Inflationary pressure in US market warrants close monitoring as it may in time affect retail demand.

AGOA uncertainty: expires in December; extension bill needs House and Presidential approval after passing Senate; company operating with the assumption of extension but flags uncertainty still exists.
Any uncertainty (e.g., AGOA beyond December) is not favorable; earlier clarity would be beneficial.

subsections.label: Overall growth and margin outlook
points: When asked if mid-teens growth guidance holds given strong Q1, management said the earlier ~15% figure 'seems very straightforward' and company 'probably should do better than that.'
Order placement visibility for Spring '27 (executed Q3 FY27) and customer projections indicate fairly good revenue traction similar to Q1.

Regardless of Indian incentive changes (RoSCTL halving scenario) or African incentive changes, EBITDA margins expected to be higher than current base, aided by BTPL contribution, rupee cushion, and continuing operational efficiencies.

subsections.label: Africa outlook
points: Africa revenue visibility currently pegged at $112-115 million versus original $120 million target, with company still pushing to bridge the gap over the remaining half of the year.
Africa double-digit EBITDA margin (bounce back from current 8%) expected around Q4 FY27 or early Q1 FY28, with H2 being a differentiating factor.
AGOA extension expectation (2 years) underpins confidence in Africa order booking for H2 and beyond, though genuine uncertainty exists pending House/Presidential approval.

subsections.label: BTPL outlook
points: BTPL, once merged (Q3 FY27), expected to generate mid- to high single-digit EBITDA margin, contributing positively to Gokaldas.
Targeting EBITDA positive from Q3 FY27 and PBT positive in Q4 FY27 — a slip from the prior call's target of H1 breakeven.
Capacity, product mix (linen, linen blends, bottom-weight fabrics) and rising average realization expected to continue improving BTPL performance.

subsections.label: Capacity-linked revenue outlook
points: Planned 2,000-3,000 new machines by end of this year — expected to contribute to FY29 and beyond revenue at ~INR175-200 crore per 1,000 machines.
Jharkhand and Karnataka new units (INR100 crore combined capex) expected to come on stream H2 FY28 and realize full potential (INR350 crore combined revenue) in FY29.
Already-commissioned expansions (Bhopal Phase 2, Karnataka, Ranchi) expected to add ~INR275 crore revenue; further new expansions expected to add another ~INR250 crore next year.
European FTA, if executed by H2 CY2027, expected to open a large duty-free market with tremendous growth advantage.

Africa visibility at $112-115 million against the earlier $120 million target; still pushing for the full $120 million with about half a year left to bridge the balance.
Double-digit Africa EBITDA is expected to bounce back from the current 8% by Q4 or early next Q1; H2 will be a differentiating factor.
BTPL should be EBITDA positive by Q3 FY27, having missed the earlier H1 breakeven target; PBT positive is targeted for Q4 FY27.

By the time of merger, BTPL anticipated to generate mid- to high single-digit EBITDA margin and contribute positively to Gokaldas.

Total capex of about INR100 crores for both new Jharkhand and Karnataka units (INR70-75 crores this year), to come on stream H2 FY28, generating combined steady-state revenue of INR350 crores, full potential realized by FY29.

Bombay Rayon (BTPL) in FY28 should be contributing an EBITDA margin closer to 12%.

Q1/Q2 revenue run rate of about $24-25 million, then ramping to $32-33 million per quarter in H2 to reach the $115-120 million full-year target.
Revenue for BTPL in FY27 should be in excess of INR1,000 crores based on current momentum.
Bhopal will add INR175 crores and Karnataka unit INR125 crores in revenue at steady state (~INR300 crores combined).
Two additional planned units, at steady state (likely FY28 or later), can add another INR300-odd crores of revenue.
Capex for both new units combined should be of the order of INR80 crores to INR100 crores, spread over 2 years.
To sustain at least 15% kind of growth, company will work on the capex required to manage and deliver that growth.

risk_register.risk: Logistics/shipping disruption (Strait of Hormuz, Houthi, China typhoons)
risk_register.note: Container availability constraints and shipping delays continue; management believes current period is the worst and expects easing over next 2 quarters.

risk_register.risk: US retail demand trajectory / inflation
risk_register.note: US import growth pace softened in June; inflationary pressure in US market warrants close monitoring as it may affect retail demand in time.

risk_register.risk: Tariff volatility
risk_register.note: On tariff side, situation currently looks good per management, though still in a 'tariff volatile world'; company gearing for volatility.

risk_register.risk: AGOA expiry (December) uncertainty
risk_register.note: AGOA expires in December; extension bill passed Senate with bipartisan support but still needs House and Presidential approval; genuine uncertainty remains despite business booking proceeding regardless.

risk_register.risk: Wage/labor cost inflation
risk_register.note: Steep minimum wage hikes in select states this year (Haryana +35%, Noida +25%) versus Karnataka's CPI-linked +5%; India Q1 saw INR20 crore incremental wage cost YoY.

risk_register.risk: Karnataka non-textile minimum wage proposal
risk_register.note: Considered 'outrageous' and high by management; not expected to apply to textiles/apparel but matter still being settled in policymaking.

risk_register.risk: Raw material cost inflation (cotton, MMF/polyester, fuel, chemicals)
risk_register.note: Fabric costs largely pass-through, but ancillary costs (poly bags, cartons, fuel) caught company by surprise in Q1 as unpriced; being factored into pricing going forward; utilities/chemical cost hit of INR5-6 crore in Q1.

risk_register.risk: US-Iran geopolitical tension / shipping reroutes
risk_register.note: Renewed US-Iran engagement has resulted in shipping reroutes and elevated freight costs, introducing uncertainty to global supply chain.

risk_register.risk: US reciprocal/penal tariffs on Indian apparel imports
risk_register.note: Penal tariff peaked at 50% for much of FY26; withdrawn in February, followed by Supreme Court ruling reducing tariff to 10% until July 24, 2026; possible Section 301 tariff (~20%) could be reimposed from end of July.

risk_register.risk: AGOA uncertainty for Africa operations
risk_register.note: AGOA restored till December 2026; renewal beyond that remains undecided, with US administration favoring country-by-country deals; management believes further extension likely but not certain.

risk_register.risk: Middle East (Iran) war raising raw material and logistics costs
risk_register.note: Increased cost of fuel, packaging, polyester, trims, cotton, and shipping; also caused LPG shortages affecting oven utilization, requiring switch to electric components.

risk_register.risk: Russia-Ukraine war pressure on EU markets
risk_register.note: Continued pressure on EU demand though it did not impact supply chains as much as the Middle East war.

risk_register.risk: Inflation impacting consumer spending
risk_register.note: Inflation across economies due to higher fuel prices could impact consumer spending in key markets like the US.

risk_register.risk: Customer resistance to input cost pass-through
risk_register.note: Company may only partially pass on price increases to customers in H2 due to customer resistance and competitive absorption of costs by Southeast Asian and Chinese under-utilized players.

risk_register.risk: Tariff refund pass-through uncertainty
risk_register.note: Unclear whether U.S. tariff refunds obtained by brands will be passed back to the supply chain; ongoing disputes (e.g., Nike class action) add uncertainty; company is not counting on any benefit.

risk_register.risk: Labor cost inflation in India
risk_register.note: Sharp wage hikes announced in Haryana (35%) and UP (25%) in response to labor unrest and rising living costs, spreading across regions.

risk_register.risk: Labor availability constraints in South India and NCR
risk_register.note: Company depends on migrant labor in these regions; challenges remain for second-shift operations, especially for women labor in the South.

risk_register.risk: U.K. and EU FTA delays
risk_register.note: U.K. FTA ratification delayed due to political events and other issues (e.g., steel); EU FTA requires ratification by 27 individual countries, expected to conclude around 2027; benefits not factored into FY27 outlook.

risk_register.risk: Working capital increase
risk_register.note: Working capital rose by ~INR200 crores in FY26 due to receivables, inventory buildup, and customer mix; company targets reduction of INR75-100 crores in FY27.

risk_register.risk: Underperformance of acquired entities (Atraco, fabric businesses) vs internal targets
risk_register.note: Not up to targets in FY26 due to extraordinary tariff disruption; expected to perform as per plan in FY27.

risk_register.risk: Unknown future geopolitical/tariff disruptions
risk_register.note: Management repeatedly caveats guidance with uncertainty over what disruptions may be unleashed in the year ahead.

risk_register.risk: Competitive pressure from Vietnam and China in synthetics
risk_register.note: China's scale in fiber/yarn/fabric ecosystems and Vietnam's proximity-driven supply chain give both regions a cost/quality edge in synthetic garments versus India.

risk_register.risk: Bangladesh energy disruptions and diesel availability
risk_register.note: Power cuts and diesel shortages in Bangladesh create volatility, though most operators manage deliveries; customers remain wary of expanding aggressively there.

themes.note: Section 301 tariff places India on equal footing with competing sourcing destinations, preserving advantage over China/Vietnam (12.5% tariff); India-UK FTA brings parity with Bangladesh/Vietnam and advantage over China.

key_takeaways: Consolidated income for the quarter grew 21% year-on-year; Consolidated EBITDA rose 17% year-on-year, with India operations up 14%.

India business grew 16% year-on-year, supported in part by the transition to the lower tariff regime under Section 122; Indian apparel exports as a whole declined 12% year-on-year during the same period.
Africa business delivered exceptional 45% year-on-year growth, supported by the renewal of AGOA, partly drawing from a weak Q1 of the previous year.

BTPL merger process is on track and is expected to conclude in the third quarter of this year; the unit is operating at a capacity of about 50 lakh meters a month, expected to grow by another 30% in the near future.
We onboarded 1 new customer during the quarter with operations expected to commence in Q2.

The U.S. tariff announced under Section 301 places India on an equal footing with competing sourcing destinations while preserving an advantage over China and Vietnam, both of which are subject to a tariff of 12.5%.
The implementation of India U.K. free trade agreement will bring India to parity with Bangladesh and Vietnam in the U.K. market, while providing a duty advantage over China.

We have a strong order book visibility across our customer base. We continue to diversify our customer portfolio and remain confident in our ability to convert improving market conditions into performance through superior execution and operational excellence.

quarters.summary: Management believes the worst of the tariff-driven disruption is behind the company; with penal U.S. tariffs normalized to 10% (until July 24, 2026) and AGOA restored till December 2026, FY27 revenue and margin outlook has improved. India margins are expected to improve a couple of percentage points YoY, Africa EBITDA margin is targeted at 8-10% in H2 FY27, and BTPL is expected to turn EBITDA breakeven in H1 FY27 and EBITDA positive (6-7%) in H2 FY27, with merger into Gokaldas expected to conclude in Q3 FY27.

subsections.label: EBITDA margin drivers
points: EBITDA margin was sustained at previous year's level, absorbing a severe financial setback in terms of tariff burden share.
Standalone Q4 margin improvement was largely because of sheer volume/revenue growth and resulting operating leverage; no tariff reversals were factored into margins.
Half of Q4 was impacted by the 50% penal tariff which was withdrawn mid-February; post that, shipments did not carry the tariff discounts offered until mid-February, aiding margin improvement.
Tariff rebates (up to 15%) went away once penal tariff was withdrawn from mid-February; sharper pricing (about 3%) given in H1 continues but will be removed in H2.

Other Indian subsidiaries (non-Gokaldas, e.g., Matrix) had minor setbacks in Q4 because tariff remained at ~50% in Q3/Q4 and some customers pivoted to other regions instead of asking for discounts; expected to reverse in FY27 as tariffs normalized.

subsections.label: Working capital
points: Working capital deployed increased in Africa due to customer mix in Q4 and a year-end factor where receivables took longer to mature.
Fabric-related working capital increases also contributed.
Additional raw material import was advanced to cater to Q1 FY27 order execution due to Chinese holidays, requiring incremental inventory investment.
Incremental volume buildup in Atraco also added to inventory needs.
Company is working with customers on early payment programs to manage receivables.
BTPL merger into Gokaldas will bring incremental working capital requirement, but also its own revenue stream.

subsections.label: Tax expense
points: Rise in tax expense mainly belongs to the standalone entity because at a consolidated level, losses of overseas entities (Atraco) and new fabric-business investments are not eligible for tax credit/set-off, inflating the effective consolidated tax rate.
At the individual entity level in India, tax rate is normal at 25.17%.

subsections.label: BTPL performance
points: BTPL lost about 4-5% at EBITDA level in Q4 FY26.
BTPL revenue for FY27 expected to exceed INR1,000 crores based on current momentum.
Captive fabric consumption by Gokaldas from BTPL is about 30-35% of BTPL output.

key_figures.label: Indian apparel exports decline Q4 FY26
Africa business growth Q4 FY26 (AGOA extension)
Expected revenue growth FY27 (excl FTA benefits)

subsections.label: Demand environment
points: U.S. and U.K. retail sales witnessed strong growth in CY25; U.S. sales continue strong in early 2026 while U.K. is showing signs of waning.

Despite strong sales, U.S. retailers have started paring down imports from H2 CY25 owing to market and tariff-related uncertainties, which could pare down inventory and provide cushion for future growth.
Company's revenues never dipped even during the 50% tariff regime; revenue was maintained and even slightly grew despite discounts, reflecting strength of customer relationships.
Order book for Africa operations is described as fairly strong; company currently working on Q3/Q4 Africa orders with strong traction.

Company is currently booking orders for spring '27; order flow is good but customers are being conservative given inflation/gas price concerns in the U.S., with orders expected to be topped up closer to date.
Company's order book is relatively robust and strong despite customer conservatism.

subsections.label: Tariff impact on demand history
points: Reciprocal tariff (in addition to MFN tariffs) remained at a staggering 50% for a significant part of the year, higher than most countries including China.
Company offered a net discount of over INR90 crores for the year to customers to offset tariff burden (net of discounts imposed on its own supply chain).
Withdrawal of penal 25% tariff in February and subsequent U.S. Supreme Court ruling against the tariffs led to a 10% tariff being imposed until July 24, 2026.
AGOA got restored till December 2026, restoring competitiveness of main production centres and improving FY27 revenue/margin outlook.

key_figures.label: Africa revenue run rate Q1/Q2 FY27
Africa revenue for remaining two quarters FY27
New customer contribution to revenue in first year

subsections.label: India vs Africa business performance
points: India business operations grew 2% in Q4 FY26 despite steep tariffs; Africa business, supported by AGOA extension, expanded 17% YoY in Q4.
India operations grew 10% YoY in FY26 despite U.S. tariff-related uncertainties.
Africa business declined 19% in FY26, primarily impacted up to Q3 due to AGOA uncertainties leading to reduced order book.
Africa business witnessed healthy growth and will continue its growth momentum in FY27 post AGOA renewal.
Africa EBITDA margin anticipated to reach 8-10% in H2 FY27, driven by strong order flow and operating leverage.

Other Indian subsidiaries (Matrix and others) had minor Q4 setbacks due to continued high tariff (~50%) in Q3/Q4, with some customers pivoting to other regions rather than seeking discounts; expected to reverse in FY27.

subsections.label: New customers
points: Company signed up two new premium customers in FY26 for India operations — one American, one European — that will begin yielding revenue from FY27.
Growth of revenue from European customers continues to be strong.
For Africa operations, company onboarded two new customers — one American, one European — that will begin operations in FY27.

Company is being selective in adding new customers to avoid overhead from managing multiple new customers depressing profit in the initial period; may add one or two more premium customers currently in discussion.
Contribution from new customers in the first year expected to be single-digit percentage of total revenue (~5%), scaling up in subsequent years.
Existing customers provide enough order flow to absorb additional capacity, supporting sustained growth momentum.

subsections.label: Margin outlook by segment
points: Steady-state (FY28, absent disruptions) India EBITDA margin estimated at 13-13.5%.
Steady-state Africa EBITDA margin estimated at 10-10.5% for FY28.
BTPL EBITDA margin estimated closer to 12% in FY28, rising to ~14% in FY29.

American customers generally give better margins than European due to larger order volumes/run sizes and larger retailers; European retail base is more fragmented and fashion-oriented, requiring multiple customers to match the revenue of one American customer.

subsections.label: India capacity expansion
points: Karnataka (Kolar Gold Fields) facility has half the factory yet to ramp up; ramping in Q1/Q2 to full capacity utilization.

Second unit in Madhya Pradesh (Bhopal) is being commissioned; lines are expanding and expected to reach full capacity utilization by Q3 FY27 (Sept-Oct onwards) with 1,000 machines operating at full capacity.

Company has option to commission 2 new factories, decision to be taken next quarter depending on tariff/geopolitical situation; more likely to sustain growth into latter half of FY27 but particularly FY28.
Additional capex for the two new units will be incurred in FY28 as lines are added; some revenue may fructify in early FY28.
Debottlenecking capacities will continue across all existing facilities, contributing additional incremental revenue beyond the specific unit figures given.

subsections.label: Africa capacity expansion
points: Capacity expansion in Africa already happened last year; factories and operations are completely aligned.
Additional tailwind opportunity exists through second shift operations without significant further capex; one factory already running ~20-25% of capacity on 2 shifts successfully.
Labor availability is easier for second-shift recruitment in Africa vs. India given the need for jobs there.

subsections.label: Labor / shift operations in India
points: In Ranchi, 2 shifts are operating successfully as labor force there is more amenable.
In Madhya Pradesh, 2 shifts are possible but only in part of the factory.
Second shift is not feasible in the South due to cultural/family factors among (particularly women) labor force; less flexibility found in rest of India outside Central India/Ranchi.

subsections.label: Regional dynamics
points: Most U.S. retailers and many EU retailers continue to diversify away from China-based suppliers, helping growth of other sourcing regions including India.
India remains a strong long-term prospect for sourcing; trend of consolidating in favor of stronger suppliers continues.
FTAs with the European region could help strengthen the industry's prospects.

European customers consider they have overinvested in Bangladesh (which is duty-free to Europe); once an EU-India FTA arrives, they intend to diversify out of Bangladesh to some extent as a level playing field emerges between India and Europe.

American customers view Bangladesh as now relatively stable under the new BNP government and continuing to be a low-cost region, but concerns remain about Bangladesh's vulnerability to oil shocks given import dependence and low BoP surpluses.
Overall impression: Bangladesh remains cost-effective and politically more stable but customers are looking to diversify, with India standing out as a viable diversification option.

Vietnam is gaining share as China loses share, driven by Chinese players relocating/setting up factories in Vietnam to leverage Chinese raw material supply chains (fiber, yarn, fabric) despite higher Vietnamese labor costs.
Vietnam labor costs near large cities approaching $400 vs hinterland $250-300+, still costlier than India's ~$210, but value chain advantages sustain Vietnam's cost-effectiveness for synthetics.

Roughly two-thirds of global apparel trade is synthetic-based (polyester/nylon), where China has global-quality capacity that India lacks; synthetic garments (preferred fall-winter) favor China/Vietnam-linked supply chains.
Cotton-based garments (preferred spring-summer) favor India/Bangladesh, giving second-half seasonality advantage to Indian apparel manufacturers.

Gokaldas leads in synthetic manufacturing in India, growing strongly in outerwear; fabric for synthetics still largely dependent on China, Vietnam, Taiwan, Korea, though domestic fabric capacity (e.g., Vardhman) is increasing.

Kenya (bulk of Africa operations) tariff to remain at 10% under Section 301 regardless of AGOA status since Africa is not under Section 301 investigation, providing a sustainable regional tariff advantage.

subsections.label: AGOA / Africa specific
points: House of Representatives approved a 3-year AGOA renewal but administration reduced it to 1 year; belief is AGOA may be extended by 1-2 more years towards year-end, enabling US to pursue country-by-country deals.
Ongoing FTA discussion with Kenya; management not confident it concludes by end of this year but feels AGOA may get extended, providing relief.

If AGOA renewal is delayed again, unlike the last time (when Africa business was not resilient and management refused to share tariff burden with customers, leading to a revenue drop), this time the customer base is more diversified, multiple conversations have occurred to ensure business flow continuity regardless of AGOA status, and the company is open to addressing AGOA-related tariff issues given its scale.

subsections.label: Raw material cost pressures
points: U.S./Iran war impacted textile value chain with increased cost of raw materials like fuel, packaging, polyester and trims.
Cotton prices have risen due to higher yarn exports to China, substitution from MMF to natural fibers, weather-related disruptions, etc.
Shipping costs have increased as well.
Cotton prices depending on cotton yields may probably ease off starting October-November this year.
Cotton/raw material price increases will eventually be a pass-through for the company in pricing of goods produced.
LPG shortages caused by Iran war meant ovens run on LPG had utilization challenges; company had to switch to electric components, which took time to implement.
Middle Eastern war disruption has been much more significant for supply chains than the Russia-Ukraine war, which impacted European demand but not supply chains.

subsections.label: Hedging policy
points: Company hedges receivables for future quarters: ~80% of revenue hedged for the next two quarters, and ~50% for the third and fourth quarters ahead.
Hedges for ~80% of revenue up to Q2 are locked at rates ranging from INR87 to INR91 per dollar.
Rupee weakened faster than expected recently, making hedges counterproductive in the near term; rupee depreciation advantage is not yet reflected in numbers and will likely only flow in H2.
Company does not speculate on rupee movement in either direction.

subsections.label: Labor cost and availability
points: Labor availability differs by region: strong in Central India (MP), Ranchi; challenging in South India and NCR, requiring dependence on migrant labor.
Incremental expansion is targeting rural/hinterland areas to tap labor availability, including deep rural regions in the South.

Haryana state government announced a 35% wage increase from April 1 in response to labor unrest and high living costs for migrant labor in the Gurgaon-Manesar belt; UP responded with a 25% increase as unrest spilled over to Noida/UP.
Rupee depreciation could offset some labor cost inflation pressure.
Labor cost inflation may bring stability by reducing attrition/absenteeism, aiding productivity, though this remains a challenge to grapple with over the next 1-2 years.
Vietnam, China labor costs are around $300+, while India is still at about $210, providing some cost headroom for India that must be offset with productivity gains.

subsections.label: Customer relationships and competitive positioning
points: Company's revenues never dipped even during the 50% tariff regime; revenue maintained and even slightly grew despite discounts, demonstrating strength of customer relationships with substantial American customer base.
With tariffs leveled off to a global equal tariff, competitive advantage vs rest of world/Asia is sustained even if Section 301 tariff (~20%) is imposed from end of July.
Weaker rupee will add competitive advantage in the future once hedges roll off.
Company watching how U.S. retail sales pan out in H2 CY26/early '27; currently booking spring '27 orders.

Southeast Asian and Chinese players are willing to absorb some cost increases strategically due to under-capacity utilization, creating competitive pressure on passing through input cost inflation to customers.

Company's endeavor is to push back price increases to customers in H2 but expects only partial recovery, not full pass-through, due to customer resistance amid anticipated inflation-led demand challenges in the US.

Tariff refund uncertainty: U.S. tariff reversal portal has opened; brands are applying for refunds but it is unclear whether refunds will be passed back through the supply chain; Nike faces a class action suit over tariff pass-through; company is not counting on any tariff refund benefit.
No short-term tactical apparel demand uptick observed from GLP-1 adoption; management says it will have to wait and see.

subsections.label: BTPL merger
points: Company has initiated merger of BTPL subject to NCLT approval, expected to conclude in Q3 FY27.
Steady progress of operational improvement at BTPL; expected to turn in operating profits in H2 of the financial year.
BTPL merger will add incremental working capital requirement to Gokaldas but will also bring its own revenue stream.

subsections.label: Leadership and process building
points: Company used the tariff disruption opportunity to strengthen its leadership team, build durable processes and expand customer outreach to secure the company from future shocks.

key_figures.label: Section 301 tariffs from July for rest of the world

subsections.label: Geopolitical and tariff risks
points: FY26 marked by spectacular disruptions: reciprocal tariff imposed at the start of the year went through multiple iterations, remaining at 50% (in addition to already-high MFN tariffs) for a significant part of the year — higher than most countries including China.
War in the Middle East (Iran) imposed upward pressure on raw material costs in the latter part of the year.
War in Ukraine continued to pressure EU markets.
AGOA uncertainty led to reduced Africa order book up to Q3, causing a revenue drop of about INR180 crores.
Even if Section 301 tariff is reimposed, there is a strong likelihood it will be similar to most competing Asian nations (~20%); Africa is not under Section 301 investigation, providing comfort.
Inflation across economies due to higher fuel prices could impact consumer spending.
AGOA renewal beyond December 2026 remains undecided; US administration favors country-by-country deals rather than a pan-Africa deal, creating uncertainty on renewal duration.
Risk that AGOA delay could again trigger customer order-shifting/discount demands as happened previously, though management believes diversified customer base now mitigates this risk.

U.K.-India FTA delayed (was expected by April/May) due to political events in U.K. and other issues (e.g., steel) cropping up; EU-India FTA ratification process is long-winded, requiring ratification by 27 individual EU countries, expected to conclude around 2027.

Global capacity/demand fights among Southeast Asian and Chinese players (who are absorbing costs strategically due to under-utilization) create pricing pressure on the company's ability to pass through input cost inflation.

Bangladesh LDC status extended from 2026 to 2029; post-2029 removal is likely, but whether Bangladesh secures an EU FTA before then is uncertain since FTAs are reciprocal and depend on EU perceiving Bangladesh as large enough a market.
Labor cost inflation risk in India: sharp wage hikes announced in Haryana (35%) and UP (25%) in response to labor unrest and high living costs for migrant labor.
Uncertain future disruptions: management repeatedly notes 'we don't know what kind of disruptions will be unleashed in the year ahead' and factors this into guidance caveats.
