subsections.label: Outlook commentary
points: Company expected to continue its growth trajectory in FY27, delivering strong performance across its business.
With competitiveness of main production centres restored (10% tariff, AGOA restored), revenue and margin outlook for FY27 has improved.
Management believes worst is behind the company; even if Section 301 tariff is reimposed, it should bring India near parity with rest of Asia (~20%).
FY27 margin guidance is subject to unknown future disruptions (geopolitical events, new tariffs); company's endeavor is to do better than the couple of percentage point improvement guided.
BTPL aiming for at least EBITDA breakeven in H1 FY27, EBITDA positive in H2 FY27 with margin of ~6-7%.
Capex will be undertaken selectively depending on how the tariff regime unfolds in July, but to sustain at least 15% growth, necessary capex will be pursued.
U.K. and EU FTA benefits have NOT been factored into FY27 outlook; any FTA materialization would provide further upside.
Acquired entities (Atraco, fabric businesses) not currently performing to internal targets due to extraordinary tariff-related disruption in FY26, but expected to perform as per plan in FY27.

guidance_ledger.statement: Anticipate Africa business EBITDA margin of somewhere between 8% and 10% in H2 FY27, working towards that.
Excluding FTA factor, revenue growth should be much more than the 10-12% suggested by the analyst.
Intention is to bring down working capital by at least about INR75 crores to INR100 crores in FY27 in Gokaldas and Atraco operations.
India EBITDA margin should be of the order of 13% to 13.5% in a steady FY28 (absent major disruptions).
Africa EBITDA margin should be about 10% to 10.5% in a steady FY28.
Ratio between India and Africa revenue should be about 75%-25% or anywhere between 80%-20%.
Bombay Rayon (BTPL) in FY28 should be contributing an EBITDA margin closer to 12%.
BTPL EBITDA margin should be of the order of 14% in FY29.
BTPL aiming for at least EBITDA breakeven in H1 FY27, and intend to achieve EBITDA positive in H2 FY27, with EBITDA around 6% to 7% in H2.
There will be a couple of percentage point improvement in margins YoY on account of disruptions being behind us; endeavor will be to try to do better than that.
Target approximately $115 million to $120 million in revenue in FY27 regardless of AGOA status, up from ~$80 million in FY26.
Q1/Q2 revenue run rate of about $24-25 million, then ramping to $32-33 million per quarter in H2 to reach the $115-120 million full-year target.
Revenue for BTPL in FY27 should be in excess of INR1,000 crores based on current momentum.
Bhopal will add INR175 crores and Karnataka unit INR125 crores in revenue at steady state (~INR300 crores combined).
Two additional planned units, at steady state (likely FY28 or later), can add another INR300-odd crores of revenue.
Capex for both new units combined should be of the order of INR80 crores to INR100 crores, spread over 2 years.
Raising BTPL capacity from 70 lakh to 100 lakh meters per month would require additional capex of about INR50 crores to INR60 crores.
To sustain at least 15% kind of growth, company will work on the capex required to manage and deliver that growth.
Merger of BTPL, subject to NCLT approval, is expected to conclude in Q3 FY27.

risk_register.risk: US reciprocal/penal tariffs on Indian apparel imports
risk_register.note: Penal tariff peaked at 50% for much of FY26; withdrawn in February, followed by Supreme Court ruling reducing tariff to 10% until July 24, 2026; possible Section 301 tariff (~20%) could be reimposed from end of July.

risk_register.risk: AGOA uncertainty for Africa operations
risk_register.note: AGOA restored till December 2026; renewal beyond that remains undecided, with US administration favoring country-by-country deals; management believes further extension likely but not certain.

risk_register.risk: Middle East (Iran) war raising raw material and logistics costs
risk_register.note: Increased cost of fuel, packaging, polyester, trims, cotton, and shipping; also caused LPG shortages affecting oven utilization, requiring switch to electric components.

risk_register.risk: Russia-Ukraine war pressure on EU markets
risk_register.note: Continued pressure on EU demand though it did not impact supply chains as much as the Middle East war.

risk_register.risk: Inflation impacting consumer spending
risk_register.note: Inflation across economies due to higher fuel prices could impact consumer spending in key markets like the US.

risk_register.risk: Customer resistance to input cost pass-through
risk_register.note: Company may only partially pass on price increases to customers in H2 due to customer resistance and competitive absorption of costs by Southeast Asian and Chinese under-utilized players.

risk_register.risk: Tariff refund pass-through uncertainty
risk_register.note: Unclear whether U.S. tariff refunds obtained by brands will be passed back to the supply chain; ongoing disputes (e.g., Nike class action) add uncertainty; company is not counting on any benefit.

risk_register.risk: Labor cost inflation in India
risk_register.note: Sharp wage hikes announced in Haryana (35%) and UP (25%) in response to labor unrest and rising living costs, spreading across regions.

risk_register.risk: Labor availability constraints in South India and NCR
risk_register.note: Company depends on migrant labor in these regions; challenges remain for second-shift operations, especially for women labor in the South.

risk_register.risk: U.K. and EU FTA delays
risk_register.note: U.K. FTA ratification delayed due to political events and other issues (e.g., steel); EU FTA requires ratification by 27 individual countries, expected to conclude around 2027; benefits not factored into FY27 outlook.

risk_register.risk: Working capital increase
risk_register.note: Working capital rose by ~INR200 crores in FY26 due to receivables, inventory buildup, and customer mix; company targets reduction of INR75-100 crores in FY27.

risk_register.risk: Underperformance of acquired entities (Atraco, fabric businesses) vs internal targets
risk_register.note: Not up to targets in FY26 due to extraordinary tariff disruption; expected to perform as per plan in FY27.

risk_register.risk: Unknown future geopolitical/tariff disruptions
risk_register.note: Management repeatedly caveats guidance with uncertainty over what disruptions may be unleashed in the year ahead.

risk_register.risk: Competitive pressure from Vietnam and China in synthetics
risk_register.note: China's scale in fiber/yarn/fabric ecosystems and Vietnam's proximity-driven supply chain give both regions a cost/quality edge in synthetic garments versus India.

risk_register.risk: Bangladesh energy disruptions and diesel availability
risk_register.note: Power cuts and diesel shortages in Bangladesh create volatility, though most operators manage deliveries; customers remain wary of expanding aggressively there.

themes.label: Tariff normalization
themes.note: Penal US tariffs eased from 50% to 10% (until July 24, 2026), restoring competitiveness and improving FY27 revenue/margin outlook.

themes.label: AGOA/Africa tariff risk
themes.note: AGOA restored till December 2026 but renewal beyond that remains undecided; Africa expected to see strong revenue growth to $115-120 million in FY27.

themes.label: Input cost inflation
themes.note: Middle East war drove up costs of fuel, polyester, packaging, trims, cotton and shipping, with only partial pass-through to customers expected.

themes.label: Capacity expansion
themes.note: New capacity being added in India (Karnataka, Bhopal) and Africa (second shifts), plus BTPL capacity expansion potential, to support sustained ~15% growth.

themes.label: Customer diversification / new wins
themes.note: Two new premium customers added in both India and Africa operations, expected to begin yielding revenue in FY27, alongside strong existing customer order flow.

themes.label: China-plus-one sourcing shift
themes.note: US and EU retailers continuing to diversify away from China and Bangladesh, benefiting India and Vietnam, though Vietnam and China retain synthetics advantage.

themes.label: Labor cost inflation
themes.note: Sharp state-level wage hikes (Haryana 35%, UP 25%) reflect rising labor cost pressure in India, partly offset by potential rupee depreciation and productivity gains.

key_takeaways: In Q4 FY '26, India business operations for Gokaldas Exports grew by 2% despite the prevalence of steep tariff and the Africa business supported by an extension of AGOA expanded by 17% Y-o-Y.
In FY '26, India operations grew by 10% Y-o-Y despite U.S. tariff-related uncertainties, while Indian apparel exports witnessed a decline of 1.4%.
The company offered a net discount of over INR90 crores for the year to its customers to offset the tariff burden.

Africa business declined by 19%, primarily impacted in the period up to Q3 due to AGOA uncertainties, leading to a reduced order book for that period, resulting in a revenue drop of about INR180 crores.
Despite these headwinds, the company delivered a total income of INR4,065 crores, a 4% growth over the previous year.

The withdrawal of penal 25% tariff in February and the subsequent U.S. Supreme Court ruling against the tariffs led to a 10% tariff being imposed until July 24, 2026. AGOA got restored till December 2026.
With the competitiveness of these main production centres of the company restored, the revenue and margin outlook for FY '27 has improved.
The company signed up two new premium customers in FY '26 for its India operations, one American and one European that will begin yielding revenue from FY'27.
The company has initiated merger of BTPL subject to NCLT approval. This is expected to conclude in the third quarter of FY '27.

The capacity utilization at BTPL is approaching nearly 50 lakh meters per month, and the mill has currently a capacity of 70 lakh meters a month and can be raised to 100 lakh meters per month with an additional capital expenditure of about INR50 crores to INR60 crores.

STYRENIX.about: Incorporated in 1973, Styrenix Performance Materials Ltd manufactures, trades and sells Engineering Thermoplastics[1]

quarters.summary: Q1 FY27 was marked by heightened global macro/geopolitical uncertainty (Middle East disruption) that caused raw material price volatility, demand hesitancy in non-OEM/unorganized segments, and a resultant volume dip, even as reported margins expanded sharply due to a temporary lag between raw material cost and finished product pricing. Management guided that ABS capacity expansion remains on track for completion within FY27 (exact month not specified), SAN merchant sales will continue unaffected by captive ABS usage, no specific volume guidance was given given ongoing uncertainty, and margins/volumes are expected to normalize toward historical sustainable levels once volatility subsides, with Thailand sales build-out continuing on a multi-year validation timeline.

key_figures.label: Extra cash flow generated (last 2 quarters, per analyst estimate)

subsections.label: Margin drivers
points: Sharp YoY improvement in EBITDA and PAT margins attributed to a temporary gap/lag between raw material cost movements and finished product pricing during the volatile quarter, described by management as 'abnormally high margins' not indicative of sustainable business performance.

Management stated the benefits seen in the quarter are a 'snapshot in time' from specific events and should not be viewed as the new sustainable margin run-rate; sustainable performance should be assessed based on periods prior to these events.

Once market conditions normalize, margins and volumes are expected to revert to the company's historical annualized operating basis; no assumption of structural margin expansion should be made for analysis purposes.

subsections.label: Capital allocation
points: Company's capital allocation philosophy remains unchanged: judicious use of capital, funding planned capex from internal cash flow, and returning surplus cash not required for growth to shareholders.
No incremental change in capital allocation strategy despite additional cash flow generated (~INR100 crores over last 2 quarters) from the volatile pricing environment.

key_figures.label: Estimated demand dip across ABS/PS segments
Average quarterly demand base - ABS (analyst estimate)
Average quarterly demand base - PS (analyst estimate)

subsections.label: Demand disruption drivers
points: Disruption began in the first week of March due to Middle East conflict, with some impact seen in the prior quarter but far more pronounced in the current quarter.

Sharp raw material price increases and significant volatility from late March onward created buyer uncertainty, leading to a cautious/wait-and-watch approach particularly among non-OEM/unorganized sector buyers.
Impact on demand was more pronounced in polystyrene than in ABS; both product segments saw lower demand but to differing degrees.
OEM segment demand impact was comparatively muted versus the more significant impact on the non-OEM/unorganized sector.

Demand-supply-pricing correlation is broad-based across the polymer industry, not specific to the company; significant price increases generally trigger a cautious buying approach rather than 'demand destruction'.
In appliances end-sector, there has been a more noticeable production/demand impact; in auto sector, the effect has been muted with production numbers more or less flat.

Some destocking/restocking dynamics among customers' customers (retailers) may have contributed to the gap between end-consumer demand and reported volumes, per analyst suggestion; management partially concurred but noted actual underlying demand impact exists too.
Management expects underlying demand to return strongly once volatility normalizes, but could not quantify timing or magnitude given continued geopolitical uncertainty.

subsections.label: Pricing dynamics
points: Raw material and finished product pricing normally move in tandem under normalized conditions; extraordinary volatility created short-term gaps between the two, which drove the abnormally high margins seen this quarter.
Previous quarter's pricing was significantly higher than the quarter before it, and moderated somewhat towards the end of the quarter, though volatility persists.
Company declined to comment on current quarter (Q2 FY27) pricing levels citing continuing volatility and daily/weekly changes tied to Strait of Hormuz developments and raw material news flow.
Short-term pricing mechanisms were used with customers (e.g., auto ancillaries) to balance servicing requirements against elevated cost/availability of raw materials during the disrupted period.

subsections.label: Auto/appliance customer inventory and buying pattern
points: Most Tier 1 auto ancillary customers buy directly from the company rather than through distributors; grade specification and share of business is typically governed by OEM-driven formulas/systems.
Some smaller volumes are routed through distributors for fulfilment purposes.
Customer inventory strategy varies by company depending on import vs. local buying mix; analyst advised to reference listed ancillary companies' balance sheets for typical inventory levels.

subsections.label: SAN business
points: SAN is a relatively small market in India compared to ABS and polystyrene; company is a major player in SAN relative to market size.

Company sells close to 15,000-20,000 tonnes per year of SAN merchant sales, a figure that does not change materially year to year; the remainder of the ~100,000 tonne SAN capacity is largely used captively/in-house.

SAN merchant sales will continue unaffected by the ABS expansion and captive usage increase; company is expanding capacities across rubber, SAN and compounding sites to meet additional requirements from the ABS expansion.

subsections.label: STYROLOY / ASALAC (Thailand new grades)
points: Volumes have grown from zero business to a few thousand tonnes on an annualized basis, though breakup details are not disclosed given competitive sensitivity.

subsections.label: ABS vs Polystyrene capital allocation priority
points: Both ABS and polystyrene businesses are important to the organization; capital allocation decisions are guided by customer requirements, organizational objectives and capital allocation context.
Company has allocated capital to polystyrene in the past for expansion and will continue to do so as the business case becomes clear; current priority is the ABS expansion already underway.
No further specifics were shared on any new polystyrene expansion decision at this stage; management will update investors as and when a decision is made.

subsections.label: ABS capex progress (India, brownfield)
points: ABS capacity expansion is a ~50,000 tonne brownfield expansion, being executed while the current plant continues running.

Management reiterated the expansion will be completed within this financial year (FY27); exact month not disclosed due to complexities of commissioning within a running (brownfield) plant, as opposed to a greenfield site where exact scheduling is more straightforward.

Priorities of safety, environment and stakeholder obligations take precedence over disclosing an exact commissioning date; management indicated it would not necessarily fall precisely in Q3 or Q4, keeping the timeline broad as 'this financial year'.
Expansion covers rubber, SAN and compounding capacities in addition to ABS, to support the incremental capacity requirement.

subsections.label: Thailand utilization
points: Thailand plant is operating at fairly low utilization levels on specific products; impact on Thailand volumes from the regional demand disruption was not significant given the already low utilization base.

Management stated Thailand cost structure is higher than India's and not directly comparable; no cost increases reported in Thailand during the quarter, and no specific timeline guidance given for cost reduction.

subsections.label: Thailand export markets
points: Thailand business supplies substantial sales to China, Japan, Vietnam, within Thailand itself, and also to Indonesia, Korea and Malaysia.
Company has established sales presence including offices in Shanghai (China) and Vietnam, and sales representatives in Seoul (Korea) and Osaka (Japan) to drive validations and sales growth.
Product validation processes in these markets/sectors can take 12-24 months, progressing from trial lots to small commercial orders to larger meaningful commercial orders.

subsections.label: Southeast Asia market-building activity
points: New market-building activity in Southeast Asia remains on track with good feedback received, though this has not yet translated into significant volume growth in Thailand.

Current weak demand environment makes it more challenging to convert new business opportunities into volume, similar dynamics as seen in India; management views this as a short-term phenomenon that should ease once conditions normalize.

subsections.label: Import dynamics into India
points: No exact import/export data available as the government has restricted sharing of such trade data; management relies on customer interactions and market understanding.
No significant variance observed in import volumes into India in the last quarter compared to prior quarters — described as 'more or less similar'.

Some traditional exporting countries to India faced production challenges due to structural issues linked to disrupted energy/naphtha supply via the Strait of Hormuz, resulting in some competitors no longer quoting aggressively in the Indian market.

key_figures.label: Additional lead time for alternate styrene monomer sourcing

subsections.label: Inventory management
points: No significant change in finished goods inventory levels between quarters; production numbers have been kept in line with sales forecasts.

Raw material inventory levels were carried slightly higher at the end of Q1 FY27 versus the prior quarter, driven by uncertainty around styrene monomer sourcing previously reliant on the Middle East (Strait of Hormuz route), which is no longer a reliable option in the current climate.
Company has tapped alternate sourcing options for styrene monomer and is fully covered, though lead times from alternate (non-Middle East) suppliers are 10-15 days longer.
Butadiene is sourced locally, so no inventory/import impact from the disruption, though pricing still moved significantly.

subsections.label: Energy and logistics disruption (Thailand)
points: Thailand faced concerns around energy availability, with fuel/natural gas usage curtailed by the government in the interest of the general population.
Thailand also faced supply chain challenges on raw material availability; company managed to continue serving all clients despite multiple operational challenges.

subsections.label: Raw material price volatility (India)
points: Natural gas usage by plants was curtailed by the government, adding to cost/operational pressures.

Global pricing markers for key raw materials rose sharply due to supply chain disruption on the import side, with reduced availability of competitively priced material from traditional import sources.

subsections.label: New business development amid crisis
points: Structural supply chain disruption typically triggers customers to diversify suppliers, but most customers buy for long-term usage with long specification/gestation periods, so short-term events do not typically trigger rapid new business wins.

New business development activity driven by customers' strategic (not crisis-driven) considerations continues regardless of current events; company sees no significant incremental benefit to new business development specifically attributable to the current crisis.
Some customers are looking to diversify supply chains for structural reasons unrelated to the current conflict, and the company is participating in those opportunities.

subsections.label: Thailand competitive landscape
points: Company has a differentiated product profile in Thailand's target markets, despite significant competitive intensity from large production capacity in China and elsewhere.

Migration from the legacy acquired brand to the company's own brand in Thailand has been completed, a process that took time given the brand being relatively unknown in the region prior to transition.

Management believes there remains investor/customer interest in the company's Thailand product and expects to capture opportunities over time; process is currently tracking as per expectation and strategy.

subsections.label: Geopolitical and macro risk
points: Middle East conflict-driven disruption is the primary risk factor cited, affecting raw material availability (styrene monomer, ACN sourced via Strait of Hormuz), pricing volatility, and downstream demand.
Continued high uncertainty and volatility in raw material pricing and geopolitical developments makes it difficult to predict demand, volumes, or pricing for upcoming quarters.
Energy/fuel curtailment by governments (in both India and Thailand) in the interest of general population needs added operational pressure.

subsections.label: Demand-side risk
points: Non-OEM/unorganized sector demand is highly sensitive to price volatility and prone to a wait-and-watch buying approach during periods of high uncertainty.
Appliance sector saw greater production/demand impact than auto sector during the disrupted quarter.

subsections.label: Execution risk (brownfield capex)
points: Brownfield nature of the ongoing ABS expansion (executed while the plant is running) introduces execution complexities not present in greenfield projects, making exact commissioning timelines harder to commit to while maintaining safety, environmental and compliance priorities.

subsections.label: Volume/margin normalization outlook
points: Management maintains that once market volatility normalizes, both volumes and margins are expected to revert to the company's historical sustainable/annualized operating levels; no assumption should be made of margins settling at a structurally higher level.
For analysis purposes, best to assume things normalize to prior levels rather than assume any significant margin expansion, given ongoing uncertainty on timing and magnitude of normalization.

subsections.label: ABS capex completion
points: ABS capacity expansion (~50,000 tonnes, brownfield) remains on track and is expected to be completed within FY27; exact month (8th, 9th or 11th month) not disclosed due to commissioning complexities in a running plant.

subsections.label: No volume guidance
points: Company does not provide explicit volume guidance; management noted that in line with production capabilities and capacity, most produced volumes are expected to be sold, but precise volume guidance is not possible given current geopolitical/demand uncertainty.

subsections.label: Thailand medium-term margin outlook
points: Management indicated a roughly 3-year medium-term horizon as a reasonable timeframe within which Thailand sales efforts should succeed in generating a much stronger margin profile, contingent on realizing higher volumes over time.

subsections.label: India margin/mix outlook with ABS expansion
points: For the Indian business, once the ABS expansion contributes, management suggests assuming similar margins to the existing business is the most sensible planning basis, since volume increases could be offset by higher competitive intensity — resulting in a likely 'wash' between factors.

subsections.label: SAN merchant sales continuity
points: SAN merchant sales (15,000-20,000 tonnes/year) will continue unaffected despite increased captive ABS-related usage post expansion.

guidance_ledger.statement: ABS expansion is on track and will be completed within this financial year; exact month (8th, 9th or 11th) cannot be committed to given brownfield commissioning complexities.
SAN merchant sales will continue as is and will not be impacted by captive usage increase from the ABS expansion.
Company does not give volume guidance; given current geopolitical uncertainty, it is difficult to provide any precise volume guidance for the year.

Once market conditions normalize, margins and volumes are expected to revert to the company's historical sustainable/annualized operating basis; no assumption of structural margin expansion should be made.
Over a roughly 3-year timeframe (or sooner), Thailand sales efforts are expected to succeed in generating a much stronger margin profile as volumes build.
For India business with ABS expansion, best to assume similar margins to existing business, as volume gains could be offset by increased competitive intensity, resulting in a likely wash.

Company has allocated capital to polystyrene expansion in the past and will continue to do so as the business case becomes clear; current priority remains the ABS expansion, with further updates on polystyrene to be shared as available.

Company's capital allocation philosophy remains consistent — fund growth capex, and return surplus cash not needed for growth to shareholders; no incremental change planned despite extra cash generated.

In a normalized environment, both auto and appliance sectors are expected to grow, and the existing sector split within ABS is expected to remain broadly the same, though it could shift slightly depending on relative growth rates.
Company is fully committed to doubling at least its ABS and SAN output over the next 2-3 years, in line with earlier plans, with no deviation.
Additional ABS capacities/volumes expected to come online in the second half of the year, specifically Q3 and Q4, not Q1/Q2; exact month not disclosed. No change from earlier announcements.
Once Thailand reaches 60-70% capacity utilization, the operation will start generating returns; company is still below that and working towards it.

Company expects to start receiving power from third-party source by next month, with benefits reflecting from this quarter; no quantification given for full-year savings as it depends on production volumes and other factors.

Prices may remain a little higher in the short-to-medium term versus pre-war levels due to lag before supply chain normalization; magnitude uncertain, declined to confirm peers' 15-20% higher estimate.

In a normalized scenario, India would grow similarly to ABS industry growth of 8-10% or higher given import substitution opportunity, if additional volumes are available; in the current disrupted scenario, growth is very difficult to estimate.
Import substitution opportunity in India expected to remain for the next 5-7 years, with market adding 30,000-50,000 tons of additional demand annually.
Company is not preponing the ABS capex despite competitor supply issues in Korea; capex is proceeding exactly as planned.
No current cost escalation identified for the upcoming ABS capex.

risk_register.note: Disruption began late March, intensified into Q1 FY27, driving raw material price spikes (styrene monomer, ACN, butadiene) and sourcing challenges via the Strait of Hormuz.

risk_register.risk: Thailand cost structure and low utilization

risk_register.risk: Import/export data opacity

risk_register.risk: Competitive intensity in Thailand (China capacity)
risk_register.note: Significant competitive intensity from large Chinese production capacity in Thailand's target export markets.

risk_register.risk: Continued pricing/demand uncertainty into Q2 FY27
risk_register.note: Volatility continues into the current quarter with frequent geopolitical news flow affecting raw material and finished product pricing; management declined to comment on current quarter specifics.

risk_register.risk: Middle East crisis / Strait of Hormuz supply chain disruption

risk_register.risk: Import/dumping pressure on GPPS

risk_register.risk: Customer input cost pass-through challenges

risk_register.risk: Uncertainty in unorganized/non-OE segment demand

risk_register.risk: Freight rate volatility

risk_register.risk: Sustainability of opportunistic Q4 margin gains
risk_register.note: Management noted that price expansion gains in certain segments during Q4 were opportunistic due to short-term tightness and may not be sustainable long-term.

themes.label: Input-cost inflation
themes.note: Styrene monomer, ACN and butadiene prices spiked sharply due to Middle East disruption before partially moderating, driving raw material cost volatility.

themes.label: Pricing power / spreads
themes.note: A temporary lag between raw material cost increases and finished product pricing drove abnormally high margins this quarter, not viewed as sustainable.

themes.label: Demand recovery
themes.note: Non-OEM/unorganized sector demand fell 15-25% due to price volatility-driven caution; OEM demand impact was comparatively muted; recovery timing remains uncertain.

themes.label: Capacity expansion
themes.note: Brownfield ABS expansion (~50,000 tonnes) remains on track for completion within FY27, alongside rubber, SAN and compounding capacity additions.

themes.label: Thailand integration and breakeven
themes.note: Thailand volumes held up relatively better than India this quarter given already-low utilization base; brand transition complete, market validations ongoing with 3-year horizon for stronger margins.

themes.label: Import substitution opportunity
themes.note: No significant change observed in import volumes into India despite some exporting countries facing production challenges from energy/naphtha disruptions via the Strait of Hormuz.

themes.label: Competitive positioning vs Korea
themes.note: Not specifically raised this quarter regarding Korea; competitive intensity discussed mainly in context of China's large production capacity affecting Thailand markets.

key_takeaways: Total income for Q1 FY27 stood at INR770.5 crores, a growth of 6.6% (standalone, YoY).
EBITDA for quarter 1 FY27 stood at INR201.4 crores, a growth of 133.9%.
EBITDA margins for quarter 1 FY27 improved to 26.1%, an increase in 1,420 basis points.
Profit after tax for Q1 FY27 stood at INR137.3 crores, a growth of 150.3%.
Sales volume for Q1 FY27 stood at 38.9 KT, a dip of 26%.
Consolidated sales volume, which includes both India and Thailand, for Q1 FY27 stood at 50.8 KT.

The quarter gone by was marked by an operating environment characterized by heightened uncertainties driven by evolving global macroeconomic conditions, geopolitical developments and fluctuations across key markets.

Whatever benefits seen in margins this quarter are a snapshot in time due to specific events and not indicative of sustainable business performance; sustainable performance should be assessed based on periods prior to these events.
ABS expansion (brownfield, ~50,000 tonnes) remains on track for completion within this financial year, with exact month undisclosed due to commissioning complexities in a running plant.
SAN merchant sales (15,000-20,000 tonnes/year) will continue unaffected by increased captive usage from the ABS expansion.
Company does not give volume guidance given the current geopolitical/demand uncertainty.
pressing_questions: Can you provide the split between OEM and non-OEM demand and clarify whether the non-OEM impact was broad-based across clients or concentrated in selective pockets?
What would be the sustainable run-rate of margins once the current benefits (from the raw material-to-finished-price lag) reverse, given historical margins were around 10-12%?
On the Thailand business — costs have remained elevated for 6 quarters; any change in fixed cost reduction plans, and what is the volume outlook for Thailand for FY27/FY28?
Given end-consumer demand in auto/electronics/households hasn't fallen as much as reported volumes, should the balance 9 months see a high-teens/mid-teens catch-up in volume growth?
Once demand normalizes, should margins settle at a higher level than historical averages given import cost parity shifts and capacity additions in higher-margin products?
On inventory — how did the plants run during the low-demand quarter, and what's the status/pricing/timing of alternate raw material sourcing for styrene monomer and ACN?
Will SAN merchant sales from the existing plant completely stop from Jan '27 due to captive ABS usage?
How does management intend to utilize the additional cash flow (~INR100 crores over 2 quarters) generated during this volatile period?
Can you give an exact timeframe (e.g., Q3 vs later) for when the ABS capex will go live, given we are 4 months into the year?
What is the SAN production bifurcation between in-house use and merchant sales, and what is the ideal auto-OEM vs non-auto mix targeted for FY27/FY28?
Have new customers been won in India/Thailand as a direct result of the supply chain crisis (B2B customers seeking new/alternate suppliers)?
By which quarter can the ABS expansion be expected to go live, and is there any volume guidance for this year?

quarters.summary: Q4 and FY'26 results showed strong margin expansion driven by supply chain disruptions (Middle East/Strait of Hormuz crisis) pushing up both raw material and finished product prices in tandem; management believes prices may settle higher than pre-war levels in the short-to-medium term but remains cautious on long-term sustainability. ABS capacity expansion in India remains on track for H2 FY'27 (Q3/Q4), while polystyrene/HIPS expansion decision remains under evaluation; Thailand operations continue working towards 60-70% utilization for breakeven, with volume dip attributed to prior-year brand-transition prebuying rather than raw material availability issues.

key_figures.label: Cash flow difference between consol and standalone (implied Thailand capex)

subsections.label: Quarterly performance drivers
points: EBITDA and PAT growth in Q4 FY26 driven partly by product mix (lower GPPS sales in the quarter) and by opportunistic pricing gains in certain segments due to short-term tightness in the market created by supply disruptions.
Management stated there was no significant inventory gain for the quarter.
Price expansion for certain segments was opportunistic and considered not sustainable long-term.
Total income for the year was lower YoY on a standalone basis, described as 'more on the pricing-driven things'.

subsections.label: Other income breakdown (consolidated)
points: Other income of INR11.8 crores (consolidated) includes forex gains in Thailand, income from services provided from Thailand facilities, scrap sales, and other miscellaneous items.

subsections.label: Balance sheet / capital allocation
points: Company maintained a healthy return ratio with a strong and prudent balance sheet on a standalone basis (ROE ~25%, ROCE ~32% for FY26).
A cash flow difference of approximately INR60 crores between consolidated and standalone figures was attributed to capex in Thailand.

subsections.label: Volume trends by product line (India)
points: ABS and HIPS grew year-on-year in Q4, while GPPS sales declined significantly due to muted demand and pricing pressure from imports/dumping and an active unorganized market.
Company chose not to aggressively participate in GPPS segments not backed by contracts or formulas, contributing to volume decline.
Q4 has nuances such as 28 days in February and periodic annual shutdowns that affect quarter-on-quarter comparability.
Management does not provide product-wise volume breakout as competitors also do not disclose this.

subsections.label: Thailand volume dynamics
points: Thailand Q4 volume decline (20-30%) attributed to a prior-year (Jan-Mar FY25) anomaly where customers over-bought under the INEOS/Novodur brand due to fear of supply disruption during the brand transition to Styrenix's own brand, not to current raw material availability issues.

Jan-March quarters are typically lower for Thailand due to seasonality, as many Far East customers follow a Jan-Dec calendar and buy more heavily toward December due to rebates and volume commitments.
Business continuity in Thailand has been largely retained despite the brand transition.
Management recommends looking at annualized (April-March) numbers for Thailand as more defensible for assessing run-rate, noting significant room to grow from current levels.

subsections.label: Pricing/contract structure
points: In ABS, 60-70% of volume is formula/contract based; remaining balance also follows an understood pricing mechanism even if not formally contracted.
In HIPS, formula-based/OEM-linked business now exceeds 50%, higher than before.
In GPPS, the company has stepped back from unorganized, non-contract-backed segments, contributing to volume decline.
Overall, more than 70% of company business now follows some form of formula-based pricing.

Monthly pricing is generally maintained with long-term value customers, with formulas incorporating certain publication prices; small gaps between spot procurement and formula pricing are managed within the formula.

subsections.label: Margin/product mix differences
points: HIPS commands better margins than GPPS because HIPS demand (air conditioning, refrigerators, packaging) is more organized, growing well, and involves specialized grades that are not easy to switch between suppliers.
GPPS has a smaller organized segment and larger unorganized segment where switching based on cost is easier, resulting in lower margins.
Spot-market margins for specific grades (where competitors like Korea have supply issues) have been better; contract/formula-based margins are similar to slightly better YoY.

key_figures.label: Thailand Jan-Mar prior year volume reference

subsections.label: ABS capacity expansion (India)
points: ABS expansion is on track with no change from earlier indicated plans/timelines.
Additional capacity and volumes expected to come online in second half of the year, specifically in Q3 and Q4 (not Q1/Q2); exact month not disclosed.
Capex commitments have already been made; cash flow impact will follow as machinery arrives and construction/commissioning completes.
Company is not preponing the ABS capex despite competitor (Korea) supply issues; proceeding exactly as planned.
No current cost escalation identified for the upcoming ABS capex.
Plan to incorporate some of Thailand's higher-margin ABS production technologies into new India capacity, enabling targeting of additional product segments in India not historically served.

subsections.label: Polystyrene/HIPS expansion
points: No fresh update on timeline for polystyrene expansion; GP PS plant capacity was already expanded previously but is under-utilized due to muted demand and margin compression from imports.

HIPS expansion studies have been conducted, but management is not yet fully convinced on the decision to deploy additional capital for a HIPS plant; decision will be communicated to shareholders once made.

PS expansion has historically been a back-ended strategy (unlike ABS, which was front-ended) as the company evaluates the business case, evolving OEM share, and customer requirements before committing capital.

subsections.label: Thailand plant utilization and breakeven
points: Thailand plant is relatively small; breakeven requires reaching 60-70% capacity utilization, and the company is currently still below that level and working towards it.
Short-term gains from current market tightness in Thailand should not be mistaken for a structural change in the breakeven target; long-term target utilization guidance remains unchanged.
Management previously estimated breakeven utilization around 65-70%, reaffirmed as unchanged despite short-term favorable conditions.

subsections.label: Power sourcing initiative
points: Company expects to start receiving power from a third-party source (power sourcing agreement) by approximately next month, which should start reflecting benefits from the current quarter, though this is described as guidance from a third party and should be taken with caution.

No quantification of expected savings provided for the full year, as savings are a function of production volumes and other factors that are currently hard to predict given demand contraction from price increases.

subsections.label: Import substitution opportunity in India
points: Despite a new (third) player entering the Indian market and existing players adding capacity, a shortfall of more than 100,000 tons of import substitution opportunity remains.
Market is expected to continue adding 30,000-50,000 tons of additional demand every year, sustaining import substitution opportunity for the next 5-7 years.
Comparison drawn to smaller economies like Vietnam (400,000 ton market) to illustrate growth potential relative to India's larger economy.

subsections.label: Thailand/global positioning
points: Thailand seen as strategically well placed from a longer-term geopolitical view; has not been severely affected in its ability to procure and produce despite the Middle East crisis.
Company recently exhibited at CHINAPLAS, engaging with large customers in EV and appliance spaces in China and Far East, reinforcing Thailand's importance for supplying these growing regions.

Thailand viewed as a critical asset for positioning the company as a preferred global supplier over the next 2-3 years, extending capability beyond India into Asia and potentially the rest of the world.

subsections.label: Raw material availability
points: Despite global supply chain disruptions from the Strait of Hormuz closure affecting flow of oil and petrochemical products, the company has not faced significant disruption to manufacturing; only minor disruptions occurred, not requiring significant reporting or concern.
Company procures raw materials from multiple global sources, a long-standing strategy providing diversification and flexibility to source based on time, cost and other factors.
Availability of raw materials in Thailand is also currently not a serious issue.

A major competitor positioned in Korea, previously vertically integrated into styrene production, stopped producing styrene a year or two ago and now imports it, illustrating that vertical integration into monomer commodities offers limited value in the current market.

subsections.label: Regional impact of disruptions
points: Korea has been notably affected by the crisis, partly due to its dependence on gas from Qatar as fuel for plants, impacting both cost and availability of raw materials.
Raw material price increases (styrene, acrylonitrile, etc.) have occurred globally rather than in one specific region; minor regional arbitrage normalizes quickly.
European ABS/PS plant shutdowns (e.g., INEOS, smaller Chinese players) occurred prior to the current Middle East disruptions and are considered largely unrelated to the current crisis.

subsections.label: Freight rates
points: Incoming freight rates rose sharply; containerized cargo rates have not moved significantly since, with maybe a slight correction.
Bulk freight rates have softened somewhat due to demand destruction in bulk petrochemical materials.
Freight rates continue to fluctuate on a day-to-day basis, making trends difficult to track.

subsections.label: Customer demand qualitative view
points: No significant uptick or downtick in demand seen from large OE customers in automotive, appliances and packaging; demand described as 'a little bit muted' at current price levels, with most large OE customers buying consistently.
Company will need to monitor how customers manage inventory clearance and price pass-through over the next few months; some slowdown risk acknowledged.
Greater caution/muted demand observed in the unorganized/smaller customer market due to pricing direction uncertainty, more so than in the OE segment.

Non-OE/unorganized segment buying behavior is more sentiment-driven, based on near-term expectations, and is currently muted due to uncertainty; better margins achievable there when supplying grades not easily available from other suppliers.

subsections.label: Competitive positioning
points: Structural weaknesses observed in competitors (e.g., Korea) due to Middle East crisis and supply issues; company sees potential benefit but outcome uncertain.

Company believes customers do not give preference to suppliers with local raw material supply or vertical integration, since underlying monomers are commodities with limited regional arbitrage; vertical integration could even be a negative given generally low spreads on raw materials in a normalized scenario.
Company positioned to capture better margins in specific grades where competitors (notably Korea) face quality/supply issues.

subsections.label: Geopolitical/supply chain risk
points: Strait of Hormuz disruption (Middle East crisis) causing global supply chain disruptions in benzene, ethylene, crude and other petrochemical inputs, impacting styrene monomer and acrylonitrile prices globally.
Uncertainty over duration of the Middle East crisis; management stated it is not qualified to predict when or how the crisis will resolve.
Potential demand contraction due to price increases stemming from the crisis, making volume forecasting difficult for the remainder of the call period.

subsections.label: Import/dumping pressure
points: GPPS segment facing margin compression and volume pressure due to imports/dumping and an active unorganized market.
PS imports and unorganized market activity have been cited as reasons for backing away from certain GPPS volumes.

subsections.label: Demand-side caution
points: Customers in automotive, appliances and packaging facing their own challenges passing through input price increases, creating potential for demand slowdown.
Greater uncertainty and caution particularly in the unorganized/smaller customer segment regarding pricing direction.

subsections.label: Strategic outlook (2-3 years)
points: Company committed to doubling at least its ABS and SAN output over the next 2-3 years, in line with previously communicated plans, with no deviation.

Management believes Indian demand will grow and remain robust regardless of short-term volatility and demand fluctuations, and the company aims to be the preferred supplier/partner for most relationships going forward.
Thailand expected to play an increasingly critical role in positioning the company as a preferred global supplier over the next 2-3 years, extending capability beyond India.

subsections.label: Pricing outlook
points: Management believes prices will likely remain a little higher in the short-to-medium term compared to historical (pre-war) levels due to lag between current supply chain disruption and eventual normalization, but declined to specify exact magnitude (declining to confirm the 15-20% higher 'new normal' suggested by peers).

subsections.label: Volume/growth outlook FY27
points: In a normalized scenario, India volume growth is expected to continue at similar levels to ABS industry growth (8-10%) or higher, given import substitution opportunity, assuming additional volumes are available; but in the current disrupted scenario, providing volume estimates is very difficult.

risk_register.note: Disruption to flow of oil and petrochemical inputs (benzene, ethylene) causing global price increases in styrene, acrylonitrile and other monomers; duration and resolution highly uncertain.

risk_register.note: Korea affected more severely due to dependence on Qatar gas as fuel, impacting cost and availability of raw materials for Korean competitors.

risk_register.risk: Demand contraction from price increases
risk_register.note: Some demand contraction observed given price increases; makes volume forecasting difficult until situation normalizes.

risk_register.risk: Import/dumping pressure on GPPS
risk_register.note: Muted demand and margin compression in GPPS due to imports and active unorganized/dumping market; company has stepped back from unattractive segments.

risk_register.risk: Customer input cost pass-through challenges
risk_register.note: Auto, appliance and packaging customers facing difficulty passing through their own input cost increases, which could lead to demand slowdown.

risk_register.risk: Uncertainty in unorganized/non-OE segment demand
risk_register.note: Greater customer caution in the unorganized market due to uncertainty over future pricing direction, leading to muted buying.

risk_register.risk: Freight rate volatility
risk_register.note: Incoming freight rates rose sharply; day-to-day fluctuations make tracking difficult, though bulk rates have softened somewhat on demand destruction.

risk_register.risk: Sustainability of opportunistic Q4 margin gains
risk_register.note: Management noted that price expansion gains in certain segments during Q4 were opportunistic due to short-term tightness and may not be sustainable long-term.

themes.label: Input-cost inflation
themes.note: Middle East crisis/Strait of Hormuz disruption pushed up raw material (styrene, acrylonitrile) prices globally, but finished product prices moved in tandem, preserving spreads.

themes.label: Capacity expansion
themes.note: ABS capacity expansion in India remains on track for H2 FY27 (Q3/Q4); PS/HIPS expansion decision still under evaluation and back-ended.

themes.label: Import substitution opportunity
themes.note: India ABS/PS import substitution opportunity expected to persist for 5-7 years with 30,000-50,000 tons/year additional demand.

themes.label: Thailand integration and breakeven
themes.note: Thailand volume dip attributed to prior-year brand-transition prebuying, not raw material issues; breakeven still targeted at 60-70% utilization.

themes.label: Pricing power / spreads
themes.note: Company believes prices may settle higher than pre-war levels in short-to-medium term due to supply chain lag; Q4 margin gains partly opportunistic and product-mix driven.

themes.label: Demand recovery
themes.note: OE customer demand in auto, appliances, packaging described as muted but stable; unorganized/non-OE segment demand more cautious due to pricing uncertainty.

themes.label: Competitive positioning vs Korea
themes.note: Structural weaknesses in Korean competitors due to crisis seen as a positive for Styrenix's ability to capture better margins in specific grades.

pressing_questions: Is it possible to quantify the inventory gains during the quarter?
We are seeing a volume dip into the Indian business, but some 20%, 30% dip into the Thailand business — any particular reason?

Does it make sense for us to prepone our capex on ABS and maybe capitalize and gain more market share given Korea's supply issues?
When can Thailand operations be at the breakeven point assuming normalized spread?

ARVIND.about: Arvind Limited (‘the Company’) is one of India’s leading vertically integrated textile company with the presence of almost eight decades in this industry. It is among the largest denim manufacturers in the world. It also manufactures a range of cotton shirting, denim, knits and bottom weights (Khakis) fabrics and Jeans and Shirts Garments. [1]

quarters.summary: Management flagged a sharp reversal in the tariff/macro picture versus the prior quarter, with US tariffs on India rising to 50% and creating high uncertainty. Q2 FY26 consolidated revenue grew 8.4% YoY to ₹2,371 crore with highest-ever quarterly EBITDA of ₹262 crore (+13% YoY) and PAT of ₹107 crore (+70% YoY), though margin expansion was compressed by ~₹23 crore of tariff-related discounts; adjusting for this, margins would be ~12%, in line with medium-term guidance. Q3 tariff impact is expected to rise further, but management expects offsetting cost savings to also increase, aiming to keep profitability broadly stable, while the AMD demerger into Irvind Advanced Materials Limited (AML) is completed with no immediate listing/monetization plan and growth engines (integrated apparel and AMD) target 20% growth trajectories with diversification away from US concentration.

key_figures.label: US direct business as % of revenue

subsections.label: Margins and tariff impact
points: Management attributed margin compression to tariff-linked discounts absorbed during the quarter: 'visible margin compression primarily stems from the tariff-related discounts absorbed during the quarter.'
Adjusting for the ~₹23 crore tariff impact, margins would have been closer to 12%, fully aligned with medium-term guidance.
Q3 expected to see higher tariff-related impact than Q2 because some punitive tariffs were implemented after Q2 orders were locked: 'It will increase from here… Q3 is pretty locked in.'
Management expects offsets (cost savings) to rise as well, aiming to keep profitability trajectory broadly stable.

subsections.label: Segment margins
points: Textile EBITDA margin: ~10%
AMD EBITDA margin: 13.6%

subsections.label: Capital allocation, liquidity posture, and returns
points: FY26 capex revised down to ₹400-450 crore, with ₹220 crore spent so far.

Reason is primarily timing prudence rather than strategy cancellation: 'we slowed down… all expansion for a period of time… One quarter went in wait and watch… more like a delay or postponement of spending.'
Leverage stable versus Mar 2025.
Working capital days held steady despite higher sales, attributed to system efficiencies.
Reiterated confidence in 20% ROCE medium-term target.

subsections.label: Shiprocket stake
points: Described as non-strategic; board will decide post-IPO.
Disclosed book value ~₹105 crore for the shares held.

key_figures.label: Garmenting share of turnover (highest tariff impact)

subsections.label: Two growth engines at scale: integrated apparel + AMD
points: Management emphasized two scaled platforms with similar revenue critical mass: integrated textile & apparel and AMD, each cited at ~₹2,000 crore 'run-rate' (integrated apparel explicitly described as '2000 crore run rate on a quarterly basis').
Q2 garmenting volume 10.7 million pieces, with management asserting 15-18% consistent growth and expecting H2 to be seasonally stronger.

subsections.label: Domestic/B2C business
points: Cited a 'thousand crore plus' domestic B2C business, expected to grow >20% this year.
Marketing tie-up with Kaun Banega Crorepati positioned as brand-building investment.

subsections.label: Business mix resilience
points: Some AMD sub-lines 'virtually not affected by tariffs.'
Garmenting is only ~20% of turnover, where tariff impact is highest.

key_figures.label: Recycled products share of global textile volume

subsections.label: Sustainability & innovation: capex-backed process shifts and circular materials
points: Commissioned India's first supercritical CO2 dyeing facility at Sankage with SNM Group and Devin Supercritical; ₹25 crore investment; waterless dyeing.
Claimed potential savings: up to 76% water, 67% energy, 90% chemicals.

Circularity partnership with US-based CERC Incorporation: integrating next-generation recycled fibers enabling high blend percentages due to quality; company will buy fiber, spin into yarn, and incorporate into products.

Management framed this as 'future-ready' for regulation (e.g., Europe recycled-content mandates), not as a near-term volume/profit driver: recycled products are 'less than two to three percent' of global textile volume; focus is 'not on realization… [but] driving more volume adoption.'
Climate targets: net-zero targets validated by SBTi, aligned to 1.5°C pathway to net zero by 2050.

subsections.label: Operational KPIs: capacity tightness and volume strength
points: Denim: highest volume in recent years at 15 million meters; operating at full capacity.
Woven: near-highest volume at 35 million meters; also full capacity.

Garmenting: 10.7 million pieces in Q2; management reiterated capacity/volume ramp with FY26 dispatch expectation '40 to 43' million pieces, exit capacity FY26 'cross 45' million pieces, and FY27 capacity target '55 is the right number for next year.'

subsections.label: Varanasi garmenting capacity update
points: Facility 'back on stream'; commercial operations expected late Q1 to early Q2 (as stated).

subsections.label: Geographic diversification
points: Explicit pivot away from US concentration, particularly in AMD: 'clear pivot is happening' toward Australia, Middle East, UK, plus EU and India.
UK FTA: management is engaging customers, but benefits expected next year due to implementation lag: 'benefit to start flowing in next next year.'

subsections.label: Tariff exposure: direct vs indirect
points: Total US exposure ~35%, split into direct (~22%) and indirect (~14-15%).
Direct: exports shipped to the US that 'attracts the full fifty percent' tariff.
Indirect: supply that ultimately reaches the US via third countries (e.g., Bangladesh/Sri Lanka), with different economics but still impacted.

subsections.label: Cost and efficiency: offsets to tariff pressure
points: Cost actions initiated in earlier quarters are now yielding 'structural and lasting savings' and are being intensified.
Supplier negotiations ('asking for discounts to our strategic suppliers').
SG&A reduction, hiring freeze ('frozen non-essential hiring').
Energy conservation and operational efficiency.

Strategic takeaway: margin expansion efforts are being used to hold the line rather than expand: 'that whole exercise has sort of got postponed… our effort is keeping us in the same place as far as margins is concerned.'

subsections.label: Working capital
points: Working capital days held steady despite higher sales, attributed to system efficiencies.

subsections.label: How discounts are negotiated / commercial discipline
points: Not passing on full tariffs; instead discounts are negotiated based on competitiveness and qualification constraints: 'Most customers, we are not passing on the full tariffs… it's more like discounts that we give… relative to… competing geographies.'
Tariff burden is shared across the supply chain: 'gets distributed between yarn, chemicals… garment makers, the brand itself, and the consumer.'

Support is selective and tied to volumes/commitment: 'We extended selective support, including discounts wherever necessary, but always in exchange for higher volumes and stronger commitment for the future.'
If economics don't work, they allow volume to move: 'we allow them to shift the volume elsewhere if it's not making sense for us.'

subsections.label: Customer sourcing behavior amid tariff uncertainty
points: Customers are currently behaving as if tariffs may ease at some point; if the tariff regime persists longer, customer sourcing behavior could change: 'customers are factoring in… at some point… certain aspects of the tariff will go away… If they prolong… how the customers will behave… that's still an uncertainty.'

subsections.label: AMD demerger completed
points: NCLT approved the scheme; AMD is now housed in Irvind Advanced Materials Limited (AML), effective 1 Sep 2025.

Rationale is primarily structural flexibility rather than immediate capital markets action: 'house it in a vehicle that allows us flexibility on how we look at the business… Right now there are no step plans.'
On separate listing: 'It will depend on the board… Right now the focus is… driving a twenty percent growth trajectory with improved profitability and return on capital employed.'
The stated objective is operational/strategic flexibility rather than monetization or listing, and monetization/listing is explicitly not imminent.

subsections.label: Macro & Tariff Regime: thesis reversal and planning uncertainty
points: Management described a sharp reversal versus the prior quarter: 'Three months on, the picture has changed completely… almost a 180-degree turn.'

India has moved from a perceived relative advantage to 'the most disadvantageous position' as the US expanded tariff coverage and took tariffs to 50%, described as 'perhaps the highest among the competing markets.'
Tariff visibility remains low and outcomes depend on policy and demand response: 'till this tariff resolution comes, that uncertainty will always remain.'
Risk that US consumption could slow once higher-priced goods fully hit retail: 'The expensive goods are only now hitting customers… will consumption fall?… highly uncertain.'

key_figures.label: Varanasi garmenting commercial operations expected timing

subsections.label: Growth outlook & demand signals
points: Growth guidance tone (especially AMD) is constructive for H2: expect to return to ~18-20% growth, with Q3 'definitely' around ~20%+ and Q4 directionally positive but less certain: 'Q4 is too far to predict.'
Order book / early shipment: management rejected the idea that Q2 was driven by early shipments: 'virtually zero impact of early shipment… tariff impacts are fully crystallized.'

Reiterated confidence in 20% ROCE medium-term target.
FY26 dispatch expectation '40 to 43' million pieces.
Exit capacity FY26 'cross 45' million pieces.
FY27 capacity target '55 is the right number for next year.'

Benefit to start flowing in next next year.

We should be able to grow in the mid-teens rather than 10%. That is our ambition going forward.
That's one of the key inputs to why at AMD, we have a 20-plus percent growth aspiration.

guidance_ledger.metric: Dalco-GFT historical revenue growth vs margin growth
guidance_ledger.statement: The historical track record of the company is to grow revenue in double digits as well as margin in high teens. We expect that with the combination of markets that we are in, we will continue to maintain that 10% to 12% revenue growth and mid-teens margin expansion or margin growth rather.
There is already a plan to put in approximately $5 million of capex every year.
Our expectation from India is approximately 18% to 20%... we will still want to grow in the high teens and hopefully 20% plus.
Our current thinking and medium-term plan is to quickly pay down the debt... our aim would be to almost wind this down over the next couple of years.
The financial ratios post acquisition of Dalco-GFT is within the covenants that we have already signed in for. We expect this to improve in 12 months' time.

guidance_ledger.metric: India line of business for Dalco-GFT technology
guidance_ledger.statement: The expectation is that some point in the next 2.5 years, we will fire that process till then we will be very busy accelerating the U.S. business.
The capex plan for this year should be ready in 3 to 4 months.
When we do the quarter 1 financials at that time, the whole financials of Dalco-GFT will be there.

key_takeaways: Tariffs are the dominant variable: Q2 absorbed ~₹23 crore impact; Q3 impact will rise, but management expects rising offsets via cost initiatives. Monitoring point: whether cost-out can keep pace if punitive tariffs persist and/or US demand softens.

Capacity utilization is high in core textiles (denim/woven at full capacity), while garmenting is scaling toward 45m → 55m capacity path; near-term revenue growth likely hinges on execution and mix amid tariff pricing pressure.
AMD demerger is completed but monetization/listing is explicitly not imminent; the stated objective is operational/strategic flexibility.

Diversification is not just rhetoric: repeated emphasis on non-US geographies (UK/EU/Middle East/Australia) and on business mix resilience (some AMD sub-lines 'virtually not affected by tariffs,' garmenting only ~20% of turnover where impact is highest).
Sustainability investments are concrete (CO2 dyeing commissioning, recycled fiber integration) but framed as strategic positioning for customer/regulatory pull rather than immediate scale economics.

quarters.summary: Arvind Limited, via wholly owned subsidiary Arvind Advanced Materials Limited (AAML), announced acquisition of 61% stake in Dalco-GFT (a US needle-punch nonwoven company) valued at $136 million (7.75x CY2025 EBITDA). Management expects the deal to accelerate AAML's global footprint, reduce supply-chain risk, and be margin- and EPS-accretive at Arvind consolidated level; growth aspiration for Dalco-GFT is mid-teens (vs historical 10%), with capacity utilization at 85% and ~$5 million annual capex planned. Financing is via debt raised in both US ($50 million) and India ($60 million) entities; company expects to pay down debt over the next couple of years while remaining within existing covenants.

key_figures.label: AAML revenue/sales scale referenced for employee execution

subsections.label: Order book / demand characteristics
points: No obvious seasonality in the business; because automotive is a large part of the business and production is specced into platforms, production throughput remains fairly constant at ~85% utilization.
Growth is expected to come from additional capacity addition and incremental uptick from other segments, pushing utilization toward 90%+ before further capacity addition.
Customer contracts typically cover about 50% share of the specced part with a contractual life of about 5-6 years, tested during due diligence.

key_figures.label: Manufacturing units
key_figures.unit: units (South Carolina and North Carolina, US)

key_figures.label: Additional lines that can be accommodated
Time gained/avoided by acquisition vs building from scratch
Years facility space sufficient for line additions

subsections.label: Capacity & utilization detail
points: Dalco-GFT has 2 manufacturing units in the US (South Carolina, North Carolina) with combined capacity of 75 million pounds and utilization currently ~85%.
Company has 6 production lines; 3-4 have just been upgraded; there is sufficient capacity for the next year with capex refinement underway to cover following year as well.
Facility space can accommodate 3 more lines; capacity will not be a constraint to targeted mid-teens growth.

Each new capacity line costs roughly $4.5-5 million; the $5 million/year capex thumb-rule represents approximately 1 line of capacity, though actual annual spend may vary (e.g., $8 million in one year then a pause) depending on product type and GSM.

subsections.label: Rationale for locating manufacturing close to consumption
points: Needle punch nonwovens are high-loft materials with a large amount of air gaps by design, meaning transportation is effectively 'shipping air' — hence products must be manufactured within roughly 500-700 miles of the consumption point to avoid excessive transportation costs.

No plans to expand into new geographies like Texas or Mexico yet since there is still significant headroom for growth within existing 2 facilities without needing to branch beyond the current operating radius.

subsections.label: Capex plan for FY
points: The capex plan for the (US) business for this year should be finalized within 3-4 months; until then, growth headroom exists via improving capacity utilization.

subsections.label: Geographic footprint
points: Dalco-GFT operates only in the US market currently — not present in Mexico or Canada despite automotive opportunities there, because manufacturing needs to be local to the point of consumption (radius of ~500-700 miles) to avoid high transportation costs on high-loft, air-heavy products.
Potential future expansion into logical adjacent areas like Texas or Mexico once current facilities are fully utilized, but no deep planning done yet given ample headroom in existing 2 facilities.
Acquisition is expected to accelerate AAML's global footprint and reduce supply-chain risk associated with the current geopolitical situation.

subsections.label: Raw materials & sourcing
points: Key raw material is staple fiber, generally polyester or polypropylene or a combination, both polymer-based and petroleum-linked.
About 65-70% of polymers are sourced locally in the US, with the remainder sourced from Korea and Vietnam, predominantly still US-based sourcing.
Working capital is about 60 days, in line with Arvind Limited's existing working capital cycle, and expected to continue at that level.

subsections.label: Cost inflation
points: Only inflationary pressure noted is on raw materials since polymers are petroleum-linked and prices have risen; impact so far assessed as manageable based on recent on-ground analysis in the US.

Some cost increases have been successfully passed on to customers; situation is evolving and being monitored, particularly amid ongoing geopolitical/war situation, but not seen as a potential derailer currently.

key_figures.label: Noise and vibration reduction segment growth rate
Automotive category growth rate (high single digits)

subsections.label: Competitive landscape & customer base
points: Automotive segment (largest segment) grows at 3-4%, while noise and vibration reduction (main product category) grows faster at 6-7%.

Company is present with the 6 largest Tier 1 suppliers to automotive OEMs; platforms specced into are a mix of American, Japanese and Korean players; hard diligence on platform quality came back positive.

Geotextiles segment offers large opportunity given US infrastructure bill; company is a young entrant in this segment where a couple of larger competitors exist, giving room to take market share with modest investment in team/people.
Roofing and flooring are other segments beyond automotive that will contribute to growth beyond the natural automotive growth rate (high single digits), pushing overall growth to mid-teens.
In automotive, ~85% (later specified up to 88%) of products are sole-sourced by the customer from the company only, reflecting deep, sticky customer relationships.

Company is well balanced across customers, has deep relationships with all meaningful customers, and excellent performance track record/customer reviews; considered top quartile on delivery, price and innovation within automotive.
Customer contracts typically have ~50% share of the specced part with contractual life of about 5-6 years, tested during due diligence.

88% sole sourcing example given: Honda CRV wheel well liner — company provides nonwoven material which customer molds into wheel well liner used on the assembly line; in 88% of such cases, only one company's product is used for that model.
Once specced into a car platform (life 6-7 years), suppliers generally are not displaced unless something goes materially wrong with the product.
For AMD (Advanced Materials Division) overall, management has a 20%+ growth aspiration; acquisitions must have significant headroom for growth to fit that objective.

subsections.label: Key customers (automotive)
points: Dalco-GFT's direct customers are Tier 1 suppliers (Dalco-GFT positioned as Tier 2); Tier 1 customers in turn supply OEMs including Hyundai, GM and others.

subsections.label: India market entry plans (future)
points: India market for these products currently much smaller than the US market but expected to grow significantly in future.

India market operates differently — the biggest players in India often act as both Tier 2 and Tier 1; company will need to work out how to enter India, and detailed plans are premature at this stage — that is considered the 'second horizon' of synergies, after first dialing up US segments.
Plan is to fire the India entry process at some point within the next 2.5 years; until then, focus remains on accelerating US business.
