risk_register.risk: Weak self-employed/professional loan penetration versus NBFCs
risk_register.note: Banks including SBI have weaker collection mechanisms vs NBFCs, limiting penetration into self-employed/professional personal loan segments where NBFCs grow 20-25% vs banks' 10-11%

risk_register.risk: West Asia / Middle East geopolitical conflict
risk_register.note: No impact on slippages or asset quality so far; MSME clusters like Morbi and hydrocarbon companies show P&L stress but minimal credit exposure; ECLGS being made available proactively; credit cost and credit growth guidance maintained unless macros dramatically deteriorate.

risk_register.risk: Technology/cybersecurity risk from advanced AI
risk_register.note: Technology risk is becoming systemic as AI models can identify and exploit vulnerabilities at scale; industry moving to coordinated resilience frameworks with regulators.

risk_register.risk: Transition to ECL-based provisioning (April 2027)
risk_register.note: Models built on draft/final guidelines; impact number not disclosed yet; expected smooth transition without significant impact on capital or credit growth ability over 3-4 years.

risk_register.risk: Global macro uncertainty / geopolitical and climate disruptions
risk_register.note: IMF projects elevated global uncertainty; India outperforms but geopolitical and climate risks remain key concerns; inflation has upward bias from energy prices and weather.

risk_register.risk: Treasury/bond yield volatility
risk_register.note: Sharp yield movement impacted treasury income in Q4, but low fair-value portfolio exposure limited the hit; forward view expects yields to stabilize in 6.75-6.9% range.

risk_register.risk: Corporate book shift to T-bill linked pricing depressing yields
risk_register.note: Large well-rated corporates moved back from capital markets to bank borrowing on T-bill linked terms, depressing yields; bank plans to shift these back to MCLR or widen spreads during FY27.

risk_register.risk: MSME cluster stress (e.g., Morbi)
risk_register.note: Morbi ceramics cluster impacted by unaffordable gas costs, reduced production; overall credit exposure to the cluster is minimal but ongoing support being assessed.

risk_register.risk: Non-fund based exposure provisioning
risk_register.note: Provisioning for non-fund credit exposure (per Basel 3 disclosures) will be required per RBI guidelines effective 1 April 2027.

themes.label: NIM trajectory
themes.note: Domestic NIM held resilient at 3% with ~7 bps uptick from lower cost of deposits; full-year 3% guidance reiterated with no significant NIM impact expected from FCNR(B) flows.

themes.label: Asset quality strength
themes.note: Gross and net NPA ratios remained at their lowest level in over two decades despite a sequential uptick in slippages, which management does not view as indicative of stress.

themes.label: Digital transformation (YONO)

themes.label: ECL provisioning transition
themes.note: Numbers deferred to Q2 pending IT system readiness; management assures no major capital adequacy impact given capital augmentation and regulatory transition dispensation.

themes.label: FCNR(B) deposit mobilization
themes.note: $6 billion mobilized to date toward an estimated $10 billion (~₹1 trillion) target, expected to reduce bulk deposit reliance without significant NIM impact.

themes.label: Credit growth guidance
themes.note: Overall and corporate credit growth guidance revised upward to 14-15%, anchored on nominal GDP expectations of 12-12.5% plus historical 2-3% premium.

themes.label: Collection capability buildout

key_takeaways: Net profit reached a record ₹21,121 crore, supported by healthy operating performance and disciplined cost management.
Operating Profit grew by 9.77% year-on-year, while domestic Net Interest Margin remained resilient at 3%, reinforcing confidence in maintaining guidance for the financial year.
Balance sheet continued to expand with total business crossing ₹110 trillion, deposits exceeding ₹60 trillion, and advances crossing ₹50 trillion.
Growth has remained broad-based across retail, agriculture, MSME and corporate segments, reflecting healthy demand.
Gross and net NPA ratios have further improved and remained at their lowest level in over two decades.
Digital transformation continues to be an important differentiator, with encouraging customer adoption of the new YONO platform and steadily growing digital acquisitions.
Subsidiaries have continued to perform well, with the successful listing of SBI Funds Management Limited marking another significant milestone in unlocking value within the SBI group.
Credit growth guidance revised to 14-15% (corporate credit growth revised to 14-15%), anchored on nominal GDP expectations of 12-12.5%.

quarters.summary: SBI's FY26 performance showed record profitability, robust credit and deposit growth, industry-leading asset quality, and improved capital ratios. Management reiterated FY27 guidance of domestic NIM above 3%, credit growth of 13-15%, credit cost of 50 bps, and ROA >1% with ROE guidance of minimum 15% through cycles, while flagging Q4 NIM compression driven by rate cuts and corporate book mix shift to T-bill linked loans, treasury MTM losses, West Asia conflict-related risks (mitigated via ECLGS), and the upcoming transition to ECL-based provisioning from April 2027.

subsections.label: Q4 vs Q3 profit decline drivers
points: Operating profit and net profit declined QoQ, dragged by treasury trading/valuation losses (~Rs 3,500 crores per analyst estimate) and higher overheads.
Q4 MTM loss of Rs 4,520 crores versus only Rs 143 crores in Q3 explains why Q3 profit was higher than Q4.
Comparison with Q4 of the previous year is distorted because that quarter had a one-time gain of Rs 3,800 crores on security receipts plus positive treasury gains, which were absent this year.
MTM loss is routed through other/non-interest income, not NII.

subsections.label: NIM/NII decline drivers
points: Full year exit NIM guidance of 3% domestic was met, but quarterly NIM naturally has seasonality; guidance is always annual, not quarterly.
Two reasons for NII impact: 25 bps rate cut reflected fully in EBLR portfolio in Q4, and 5 bps MCLR cut also fully factored in Q4.
Composition shift: EBLR plus T-bill linked floating rate loans in corporate book rose from 43% (previous year) to 49% (Q4FY26), which depresses yields when loans move from MCLR to T-bill pricing.

Large well-rated corporates who were earlier accessing capital markets (CP etc.) have moved back to bank borrowing, and these facilities are largely T-bill linked — this shift is a relationship-value gain not fully visible in NIM but visible in ROA and fee income.
Company plans to move as many T-bill linked loans back to MCLR-based pricing as possible in the current financial year, or increase spreads over T-bill for relationship clients.
Management does not expect further NIM dip going forward and reiterates confidence in 3% full-year domestic NIM for FY27.
Yield on advances decline driven by repo rate cut impact and shift in corporate credit composition; cumulative 12-month domestic yield down 11 bps.

subsections.label: Slippages and asset quality commentary
points: Q4 slippages increase is not a matter of concern; Rs 850 crores already recovered/pulled back as of the call date.
No structural issue in asset quality; slippages mostly from agriculture and some SME, seasonal in nature.
No impact from West Asia conflict on slippages so far.
Company does not disclose gross slippages typically (only Q1 full-year figure disclosed, subsequently net); no predominant concerning movement noted.

subsections.label: Treasury and bond yield outlook
points: Internal treasury guidance previously expected bond yields moving up to 6.75%; there has been a sharper movement but current view is a range of 6.75-6.9% unless West Asia conflict or fiscal imbalances worsen.
Some profitable securities were sold (switches) during the quarter, contributing to trading profits and moderated portfolio yield versus rising G-sec yields.
Sales beyond the 5% allowed threshold were undertaken as permitted.

subsections.label: Liquidity Coverage Ratio (LCR)
points: LCR averaged ~124% in Q4FY26 versus ~135% in Q3FY26, reflecting liquidity consumption amid 17% credit growth.
New LCR guidelines effective April 1 expected to provide 3-4% improvement.
Bank targets a comfortable LCR range of 115-120%, given a preference for 10-15% buffer over the 100% regulatory minimum; entered the year around 125%.

subsections.label: Cost-to-income and overheads
points: Cost-to-income ratio guidance is to remain contained below 50%; would have ended year at 47-48% but for weak treasury income.
Other Opex bunching in Q4 is a recurring pattern due to payment cycles, not intentional; management will explore spreading expenses more evenly across quarters.

Salary cost uptick from PLI-related payout not booked in staff expenses this quarter due to ongoing debate on government PLI basis; instead booked under other provisions — total impact is broadly similar if combined.

subsections.label: Capital and value unlocking
points: CET-1/capital augmentation expected from planned listing of SBI AMC this financial year.
SBI holds ~7.3% stake in NSE within the group; bank has given in-principle consent to participate in NSE OFS, with participation extent to be determined by the board.
Once NSE lists, SBI's shareholding will be available to mark-to-market as a hidden reserve, currently not marked to market in the books.
Reserves and surplus stood at Rs 5,95,000 crores (per presentation page 55); fair market valuation on balance sheet expected to rise further with such unlocking.
Current capital position can fund credit growth of almost Rs 12 trillion; further augmentation will help going forward.

subsections.label: Current account deposits
points: Current account growth appeared to slow to single digits versus 20-25% growth seen a few quarters back, but this is a period-end comparison effect, not underlying weakness.
FY25 (March'25) saw an unusually large ~Rs 50,000 crore government fund release in the last days of March, inflating the base; this inflow was absent in FY26.

Despite that base effect and a 21% YoY decline in government current account deposits, non-governmental current account deposits grew 23% YoY — termed the best current account performance ever for SBI.
Current/business account customers also create cross-sell opportunities for other transactional banking products, fee income, and potential future lending relationships.

subsections.label: Forex/derivatives unwind
points: RBI-directed forex open position unwind resulted in a Q4 MTM impact of Rs 100 crores; complete unwinding on 10th April resulted in a net loss of Rs 57 crores.

subsections.label: DICGC premium
points: Bank expects to benefit from reduced DICGC premium next year but declined to disclose the specific number as it is not a disclosable item under regulation.

key_figures.label: Corporate loan growth reported in last two quarters

subsections.label: Gold loans
points: Gold loan market is highly diversified with average ticket size of ~Rs 2.5 lakhs in SBI's book; this is a price-sensitive segment unlike smaller-ticket borrowers at NBFCs willing to pay any rate.

Gold loans are an efficient equity/ROE product due to zero risk weight, with average LTV of 52% indicating safe lending, and yield of 8.5-9% considered good for a near-zero-capital, near-zero-NPA product.
Bank aims for strong but qualitative growth in this segment rather than purely chasing volume/NIM via higher rates.

subsections.label: Auto loans and cross-sell (Xpress Credit)
points: Auto sector loan growth was muted at 8.5%; management expects improvement with peace-making efforts, mediation, and softer oil prices.
Auto loan itself is a low-margin 'hook' product (dealer commissions eat into profitability) but drives other product engagement and cross-sell.
Xpress Credit has built a good base as an initiative over the past few years.

subsections.label: Products-per-customer (PPC) / cross-sell strategy
points: Current PPC (financial products) is around 3; some customers take 8-10 products from SBI indicating headroom; target is to reach a PPC of 5.
Strategy involves redeploying branch workforce (freed up by digital channel migration) into sales and upselling roles.
Mutual fund and insurance business is tracked at branch level and district level; YONO has deep integration with subsidiary product distribution.
Insurance cross-sell is managed carefully for suitability given industry concerns about mis-selling, though SBI's mis-selling incidence is stated to be the lowest.

subsections.label: MSME risk mitigation
points: Business Rule Engine (BRE) launched several quarters back shows lower delinquencies in BRE-underwritten portfolio versus non-BRE portfolio, indicating more robust underwriting models.
CGTMSE coverage has shifted predominantly to CGTMSE-eligible loans (58% of eligible universe covered), replacing partial collateralization, improving mitigation and recourse.

subsections.label: Market share strategy
points: Bank is deliberately pursuing district-level market share growth; district-level market share data is now available and used strategically, down to branch-officer awareness level.
Even in districts where SBI already has 60% market share, guidance is to grow 1 percentage point per year in every district.
25% market share (of GDP) is described as 'a little farther' but achievable in 4-5 years at the 1%-per-year pace.
Growth strategy is being aligned with rural/district banking expansion and government objectives, including a globalization angle mentioned by an analyst.

subsections.label: Middle East / West Asia exposure
points: SBI has two large Middle East offices: Bahrain and DIFC Dubai, both primarily wholesale banking; Bahrain retail operations are small and Dubai has no retail operations.
Tel Aviv branch does mostly non-funded business (guarantees, largely defence-related for Indian entities).
98%+ of the Middle East corporate book is either sovereign or bank/sovereign-related exposure; minimal direct exposure to medium enterprises or corporates in the region.

Retail exposure via GCC-worker housing loans is concentrated in Kerala and described as 'very small'; no asset quality impact observed as GCC workers have largely stayed in place and GCC countries are normalizing.
Staff temporarily relocated from GCC countries to Mumbai have largely returned, indicating stabilization.
Total India-linked exposure to the Middle East (including trade finance) is USD 10-12 billion globally, with no current concern flagged.

subsections.label: CASA / deposit campaign
points: Bank launched a campaign called 'ABCD - All Branches to Contribute to Deposits' to help mobilize deposits and improve CASA/market share.
Savings bank growth was double-digit (10%) on a large base, aided by this campaign.

key_figures.label: New savings accounts originating on YONO

subsections.label: Project Saral
points: Operations process re-engineering initiative aimed at simplifying the bank at scale, simplifying customer journey and releasing capacity within the system to focus on relationship building and business growth.

subsections.label: Analytics 2.0
points: Building a more digital-native, intelligence-led organization; data and AI becoming central to decision-making across credit, risk and customer engagement.

subsections.label: Liability franchise / YONO strategy
points: Strengthening liability franchise as savings shift towards market-linked instruments, deepening engagement through YONO, expanding ecosystem partnerships, and creating offerings for diverse segments.
Balance sheet strategy is moving from volume-led expansion to value-accretive growth with sharper focus on granularity, product competitiveness and risk-adjusted returns.
Expansion into new growth areas including startups, alternative investments, ecosystems and global trade to diversify and future-proof the portfolio.

New YONO 2.0 platform drove strong adoption: 4 crore registrations within 3 months of launch, total users crossing 10 crore, and 66% of new savings accounts in FY26 originating on YONO, confirming digital-first banking is embedded in customer behaviour.

subsections.label: NSE stake / listing / value unlocking
points: SBI (within group) holds ~7.3% in NSE; bank has given in-principle consent to participate in the NSE OFS, with the extent of participation to be determined by the board.
Once NSE lists, SBI's NSE shareholding (currently not marked to market) will become available as a reserve to mark to market, unlocking hidden value.
Bank has also embarked on listing SBI AMC, expected to complete this financial year, resulting in capital augmentation/CET-1 benefit.

subsections.label: CHAKRA initiative for sunrise sectors
points: CHAKRA initiative launched to support sunrise sectors such as green hydrogen, data centres, new renewable energy models, small modular reactors, and semiconductors.
These sectors require composite funding structures beyond vanilla loans — potentially mezzanine or equity funding — which CHAKRA is designed to handle.

subsections.label: Energy transition / infrastructure opportunity
points: Transmission infrastructure identified as one of the most important emerging investment areas, with large ticket size projects under discussion; structure (SPV vs company-led) not yet finalized.
Battery Energy Storage Systems (BESS) proposals — large number currently being processed.
Pump storage hydro projects starting to emerge as tenders shift toward round-the-clock power combining BESS/pump storage hydro with solar/wind.

Data centre financing: bank funds both infrastructure (developer/shell) and GPU/fit-out as a package, focusing largely on the hyperscaler model given assured demand and client quality; Mumbai has significant data centre activity.
Greenfield data centre projects allow the bank better pricing ability.
Smart metering: significant work already done, with further opportunities identified.

subsections.label: West Asia / geopolitical conflict
points: No impact of West Asia conflict on slippages so far; slippages are seasonal (agriculture, some SME) with no structural asset quality concern.
Company is sticking to 50 bps credit cost guidance and 13-15% credit growth guidance even factoring in the West Asia conflict, unless macros are dramatically disturbed.

MSME clusters such as Morbi (ceramics/gas-dependent) are impacted by unaffordable gas costs leading to reduced production; overall credit exposure to the cluster is minimal but some support may be needed.
Hydrocarbon/oil companies impacted at P&L level but have strong balance sheets; management does not see this translating into a credit issue.
Broad-based stress is not visible yet; only pockets/clusters are impacted.

subsections.label: ECLGS 5 (Emergency Credit Line Guarantee Scheme)
points: ECLGS is viewed as a proactive, pre-emptive government measure; scheme size is Rs 2,50,000 crores with a separate Rs 5,000 crores allocation for airlines.
No customers have yet approached the bank for ECLGS; operationalizing guidelines will take about 8-10 days, and the bank is proactively reaching out to customers.

Full ECLGS limit available to SBI's MSME and non-MSME customer base is estimated at Rs 70,000-80,000 crores; expected utilization is not more than 30%, worst case 30-40%, potentially higher if the conflict escalates.

subsections.label: ECL (Expected Credit Loss) provisioning transition
points: Transition to ECL-based provisioning effective from April 2027 is viewed as a significant regulatory step; bank is confident of a smooth transition.

Models have been built based on draft guidelines and further tweaked based on final guidelines; management declined to give an impact number, indicating more clarity will emerge after Q1FY27 (June quarter).
Transition is expected not to significantly impact ability to fund credit growth or capital ratios; expected to be smooth over the next four years.
No provisioning has yet been made based on ECL as of the call date.
Provisioning for non-fund credit exposure (per Basel 3 disclosures) will also be required per RBI guidelines effective from 1 April 2027.

subsections.label: Technology/cybersecurity risk
points: Technology risk is becoming a systemic risk; emergence of advanced AI models capable of identifying and exploiting vulnerabilities at scale has changed the cybersecurity paradigm.
Industry is moving towards coordinated, system-wide resilience frameworks in partnership with regulators, government, and other stakeholders.

subsections.label: Macro environment risk
points: Global economy remains in a phase of elevated uncertainty; geopolitical developments and climate-related disruptions remain key risks.
Inflation expected at 3.8% near-term with full-year estimate of 4.6%, with upward bias from energy price movements and weather-related uncertainties.
Credit growth is a function of macros; bank does not want to grow significantly higher than what macro growth (GDP, inflation) can support.

key_figures.label: SBI corporate credit growth guidance FY27

subsections.label: NIM guidance
points: Guidance is domestic NIM above 3% for the full year FY27; company does not give wholesale/global bank NIM guidance.
Guidance is always annual, not quarterly, given seasonality in a large loan book.

subsections.label: Credit growth guidance
points: FY27 credit growth guidance of 13-15%, lower than FY26 actual of 16.87%, but management believes hitting the higher end is feasible absent significant West Asia escalation.
Corporate credit guidance for FY27 is 12-13%; RAM (Retail, Agri, MSME) growth is expected to primarily drive the 13-15% overall growth.

Credit growth is calibrated against nominal GDP growth (real GDP 6.5-6.9% + ~4% inflation ≈ 10.5-11% nominal), with the bank building ~3-4% premium over that; if macro numbers don't materialize, growth ambition will be scaled back accordingly.

subsections.label: Return ratios guidance
points: ROA guidance of greater than 1% through the cycle, including through the ECL provisioning transition period (3-4 years).
ROE guidance of minimum 15% through the cycles.

subsections.label: Cost-to-income guidance
points: Guidance is to keep cost-to-income ratio contained below 50%.

subsections.label: Credit cost guidance
points: 50 bps credit cost guidance maintained, consistent with guidance given over the last three years, unaffected by West Asia conflict developments as things currently stand.

subsections.label: LCR guidance
points: Bank targets comfortable LCR range of 115-120% (10-15% buffer over 100% regulatory minimum), expecting some moderation from current ~125% as credit growth continues, partly offset by 3-4% improvement from new LCR guidelines effective April 1.

themes.label: NIM trajectory
themes.note: Domestic NIM at 3.03% for FY26 met annual guidance despite Q4 dipping to 2.93%, driven by rate cuts and corporate book mix shift to T-bill linked loans; FY27 guidance reiterated at above 3%.

themes.label: Asset quality strength
themes.note: Gross NPA at 1.49% and Net NPA at 0.39%, both improving YoY, with PCR at 74.36%, described as a two-decade low validating underwriting discipline.

themes.label: Treasury volatility
themes.note: Q4 MTM loss of Rs 4,520 crores versus Rs 143 crores in Q3 dragged profitability; management expects yields to stabilize in the 6.75-6.9% range going forward.

themes.label: Digital transformation (YONO)
themes.note: New YONO crossed 4 crore registrations in 3 months, total users above 10 crores, and 66% of new savings accounts originated on YONO in FY26.

themes.label: West Asia conflict exposure
themes.note: Management sees minimal direct exposure (mostly sovereign/bank in Middle East, small Kerala-linked retail exposure) and no asset quality impact so far, though ECLGS is being made available proactively.

themes.label: ECL provisioning transition
themes.note: Transition to ECL-based provisioning from April 2027 is expected to be smooth over 3-4 years without significant capital or growth impact; no impact number disclosed yet.

themes.label: District-level market share expansion
themes.note: Bank targets 1 percentage point market share growth per district per year, aiming for 25% share of GDP in 4-5 years, supported by campaigns like 'ABCD - All Branches to Contribute to Deposits'.

key_takeaways: Net profit reached a record high at Rs 80,032 crores, up 12.88% year-on-year, supported by 11.25% year-on-year growth in operating profit with a domestic NIM at 3.03%, supporting our guidance to maintain NIM above 3%.
As total business crosses the Rs 109 trillion mark, this performance showcases our strengthening market position and sustained customer trust.

We achieved resilient deposit growth of 11.03% year-on-year by about Rs 6 trillion driven by strong inflows in retail term deposits which grew by 14.77% and a double-digit savings account growth at 10.6%.
The credit growth has been robust and was up 16.87% year-on-year as on March 26, which was driven by all the segments registering double-digit growth.

The asset quality continues to be industry leading with gross NPAs at 1.49%, improving by 33 basis points and net NPA at 0.39%, further improving by 8 basis points on year-on-year basis. The PCR was at 74.36%.
Strengthening our capital position, our CAR has improved by 115 basis points year-on-year and stands at 15.4%, which is well above the regulatory requirements.

The strong adoption of a new YONO, crossing 4 crore registration within three months of launch and bringing total users above 10 crores confirms that digital-first banking is now deeply embedded in customer behaviour. 66% of new savings accounts originating on YONO platform in FY26 demonstrates our successful transition to a digital-first institution.
Our emphasis has always been on efficiency and return matrix, with ROA consistently greater than 1% and ROE at 18.5% at the end of Q4 FY26.

TATASTEEL.about: Tata Steel Ltd is Asia's first integrated private steel company setup in 1907.[1] The company has presence across the entire value chain of steel manufacturing from mining and processing iron ore and coal to producing and distributing finished products.[2] The company has a target to increase domestic steelmaking capacity to 30 MnTPA by 2025.[3]

quarters.summary: Management framed Q1 FY27 as resilient despite West Asia-driven supply-chain disruption (unplanned costs ~₹1,200 crore) and Chinese exports depressing global prices. India NSR expected to be ~₹1,500/ton lower QoQ in Q2 but EBITDA expected higher on volume recovery; UK trending toward EBITDA breakeven in H2 (possibly pushed one quarter) with realizations +£80/ton QoQ expected; Netherlands DSP restart trial from Aug 5 is a key near-term catalyst with Q2 realizations +€10/ton QoQ expected; NINL 4.8 mtpa expansion approved (₹33,873 crore, 48 months) as major India capital allocation event; Europe expected to reprice structurally in phases as safeguards/CBAM reshape supply.

DSP is ~20% of Netherlands production; shutdown since first week of April due to chrome emissions exceedance
Q1 EBITDA only €4m despite revenue/ton +€87, as costs/ton rose +€118 from volume loss and higher raw materials

Restart plan: approval received to run DSP for 4-week trial from Aug 5; management confident emissions now controlled after changing rollers (dry/wet), expects permission to operate beyond trial if data supports

subsections.label: Technical clarification (Netherlands)
points: CEO: issue is specific to DSP tunnel furnaces and roller materials; other plant areas and new-build assets are not impacted

subsections.label: Environmental progress since 2020 (Netherlands)
points: Undercooked coke incidents reduced by 98%, now <0.011% of pushes, below industry average
CO2 intensity ~1.66 tCO2/t crude steel, amongst the lowest among integrated producers

key_figures.label: MBK mines iron ore capacity expansion

subsections.label: NINL (Nilachal) expansion
points: Board approved 4.8 mtpa expansion at NINL, central to 'deepening presence in high margin and branded long products'
Investment of ₹33,873 crore (core steelmaking expansion) to take NINL to ~6.2 mt in phase 1; stated longer-term ambition of 10 mt at the site
Timeline: 48 months to commission
NINL merger into Tata Steel progressing; expected completion by end of FY27

subsections.label: Mining capacity expansion
points: Expanding iron ore mining capacity at MBK mines by 15 mtpa in phases; capex additional to the steel expansion capex

subsections.label: Capex intensity — NINL vs Kalinganagar
points: Management: NINL should be viewed 'more like a greenfield' project because it needs enabling infrastructure, layout, and environment compliance
Kalinganagar phase 2 benefitted from phase 1 enabling assets and the existing HSM, unlike NINL
Also cited FX impact on imported equipment as a factor in capex intensity

key_figures.label: UK safeguards contract renewal marker month
UK EAF piling and OEM packages ordered

subsections.label: Europe market structure outlook
points: Europe expected to reprice structurally, with UK and EU safeguards as key drivers
Price improvement expected in phases (not a sudden spike) as quotas/CBAM change the supply stack
Noted that imports availability tightens meaningfully, with commentary that a large portion of imported volume is effectively removed under new constraints
UK prices recovering toward historical relationship with Europe, having previously been 'well below' Europe for about 1 year
Further UK upside depends on product-category quota recalibration and contract renewals, with November a key marker

subsections.label: Strategy emphasis
points: Strategy continues to shift toward mix, downstream/solutions, approval-based segments, and selective upstream growth

subsections.label: NINL merger
points: NINL merger into Tata Steel progressing; expected completion by end of FY27

subsections.label: Capital allocation stance
points: India-led growth with more downstream weighting; Europe assessed independently

India upstream optionality discussed (existing assets plus Maharashtra in phases), but management emphasized value creation and sequencing versus pure market-share pursuit

guidance_ledger.statement: Q2 India NSR expected ~₹1,500/ton lower than Q1 (longs weaker due to monsoon slowdown; flats more resilient with strong auto).
Despite NSR softness, management expects higher Q2 EBITDA (₹ crore) vs Q1 due to higher volumes.
Board approved 4.8 mtpa expansion at NINL; investment ₹33,873 crore to take NINL to ~6.2 mt in phase 1; longer-term ambition 10 mt at the site; 48 months to commission.
NINL merger into Tata Steel progressing; expected completion by end of FY27.
Expanding iron ore mining capacity at MBK mines by 15 mtpa in phases.
Management reiterated trajectory toward EBITDA breakeven in H2, possibly 'pushed by one quarter,' but still aiming Q3/Q4 'closer to break-even.'
Q2 expected +£80/ton realization vs Q1, but not all to margin because UK is substrate-fed.
Mitigation via restart/ramp alternate facilities (Llanwern cold mill, pickle line); expects normalization by Q3/Q4.
Management expects Q2 better than Q1 (DSP disruption should reduce if trial progresses).
Netherlands Q2 realizations expected +€10/ton QoQ (but volume normalization hinges on DSP).
Restart plan: approval received to run DSP for 4-week trial from Aug 5; management confident emissions now controlled, expects permission to operate beyond trial if data supports.
Additional ~₹300 crore/quarter (₹1,200 crore/year) depreciation due to mining assets facing re-auction/bidding in 2030.
Europe expected to reprice structurally in phases (not a sudden spike) as quotas/CBAM change the supply stack.
UK prices recovering toward historical relationship with Europe; further upside depends on product-category quota recalibration and contract renewals (November a key marker).
Guided to ~100 kt this year in shipbuilding, with ambition to scale to 0.5 mt.
Company has largely completed engineering, but will not proceed until clarity on regulatory framework certainty, government funding/policy support, and market support (CBAM/safeguards/ETS dynamics).
In FY2027 we are aiming to achieve cost transformation related savings of ~Rs 7,100 crores vs. FY2026 levels.
We intend to increase capex in FY2027 to around Rs 20,000 crores of which more than 60% will be spent in India.
The volume will be at least 2 million tons better in this financial year compared to the previous financial year with most of it coming in India.
Between July and September, we should be able to get the FID.
Once we get the FID, the target date is somewhere around 2029-30.
In India we expect 1Q to be about Rs. 6,000/t higher than 4Q.
In UK, we expect it to be about £80/t higher in 1Q compared to 4Q.
In Netherlands we expect it to be about €80/t higher in 1Q compared to 4Q.
The delta increase we expect in 1Q for India over 4Q is $15/t.
In Netherlands, the delta coal cost increase is about $10/t.
The iron ore increase in Netherlands is expected to be about $5/t in 1Q over 4Q.
We expect margin expansion in India and in UK, and some margin compression in Netherlands because of the issues that we've had with the DSP.

Until two months back, we were expecting at least 8-10% growth in steel demand going forward. Now, if we are going to recalibrate the GDP and say that the GDP will grow a bit less, then the steel demand may grow a bit less as well.
We are expecting maybe 30% of the benefit to come in this quarter and 70% of the benefit to come in next quarter.

The EBITDA losses will shrink this quarter compared to last quarter and will shrink again the next quarter; whether the shrink is enough to be positive next quarter is something we are still working out.
We hope to be EBITDA positive during this year, now that the prices have started improving.

Typically good EAFs work in the range of 6 to 8% EBITDA margin, and our assumption is that it is the same, but we have more value added products in the portfolio, so we should be able to get better than that.
Our base assumption for spreads is business as usual for the next 12 months at least... adjusted for a CBAM uplift... and for the coal prices that have also moved up, the spreads are no different.
Overall, the plan this year on an EBITDA basis is higher than the plan for last year and in Netherlands also.
We are increasing that from India from Tata Steel Kalinganagar to about 1.8 million tons - that is our target to increase.
The tubes business, which is now at 1.2 million tons; we want to take it to about 4 million tons.
The wires business... is about 600,000-700,000 tons, and we want to take it to a million tons.
We want to double the India capacity which we've already announced last year.
We plan to double the size of the Colors business also in the next 12-24 months.
We want our downstream businesses to at least be about 50-60% of our volume.
So, we are fairly advanced in that. We'll take a few months and come back and announce it, and then going to ensure that we can execute it quickly.
Hopefully in the next three months or so, we will give you an update about where we are on the land and more specifics about it.
Even with the existing sites between Kalinganagar, Meramandali and Neelachal plus Jamshedpur at 11 million tons, we already have the optionality to grow to 45-50 million tons in India.
Once we start the Maharashtra site... that potentially adds another 6-10 million tons.

risk_register.risk: West Asia war-driven cost increases (energy, freight/insurance, gas, logistics)
risk_register.note: Unplanned costs of about ₹1,200 crore directly attributed to the West Asia war; mitigations/alternate sourcing expected to taper impact in coming quarters.

risk_register.risk: Chinese export volumes depressing global steel prices
risk_register.note: Chinese exports of 9–10 million tons a month cited as depressing global prices.

risk_register.risk: UK import quota levels remaining high despite revised safeguards
risk_register.note: Quotas still '70–80% of the demand' in some categories (galvanized, tubulars, packaging) and 'not fully aligned' with fairness intent, despite 51% reduction in tariff-free quotas and higher duties.

risk_register.risk: UK Port Talbot pickle line fire
risk_register.note: Fire on June 3, 2026; no injuries; insurance recovery underway; Q1 impact ~10 kt volume, ~£5m EBITDA; normalization expected by Q3/Q4.

risk_register.risk: UK EAF high-voltage grid connection delay by National Grid
risk_register.note: Risk flagged; company working with stakeholders to mitigate.

risk_register.risk: Netherlands regulatory/'social license' uncertainty
risk_register.note: Management stressed Netherlands standards can be beyond EU norms and 'without precedent,' complicating long-term capital decisions.

risk_register.risk: Netherlands DSP shutdown due to chrome emissions exceedance
risk_register.note: Shutdown since first week of April; caused sharp earnings compression; 4-week restart trial approved from Aug 5.

risk_register.risk: Netherlands legal/prosecutorial exposure
risk_register.note: Prosecutor intends to proceed; currently 'essentially on the company,' with possibility of individuals named later (not yet); hearing referenced for Nov 20.

risk_register.risk: Regulatory/market uncertainty delaying Netherlands decarbonization (DRI/EAF) investment
risk_register.note: Engineering largely complete but proceeding contingent on regulatory framework certainty, government funding/policy support, and market support (CBAM/safeguards/ETS dynamics); EU ETS phase-out slowdown reduces near-term pressure but also reduces CBAM uplift, affecting investability.

risk_register.risk: India steel demand growth moderation with GDP recalibration
risk_register.note: Not directly re-addressed this quarter in the summary provided (raised as prior guidance).

risk_register.risk: Material uncertainty at Tata Steel Netherlands (going concern) due to regulatory letter on CGP permit revocation
risk_register.note: Post Balance Sheet date letter from local environment agencies regarding intent to revoke permits without specifics; caused auditors to flag material uncertainty as no definitive closure pathway/timeline is articulated.

risk_register.risk: Coke and Gas Plants (CGP) closure cost and physical transition risk
risk_register.note: Plants are 40-50 years old; some regulatory standards not technically achievable; closure must be safe, planned, controlled and sequential; cost penalty from market coke purchase partially offset by CO2 reduction benefit.

risk_register.risk: UK EAF electricity infrastructure delay
risk_register.note: National Grid formally alerted a delay of 6-8 months (potentially higher) versus original plan; critical for project commissioning; commissioning delay estimate revised from 18 months to 12 months.

risk_register.risk: West Asia geopolitical conflict impact on costs and supply chain
risk_register.note: Increased costs and supply chain risks around energy, freight and raw materials; downstream lines (galvanising, tinplate, colour coated) faced shortage of critical inputs like Propane, now largely resolved.

risk_register.risk: UK weak demand and low-cost imports
risk_register.note: Weak demand conditions and influx of low-cost imports have continued to weigh on performance, with EBITDA losses of around £98/t in FY2026.

risk_register.risk: Netherlands regulatory landscape evolving beyond EU norms
risk_register.note: Local regulatory authorities proposing standards that go beyond prevailing EU norms and global practices.

risk_register.risk: TSN mass claim lawsuit
risk_register.note: No material update; company has time to file defence; experts studying claim details.

risk_register.risk: India construction/MSME softness
risk_register.note: Construction demand slowdown; MSME segment facing working capital pressure; long products facing pressure from secondary producers in May.

risk_register.risk: Macro/GDP recalibration risk to India steel demand
risk_register.note: If GDP growth recalibrated lower amid current macroeconomic situation, steel demand growth (previously expected 8-10%) may also moderate.

risk_register.risk: Netherlands DSP production loss impact
risk_register.note: ~1.5 months (~200,000 tons) of lost DSP production expected to cause margin compression in Netherlands in the near term despite price hikes.

risk_register.risk: Labour/workforce restructuring risk from facility shutdowns
risk_register.note: Permanent shutdown of any facility (e.g., CGP) will require workforce restructuring, as was done in UK; more complex if unplanned.

themes.label: West Asia conflict cost/supply pressure
themes.note: Unplanned costs of ~₹1,200 crore directly due to West Asia war (energy, freight/insurance, gas, logistics); mitigations expected to taper impact.

themes.label: UK safeguard policy tailwind
themes.note: Revised safeguards cut tariff-free quotas 51% and raised duties, but quotas still cover 70–80% of demand in some categories; not fully aligned with fairness intent.

themes.label: Netherlands CGP regulatory uncertainty
themes.note: DSP shutdown since April due to chrome emissions exceedance; restart trial from Aug 5; broader 'social license' and legal exposure persists with Nov 20 hearing referenced.

themes.label: Downstream/value-added mix shift
themes.note: Auto, branded longs, digital, construction solutions and downstream businesses (tubes, tinplate, wires, Colors) posting strong growth; strategy explicitly prioritizes downstream/approval-based segments over pure upstream scale.

themes.label: Capacity expansion optionality & pacing
themes.note: NINL 4.8 mtpa expansion approved (₹33,873 crore, 48 months) plus MBK mining capacity expansion by 15 mtpa in phases; NINL viewed as more like a greenfield project vs Kalinganagar phase 2.

themes.label: Deleveraging & balance sheet strength
themes.note: Net debt/EBITDA at 2.3x, within the stated 2.5–3x through-cycle range, with liquidity of ₹45,950 crore including ₹13,200 crore cash.

themes.label: UK EAF transition
themes.note: 3 mtpa scrap-based EAF largely on schedule (35% piling, all major OEM packages ordered), though grid connection timing with National Grid flagged as a risk.

key_takeaways: Resilient quarter despite external shocks: Management framed Q1 as resilient amid West Asia-driven supply-chain disruption and Chinese exports of "9–10 million tons a month" depressing global prices.

Consolidated performance improved despite "unplanned cost increases of about ₹1,200 crore… directly due to the West Asia war" (energy, freight/insurance, gas, logistics). Mitigations/alternate sourcing are expected to taper the impact in coming quarters.
Strategy emphasis continues to shift toward mix, downstream/solutions, approval-based segments, and selective upstream growth—explicitly not chasing upstream scale "unless it creates value."
Board-approved NINL 4.8 mt expansion (₹33,873 crore; 48 months; phase-1 to 6.2 mt; long-products focus; 10 mt longer-term ambition).
Netherlands DSP restart approval (Aug 5, 4-week trial) is a near-term catalyst; Q1 profitability was heavily impaired.
UK fire disclosure (Port Talbot pickle line) quantified impact (10 kt; £5m EBITDA) and normalization timeline (Q3/Q4).
Accelerated depreciation adds a ₹1,200 crore/year non-cash drag (mechanical/regulatory-driven).
Clear articulation that Europe decarbonization capex (Netherlands) is under re-assessment pending regulatory certainty and investability; UK EAF remains committed/on schedule.
No interest in UK nationalized assets; focus remains on Port Talbot EAF transformation.

quarters.summary: Tata Steel delivered a strong FY2026 with consolidated EBITDA up 35% YoY and margin expansion across geographies despite subdued pricing. Management expects margin expansion in India and UK in 1QFY27 driven by higher realisations, some margin compression in Netherlands due to DSP-related production loss, and flagged material uncertainty at Tata Steel Netherlands (TSN) linked to a post-Balance Sheet Date regulatory letter on Coke and Gas Plant (CGP) permits; UK EAF project faces ~12-month electricity infrastructure delay; NINL merger and expansion progressing with FID expected Jul-Sep 2026 and first steel targeted 2029-30; FY2027 cost transformation savings target ~Rs 7,100 crores; capex guided up to ~Rs 20,000 crores in FY2027 with >60% in India.

subsections.label: Quality of earnings & cost transformation
points: Focus is clearly on the quality of earnings amid multi-year trough in steel prices and unprecedented uncertainty.

Key cost efficiencies in India driven by purchase optimisation of spares, reduced refractory consumption, increased use of coastal waterways (structural cost advantage over other transport modes), higher power wheeling and a leaner coal mix.
UK cost benefits driven by calibrated and focused spending on maintenance costs, stronger spares-management discipline and insourcing of product testing.

Netherlands cost benefits driven via optimisation of coal blend leading to decline in procurement costs and deployment of value-in-use concept to improve operating efficiencies such as fuel rate, scrap consumption etc.
Key variation to 100% compliance on the cost transformation program was the delay in the TSN restructuring, which has since been completed.
Working capital efficiency enhanced with cash release especially in India and Netherlands through focused management of working capital.

subsections.label: Balance sheet & deleveraging
points: Post pandemic, prioritised deleveraging in FY2021 & FY2022 including prepayment of $3.6 billion of offshore obligations.

Focus for last few years has been on onshoring of overseas debt to mitigate INR depreciation risk; equity stake acquisitions in Tata Steel Holdings Pte. Ltd over past three years largely relate to this onshoring initiative.
By FY2028 overseas debt will reduce further as overseas dollar bonds are repaid; only remaining overseas debt will be working capital lines for overseas businesses.

Debt prepayment of ~Rs 9,100 crores from internal cash during the year is masked on financial statements by FX revaluation (overseas debt valued at Rs 94/$ vs Rs 88/$ a year back) and increase in leased assets.
Tata Steel remains one of few steel companies globally rated investment-grade by international rating agencies.

subsections.label: India business as core growth engine
points: India now contributes ~74% of Tata Steel's total crude steel production.
India EBITDA margin of 24% similar to the 10-year average even in a challenging year.
Kalinganagar Phase 2 capacity expansion is now complete, complemented by focused investments in downstream facilities and portfolio simplification, strengthening product mix and margin profile.

subsections.label: UK operations
points: Steel prices remained below £500/t until end of February; onset of West Asia conflict along with UK government tighter safeguard announcement drove meaningful uplift in hot rolled prices.
Most of the recent spot price movement expected to flow through P&L in 1QFY27 and 2QFY27.

UK safeguard measures originally introduced to support domestic production are set to expire 30th June 2026; revised regime from 1st July 2026 proposes ~60% reduction in import quotas and tariff increase from 25% to 50%, aiming for 40-50% of steel demand met via domestic production.
Weak demand conditions and influx of low-cost imports have continued to weigh on performance historically.
With price increases coming through in 1Q, quarter-on-quarter improvement in earnings expected going forward.

subsections.label: Netherlands operations
points: Liquid steel production broadly stable; deliveries slightly below production level.
Policy measures including tighter safeguards effective 1st July and ongoing CBAM implementation reshaping trade flows and enabling preference for local supply.
4Q higher volumes and improvement in costs were mostly offset by drop in realisations QoQ.
Netherlands continues to perform exceedingly well on cash flow management and is effectively net debt free despite challenging operating/regulatory conditions.

subsections.label: NINL merger
points: Board approval received to merge NINL with Tata Steel Limited subject to necessary approvals; transaction targeted to complete in FY2027.

subsections.label: Capex plans
points: Total capex in FY2026 was ~Rs 14,000 crores consolidated; intend to increase to ~Rs 20,000 crores in FY2027, of which more than 60% will be spent in India.

subsections.label: India demand outlook
points: India demand expected to be strong as long as there is infrastructure-led growth; this has been more infrastructure-investment led than consumption-led.
If current macro situation causes GDP recalibration lower, steel demand may grow a bit less as well.
Automotive sector quite strong and continues to be strong; passenger vehicle and two-wheeler segments strong; need to watch impact of rising fuel prices on commercial vehicles.
Construction had a bit of a slowdown, partly due to labour unavailability (attributed to elections) and some MSME working capital pressure.
Long products softer in May driven by secondary producers struggling with working capital, high cost, disposing steel; gap between secondary and primary producer prices has increased.

Flat products holding up better, supported by rising China prices (+$20-25/t in last 3-4 weeks), falling Chinese exports (below 10 million tons after a while, down for first four months of year), and growing export options for Indian flat producers aided by weaker Rupee.
Flat products closely tied to auto demand, both directly and indirectly, and auto has been strong so far.

subsections.label: Retail & branded growth
points: FY2026 marked shift from engagement-led initiatives to solution-oriented partnerships anchored in innovation and AI-led enablement.
Tata Tiscon achieved best-ever annual volumes; Tata Steelium achieved robust ~28% YoY volume growth.
Tata Tiscon sales mix has shifted heavily toward retail (individual house builders) versus projects, as retail is more attractive/profitable than the price-competitive projects market.
Aashiyana is an order generation platform for individual house builders; fulfilment via physical distribution chain across India within 72 hours, through 10,000+ dealer network.

Online platform includes all Tata Steel products (steel, Tata Pravesh, tubes, wires) but 90-95% of sales is Tata Tiscon; no current plans to spin off/monetise the platform as it is viewed as a strategic route-to-market channel.
Orders now come from Indians living abroad building/buying steel for relatives' homes in India, reflecting expanded customer reach via the platform.

subsections.label: Automotive & Special Products
points: Delivered best-ever quarterly and annual volumes.

CAGL at Kalinganagar (state-of-the-art) secured over 25 new grade approvals across ultra-high strength steels and coated products, enabling customers to meet evolving safety and lightweighting requirements.

subsections.label: Downstream businesses
points: Tubes, Wires and Colors achieved best-ever sales; Tinplate witnessed record annual sales of PAXEL edible oil cans.
Plan to double India packaging capacity (already announced last year) and double the size of Colors business in next 12-24 months after buying out BlueScope's JV share.

Objective is to sell less HRC in the market (commodity, price-pressured, sold to tube makers) and more value-added products (cold rolled, galvanised, packaging steel) to better manage cyclicality and protect profitability.
Target for downstream businesses to be at least 50-60% of total volume.

subsections.label: Value-added mix & Ludhiana economics
points: Downstream businesses add anything from 5-10% incremental EBITDA even if steel is transferred at market prices.

Ludhiana (scrap-based EAF) profitability from a conversion point of view will be lower than integrated route, but net of freight, realisation is higher because ~Rs 3,000/t transportation cost (Jamshedpur to Ludhiana) is saved.

Ludhiana less exposed to weakening rupee and coal price increases since it uses scrap rather than imported coal/iron ore; would benefit further if carbon taxes are introduced given greater carbon efficiency.

subsections.label: UK slab supply model ('fifth hot strip mill')
points: Port Talbot facility in UK is effectively now the fifth hot strip mill for Tata Steel; system economics on slab transfer improve total consolidated Tata Steel EBITDA even when standalone UK EBITDA looks weak.
Model of supplying slabs from India to UK will continue until the EAF starts.

subsections.label: Segmental demand nuances (Tiscon/Steelium)
points: Tata Tiscon sold to both projects and retail; retail preferred as more attractive/profitable than projects (price-competitive market).

Steelium sales depend on further value-addition options available (e.g. as galvanising lines ramp up at Kalinganagar, less cold-rolled steel is available to sell externally, redirected to auto or galvanised applications for better realisations).

subsections.label: Netherlands DSP suspension
points: Direct Sheet Plant at IJmuiden was temporarily suspended following emission observations; issue has now been resolved and plant expected to restart soon with due regulatory clearance.
DSP closure and trials being run; expected back up later this month if all requisite approvals are received.
DSP suspension is distinct from the CGP issue — related to emissions from the DSP exceeding limits, declared transparently to regulator and jointly reviewed.

subsections.label: Coke and Gas Plants (CGP) closure
points: Given the age (40-50 years old) of Coke and Gas Plants, company is considering planned closure in the future; several measures have been undertaken over the last 2 years to enhance environmental standards.

Company has agreed to close CGPs in a planned, controlled and safe manner in the future after careful assessment; some regulatory standards required are above global industry standards and not technically achievable/followed anywhere else.
Discussions ongoing with the Province and Environment Agencies on timeline for controlled, sequential and safe closure.
Coke ovens cannot be shut down in an unplanned manner — described as more like a chemical factory than a steel factory; cooling down requires time and there is a 'make safe' and permit requirement.
Company was anyway planning to shut CGPs down soon after first phase of DRI-EAF would have come up; current situation may accelerate this timeline.

If closure proceeds, coke/gas would be sourced via market purchase, potentially including from India; cost penalty expected due to loss of coke oven gas energy source and added freight, partially offset by CO2 reduction benefit — net impact depends on transition timing.
Permanent shutdown of any facility triggers restructuring of associated labour, as was the case in the UK; unplanned shutdown makes this a lot more complex to handle.

subsections.label: NINL expansion progress
points: Initial site preparation work has started; permissions being obtained on different parts.
FEL3 (basis for final capital allocation) is very advanced; announcement expected in the next few months.
Careful, regulatory-compliant approach being taken given the site's scale (10 million ton site), aiming to be tight on capex.

subsections.label: UK EAF project progress
points: Major demolition works completed.
Securing access to higher-power electricity is critical for the planned transition; National Grid has formally alerted a delay in its connectivity project.
Company in conversation with National Grid and UK Government on resolution.

Working to get at least a partial electricity connection (even one line) as soon as plant is ready, to run trials and test equipment without wasting time, aiming to compress ramp-up and protect targeted project IRR.

subsections.label: Capital allocation philosophy / brownfield optionality
points: Company has optionality to operate parallelly across four sites (Kalinganagar, Meramandali, Neelachal, Jamshedpur) versus historically sequential expansion when operating only out of Jamshedpur.
NINL 5 MTPA blast furnace will be an exact replica of the Kalinganagar 5 million ton blast furnace (steel melt shop will differ as it is a long products plant).

Approach has changed: projects are now announced only after all approvals are obtained and FEL3-level detailing is complete, improving ability to stick to schedule and cost (e.g., Ludhiana built in 2 years, started ahead of schedule).

Cost of iron ore and coal in India rising (bidding over 100% for iron ore, coal import dependency with weak INR), shifting value pools downstream rather than upstream — driving greater focus on downstream investment.
Execution capacity constraints in India (limited pool of contractors executing projects) is a consideration in pacing expansions.
Brownfield expansion allows lower cost of expansion and better pacing vs a large single M&A bullet (e.g., Bhushan acquisition required ~Rs 35,000 crores in one go).

subsections.label: Maharashtra greenfield site
points: Land identified; discussions ongoing with government; more definitive update expected in next 3 months on land and mining specifics.
Approach described as 'definitive' rather than merely circumspect — company knows exactly what it wants to do and is working with government support.

subsections.label: UK market
points: Subdued demand dynamics reflected in annual deliveries.
Welcomed recently announced revisions to safeguard measures (60% reduction in tariff-free quotas, higher duties) expected to support more balanced market environment.
Continued and calibrated policy support seen as critical to enable sustained recovery.

subsections.label: Netherlands market
points: Policy measures including tighter safeguards effective 1 July and ongoing CBAM implementation are reshaping trade flows and enabling preference for local supply.
Company deeply engaged with the Province of North Holland and environmental regulators on emission compliance and future of coke/gas facilities.

subsections.label: Export dynamics
points: Indian flat product producers now have export options with export prices not too bad; weaker Rupee is helping exports.
China's exports have come down to less than 10 million tons after quite a while; first four months of the year Chinese exports are down.

subsections.label: West Asia crisis supply chain impact
points: Developments in West Asia have increased costs and supply chain risks around energy, freight and some raw materials.

In India, upstream operations largely unaffected, but some downstream galvanising, tinplate and colour coated lines were impacted by shortage of critical inputs like Propane; most lines are now back in full operation and company actively working to mitigate.
Downstream operations initially faced supply chain constraints; mitigated via alternate fuels, alternate shipping routes and preponing shutdowns in some cases.
Cost transformation program in FY2027 expected to progressively help mitigate a portion of these pressures.
Improved pricing trends across India, Netherlands and UK should help absorb near-term cost pressures from West Asia crisis.

subsections.label: Logistics consolidation (TMILL/BRPL)
points: TMILL started as a port operations and shipping logistics company, but 80% of revenue now comes from ground and rail movement; one of the biggest rake operators in the country, managing warehouses for just-in-time procurement delivery.
TMILL exploring waterways movement, connecting Kalinganagar to Paradip and onward to Angul, aligned with government focus on waterways.
Buying out IQ Martrade (German logistics partner of 20+ years); Tata NYK remains a separate shipping JV; TMILL going forward will be Tata Steel and NYK focused on ground logistics.
Slurry pipeline JV with Lloyds (Brahmani River Pellets Limited - BRPL) to be expanded; plan to double slurry pipeline capacity, potentially extending to Western India later.

Rationale for raising TMILL stake to 74% (from 51%) is to consolidate for synergies in manufacturing excellence and supply chain leverage; venture has been profitable, paying dividends, with capital returned multiple times over for all partners.

subsections.label: Customer relationship shift
points: FY2026 marked a shift from engagement-led initiatives to solution-oriented partnerships anchored in innovation and AI-led enablement, scaling the branded and retail segment.

subsections.label: Discerning segments (shipbuilding, oil & gas)
points: Strengthened presence in shipbuilding and oil & gas, aided by international certifications enabling participation in higher-specification and globally competitive orders with stringent quality/reliability requirements.

subsections.label: Construction innovation
points: Deployed InQuik modular bridge system at Varanasi-Ranchi-Kolkata Expressway in just 24 days.
Introduced first-of-its-kind Mobile Bore Pile Cage solution, significantly enhancing on-site efficiency.

subsections.label: Market share philosophy
points: Company more focused on market share in key attractive segments (aiming for at least twice overall market share in those segments) rather than aggregate market share.
Intends to remain the dominant, number one player in automotive, oil & gas and its retail franchise segments.

Optionality to grow upstream capacity exists (45-50 MTPA at current sites plus 6-10 million tons at Maharashtra), giving flexibility versus peers who are adding capacity aggressively; pacing decided based on demand, balance sheet and other factors.

subsections.label: NINL merger
points: Board approval received to merge NINL with Tata Steel Limited, subject to necessary approvals; transaction targeted to complete in FY2027.

subsections.label: Consolidation of JV partners in India
points: Company buying out JV partners across the value chain (e.g., bought out Colors/BlueScope JV) to leverage manufacturing excellence and supply chain synergies rather than operate fragmented.
Philosophy: in India (home market/core strength), company prefers to build capacities by itself rather than via JV, though it retains a JV with Nippon Steel for a continuous annealing line.
India growth strategy is not being held back by, nor dependent on, developments in the European portfolio.

subsections.label: Netherlands JLoI and Final Investment Decision
points: Joint Letter of Intent (JLoI) with the Dutch government has condition precedents on both company and government sides, some requiring regulator fulfilment too.

Company will not commit binding investment unless contractually guaranteed (not just grandfathered) to run its course over the investment recovery period; government is itself an investor in this equation.
Not yet at Final Investment Decision (FID) stage; regulatory landscape assessment is an ongoing fulcrum in the process.
Company will not use public money for investments that are at risk without adequate certainty.

subsections.label: TMILL / logistics consolidation
points: Raising stake in TM International Logistics Ltd (TMILL) from 51% to 74% (balance held by NYK) to consolidate control over logistics value chain.
Buying out IQ Martrade (German logistics partner); expanding BRPL slurry pipeline JV with Lloyds.

subsections.label: Maharashtra greenfield expansion
points: In active discussion with government; land identified; more definitive specifics expected within next 3 months on land and mining aspects; described as a 'definitive' rather than tentative plan.

subsections.label: Netherlands regulatory/going concern uncertainty
points: Post Balance Sheet date, company received a letter from local environment agencies regarding intent to revoke permits without specifics — this creates material uncertainty for TSN in preparing financial statements.
Local regulatory environment evolving, with authorities proposing standards beyond prevailing EU norms and global practices.
Material uncertainty stems solely from the letter's lack of definitive pathway, dates or transition specifics — not from the underlying closure decision or financial cost itself.
If closure of CGP proceeds without a mutually agreed safe/controlled timeline, situation becomes unmanageable from a physical operations standpoint.
Auditors flagged material uncertainty on TSN going concern basis in financial statements due to this letter.

subsections.label: Netherlands mass claim lawsuit
points: No material update; company has time to file its defence on the mass claim; experts studying the parts raised in the claim before submission.

subsections.label: UK electricity infrastructure delay
points: National Grid has formally alerted that its connectivity project for the EAF is delayed; delay of 6-8 months (potentially higher) versus original plan; this is critical for project commissioning.

subsections.label: West Asia conflict / geopolitical risk
points: Developments in West Asia have increased costs and supply chain risks around energy, freight and some raw materials.
Downstream operations (galvanising, tinplate, colour coated) faced input shortages (e.g., Propane); most now resolved.

subsections.label: UK demand & import competition
points: Weak demand conditions and influx of low-cost imports have continued to weigh on UK performance historically.

subsections.label: India construction/MSME softness
points: Construction demand had a bit of a slowdown; some pain seen with MSMEs due to pressure at that end of the value chain and working capital issues.
Long products facing pressure in May from secondary producers struggling with working capital and high costs.

subsections.label: Macro/GDP risk to steel demand
points: If GDP growth is recalibrated lower amid current macroeconomic situation, steel demand growth expectation (previously 8-10%) may also moderate.

subsections.label: India outlook
points: Realisations expected ~Rs 6,000/t higher in 1Q vs 4Q, including part of the auto contract increases (most auto benefit expected in 2Q — ~30% in 1Q, 70% in 2Q).
Coal consumption cost expected to increase by $15/t in 1Q over 4Q.
Overall margin expansion expected in India despite added West Asia-related costs beyond coal and iron ore.

Volume guidance of at least 2 million tons higher in FY2027 vs FY2026, mostly from India as Kalinganagar ramp-up is largely complete; Ludhiana contributing only 0.5 million tons of that as it is still ramping up.

subsections.label: UK outlook
points: Realisations expected ~£80/t higher in 1Q vs 4Q; margin expansion expected in UK.

EBITDA losses expected to shrink this quarter compared to last quarter, and shrink again next quarter; whether this reaches positive territory next quarter still being worked out given Middle East gas price/energy cost impact.
Company hopes to be EBITDA positive during this year, aided by improving prices, ahead of EAF start.
Post-EAF, typical EAF operations run in 6-8% EBITDA margin range; company expects to do better given more value-added product mix.

subsections.label: Netherlands outlook
points: Realisations expected ~€80/t higher in 1Q vs 4Q; coal cost expected up $10/t and iron ore cost up $5/t in 1Q vs 4Q.
Some margin compression expected in Netherlands due to DSP-related production loss (~1.5 months, ~200,000 tons) despite price hikes.

Base case assumption for Netherlands spreads is business-as-usual for next 12 months (FY2027/28), adjusted for CBAM uplift and higher coal prices, with no adjustment for CGP-related scenarios in the base case.
Overall plan for the year on an EBITDA basis is higher than the prior year plan, including for Netherlands.

subsections.label: NINL
points: FID targeted between July and September 2026; once achieved, target date for first steel is around 2029-30.

guidance_ledger.statement: In FY2027 we are aiming to achieve cost transformation related savings of ~Rs 7,100 crores vs. FY2026 levels.
We intend to increase capex in FY2027 to around Rs 20,000 crores of which more than 60% will be spent in India.
In India we expect 1Q to be about Rs. 6,000/t higher than 4Q.
In UK, we expect it to be about £80/t higher in 1Q compared to 4Q.
In Netherlands we expect it to be about €80/t higher in 1Q compared to 4Q.
The delta increase we expect in 1Q for India over 4Q is $15/t.
In Netherlands, the delta coal cost increase is about $10/t.
The iron ore increase in Netherlands is expected to be about $5/t in 1Q over 4Q.
We expect margin expansion in India and in UK, and some margin compression in Netherlands because of the issues that we've had with the DSP.
The volume will be at least 2 million tons better in this financial year compared to the previous financial year with most of it coming in India.
Between July and September, we should be able to get the FID.
Once we get the FID, the target date is somewhere around 2029-30.

Until two months back, we were expecting at least 8-10% growth in steel demand going forward. Now, if we are going to recalibrate the GDP and say that the GDP will grow a bit less, then the steel demand may grow a bit less as well.
We are expecting maybe 30% of the benefit to come in this quarter and 70% of the benefit to come in next quarter.

The EBITDA losses will shrink this quarter compared to last quarter and will shrink again the next quarter; whether the shrink is enough to be positive next quarter is something we are still working out.
We hope to be EBITDA positive during this year, now that the prices have started improving.

Typically good EAFs work in the range of 6 to 8% EBITDA margin, and our assumption is that it is the same, but we have more value added products in the portfolio, so we should be able to get better than that.
Our base assumption for spreads is business as usual for the next 12 months at least... adjusted for a CBAM uplift... and for the coal prices that have also moved up, the spreads are no different.
Overall, the plan this year on an EBITDA basis is higher than the plan for last year and in Netherlands also.
We are increasing that from India from Tata Steel Kalinganagar to about 1.8 million tons - that is our target to increase.
The tubes business, which is now at 1.2 million tons; we want to take it to about 4 million tons.
The wires business... is about 600,000-700,000 tons, and we want to take it to a million tons.
We want to double the India capacity which we've already announced last year.
We plan to double the size of the Colors business also in the next 12-24 months.
We want our downstream businesses to at least be about 50-60% of our volume.
So, we are fairly advanced in that. We'll take a few months and come back and announce it, and then going to ensure that we can execute it quickly.
Hopefully in the next three months or so, we will give you an update about where we are on the land and more specifics about it.
Even with the existing sites between Kalinganagar, Meramandali and Neelachal plus Jamshedpur at 11 million tons, we already have the optionality to grow to 45-50 million tons in India.
Once we start the Maharashtra site... that potentially adds another 6-10 million tons.

themes.label: Deleveraging & balance sheet strength
themes.note: Net Debt/EBITDA improved to 2.3x from 3.3x two years back; continued onshoring of overseas debt to mitigate INR depreciation risk; investment-grade rating maintained.

key_takeaways: Tata Steel delivered a strong performance in FY2026, with improved margins expanding across operating geographies despite subdued pricing and challenges during the year.
India is the key anchor of our growth strategy, with annual crude steel production and deliveries increasing by 8% YoY to around 23 million tons.

Our Consolidated EBITDA increased by 35% YoY from Rs 25,802 crores in the full year ended Mar'25 to Rs 34,848 crores in the full year ended Mar'26. The consolidated EBITDA margin expanded by 320 bps from ~12% to ~15%.
Our full year performance demonstrates the impact of the cost transformation program, which has achieved Rs 10,868 crores of savings across geographies.

UK losses have narrowed by £168 million to -ve £217 million while Netherlands EBITDA almost tripled to €267 million. Combined, UK & Netherlands EBITDA turned positive for the financial year 2025-2026.
We have received the Board approval to merge NINL with Tata Steel Limited subject to necessary approvals and permissions and will be looking to complete the transaction in FY2027.

We have received a letter post the Balance Sheet date from the local environment agencies regarding their intent to revoke permits without any specifics-this causes the material uncertainty element for Tata Steel Netherlands while preparing the basis of preparing the financial statements.

Effective 01st July 2026, the revised safeguard regime proposes a ~60% reduction in import quotas alongside an increase in tariffs from 25% to 50%, with the objective of ensuring that 40-50% of steel demand is met through domestic production.
Work is progressing on the ~3 MTPA scrap based Electric Arc Furnace in the UK... National Grid has formally alerted to us that their connectivity project is delayed.
Our year end Net Debt to EBITDA has reduced to 2.3x compared to 3.3x two years back.
Board has proposed Dividend of Rs 4 per share for fully paid share of face value of Rs 1 each.
pressing_questions: Given so much regulatory uncertainty in the region and constant surprises, is there a case to revisit our entire investment plan in the region?

You mentioned that regarding the coke oven you may buy coke from India or somewhere else. Just trying to understand this because the auditors have flagged the material uncertainty to going concern... can you clarify this and in case we shut down these facilities for 5 years before DRI comes, then what do you do with the labour there?

How do you grandfather regulatory changes, when the regulatory landscape can change later also after you make the investment... in case there is a plan to not go ahead with this investment, does it mean you accelerate India investment, and why not explore global majors for tie ups like some other players are doing?
Given that we only have the EAF coming on stream, will there be any debottlenecking at Jamshedpur which can add to the volumes?

If you look at your annual reports over the last five years, it has been vacillating between 35-40 MTPA of India capacity by FY2030... why can't we have parallel expansions across our projects?... What is stopping us? Why are we being so circumspect about it?

How should we look at normalised spreads for Tata Steel Netherlands, if one had to assign a particular scenario with a higher probability? Likewise for UK, before and after EAF, for both the variables, how is it that one should understand the impact of CBAM?
Given that we are still in the process of getting all the approvals for NINL, what is the earliest estimate of the first steel?

ECLERX.about: EClerx Services Ltd incorporated in 2000, provides business process management, automation and analytics services to a number of Fortune 2000 enterprises, including some of the world's leading financial services, communications, retail, fashion, media & entertainment, manufacturing, travel & leisure and technology companies[1]

quarters.summary: Growth remained resilient in Q1 FY27 with the 12th consecutive quarter of sequential growth and revenue crossing an annualized run-rate of over USD 500m, but margins reset sequentially due to wage increments and mix headwinds; management expects another quarter of sequential growth despite a mixed macro, and remains confident of hitting the full-year EBITDA range of 24-28% (midpoint being the practical expectation), with BFSI expected to inflect positively from H2.

subsections.label: Margin bridge
points: Sequential margin decline was driven mainly by wage increases.
EBITDA compression of 260 bps QoQ primarily from wage increments (210 bps) and computers/network infrastructure costs (40 bps), partly offset by a 60 bps reduction in SB.
Mix headwind: new sites (Cairo, Lima; Manila scaling) run lower gross margin than India; CFO flagged that change in revenue mix will have some downside on margin.

Higher other operating expenses due to communications/network infrastructure and facility build-out; CFO does not expect computing/networking costs to structurally trend down near-term as equipment has become more expensive.
CFO linked capacity expansion (new seats) to higher depreciation and interest this quarter.

subsections.label: Cash flow
points: Cash conversion (OCF/EBITDA) at 38%; CFO cautioned Q1 is seasonally lower because annual variable payouts are paid in this quarter.

subsections.label: Utilization & staffing
points: Utilization at 76.5%, up vs Q4.
Total headcount down 0.6% QoQ, but billed headcount increased due to higher utilization.

subsections.label: Working capital & attrition
points: DSO at 79 days.
Attrition at 21%, flat QoQ.

subsections.label: Margin framework
points: CFO reiterated confidence of meeting the stated full-year EBITDA range of 24-28%, despite near-term pressures.
CFO suggested using the midpoint of the range as a practical expectation, noting higher than that is going to be a little difficult.
