subsections.label: Margin drivers
points: FY26 margins impacted by 580 bps due to significant step-up in renovation expenditure (upgrading owned hotel portfolio), investments in technology, and GST-related change effective during the year (only half-year impact in FY26, full-year impact going forward).

GST impact expected to decrease YoY as number of customers paying rate below Rs. 7,500 keeps reducing with price hikes and ARR growth; all current future supply planned under upper upscale Aurika brand, largely unaffected by GST change.
Expect renovation, tech and GST expense heads together to reduce to ~3.7% of revenue by FY28 and onwards, leading to corresponding EBITDA margin expansion.
Typically renovation spend is 50% OPEX, 50% CAPEX; includes replacement of air conditioning systems, pumps, DG sets etc. for Keys portfolio and older Lemon Tree hotels.
One-off items (ex gratia, Delhi property tax, new Labour Code impact, ~Rs.25-30 crore, ~2% of income) will disappear from P&L from FY27, a permanent saving.
Combined saving expected: ~1% of revenue every year from GST, tech and renovation reduction, plus Rs.25-30 crore permanent saving from one-off removal.

subsections.label: Debt and capital structure
points: Total borrowings reduced to Rs.1,500 crore from Rs.1,699 crore YoY; cost of debt fell to 7.42%, down 115 bps YoY.
Current debt-to-EBITDA is about 2.25x; company describes itself as conservative versus a technically feasible 4x for a high-growth stable-earnings company.
If Rs.1,500 crore of capital deployed for Fleur growth, debt could rise to mid Rs.2,500-3,000 crore consolidated (Fleur), temporarily raising debt-to-EBITDA until new EBITDA flows in.

subsections.label: Standalone Lemon Tree margin trajectory
points: Pro forma Lemon Tree standalone EBITDA margin currently at 60% versus a steady-state flow-through guidance of 70%+, due to increased corporate operating expenses (tech investments, new hiring in operations, marketing, revenue, digital, sales) that have an immediate P&L impact but a lag effect on revenue contribution.
As fee income grows and pro forma normalizes, margin expected to move to 70% and potentially 75-80% steady state as all signed hotels start contributing fee income.
On steady state, EBITDA margin of 75-80% with tax at 22-25% would translate into ~60% PAT margin, since Lemon Tree standalone will have no depreciation or interest.

Current quarter PAT margin is 40% versus 45% in FY25; management explains this via technology/corporate expense investment being treated as an investment to be monetized as fee income grows faster than fixed costs.

subsections.label: Capital allocation
points: Post restructuring, Lemon Tree expected to be a zero-debt, cash accretive company; management/Board to decide on dividend distribution or shareholder give-back policy; Lemon Tree will effectively move into distribution of profit to shareholders.
Fleur is not currently seen as a dividend distributing company; capital will be deployed for growth as it can add more shareholder value by growing the business rather than distribution.

No current plan to invest in F&B (not core competence); would only consider acquiring asset-light platforms at the right value adding to brand/customer/technology portfolio, with a very high hurdle rate given preference for shareholder returns over low-conviction acquisitions.

subsections.label: Signings-to-openings conversion methodology
points: Most management contracts are for hotels under construction, not conversions; best way to estimate openings in a given year is to look at what was signed roughly 3 years prior.

FY26: opened ~1,500-1,600 rooms against having signed under 2,000 rooms about 3 years ago — broadly in the right trajectory; signed 5,000 rooms this year, implying ~5,000 rooms should open roughly 3 years later (with some possible delays but rarely earlier openings, occasionally 6-month or greater slippage if owner runs out of finance).

Management declined to give explicit total management fee guidance for FY27-28, citing risk of being held to a number if slippage occurs; instead pointed to a similar clip of ~2,000 rooms opening in FY27 as last year.

subsections.label: Geographic pipeline expansion
points: Large majority of hotels are currently concentrated in North and West India; expansion opportunity exists in the Southern region, Eastern Coast, Bengal and further east as the company goes deeper into India.

General direction: signing 55+ hotels per year while opening ~25 hotels annually, with openings typically occurring about 3 years after signing; pipeline growth expected to translate into accelerating openings as hotels signed a couple of years ago become operational.

subsections.label: Demand environment and pricing strategy
points: Company shifted strategy in mid-March to focus on occupancy growth rather than price growth given demand-shrinking macro environment (geopolitical tensions, aviation disruptions); adjusted pricing to maintain occupancy premium versus market while broadly maintaining YoY price levels rather than dropping prices aggressively.
Strategy has resulted in occupancy hitting a 'ceiling' this quarter (unprecedented), while average rate growth has been roughly flat; this approach will continue if war-related uncertainty persists.

B2C/direct booking business has grown strongly ('gone through the roof'), while corporate travel has slowed as corporates instruct staff to reduce travel due to rising airfares and war-related concerns; corporate travel dries up quickly in war situations since it is typically a CEO/CXO-level decision.

Retail/non-corporate segment continued growing with the company gaining more market share than last year; occupancy this year is better than the same period last year despite last year's shorter Sindoor conflict versus this year's ongoing war next door.

subsections.label: Long-term growth outlook (openings and fee income)
points: Company signing 5,000 rooms a year currently, expected to accelerate with newly hired top-line business development leadership; addressable market cited as 2.5 million unbranded rooms in India, largely in company's mid-market to upper-mid-scale sweet spot.

If Fleur adds 2,500 planned rooms plus ~800-1,000 rooms under construction, Fleur's operating asset base could increase 60% over the next 3 years, with resulting fees flowing directly to Lemon Tree (barring any hotels going to other brands).

Managed portfolio expected to open ~2,000 rooms in FY27, rising to ~3,000 in FY28 and ~4,000 in FY29 as pipeline signed now converts to openings; newly opened hotels have subdued fee income in first 12-18 months before stabilizing, after which fees can increase 50-60%.
FY23-FY26 fee income CAGR for managed portfolio was 27% per year; management declined to share specific forward fee income projections.

subsections.label: Aurika vs Keys RevPAR divergence
points: RevPAR growth is very subject to micro market; Aurika operates only 2 hotels (Mumbai and Udaipur) while Keys spans many cities (Ludhiana, Visakhapatnam, Bangalore, Trivandrum, Cochin, Pune etc.), so quarterly comparisons are not like-for-like.

In Mumbai micro market, about 5 new hotels opened in the last year (Accor Fairmont, Ginger, ICONIQA, Novotel, Radisson etc.) adding ~2,000 keys, creating a temporary supply glut that Mumbai is expected to absorb over time.

Udaipur is a seasonal wedding market; growth was muted partly due to IndiGo shutdown impact in December spilling into January, and the war impacting discretionary/airport-market demand from mid-March through April.

Full-year RevPAR growth for Aurika was 19% and for Keys was 20%; Keys number reflects only the first 2 fully renovated hotels — this growth rate expected to continue for ~2 more years until entire Keys portfolio renovation is complete and stabilized.

subsections.label: Aurika occupancy/ARR quarter dynamics
points: Aurika Q4 occupancy decline of 2% was due to a large wet lease in Aurika Mumbai going away (a one-off), which was compensated by rate change/segment shift — wet lease was about 8% of occupancy, replaced by about 6% of other demand at better rates.
Q4 performance in Aurika is essentially a March performance; January was reasonably good, February excellent, March saw war-driven air traffic decline creating challenges filling the hotel.
Q4 blended ARR increase of ~5% for Aurika was contributed by both Mumbai (~4%) and Udaipur (~15%), with Udaipur weighting the average slightly higher but not materially so.

Retail pricing in Q4 fluctuated with demand: went down in March (demand drop), up in February, down in first two weeks of January, up in the second two weeks; corporate pricing does not change, but corporate demand itself dropped in March.

subsections.label: Keys renovation and ARR trajectory
points: Two years ago, Keys ARR was ~Rs.3,000-something and Red Fox ARR ~Rs.4,000-something; management target was for Keys to move towards Red Fox's ARR post renovation.

A fully renovated example hotel (100 rooms) now delivers Rs.11 lakhs EBITDA per room; not all Keys hotels will match this, hence conservative target of Rs.60 crore EBITDA (implying <Rs.6 lakhs/room across 930+ rooms).

Keys occupancy in Q4 was 64%, partly because a few hundred rooms were shut for renovation during the year; management aspires for Keys occupancy to reach Red Fox's mid-70s occupancy level, with ARR potentially reaching Rs.5,400-5,500 (not necessarily Rs.6,000) to hit the Rs.60 crore EBITDA target.

subsections.label: Management fee dynamics
points: Third-party management fee growth (23% FY26) driven by both same-store and scale/net addition of hotels in the base; Fleur fee growth (8% FY26) is same-store since no additional rooms were added to that base during the year.

A large part of fees comes from incentive fee (1% to 5% of revenue based on GOP/hotel-level EBITDA slab); aggressive renovation of owned portfolio (including Fleur hotels) combined with GST impact reduced EBITDA margins, which significantly affected incentive fees; incentive fees expected to rise proportionately as EBITDA recovers.

FY23-FY26 CAGR of managed portfolio fee income was 27% per year; expected to grow faster as base scales, though fee income growth for newly opened hotels is subdued in first 12-18 months before stabilizing (fees can increase 50-60% once a hotel stabilizes).

subsections.label: Negotiated vs retail room-night mix
points: Negotiated (corporate) room nights typically carry lower rates than non-negotiated (retail); in March, corporate business dropped sharply, prompting the company to build occupancy through retail bookings at slightly lower rates.
Full-year negotiated ratio change (55.4% vs 56.1%, -50bps) is not material; the shift is largely driven by Q3/Q4 dynamics when corporate demand dropped and retail demand was pursued to compensate.

Long-term strategy is to reduce dependence on concentrated corporate demand and build distributed retail (C2B) demand; target is 65% retail/direct business as portfolio scales to 20,000-25,000 operating rooms, sourced through OTAs, website, loyalty program, and direct-to-hotel/call centre channels.

subsections.label: Loyalty program
points: Loyalty program was rehashed a couple of years ago; currently has about 24 lakh guests, driving ~48-50% of annual room nights, with first-time loyalty sign-ups contributing 25% of annual room night volume — benchmarks considered solid versus international chains.

Technology investment to date has focused on operational seamlessness (revenue management system, market tool, sales force automation); next phase will focus on legacy PMS system transformation, website/booking engine and loyalty engine over the next couple of years to drive more direct/retail business.

subsections.label: Demerger structure
points: Warburg Pincus has completed purchase of APG's stake in Fleur.
Lemon Tree will transfer 17 hotels and development capabilities to Fleur in exchange for which Lemon Tree shareholders will receive Fleur shares, leading to Fleur's separate listing.

Scheme will result in 2 distinct financially sound businesses: Lemon Tree Hotels as pure-play asset-light company (hotel management, brand, loyalty, distribution, digital services) and Fleur Hotels as a large-scale growth-oriented ownership/leasing platform with in-house development capabilities.
Each entity will have its own management team, capital structure and growth priorities while continuing long-term operating agreements and strategic alignment.

Post reorganization, Lemon Tree will emerge debt-free, high-margin, high ROCE, generating strong free cash flow from fees and brand-related income; Fleur will consolidate ownership of the group's existing hotels, all fully renovated by demerger time.

Post-scheme, Lemon Tree shareholders will effectively own ~74% of Fleur (33% direct + 41% indirect through Lemon Tree), versus 59% Lemon Tree currently owns directly in Fleur — before any Warburg primary infusion.

Post scheme, long-term management contracts give Lemon Tree stable/growing fee income from Fleur; Fleur can underwrite new opportunities with certainty/speed with Lemon Tree as management partner, while retaining strategic flexibility for other brands where warranted.

Patanjali Keswani continues to chair both companies with direct ownership in each; primary focus will be Fleur pipeline/growth as Executive Chair; will cease executive role in Lemon Tree from March 2027, transitioning to non-Executive Chair.

subsections.label: Demerger approval timeline
points: CCI approval received in April; company is currently at the stage of shareholder and SEBI approval, which is the normal process before NCLT filing.
Only about 1 month of delay from earlier estimate; typically takes 3 months for stock exchange process; this is a somewhat conservative estimate given procedural steps.

Key uncertainty is NCLT timeline (first motion order, second motion, shareholder and creditor approvals in between) — could take 6, 9 or 12 months; outer limit given is 18 months from now if it takes longer, or 12 months if resolved earlier; management does not expect completion to slip to end of CY27.

subsections.label: Fleur brand-agnostic operating model
points: When Warburg invested, they checked the quality/economics of Lemon Tree's management contracts versus peers and were satisfied with alignment.

If a new Fleur asset makes more sense for another brand to operate, that will be allowed to happen; but given the long Fleur-Lemon Tree relationship and Lemon Tree's mid-market/upscale delivery record, Lemon Tree will also be considered — approach is brand-agnostic with the caveat that Lemon Tree should not be discriminated against.

Example cited: company bid via NCLT for a 5-star hotel run successfully by another international brand; lost the bid to an ultra-high-net-worth individual outbidding them, but had they won, they would have retained the existing operator's management contract.

subsections.label: Fleur pipeline and investment strategy
points: Fleur to become India's largest hotel platform by inventory post-scheme (5,600 rooms, 39 operational hotels); operates pan-India but economics concentrated in top 6 cities with structurally high barriers to entry and growing demand.
Design finalized for Aurika, Nehru Place (North India's largest hotel, 572 rooms), currently under final approval stage before construction commencement.
Plan to open 2 of 3 blocks of Aurika Naldehra, Shimla by Q2 to capture increased summer demand.

Signed a license deal in January 2026 for a 47-room heritage Aurika Hotel at Varanasi, located on the ghat adjoining the River Ganges, with potential for very high rates due to strategic location and deep year-round Varanasi market demand.
Aurika is described as the highest ARR and margin product; growing Aurika portfolio elevates the group's overall profile, improves financial metrics, and strengthens the brand network.

Combined with Warburg Pincus primary investment commitment and strong internal accruals, Fleur now has capital structure and institutional backing to expand top line; focus areas are urban markets with structurally deep demand, leisure markets, and international destinations frequently visited by Indian travellers.

Fleur evaluates a healthy and growing number of opportunities across deal types (acquiring existing assets or developing new hotels); Fleur's peer-leading margins and in-house development capabilities compress time/risk in underwriting new opportunities; disciplined on returns though flexible on deal structure.

2,500 additional rooms target under various stages of discussion; investment focus on upscale/upper upscale (Aurika and Lemon Tree Premier) concentrated in top 6 cities, plus selective international destinations Indians travel to and very selective leisure markets; considering greenfield, operating-hotel acquisitions, and brownfield assets.

Acquisition valuations currently range from 8x to 16x EBITDA (higher for trophy assets, which company is not interested in); for acquired operating assets, main additional investment would be renovation (adjusted into acquisition price); self-built greenfield is cheaper but takes longer to market.

Timeline for 2,500 rooms is not expected to be 5-6 years: immediate for acquisitions, 1-2 years for acquisitions needing renovation, ~4 years for greenfield (company typically builds hotels in 3-4 years absent force majeure).
When investing own money in greenfield, focus is more on Lemon Tree Premier and Aurika brands; may also selectively acquire mid-market hotels that make sense in their micro market.

subsections.label: Geopolitical and macro headwinds
points: FY26 impacted by intermittent global headwinds including renewed geopolitical tensions in the Middle East, aviation disruptions (IndiGo shutdown in December spilling into January) and GST changes during the year.

War-related uncertainty (described as the U.S. war against Iran) started affecting the business marginally in early March, became very significant by mid-March, and continued into April; May was surprisingly good.

Corporate travel is the first segment to dry up during war/uncertainty periods since it is typically a single CEO/CXO decision; example cited of a large company (100,000 employees, ~100,000 room nights/year) instructing maximum travel reduction due to rising airfares and war concerns.

Prolonged uncertainty/volatility is a bigger macro concern than the war itself — oil prices, inflation, and current account deficit could adversely affect the Indian economy if the situation persists without conclusion.

Fortunately, war impact was largely confined to March and April; if the situation does not deteriorate further, company expects to perform reasonably well; if resolved, expects to perform even better.

subsections.label: Cost pressures
points: Margins adversely affected by hard calls taken to do catch-up renovation; shocks this year included renovation catch-up, ex gratia payments, Labour Code impact and GST impact, which affected the company to a significant level.
Company's cost structure, considered its 'moat', has been affected and management's current focus is on bringing costs under control and restoring EBITDA margins to earlier levels.

subsections.label: Micro-market supply risk
points: Aurika Mumbai affected by a temporary supply glut as ~5 new hotels (including Accor Fairmont, Ginger, ICONIQA, Novotel, Radisson) opened in the same micro-market adding ~2,000 keys; Mumbai is expected to absorb this supply glut over time.

Aggressive competitor moves to capture domestic demand cited as a potential risk if peers get more aggressive throughout FY27, though management notes its B2C/retail business has grown strongly even as corporate travel slowed.

subsections.label: Demerger execution risk
points: NCLT approval timeline is uncertain and could range from 6 to 18 months, creating timeline risk for demerger completion; process involves multiple procedural steps (first motion order, second motion, shareholder and creditor approvals) beyond company's control.

subsections.label: Cost and margin outlook
points: Management declined to give explicit financial guidance for total management fees FY27-28 or a 5-year CAGR target, citing risk if actuals slip from stated numbers; instead offered directional commentary (signing pace, opening pace, fee growth trends).

Renovation spend is expected to normalize to management's stated normal range of 1.2-1.4% of revenue once the current portfolio-wide renovation catch-up (which is 85% complete on ~4,000 rooms needing heavy renovation) is finished; possibly even lower at ~1.0-1.1%.

Combined GST + tech + renovation expense reduction of ~1% of revenue per year expected, plus a Rs.25-30 crore permanent saving from disappearance of one-off costs (ex gratia, property tax, Labour Code impact) starting FY27.

subsections.label: Fleur growth outlook
points: Fleur targets adding 2,500 rooms over the next 2-3 years via a mix of greenfield, acquisitions of operating assets, and brownfield development, backed by Warburg Pincus capital and internal accruals.
Combined with Nehru Place and other committed capital, company has potential to deploy up to Rs.3,000 crore over the next 12-18 months, contingent on deal availability.

key_takeaways: FY26 was the best year in Lemon Tree's history across Occupancy, ARR, Revenue, EBITDA, PBT, PAT and Cash Profit; Q4 FY26 was the best ever fourth quarter on the same parameters.
For the full year FY26, total revenue stood at Rs. 1,452.7 crore, up 13% YoY; Net EBITDA stood at Rs. 699.3 crore, up 10%; PAT grew 19% to Rs. 288.3 crore; Cash Profit grew 16% to Rs. 443.1 crore.
Net EBITDA margins for FY26 was 48.1% compared to 49.4% in FY25, a contraction of about 126 bps, impacted by 580 bps due to renovation expenditure, technology investments and GST-related change.
Total borrowings brought down to Rs. 1,500 crore from Rs. 1,699 crore versus a year ago; cost of debt fallen to 7.42%, down 115 basis points versus a year ago.
Combined operational and signed pipeline inventory stands at 22,581 rooms across 268 hotels, of which 131 hotels and 11,811 rooms are already operational.
Post-scheme, Fleur will be India's largest hotel platform by inventory with 5,600 rooms and 39 operational hotels; Lemon Tree shareholders will effectively own close to 74% of Fleur Hotels.
CCI approval for the demerger came in April; company is at the stage of shareholder and SEBI approval; NCLT timeline could range from 12 to 18 months from now.

Post reorganization, Lemon Tree will emerge as a debt-free, high-margin, high ROCE company generating strong free cash flows from fees and brand-related income; steady-state PAT margin targeted at ~60%.
pressing_questions: Given the macro environment, especially with both largest domestic carriers announcing capacity cuts for the next 3 months, how should one think about the occupancy and RevPAR growth environment for the next 2-3 months and full year FY27, especially given most capacity reduction is on metro-to-metro routes?

On signings-to-openings conversion, while 55 hotels were signed during FY26, openings stood at just 20 hotels with only 1 hotel opened in Q4 — how confident is management about FY27/FY28 openings of ~4,500 Keys, and what should total management fee look like for FY27/FY28 if this is on track?
What is the new timeline for the Fleur demerger given the earlier 12-month estimate versus the slide's mention of 12-15 months for SEBI and other approvals?

On the pro forma Lemon Tree standalone entity showing 60% margins, why are margins at the lower end versus an expected ~70% range given the asset-light portfolio, and where could this margin trajectory go?
Have we set aside any total CAPEX or capital outlay specifically for the proposed addition of 2,500 Keys across Fleur, and with or without it, what peak debt number is the company comfortable with?
For the next 5 years, what CAGR growth does management foresee for Lemon Tree as the asset-light platform owner, given the freed-up capital and opportunity?

REGAAL.about: regaal Resources Limited (RRL) is a leading agro-processing company in India, specialising in the manufacturing of maize starch, speciality starches, food-grade starches, and starch derivative products.

quarters.summary: Q1 FY27 marked an inflection point: major capacity commissioning (crushing doubled to 1650 MTPD, new liquid glucose and Maltodextrin facilities, cogen power expansion) was completed during the quarter, and the company is now transitioning into a ramp-up/utilization phase. Management guided full-year FY27 crushing volume of at least ~4 lakh tons, value-added mix rising to 20-22% of turnover, expects utilization and EBITDA per ton to improve progressively from Q2 FY27, but refrained from giving specific EBITDA-per-ton, margin, or export-mix guidance citing raw-material/finished-product price volatility outside its control; peak debt is expected in H1 with deleveraging in H2 as working capital normalizes.

subsections.label: Profitability drivers
points: Value-added growth of 30.3% YoY and margin expansion to 39.8% (from 25.1%, +1477 bps) driven by a decisive shift towards higher margin, manufacturing-led revenue.
Operating income declined 18% YoY on account of a deliberate reduction in low-margin trading activity; trading contribution fell from 19.5% to 3.3% of revenue.
Improvement in value-added flowed through to Operating EBITDA (up 26.6% YoY to Rs.30.98 crores, margin 15.3%, +540 bps) and PAT (up 47% YoY to Rs.13.33 crores, margin 6.6%, +291 bps).

Management attributed the 47% YoY PAT jump majorly to operating leverage rather than raw material cost movement, noting last year's trading activity was ~19% of Q1 turnover versus 3% this year, and trading margins are much lower than manufacturing margins.
EBITDA per ton was Rs.4,450 in Q1 FY27, versus Rs.4,742 in FY26 and ~Rs.3,100 in FY23 (historical reference).
Interest cost this quarter was 7.9%.

subsections.label: Working capital / balance sheet
points: Cash conversion cycle of 130 days (analyst referenced inventory days of 208) driven largely by higher inventory levels built to support the expanded 1650 MTPD capacity.

Incremental capacity was commissioned only late in the quarter, so revenue contribution had not yet fully flowed through, leaving inventory elevated relative to current revenue base; inventory days expected to normalize progressively as utilization ramps up.

Inventory days are seasonally higher in Q1 and Q2 due to advance maize procurement; this seasonal effect is more pronounced this year given significantly higher crushing capacity and larger expected volumes.
Net debt of Rs.735.32 crores reflects funding of the expansion program plus seasonal raw material procurement.
All debt raised for the new capex qualifies for interest subvention under Bihar's Industrial Investment Promotion Policy, containing effective cost of borrowing.
Major phase of the capex cycle substantially behind the company as of quarter-end (~Rs.552 crores incurred of ~Rs.664 crores total outlay as of 30 June 2026).
Company expects free cash flow generation to strengthen as expanded capacity ramps up, enabling greater reliance on internal accruals and progressive deleveraging.

Peak debt for the year is already being reached in H1 due to working capital build (inventory); debt expected to reduce in H2 as working capital normalizes — historical pattern shows working capital debt coming down to ~40% of peak by Q4 (e.g. Rs.100cr peak -> Rs.40cr).
Net interest cost guided at Rs.39-40 crores for FY27.

subsections.label: Interest subvention clarification
points: Company draws multiple different loans for different projects/capacities, each eligible for subvention.

Old regime capped subvention at Rs.20 crore per project (applicable to the 825-ton liquid glucose/MDP project registered in 2024); amended policy (passed ~Nov-Dec FY25) raises cap to Rs.40 crore, including for earlier-approved projects whose production had not yet started, but final government clearance is still awaited, so it has not been reflected in the presentation.

subsections.label: Value-added product portfolio expansion
points: Plans during FY27 to enter high-value derivatives including Dextrose Anhydrous, Dextrose Monohydrate and Hydrol, while expanding beyond existing Dextrin and edible starch range into specialized modified starches such as cationic starch, carboxymethyl starch, pre-gel starch and spray starch.
Maize-to-starch conversion (value addition) rate has become better in Q1 FY27 compared to Q4 FY26.

Different value-added products carry different value addition: some have up to 100% value addition, others 35%-40%, on a mixed basis; maltodextrin powder has higher margin and higher value addition but lower volume (50 tons) versus liquid glucose (180-200 tons).

Modified starch products target specific end-use segments: cationic starch and carboxymethyl/oxidized starch for paper mills (existing customers), pre-gel starch for food industry and also usage in batteries (new area), carboxymethyl starch for oil drilling (small volume ~20-30 tons of total 1,000-1,100 ton capacity).
Value-added product share of turnover was ~3% in FY26, expected to reach 20-22% in FY27, with capacity build-out targeting an eventual 50:50 split between starch and value-added capacity.

subsections.label: Go-to-market strategy for value-added add-ons
points: About 80-90% of new value-added products will go into current channel (existing dealers and institutions) — e.g., cationic starch will be supplied to existing paper mill customers.
Remaining 20-30% requires new customer development, which management does not view as difficult given the strong existing base.
For liquid glucose, company has acquired big MNC customers (India's biggest MNCs) and is now billing them directly.

White labelling base has increased — new customers added under the 'India White' brand, and existing customers have increased their off-take; both cross-selling from existing customers and new customer additions are occurring.

subsections.label: Co-products
points: Management has not significantly explored turning co-products into high-value-added products such as animal feed; noted a small possibility of a feed plant but this is a completely different business line not yet explored for margin/value-addition potential.

subsections.label: Workforce
points: Current employee count stands at 719.

subsections.label: Capacity commissioning
points: Centerpiece of the quarter was commissioning on 26 May 2026 of doubled crushing capacity (825 to 1650 MTPD), alongside new liquid glucose facility (180 TPD), Maltodextrin powder facility (50 MTPD), and cogeneration power plant expansion (7.1 MW to 15.8 MW).

These investments established Regaal as the largest maize wet milling facility in eastern India, strengthening ability to capture value across the maize processing chain and broadening product portfolio.
Expanded plant actually started operations around 1st/2nd June 2026 (commissioning recorded 26 May).

subsections.label: Utilization ramp-up
points: Capacity utilization of 71.4% for the quarter (maize crushing volume of 69,689 metric tons vs 64,770 in Q1 FY26, an incremental 5,500 tons / 8%) should be viewed in context of commissioning and integration of doubled capacity; planned shutdown days during the quarter temporarily lowered utilization.

With major commissioning and integration now complete, utilization expected to improve progressively from Q2 FY27 as incremental volumes contribute more meaningfully to revenue; Q2 FY27 crushing guided at 100,000-110,000 tons.
9 days of shutdown for integration of both plants during April and May resulted in a loss of ~7,200 tons (9 days x ~800 tons/day).

Management hopeful of reaching maximum utilization within FY27, based on past experience of achieving good utilization after expansions; target capacity utilization of 90-95%, with expected utilization for the 1,650 MT capacity at 75-80% over the next 3 quarters.
FY26 full-year crushing was ~2,65,000 metric tons; FY27 expected crushing is >4,00,000 metric tons.

subsections.label: Value-added product ramp-up
points: Entire incremental Q1 volume (5,500 tons) went into liquid glucose and a small part of maltodextrin powder production.
Liquid glucose has reached ~70% of capacity utilization and is on an increasing trend.

Maltodextrin powder ramp-up slower as samples need approval from various customers/MNCs; existing customers being catered to while new customer development is ongoing; expected to reach target level in 2-3 months.
Modified starch basket (cationic, carboxymethyl, pre-gel, spray starch) trials have started and expected to be completely online within September 2026.
Dextrose products (Dextrose Anhydrous, Dextrose Monohydrate, Hydrol) expected to see 'light of day' by Q4 (before March).

subsections.label: Infrastructure build-out
points: Building supporting infrastructure for growth: additional 50,000 tons of storage across two new silos, a 50,000 sq ft maize godown, and a 1.6 MW methane gas-based power plant.

subsections.label: Future capacity expansion stance
points: Management stated it is too early to talk about another expansion; company is focused on stabilizing the current expansion at this point; team has met with ministers in Karnataka regarding some capacity but no near-term plans confirmed.

CAPEX plans for FY27 focused on stabilization — reaching 90-95% capacity utilization, marketing value-added basket at good prices, improving results, decreasing debt — before considering further expansion.

subsections.label: Export expansion
points: Export contribution more than doubled to 10.4% in Q1 FY27 from 4.9% in Q1 FY26 (also cited in Q&A as up from 5% to 10%), reflecting growing acceptance of products across international markets.
Company is opening new markets across South and West to sell products domestically, and pursuing new export geographies internationally.
Team has visited new export opportunities; company will attend trade fairs scheduled in September, with CMD attending personally.
Management could not commit to a specific export target/guidance but expects export share to increase further given expanded capacity; growth will depend on securing orders and ability to supply.
Indian maize prices are low compared to Ukraine and USA prices; per industry association calculations, at maize price of Rs.24-25, Indian starch exports remain very competitive.

subsections.label: Raw material sourcing geography
points: Historically (till FY26) company procured 90-95% of inventory during Rabi season (April-July); FY27 sourcing is ~80% Rabi season, with 10-15% sourced from other states (Maharashtra, MP, Karnataka) where maize is abundant.
Bihar also grows a smaller Rabi/Kharif crop (~6 lakh tons) in certain pockets not explored in the past 6-7 years; company now exploring buying 5-10% of requirement from Bihar Kharif districts.

Bihar and Karnataka maize is considered the best crop in the country due to smaller grain size (280-290 grams/100 grains vs 350-400 grams in other states), giving higher recovery of finished product and better quality.

Company procures a large portion of requirement directly from farmers at no logistics cost (FOR/freight included), and because Bihar lacks large inherent maize consumption, maize is otherwise exported to other states/companies — giving Regaal a cost advantage.

subsections.label: Strategic focus post-expansion
points: With the major investment cycle substantially behind it, company's attention is on translating enhanced capacity into higher utilization, richer product mix, stronger capital position and sustainable long-term value for stakeholders.
Company is exploring new geographies (South and West India, and new export markets) to build a more geographically diverse revenue base.
Team has met with ministers in Karnataka regarding potential future capacity, though management stated it is too early to discuss another expansion and is focused on stabilizing the current one.
Value-added products going into the existing channel are estimated at 80-90% (alternately cited as 70-80%), with the remaining 20-30% requiring new channel development.

subsections.label: Raw material / commodity price risk
points: EBITDA per ton and EBITDA margin are heavily influenced by market prices of maize (raw material) and finished starch product, which are not in the company's control; management refrained from giving specific per-ton or margin guidance for this reason.

Business is described as a 'whole number trade' — if maize prices go up, starch prices go up correspondingly, and profit/EBITDA tends to stay largely level rather than moving proportionally in percentage terms.

Maize prices have risen from ~Rs.20 (previous concall reference) to ~Rs.24 (per analyst reference; Rs.22.5-23 at company doorstep), nearing last year's peak of Rs.26-27 in the same period, but management does not see prices going very high given a seasonal pattern where Bihar maize prices rise in September and soften in October, a pattern repeated in prior years.

Company is holding substantial stock for the year, so a price rise is not seen as a major concern; if maize prices rise, starch prices should also rise, putting the company in a better position this year.

Competitive dynamics: Gujarat Ambuja and Sanstar are also adding specialty starch capacity; management states it has never faced a challenge selling its expanded output (180 to 825 tons) and is countering competitive pressure by increasing export base (5% to 10%) and entering new domestic markets.

subsections.label: Volume and utilization outlook
points: Management expects utilization to progressively improve from Q2 FY27 onward as incremental volumes contribute more meaningfully to revenue; Q2 FY27 crushing guided at 100,000-110,000 tons.
Full-year FY27 crushing guided conservatively at 'more than 4 lakh tons' as a minimum target which management hopes to achieve, versus 2.65 lakh tons in FY26.
Hopeful of reaching maximum utilization within FY27 based on past experience post-expansion, with target capacity utilization of 90-95%.

subsections.label: Margin and per-ton EBITDA guidance withheld
points: Management declined to give specific EBITDA-per-ton or EBITDA margin guidance for FY27, citing that raw material and finished product prices are not controllable variables, and margin depends on a combination of price, value-add mix, and operating leverage.
Guided that value-add and operating leverage should drive relative improvement in EBITDA per ton, assuming current prices remain constant.
On a like-for-like price basis, the company expects to perform better than before due to operating leverage and value-add, though no firm number was given.

Blended EBITDA margin guidance also withheld for similar reasons — margin depends on maize/finished product prices (not controllable), extent of value addition (controllable, increasing), and scale (controllable, increasing).

subsections.label: Export and value-added mix outlook
points: No specific export revenue target given, though management is hopeful export share will increase given expanded capacity, new markets, and trade fair participation.

Value-added product mix guided at 20-22% of turnover for FY27, with capacity built out for a 50:50 starch:value-add split eventually, and turnover-based value-add guided informally at 30-35% at higher scale (per Sanjeev Sancheti's comment), though CMD declined to commit to a firm percentage for FY27, citing this year's difficulty to gauge; a rough directional expectation of ~20% for the current year was acknowledged as 'likely' (previous guidance had referenced 25%).

subsections.label: Debt / leverage outlook
points: Peak debt for FY27 already being reached in H1 due to seasonal working capital (inventory) build; debt expected to decline in H2 as working capital normalizes, following historical pattern of working capital debt reducing to ~40% of peak by Q4.
Company expects free cash flow generation to strengthen as expanded capacity ramps up, transitioning from a CAPEX-led phase to a phase of cash generation and deleveraging.
Net interest cost guided at Rs.39-40 crores for FY27.

subsections.label: CAPEX outlook
points: No major new CAPEX plans for FY27; management wants to stabilize and consolidate the recent expansion, achieve 90-95% capacity utilization, market the value-added basket at good prices, improve results and decrease debt before considering any further expansion plans (including any potential Karnataka capacity, on which ministers were met but no firm plan exists).

key_takeaways: Q1 FY27 marks an important inflection point in Regaal's growth journey - completed a major phase of capacity commissioning and entered a phase focused on ramping up utilization, scaling volumes and capturing greater value from expanded manufacturing capabilities.

Commissioning on 26 May 2026 of a doubling of crushing capacity from 825 MTPD to 1650 MTPD alongside a new liquid glucose facility of 180 TPD, a Maltodextrin powder facility of 50 MTPD, and expansion of captive cogeneration power plant from 7.1 MW to 15.8 MW - together establishing Regaal as the largest maize wet milling facility in eastern India.

Operating income for the quarter stood at Rs. 202 crores/202.15 crores, lower by 18% YoY on account of a deliberate reduction in low-margin trading activity (trading contribution fell to 3.3% from 19.5%).
Value-added grew 30.3% YoY to Rs. 80.53 crores, with value-added margin expanding to 39.8% from 25.1% in Q1 FY26, driven by a decisive shift towards higher margin, manufacturing-led revenue.
Operating EBITDA rose 26.6% YoY to Rs. 30.98 crores with EBITDA margin expanding 540 bps to 15.3%; PAT grew 47% YoY to Rs. 13.33 crores with PAT margin improving 291 bps to 6.6%.
Contribution from exports more than doubled to 10.4% in Q1 FY27 from 4.9% in Q1 FY26, reflecting growing acceptance of products across international markets.

During FY27, plans to enter high value derivatives including Dextrose Anhydrous, Dextrose Monohydrate and Hydrol, while expanding into specialized modified starches such as cationic starch, carboxymethyl starch, pre-gel starch and spray starch.

Net debt stood at Rs. 735.32 crores; of total project outlay of approximately Rs. 664 crores, around Rs. 552 crores had been incurred as of 30 June 2026, with the major phase of the CAPEX cycle now substantially behind the company.
Management declined to give specific EBITDA-per-ton or EBITDA-margin guidance, citing raw material and finished product price volatility as an uncontrollable variable.

quarters.summary: Regaal Resources closed FY26 with strong revenue and profitability growth and commissioned a major brownfield capacity expansion (crushing capacity to 1,650 TPD, plus new liquid glucose, maltodextrin and power capacity) on May 26, 2026, at a revised capex outlay of ~INR540 crores (up from ~INR430 crores). Management explicitly declined to give FY27 guidance, stating it will wait for a quarter of stabilized operations post-commissioning and provide a comprehensive earnings outlook by end of H1 FY27; value-added product mix is expected to rise from ~2-3% in FY26 to 20-25% in FY27 and to ~35% at peak/full capacity utilization.

subsections.label: Margin drivers
points: The improvement in the operating EBITDA margin during FY26 reflects better realizations.

Margin expansion during the year was partly offset by higher freight and forwarding costs within other expenses, along with relatively higher shutdown days during March '26, which impacted crushing volumes and operating leverage during the period.

Q4 EBITDA on an absolute basis appeared lower quarter-on-quarter per an analyst's calculation, but management clarified operating EBITDA margin rose from 10.7% to 13.3% versus the analyst-cited comparison, attributing the change to costs ramped up ahead of expansion commissioning rather than underlying deterioration.
Management expects steady-state margins to be visible from the second or third quarter of FY27 as the ramp-up costs normalize.

subsections.label: Balance sheet / working capital
points: Cash conversion cycle improved to 50 days in FY26 from 93 days in FY25, driven by tighter working capital management, supported by lower inventory and receivable days.
Working capital requirement follows a sine-graph pattern: it increases in Q1, peaks around Q2, and steadily falls from Q3 to Q4; cash conversion cycle is expected to range between 50 and 75 days.

Other current assets rose from INR56 crores to INR170 crores mainly due to advances given at year-end (March) to new maize suppliers and warehouses to ensure smooth raw material flow ahead of the capacity ramp-up to 1,650 TPD commissioned in May.
Advances increased from about INR45 crores to around INR150 crores for this reason.

subsections.label: Capital allocation
points: Capex outlay revised upward from approximately INR430 crores to approximately INR540 crores due to an expanded value-added products pipeline and a larger captive co-generation plant capacity.
Of the total INR540 crores capex, approximately INR401 crores had already been spent by March 31, 2026; the balance of INR140 crores is expected to be spent in FY27.
Net debt stood at INR545.65 crores; with incremental capex during FY27, total debt (including working capital/CC) is expected to be around INR700-750 crores.
Board recommended a dividend of INR0.25 per share, subject to shareholder approval.

subsections.label: Product portfolio
points: Regaal operates an integrated maize wet milling facility with a diversified product portfolio spanning three broad categories: native maize starch, edible starch, and modified starch (white dextrin, yellow dextrin, oxidized starches).
Also manufactures value-added consumer products such as maize flour, custard powder, baking powder and icing sugar.

Wet milling process generates commercially valuable co-products: maize germ, maize gluten, maize fiber, maize steep liquor, and enriched fiber, catering to animal nutrition and food production industries.
New value-added products being added: dextrose anhydrous (DAH), dextrose monohydrate (DMH), hydrol, cationic starch, carboxymethyl starch, pre-gel starch, gulal (white-labelled), and spray starch.
DAH and DMH (constituting another ~50% increase in output) have already commissioned 230 tons; further DAH/DMH capacity expected between Q3 and Q4 (around December-January), exact date not confirmed.

subsections.label: Value-added mix ramp-up
points: Value-added product share was hardly present in FY26 (2-3%); it is being ramped up via the current capacity expansion and is expected to reach 20-25% in FY27 and approximately 35% at peak/full-year run-rate.

Most of the incremental capacity from the expansion (from ~800+ TPD to 1,600+ TPD) is being directed into value-added products rather than native starch, so the delta in native starch output will not be very high; most of the delta is in value-added products.

Management could not immediately provide a capex split (native/by-products vs value-added) but indicated a good portion of the capex has gone into value-added products, and offered to follow up separately.
Expected price premium (delta) of value-added products over starch prices is approximately 20-25%, with a firmer guidance to be given in H1.

subsections.label: White-labelling
points: White-labelling strategy started with one company and has now expanded to four companies (names undisclosed); volumes have been increasing and this is expected to increase considerably within H1.
White-labelling previously accounted for about 2-2.5% of starch quantity (approx. 6,500 units).

subsections.label: Expansion commissioning
points: On May 26, 2026, the company commissioned a significant expansion of manufacturing infrastructure, scaling crushing capacity to 1,650 TPD via addition of new derivative manufacturing facilities: liquid glucose at 180 TPD and maltodextrin powder at 50 TPD.
Simultaneously, the captive co-generation power plant was expanded by 10 MW, taking total power capacity to 15.8 MW, strengthening energy self-sufficiency.
At 1,650 TPD, Regaal now operates as the largest maize milling facility in Eastern India.
Commissioning of all facilities envisaged under the expanded capex plan (DAH, DMH, Hydrol, modified starches, etc.) is expected over the course of FY27.
The power plant is fully operational; of the new 10MW capacity, 5MW is currently being drawn as required.
Ramp-up of new production lines depends on machine-to-machine commissioning; management expects ramp-up to take no more than 15-20 days (weeks, not months) barring issues.
As is customary with large-scale commissioning, the facility will progressively ramp up to optimal operating levels over the coming weeks.
The expansion is a brownfield expansion (not greenfield), so overhead costs will not double even as capacity doubles, allowing economies of scale to benefit margins.

subsections.label: Infrastructure moat
points: 65,000 MT of maize storage capacity is spread across four humidity-controlled silos and raw material godowns, ensuring supply security through harvest and non-harvest seasons.
Facility is spread over 55 acres, with abundant land available to support future expansions.
Company is largely self-reliant on power, with approximately 81% of FY26 electricity requirement sourced from the captive co-generation plant.
Regaal is one of the few maize wet milling facilities in India to operate a zero liquid discharge unit.
Recognized as a One Star Export House by the Director General of Foreign Trade, Ministry of Commerce and Industry.

subsections.label: Employment impact
points: The expansion project is expected to create 475 additional direct employment opportunities, taking total on-role workforce to approximately 950 employees.

The expansion is also expected to generate significant indirect opportunities across contractual labor, logistics, warehousing, transportation, procurement, allied services, and the broader agriculture value chain, and to support farmer livelihoods and the rural economy.

subsections.label: Location advantage
points: Manufacturing facility located in Kishanganj, Bihar, one of India's top three maize cultivating states, contributing approximately 11.6% to India's total maize production.

Location provides direct access to high-quality raw material at competitive prices, proximity to Dalkhola Mandi and Gulabbagh Mandi (among India's largest maize markets), and a natural gateway to South Asian export markets, being close to Nepal and Bangladesh borders.
Export reach extends further across South Asia, enabling international customers to be served at competitive freight costs.

subsections.label: Distribution network
points: As of March 2026, the company had 345 customers, of which 134 were onboarded during the year.
Dealer channel accounts for 65.5% of annual revenue, reflecting the strength and depth of the distribution network.

subsections.label: International expansion
points: Company continues to build its international footprint with a particular focus on South-East Asian markets, where it sees significant long-term potential for maize-based derivatives.
Recent softening in raw material prices has meaningfully improved global cost competitiveness, enabling more effective engagement with international customers on more compelling terms.
During the period, the company secured a sizeable export order, strengthening near-term export revenue visibility and reinforcing its credentials as a reliable supplier internationally.
Starch prices have also started looking up due to the reopening of export markets.

subsections.label: Procurement strategy
points: Three-pronged procurement strategy: (1) direct purchase from farmers during Rabi season (April-July main season, with spillover in August-September); (2) 27 Farmer Procurement Centers (FPCs) across six-seven districts (20-100 km around the plant) where farmers deliver material, transported to the plant; (3) a small amount purchased from traders across different states as needed.

Company has warehouse agreements ranging from 500 meters to 80 km around the factory, holding about 240,000 tonnes of material, combined with 65,000 tonnes of own storage and four months of direct Rabi season procurement, together covering about 90% of annual requirement; the balance 10-15% is sourced across all 12 months from other states.

Trading revenue (previously 30%+ of revenue) is expected to come down considerably, near to zero, with the new capacity, as the company will not have surplus maize to trade; residual trading may occur only to capture size/MOQ discounts on raw material procurement, not for revenue generation.
Raw material availability in Bihar has never been a problem; Bihar is a net exporter of maize to other states.

subsections.label: Pricing environment
points: Maize prices have come down considerably compared to last year, which management views as beneficial for the entire industry.
Last year maize prices hovered between INR18 and INR23-24, with an INR4-5 spread of movement within the market.

Delta change in this year's procurement price vs last year is expected to be about 10% lower, translating to roughly INR1.5-2.5 (ballpark INR2) lower, though Bihar's crop has not yet fully come in (farmer deliveries began around May 15-16 due to rain delays).

Government's growing thrust on ethanol blending and maize demand, along with the government sitting on large stocks of broken rice being allocated to plants, creates uncertainty on whether maize prices will rise or fall going forward, though finished product pricing is expected to improve accordingly.

There is a significant realization delta between Q4 and Q1 for co-products (germ, gluten, fiber); starch prices have also started looking up due to the reopening of export markets, and value addition from maize to starch is higher than last year.

subsections.label: Competitive positioning
points: Growing demand for maize derivatives, coupled with strategic location, integrated infrastructure and strong sourcing capabilities, positions Regaal well to create sustainable value for stakeholders.
Recent softening in raw material prices has meaningfully improved global cost competitiveness, enabling more effective engagement with international customers on more compelling terms.

An industry peer (Gujarat Ambuja Export) was cited by an analyst as showing quarter-on-quarter margin improvement (6% to 15%), contrasted against Regaal's reported figures; management disputed the comparison basis.

subsections.label: Confidentiality on segment mix
points: Management declined to disclose the revenue bifurcation across end-industries (food, pharma, agriculture, and other sectors) on the call, citing competitive sensitivity, but offered to discuss separately off-call.

subsections.label: Policy support (Bihar BIIPP)
points: Regaal benefits from the Bihar Industrial Investment Promotion Policy (BIIPP), which provides interest subvention and State GST reimbursement, lowering effective cost of capital and supporting margin resilience.
The Bihar State Promotion Board Policy came into effect in 2016 and was amended in 2025, increasing the interest subvention; this was a temporary policy amendment.
Under the scheme, loans taken from scheduled banks for construction of factory/production infrastructure are subvented by the Bihar government up to a capped interest rate of 10% per annum.

There is a cap of INR20 crores subvention to be availed over five years; the company structures its loan portfolio strategically to consume the entire INR20 crores within five years (loans are typically for six years, so subvention is out-of-pocket for one year).
Historically, subvention amounts filed (e.g., for March/April) are typically received by June, about 90% of the time.
Interest subvention receivable is accounted for as a debit receivable and credited against interest costs in the P&L; the ~5% cost of debt reflects this net-of-subvention treatment.

subsections.label: Company positioning and strategy
points: This expansion strengthens Regaal's presence in higher value-added maize derivative products and enhances its ability to cater to evolving customer requirements across food, pharmaceutical, agriculture and healthcare sectors.
Additions are aimed at deepening presence in higher value-added derivative segments, driving margin accretion, and positioning Regaal as a more complete maize processing platform.

As project execution progressed, the opportunity set became increasingly compelling both in breadth of value-added products achievable and strategic importance of building a robust, energy-efficient facility for the long term, leading to the capex revision upward.
Management views the incremental investment as a high-conviction allocation of capital.
This was the company's first earnings call since its listing on NSE and BSE in August 2025.

subsections.label: Commissioning and ramp-up risk
points: As is customary with large-scale commissioning, the newly expanded facility will need to progressively ramp up to optimal operating levels over the coming weeks, and there is uncertainty on the exact timeline for reaching full capacity utilization.

subsections.label: Raw material price risk
points: Corn/maize prices have begun to soften, which management views constructively but wants to observe for another quarter before concluding on the structural trajectory.
Revenue is raw-material-heavy and moves with maize commodity price cycles; if maize prices fall, turnover may not rise fully in line with output growth.
Government's push to increase ethanol blending, alongside large government stocks of broken rice being allocated to plants, creates uncertainty on the future direction of maize prices.

subsections.label: Margin volatility perception
points: An analyst raised a concern that quarter-on-quarter operating margin appeared to have declined (from 19% to 14%, per the analyst's calculation) while an industry peer's margin improved over the same period; management attributed this to cost ramp-up ahead of expansion commissioning rather than a structural weakness, and pointed to operating EBITDA margin actually rising from 10.7% to 13.3%.

subsections.label: Guidance approach
points: Management has just commissioned a significant expansion and, as customary with large-scale commissioning, the facility will progressively ramp up over coming weeks.
Corn/maize prices have begun to soften, viewed constructively, but management believes it prudent to let this play out over another quarter before drawing firm conclusions on structural trajectory.

Given the inflection point of new capacities coming online alongside evolving input cost dynamics, management is refraining from a formal earnings outlook until a quarter of stabilized operations has passed.
Management expects to share a more comprehensive view of the earnings trajectory by the end of H1 FY27 (between Q1 and Q2 FY27).

Management repeatedly declined to provide FY27 sales volume guidance (previous FY26 volume was 2.65 lakh tons), capacity utilization guidance, EBITDA margin floor guidance, and value-added product premium guidance in exact terms, citing the early stage of the ramp-up.

Revenue at full utilization is expected to at least double from the prior ~INR800 crore turnover level (at 825 TPD), plus additional value-added product contribution, though actual revenue will also move with maize commodity price cycles.
In the past, the company has quickly ramped up to full capacity following expansions, and management is confident of a similarly quick ramp-up this time (within weeks, not months).

guidance_ledger.statement: We look forward to sharing a more comprehensive view of our earnings trajectory by the end of H1 FY27.
We are at present refraining from any guidance on FY27 sales volume (FY26 was 2.65 lakh tons); let the plant stabilize first.
We will reach optimum capacity, which is literally 100% of rated capacity, fairly quickly, but we will not venture the exact date now; firm guidance between Q1 and Q2.
This year (FY27) value-added mix will be closer to 20% to 25%; at peak capacity it will be about 35%.
If production is doubling, revenue will also at least double, plus value-added products, though it depends on maize prices.
Balance INR140 crores capex will be coming in FY27 (out of total ~INR540 crores, INR401 crores already spent by March 31, 2026).
With the capex coming during this financial year, total debt is expected to be around INR700-750 crores, including working capital debt.
Cash conversion cycle should roam around between 75 and 50 days.

key_takeaways: FY26 was a year of strong growth for Regaal. Our operating income grew by 23.9% year-on-year to INR 1,134.2 crores, while value-added increased by 18% to INR 295.8 crores.
Operating EBITDA for FY26 stood at INR126.6 crores, with a margin of 11.2%.
The PAT stood at INR 55.6 crores with a margin of 4.9%.

On 26th May 2026, we successfully commissioned a significant expansion of our manufacturing infrastructure. Our crushing capacity has been scaled up to 1,650 tons per day, completed by the addition of new derivative manufacturing facilities, being liquid glucose at 180 tons per day and maltodextrin powder at 50 tons per day.
We revise our capex outlay upwards from approximately INR430 crores to approximately INR540 crores.
The net debt-equity ratio improved to 1.1x from 1.9x in FY25 and the company's cash conversion cycle improved significantly to 50 days in FY26 from 93 days in FY25.

We feel it is most appropriate to wait for a quarter of stabilized operations before offering a formal earnings outlook... We look forward to sharing a more comprehensive view of our earnings trajectory by the end of H1 FY27.
At 1,650 tons per day, Regaal now operates as the largest maize milling facility in Eastern India.

So are we expecting that we'll be operating at optimum capacity starting H2 FY27? (management declined to confirm, calling it an indirect attempt to extract guidance)
What is the whole of last year, how much lower price should the maize come at versus last year? Is it a INR 1 lower, INR 2 lower, INR 3 lower, whatever be that ballpark number?
